TRANSLATION of a Letter from Mon. sieur Chauvelin to Lord Grenville; dated 17th January 1793.

Portman Square, 17th January 1793, Second Year of the French Republic.

My Lord*

t have the Honour of addressing myself to you, to beg of you to grant me an Interview. I shall proceed to explain the Motives of this Request, and you will judge them to be such as will not admit of Delay. I shall first desire of you, my Lord, Security for my Communications with the French Government. Whatever may big the Character which you acknowledge Kje to possess, you have at least never doubted of the Authenticity of the Declarations which I have transmitted to you in the Name of the French Nation. I will therefore propose to you, my Lord, either abso-. lutely to refuse hearing me, or to give Orders for my Couriers to be respected, and the Secrecy of my Letters, as well of those sent as received, to be observed.

I will then, my Lord, require to be informed whether His Britannick Majesty will receive my Letters of Credence, and if He be satisfied with the Declarations contained in the Paper which I had the Honour of transmitting to your Lordship last Sunday. 1 have hot only received fresh Orders from the Executive Cpungil of France, to insist upon a speedy and definitive Answer; but there is yet another Reason which urgently presses for the Decision of His Britannick Majesty. — I have learnt this Day, that the Law relating to Foreigners obliges them to make their Declaration within Ten Days after the 10th of January, and in case of any Foreigner, who is amenable to this Law, neglecting or refusing to make such Declaration, the Magistrates of this Country would be authorized not only to require him to do so, but even to imprison him. I know, my Lord, and all those who understand the Rights of Nations know it also, that I

cannot be implicated in this Law: The avowed and acknowledged Organ of a Government which executes Laws to which Twenty-five Million of Men have submitted themselves, my Person is, and ought to be, sacred; and even under my diplomatic Character* my Lord, I could not be ranked among the general com* noon Class of Foreigners, until His Britannick Majesty: should have definitively rejected tire Letters of Credence which He knows I have received for Him. But had I been implicated in this Law, I owe to the Government of a free and powerful Nation, which I represent, this Declaration, that it would be impossible for me to submit to it; and that all the Persecutions which it might please His Britannick Majesty to make me endure, would fall upon the French Nation, in whose Cause and fer whose Sake it would be my Glory to suffer.

After this candid Declaration, my Lord, thinking myself entitled to an equal Sincerity on your Side, I will desire of you, in the Conversation which I solicit, to inform me, what is the Conduct which His Britannick Majesty's Ministers mean to hold with respect to me, and with respect to the Persons who compose my Household, in consequence of the Law against Foreigners.

I have the Honour to be, &c.

(Signed) F. Chauvelin.

TRANSLATION of a Letter from Lord Grenville to Monsieur Chauvelin,20th January

»793-

Whitehall, 20th January 1793.

I have received, Sir, your Letter of the 17th of this Month.

I have already informed you, that His Majesty hay reserved to Himself the Right of deciding, according as He shall think fit, on the Two Questions, of acknowledging a new Form of Government in France, and of receiving a Minister accredited on the Part of any other Authority in France than that of his Most Christian Majesty. And in Answer to the Demand which yoti now make to me, Whether His Majesty will receive your new Letters of Credence ? I am to inform you, that His Majesty does not think fit, under the present Circumstances, to receive those Letters.

The Demand which you make to me is equally incompatible with the Form of an Unofficial Communication, and with the Character in which you have hitherto been acknowledged, of Minister from his Most Christian Majesty. It only remains for me then, on the Subject of your Letter, especially after what has just passed in France, to inform you, that as Agent, charged with a Confidential Communication, you might certainly have expected the necessary Measures on our Part for the Safety of your Letters, and of your Messengers; that es Minister from the Most Christian King, you would have enjoyed all the Exemptions which the Law grants to Public Ministers, recognized as such; but that as a private Person, you cannot but return to the general Mass of Foreigners resident in England.

I have the Honour to be, &c.

(Signed) Grenville.

Whitehall, January 24th 1793.

I am charged to notify to you, Sir, that the Character with which you had been invested at this Court, and the Functions of which have been so long suspended, being now entirely terminated, by the fatal* Death of his late Most Christian Majesty, you have no more any Public Character here.

PetitionVe- w^om the Petition of Gilbert Crompton, and others, ported. whose Names are thereto subscribed, being the Owners, and Occupiers of Land adjoining to the River Foss, in the City of York, or North Riding of the County of York, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Navigation Bills and Bills of Drainage, had been complied with,- and that the Committee, had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where, the same was read; and is as followeth;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. William Jessop, a Surveyor, being examined, said, That the Course of the River Foss, leading from the City of York to a certain Mill called Stillington Mill, in the Parish of Stillington, in the North Riding of the County of York, is very crooked, and in many Places ' so filled up and choaked with Weeds and Mud that a free Passage for the Water cannot be had, and that by Reason of the frequent Overflowings thereof many Acres of very valuable Land adjoining the said River are greatly injured, and considerable Damage occasioned to the Proprietors thereof: That the Stagnation of Water and Filth arising from the said River in and near the City of York, produces a serious Nuisance to the Inhabitants thereof, and its Suburbs, especially in the Summer Season, which would be entirely removed if the before-.-mentioned Land was drained: That not only an effectual Drainage of the said Land may be obtained, but also the said River may be made navigable from York to Stillington Mill, which would produce many solid Advantages to the City of York, and the neighbouring Towns and Villages through or near which such intended. Navigation would pass, by rendering the Conveyance of Coals, Lime, Corn,. and all Sorts of Merchandize, more easy and expeditious.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for , making and maintaining a Navigable Communication from the Junction of the River Foss with the River Ouse, at or near the City of York, to Stillington , in the Parish of Stillington, in the North Riding of the County of York, and for draining and improving certain Low Lands lying on each Side of the said River Foss: And that Mr. Wilberforce and Mr. Duncombe do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of the Common Brewers of the City of Common London and Parts adjacent, whose Names are there- Brewers unto subscribed, was presented to the House, and Pet, tion-read; Setting forth, That, by an Act made in the Twenty-second Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for repealing the Duties payable for Beer and Ale above Six Shillings a Barrel, exclusive of the Duties of Excise, and not exceeding Eleven Shillings a Barrel, exclusive of such Duties, and for granting, other Duties in Lieu thereof, and for other Purposes (herein mentioned, it was enacted, that, from and after the 5th Day of July 1782, the several Rates and Duties then payable for Beer or Ale above Six Shillings the Barrel, exclusive of the Duties of Excise, and not exceeding Eleven Shillings the Barrel, exclusive of such Duties, commonly called Table Beer, which should at any Time be brewed by the Common Brewer in England and Wales, should cease and determine, and in Lieu thereof there should thenceforth be raised, levied, collected, and paid, throughout England and Wales, for every Barrel of Beer or Ale above Six Shillings the Barrel, exclusive of the Duties of Excise, and not exceeding Eleven Shillings, exclusive of such Duties, commonly called Table Beer, brewed by the Common Brewer, and so proportionably for a greater or lesser Quantity, the Sum of Three Shillings to be paid by such Common Brewer; and that, since the passing of the said Act, it has proved that the Price of Eleven Shillings per Barrel, exclusive of the Duty, is not sufficient to support the ESpences, stand against the Common Contingencies of Trade, and afford even a moderate Profit to the Brewer, so that the Brewers of Table Beer have ever since been labouring under great Difficulties, which have gradually increased, owing to the high Price of Malt and Hops, the former of which Articles alone has advanced, on an Average, more than Seven Shillings a Quarter compared with the same Number of Years preceding the passing of the Act, together with the increased Price of Horse Provender, Fuel, and Labour, to which must be added the other unexpected Additions to the Capital of a Brewer, arising froip the great Advance in the Price of Horses, Casks, and other Utensils, and, in consequence, the Trade is now become altogether inadequate to its Expenditure; and that the Petitioners are deterred from endeavouring to alleviate those Grievances by brewing their Liquor of an inferior Quality, being aware that such a Measure would not only draw on them the Complaints of their Customers, but likewise occasion a still more heavy L068 by the Return of their Liqaor, as is the Usage of the Trade; and that many of the Petitioners Customers have requested to be supplied with good Table Beer, for which they are willing to pay a higher Price, but

H h from

from this the Petitioners are restrained by the aforementioned Act, by virtue of which such Beer would become subject to the Strong Beer Duty of Eight Shillings per Barrel: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to alter the Provisions of the said recited Act, in such Manner that Common Brewers may be authorized to sell Table Beer of a Price of Thirteen Shillings per Barrel, exclusive of the Duty, to such Persons as chuse to have it of that Quality, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to die Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Alderman die

Lord Mayor of London&c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

and that the said Commissioners have caused every Exertion to be made, which the Law prescribes, in making, supporting, and repairing the said Roads, but, from the great Increase of Commerce, the Carriage of Merchandize, of Coals, of heavy Materials for Building, and other Purposes, the same are become so burthensome, that, without an Increase of the Tolls, the said Roads cannot be repaired, and must remain in a decayed ruinous State, and wholly unsafe and dangerous to the Public and the Petitioners; and that it - is found by Experience that some of the Gates on the said Road are improperly placed, and might be put in a much more advantageous Situation, and that the Tolls are evaded and lessened for Want thereof; and that, taking into Consideration the great Length of the Road comprized in the said Act, the enormous Expence of making and repairing the same, the Petitioners apprehend there are too few Gates, and that the same ought and may be increased, and sufficient Tolls raised, to complete the said Roads, and in future to keep them in good and sufficient Repair, without oppressing the Public or others interested therein: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to continue and enlarge the Term and Powers of the said Act, under such Powers and Restrictions as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Bastard, Mr. Thomas Stanley, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Mr. Henry Hobart reported from the Committee, to Royal E* whom the Petition of the Governor, Sub-Governor, change Deputy Governor, and Directors, of The Royal Exchange Com,v'* Assurance, was referred; That the Committee had exa- petiuw mined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed repoti^d. htm to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition; it appeared, that by an Act passed in the Sixth Year of the Reign of King George the First, intituled, "An " Act for better securing certain Powers and Privileges, intended to be granted by His Majesty, by " Two Charters for Assurance of Ships and Mer-

123

" chandizesat Sea, and for lending Money on "tomry, and for restraining several extravagant and " unreasonable Practices therein named," his said Majesty did, by Letters Patent dated the 22d of June a 720, incorporate divers Persons, to be a Corporation in Deed and in Name, and to have perpetual Succession, and a Common Seal, by the Name of The Royal Exchange Assurance for insuring Ships and Hoods at Sea, and for lending Money upon Bottomry, " with Power to raise a Capital of One Million five hundred thousand Pounds, and to make Bye Laws and Regulations for the good Government thereof, so that the same were not repugnant to the Laws of the Land, which Charter is subject to Redemption and Power of Revocation, as in the said Act and Charter are mentioned.

It further appeared that his said Majesty did, by other Letters Patent, dated the 29th of April 1721, incorporate several other Persons to be a Corporation, for the Assurance of any Life or Lives, and against Casualties and Accidents by Fire, and to have perpetual Succession, and a Common Seal, by the Name of The Royal Exchange Assurance of Houses arid Goods from Fire, with Power to raise a Capital of Five hundred thousand Pounds, and to make Bye Laws, with a Power of Revocation, as before mentioned; Then,

Mr. George Burley being examined, said, That it will be of Public Utility if the said Corporations are empowered to grant, sell, or purchase Annuities upon or for Lives; or by or with Survivorship, which no other Corporation now is enabled to do: That the granting and purchasing such Annuities are frequently in the Hands of improper and necessitous Persons, who make an exorbitant Gain thereby, to the great Detriment of Individuals and the Public in General, which would be in a great Measure (if not wholly) prevented, if a known Office, long established, was empowered so to do; and that the Powers granted by the said Letters Patent should be extended and enlarged to the granting, selling, or purchasing of Annuities upon Lives.

And the Witness further said, That in Order to effectuate the Purposes aforesaid, it will be necessary that the Petitioners and their Successors should be empowered to take and use some other Name or Names of Incorporation, with Power to make, alter, and renew a Seal or Seals for such Purpose; and that the falsely making, forging, counterfeiting, or altering such Seal or Seals, should be attended with some Penalty or other Punishment.

Mr. William Morgan and Mr. Abraham be-

ing examined, corroborated the Evidence of Mr. Burley.

; 1 Ordered That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to

enable the Royal Exchange Assurance Companies, and their Successors, to grant, purchase, and sell Annuities upon or for Lives: And that Mr. and

Mr. Mainwaring do prepare, and bring in, the same.

'King'* Me*- Ordered, That the Order of the Day, for taking into *g« for Consideration His Majesty's most Gracious Message of SZffo1^* last, be now , .

considered. And the said Order being read accordingly; and Address The House proceeded to take the said Message into -thereupon. Consideration.

And the same was again read by Mr. Speaker.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, to return His Majesty the Thanks of this House for His most Gracious Message, and for the Communication of the Papers, which by His Majesty's Command, have been laid before us:

To offer to His Majesty our heartfelt Condolence on the atrocious Act lately perpetrated at Paris, which must be viewed by every Nation in Europe as an Outrage on Religion, Justice, and Humanity; and as a striking and dreadful Example of the Effect of Principles, which lead to the Violation of the most sacred Duties, and are utterly subversive of the Peace and Order of all Civil Society;

To assure His Majesty, that it is impossible for us not to be sensible of the Views of Aggrandizement and Ambition, which, in Violation of repented and solemn Professions, have been openly manifested on the Part of France, and which are connected with the Propagation of Principles incompatible with the Existence of all just and regular Government: That, under the present Circumstances, we consider a vigorous and effectual Opposition to these Views as essential to the Security of every Thing which is most dear and valuable to us as a Nation, and to the future Tranquillity and Safety of all other Countries:

That, impressed with these Sentiments, we shall with the utmost Zeal and Alacrity, afford His Majesty the most effectual Assistance to enable His Majesty to make a further Augmentation of His Forces by Sea and Land, and to act, as Circumstances may require, in the present important Conjuncture, for maintaining the Security and Honour of His Crown, for supporting the just Rights of His Allies, and for preserving to His People the undisturbed Enjoyment of the Blessings which, under the Divine Providence, they derive from the British Constitution.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to His Majesty by such Members of this House as are of His Majesty's most Honourable Privy Council.

King's Me*- Ordered, That His Majesty's most Gracious Message referred sage q( Monday last, be referred to the Consideration Supply11* of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

The Witness further added, That the Restriction as to repairing the Streets in East Retford, lying in the Line of the Road, has been found inconvenient; and that the same, by Reason of the great Increase in the Number of Waggons and other heavy laden Carriages which have passed through the same since the Road was made Turnpike, such Streets are become ruinous and bad, and cannot be kept in such a State as they ought to be, for the Accommodation of the Public, unless the said Restriction is repealed, and the Trustees enabled to apply Money of the Trust in Aid of such Repairs; and that there is a certain Bridge over the River Idle in the said Town of East Retford, which, from the great Increase of Waggons, and other heavily laden Carriages, passing over the same, and the additional Number of Coaches and other Pleasure Carriages, is become much more expensive to maintain and keep in Repair than it formerly was, and is also so narrow as to be very incommodious and unsafe; and that the Trustees are willing to apply jso much Money, to arise from the Tolls on the said Road, towards the widening, amending and repairing of the said Bridge, as may be found requisite and expedient for the complete Accommodation of the Public.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to continue ifhe Term, and alter and enlarge the Powers of an Act, passsd in the Sixth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for repairing and widening the Road from Bawtry, in the County of York, to East Markham Common, in the County of Nottingham, and from Little Drayton to Twiford Bridge, in the said County: And that Mr. Gaily Knight, Mr. Pierrepont, and Mr. berforce, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of the Owners and Occupiers of Corn Mills, Fulling Mills, and other Mills, upon the River Colder, near Halifax, in the West Riding of the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners being informed that Two Schemes of Navigation are now in Agitation, one for extending the Manchester, Bolton, and Bury Canal, from Bury, in Laby Rochdale,

Littlebroygh, and Ripponden, to or near to Smoerby Bridge, in Yorkshire, the Head of the Navigation from the Rivers Humbelr and Hull, and the other for making a Navigable Canal from Manchester, by Rochdale, Tod-morden, and Hebden Bridge, also to Sowerby have duly weighed and considered both the said Schemes, not only with respect to their Public Utility, but as to their Effect upon Private Property; That the first-mentioned Scheme, for extending the Canal from Bury, is, in the Judgment of the Petitioners, far preferable to the other, because no material Injury whatsoever will be done to any Mills upon the River Colder, or upon any of the Brooks that feed it, by its being carried into execution, as the Mills will not be thereby deprived of any Water, and the Communication will be nearer by many Miles, and more speedy and convenient, than by the other Line proposed, which cannot be executed without totally destroying or materially injuring a great many valuable Mills upon the River Calder, and near the Line of that proposed Canal, as well as other Private Property That the Scheme for extending the Canal from Bury as aforesaid will open a Communication between the East and West Seas, by the several trading Towns of Hull, Armine-, Rawcllffe, Knotting ley, Castleford, Wakefield, Dewsbury, Elland, Halifax, Rochdale, Bury, Man-

chester, Bolton, Wigan, Chorley, Blackburn, Lancaster, Kendall, and other Places of Commerce, which will be more expeditious and safe, and a shorter and easier Passage than in any other Line heretofore discovered: And therefore praying, That the Bill brought in, or intended to be brought in, for extending the Canal from Bury to Sower.by Bridge, may pass into a Law, and that they may be heard, by Counsel, against any Bill which may be brought in for making a Navigable Canal from Manchester, by Rochdale and Todmorden, to Soioerby Bridge, as being injurious to all the Mill Property upon that Line, and in particular to the Petitioners.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from the CNavigation, at or near

Sowerby Bridge Wharf, in the Parish of Halifax, in the West Riding of the County of York, to the Canal of his Grace the Duke of Bridgewater, in the Parish of Manchester, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, and also certain Collateral Cuts from the said intended Canal, be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Answer to Address on King's Message.

Lord Viscount Parker reported to the House, That their Address of Friday last (to return His Majesty the Thanks of this House for His most Gracious Message, and for the Communication of the Papers, which,

13

by His Majesty's Command, had been laid before this House; and to offer to His Majesty the Condolence of this House on the atrocious Act lately perpetrated at Paris: To assure His Majesty, that it is impossible for this House not to be sensible of the Views of Aggrandizement and Ambition, which have been openly manifested on the Part of France; and that, under the present Circumstances, this House doth consider a vigorous and effectual Opposition to those Views as essential to the Security of every Thing which is most dear and valuable to this Nation, and to the future Tranquillity and Safety of all other Countries; and that this House will, with the utmost Zeal and Alacrity, afford His Majesty the most effectual Assistance to enable His Majesty to make a further Augmentation of His Forces by Sea and Land, and to act, as Circumstances may require) had been presented to His Majesty; and that His Majesty had commanded him to acquaint this House, that His Majesty receives, with the greatest Satisfaction, the Assurances of their cordial and zealous Support in the present important Conjuncture.

The House proceeded to the Appointment of a Select Committee, to try and determine the Merits of the said Petition.

The Serjeant at Arms was directed by Mr. Speaker to go, with the Mace, to the Places adjacent, and require the Attendance of the Members on the Business of the House.

And he went accordingly.

And being returned;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker; and One hundred and Twenty-six Members being present;

The Counsel and Agents were called in to the Bar.

And the Door of the House being locked;

The Order of the Day for taking the said Petition into Consideration, was read.

And the Names of the Members were taken out of the Box (before prepared) put into Six Glasses, and drawn and read in the usual Manner.

And the Names of Seven Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of the Honourable Major General Thomas Bruce, being drawn,' he offered to the House, as an Excuse for not serving on the said Committee, That be was a General Officer on the Staff, and liable to be immediately ordered upon the Public Service; and the Substance of what was so alledged by him being taken down by the Clerk, and the said Member having at the Table verified the same upon Oath, the Opinion of the House was taken thereon; and he was excused from serving on the said Committee.

And the Names of Ten other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of Samuel Whitbread, Junior, Esquire, being drawn, he was nominated to serve on the said* Committee, by the Counsel for the Petitioners.

And the Names of Five other Members then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of the Right honourable Henry Dundas being drawn, he offered to the House, as an Excuse for not serving on the said Committee, That, being One of His Majesty's principal Secretaries of State, he conceived it would be attended with material Interruption to Public Business, if he was obliged to serve on the said Committee; and the Substance of what was so alledged by him being taken down by the Clerk, and Mr. Secretary Dundas having at the Table verified the same upon Oath, the Opinion of the House was taken thereon; and he was excused from serving on the said Committee.

And the Names of Four other Members, then pre-. sent, were drawn, who were not objected to.

Stourbridge, to communicate with the Petitioners Canal at Stourton, about Twelve Miles only from the River Sevetm, and the same are now completed, and are called the Dudley and Stourbridge Canals, the Objects of which Navigation were, by communicating at one End thereof with the Birmingham Canal at Tipton, and at the other End thereof with the Petitioners Carnal at Stourton, to open a nearer Communication' between Birmingham and the River Severn, and for supplying Birmingham, Worcester, and the otherTowBs near the Severn, and the Counties of Worcester, Warwick, Gloucester, and Hereford, with Coals from the several Mines lying in or Voi, 4SL

That they may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law.

Petition froM facturers, and other Inhabitants of the Town of Woverlmrup-verhampton, in the County of Staffor, and the Neighbourhood thereof, was also presented to the House, |oa ane(f S*^T and read; Setting forth, That the greatest Part of o«k Canal7 the Petitioners are settled in the said Town and its Bill; Neighbourhood, and employed in the Manufactory of Iron, Steel, Copper, Brass, and other Metals, and the principal Raw Material for converting the said Metals into Wares is Coal, the Mines of which, lying within the Compass of the said Manufactories, being of good Quality, and in great Plenty, hath seated such Manu, factories in the said Town and its Neighbourhood, which have been increasing for many Years past, and are now arrived at such a Degree of Perfection and Extent, as to become an Object of great Concern to the Commerce and Wealth of this Kingdom; anti that the Raw Material, Iron Ore, being also found with the Coal within the Circle of the said Manufactory, the Petitioners have, with great Expence, established Founderies and Iron Works, and, by Means of a cheap Supply of Cod, they manufacture a great Part Of the Iron used by themselves from the Ore, which, until a late Period, wa* brought from Rutsia and other

foreign States, and paid for in Bullion or foreign Bills of Exchange, and have also erected Smelting furnaces and Mills, for the refining and manufacturing of Copper, making of Brass, and converting other Metals from their Virgin State into Manufactures of Various Kinds, and the Whole is in a fair Prospect of arriving at that Degree of Perfection and Extension which cannot fail of yielding great Advantages to the Trade and Commerce of th*3* Kingdom, as well 'as redound to the Honour and Credit of the Manufacturer, if encouraged by the Protection and Support of Parliament; and that, in the Sixth, Eighth, Sixteenth, Twentieth, and Thirtieth Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, various Acts have been obtained for making Canals1 through the County of Stafford, ind several adjacent Counties, to open a Conveyance by Water to all the large Trading Ports in this Kingdom, which said Canals, being now finished, and some of them passing through the Whole of the said Manufactory, answer every useful and necessary Purpose, in lowering the Price of, or supplanting, Land Carriage to the different Sea Ports and Inland Parts of the Kingdom; and that the Petitioners most seriously beg Leave to' remark to the' House, that the Prosperity, and even the Existence, of the Iron Manufactory depends upon the low Price of the Raw Materials used therein, especially upon the plentiful Supply and low Price of Coal, and that, to the cheap Supply and Plenty of that Article, the said Town and Neighbourhood owe their present flourishing Trade, that the increase of Canals must also increase the Price of Coals, in consequence of which the Manufacturers will raise their Demand on their various Articles, and the Merchants will be obliged to carry this great Branch of 'British Commerce to Foreign Markets, under the Disadvantage of an advanced Price; and that the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Bill is brought into the House for Power to make a Navigable Canal, from the Dudley Canal, in the County of , to

the Worcester and Birmingham Canal, now making at, or near, Selly Oak, in the said County of and also

certain Collateral Cuts to communicate therewith, and the Petitioners are informed that Petitions are intended to be presented for making other Canals from or near the Town of Birmingham, into the County of Warwick, for the Purpose of furnishing an additional Supply of Coals into the said Counties of Warwick and Worcester, and the Petitioners beg Leave to state, that the Inhabitants of those Parts of the said Counties of Warwick, Worcester, and Gloucester, which border upon the Rivers Secern and Avon, have now a plentiful Supply of Coals upon reasonable Terms, raised at the Mines in Staffordshire and Shropshire, and conveyed along the said Two Rivers, and that there is no Manufactory of any Consequence in the Line of the new projected Canals; and that the Petitioners most seriously beg Leave further to represent to the House, that the saving of a few Shillings in the Carriage of a Ton of Manufactured Wares is of little Consequence compared with the smallest Advance upon a Raw Material, and particularly upon the Article of Coal, the Consumption of which at the Mines within the said Manufactory, in the Year 1790, amounted to 844,952 Tons, and that an Advance of One Shilling per Ton in the Price of Coal is a Loss to the Consumers and Public of 42,247/. ioj. a Year, and advances the Price of Manufactured Iron One Pound a Ton, there being Twenty Tons of Coal consumed in making One Ton of Iron; and that the Coal Mines at and near Netherton are essential to the Support and Prosperity of the Nail Manufactory, as also of many large Iron Works, and other Manufactories of heavy Wares, established at and near that Place, to all which, as well as to the Cold Mines, the Dudley Canal is already open, and capable of serving every useful and Public Purpose; and the Petitioners beg leave to remark, that the Speculation upon Canals is

now carried to an enormous Extent, that, instead of . promoting the Public Good with laudable Enterprize,;

it is become a new System of Gambling, by which the unguarded will fall a Prey to Adventurers unless protected by the Wisdom of the House: And therefore praying, That the Representations contained in their Petition may be taken into Consideration, and that the Raw Material, Coal, the fundamental Support of their Manufactory, may be preserved. and secured to them and their Posterity against all new Schemes for additional Canals to carry Coal out of that Part of the County of Stafford, and that they may be heard, by their Counsel, at the Bar of the House, against the Bill now depending for making such Canal from the Dudley Canal to the Worcester and Birmingham Canal at or near Selly Oak, and that the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table, until the Bill for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from the Dudley Canal, in the County of Worcester, toi the Worcester and Birmingham Canal, now making, at, or near, Selly Oak, in the said County* and also certain Collateral Cuts to communicate therewith, be read a Second Time; and the Petitioners are to be then heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petitions, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petitions. a

A Petition of the Right honourable Frederick Augustus Earl of Berkeley, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from the Canal

Navigation at Braunston in the County of to join the River Thames, at Nezv Brentford, in the County of 'Middlesex, and also for making and maintaining certain Collateral Cuts from the said intended Canal; and Setting forth, That the Petitioner is Owner and Occupier of the Mansion House of Cranford, in the said County of Middlesex, a Family Scat' of the Petitioner and his Ancestors for upwards of Two Centuries past, and which hath been kept up and lately improved by the Petitioner at a very considerable Expence; and that the said Canal in its intended Course through the Parish of Harlingion will run so near the said Family Seat as totally to destroy the Comfort of the Petitioner, and the Security of his Property, by making a public Way for Bargemen and others at all Hours of the Night, as well-as by Day, close to Lis Ground, and within a few Hundred Yards of his House; and that in carrying the intended Canal so near to the Petitioner's said Family Seat the Projectors appear to have wantonly, or at least unnecessarily, deviated from the obvious Line of it, notwithstanding an Application and Remonstrance on the Part of the Petitioner while the Scheme was in Agitation, and before the present Line of the Canal was finally laid down: And therefore praying, That he may be heard, by his Counsel, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law, or that he may be otherwise relieved from the Injury he is threatened with, in such Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Noblemen, and the humble Petition of the several Gentlemen and others, whose Names are thereunder written, Proprietors and Occupiers of Lands within the Parishes or Districts of Hillingdon, Harlingion, Hayes, Norwood, , and Drayton, in

the County of Middlesex, was also presented to the House, and read; Likewise taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth. That the Petitioners, in case the said Bill is suffered to pass into a Law, will be materially injured, inasmuch as several of the Lands and Grounds through which it is intended the said Canal shall pass (and of which Lands and Grounds the Petitioners are Proprietors and Occupiers respectively) will he divided from each other, to the great Detriment of the Petitioners, and particularly to such of them as are Proprietors and Occupiers of Common Field Lands; and the said Bill will also, if suffered to pass into a Law, be in other Respects injurious to the Petitioners; Vol. 48.

A Petition of the Persons thereunto subscribing, Inverness Freeholders and Owners of Land in the County of In- p^.

verness, was presented to the House, and read; Setting tion forth, That the Laws now in force in Scotland, for making and repairing Roads and Bridges, have been found insufficient in the County of Inverness, and other and further Powers are necessary to carry the Intention of the Laws into Execution; and that in some Cases Doubts have arisen as to the Description of Persons chargeable towards making and repairing the Highways, and, in general the effectual Enforcement of the Performance of the Statute Work, and the proper Application of it in the said County, is attended with much Difficulty and Trouble; and that in many Places it has been found more useful and more effectual, as well as more easy and convenient, for Persons liable in Statute Services to establish a reasonable Composition in.

Money in Lieu of actual Labour, and that, in many Respects, it will* be of real Advantage to the said County to convert the Statute Labour into Money, or to assess a cei % un Sum in Place of the Performance of such Services, and to ascertain the Rate and Mode of levying such Assessment, and also to authorize a further Sum than is at present levyable by Law to be levied for Road and Bridge Money in the said County:

And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for regulating and converting the Statute Labour in the said County of Inverness, and for the other Purposes above-mentioned, in such Manner, and under such Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Colonel Macleod, Major Maitland, Ac.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Mr. Secretary Dundas acquainted the House, That King'»Mej-he had a Message from His Majesty to this House, »ag* respect-signed by His Majesty; and he presented the same to *f‘

the House; and it was read by Mr. Speaker (all the War by Members of the House being uncovered) and is as France, followeth; viz.

GEORGE R.

His Majesty thinks proper to acquaint the House of Commons, that the Assembly now exercising the Powers of Government in France have, without previous Notice, directed Acts of Hostility to be committed against the Persons and Property of His Majesty's Subjects, in Breach of the Law of Nations, and of the most positive Stipulations of Treaty, and have since, on the most groundless Pretences, actually declared War against His Majesty and The United Provinces: Under the Circumstances of this wanton and unprovoked Aggression, His Majesty has taken the necessary Steps to maintain the Honour of His Crown, and to vindicate the Rights of His People; and His Majesty relies with Confidence on the firm and effectual Support of the House of Commons, and on the zealous Exertions of a brave and loyal People, in prosecuting a just and necessary War, and in endeavouring, under the Blessing of Providence, to oppose an effectual Barrier to the further Progress of a System which strikes at the Security and Peace of all independent Nations, and is pursued in open Defiance of every Principle of Moderation, Good Faith, Humanity, and Justice.

In a Cause of such general Concern, His Majesty has every Reason to hope for the cordial Co-opcratioft of those Powers who are united with His Majesty by the Ties of Alliance, or who feel an Interest in preventing the Extension of Anarchy and Confusion, and in contributing to the Security and Tranquillity of Europe.

G. R.

Ordered, That His Majesty's said most Gracious Message be taken into Consideration Tomorrow Morning.

TRANSLATION of a Declaration delivered by Lord Auckland to the States General of The United Provinces ,dated Hague, November 16th

1792-

DECLARATION.

The undersigned Ambassador Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary of His Majesty,

has received the King's Orders to inform their High Mightinesses the States General of The United Provinces, that His Majesty, seeing the Theatre of War brought so near to the Frontiers of the Republic by the recent Events which have happened, and being sensible of the Uneasioess which may naturally result from such a Situation, thinks it due to the Connection which subsists between Him and the Republic, that He should renew to their High Mightinesses on this Occasion, the Assurances of His inviolable Friendship, and of His Determination to execute, at all Times, with the utmost good Faith, all the different Stipulations of the Treaty of Alliance so happily concluded in 1788, between His Majesty and their High Mightinesses.

In making to their High Mightinesses this Declaration, the King is very far from supposing the Probability of any Intention on the Part of the Belligerent Parties to violate the Territory of the Republic, or to meddle in the internal Concerns of its Government. The Kino is persuaded that the Conduct which, in Concert with His Majesty, their High Mightinesses have hitherto observed, and the Respect to which the Situation of His Majesty and the Republic justly entitles them, are sufficient to remove any Ground of such Apprehension. His Majesty, therefore, confidently expects that no Events of the War will lead to any Circumstance from without, which may be injurious to the Rights of their High Mightinesses; and He strongly recommends to them to employ, in concert wih His Majesty, an unremitted Attention and Firmness to repress any Attempts which may be made to disturb the internal Tranquillity of the Provinces.

His Majesty has directed this Communication to be made to their High Mightinesses, in the full Persuasion that nothing can more effectually conduce to the Interest and Happiness of both Countries, than the Continuance of that intimate Union which has been established between them fqr the Maintenance of their own Rights and Security, and with a View to contribute to the general Welfare and Tranquillity of Europe.

(Signed) Auckland.

Hague, November 16th 1792.

TRANSLATION of a Memorial presented by Lord Auckland, His Britannick Majesty's Minister at the Hague, to their High Mightinesses The States General.

High and Mighty Lords,

The undersigned Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of His Britannick Majesty, takes the earliest Opportunity, in consequence of the express Orders of the King, to ley before your High Mightinesses Copies of all the Papers which have been exchanged, since the 27th of December last to the 20th of this Month, between Lord Grenville, Secretary of State to His Majesty, and M. Chauvelin.

The King, High and Mighty Lords, is firmly persuaded, that the Sentiments and Principles expressed on the Part of Great Britain are perfectly conformable to those which animate your Republic, and that your High Mightinesses are disposed fully to concur in ttye Measures which the present Crisis demands, and which are a necessary Consequence of these Sentiments and Principles.

The Circumstances which have led to this Crisis are too recent, and the Conduct of the King too well known, for the undersigned to have Occasion here to enter into any long Detail. It is not quite Four Years since certain unhappy and deluded Persons, assuming the Name of Philosophers, have presumed to think themselves capable of establishing a new System of Civil Society. In order to realize this Dream, the Offspring of Vanity, it became necessary for them to overturn and destroy all established Notions of Subordination, of Morals, and of Religion, which had hitherto constituted the Security, the Happiness, and the Consolation of Mankind. These destructive Projects have but too well succeeded; but the Effects of the new System which they wished to introduce, have only served to demonstrate the Folly and Wickedness of its Authors. The Events that have since so rapidly followed, surpass, in Atrocity, all that has hitherto sullied the Page of History. Property, Liberty, Security, and even Life itself, have been the Sport of this unbridled Phrenzy of the Passions, of this Spirit of Rapine, of Hatred, and of the most cruel and unnatural Ambition. The Annals of Mankind cannot present a Period in which, in so short a Space, so many Crimes have been committed, so many Misfortunes produced, and so many Tears shed; in a Word, at this very Moment these Horrors appear to have attained their utmost Height.

During all this Time the King, surrounded by His People, who enjoyed under the Favour of Providence a degree of Prosperity without Example, could not behold the Misfortunes of others without the strongest Emotions of Pity and Indignation; but, faithful to His Principles, His Majesty has never permitted Himself to interfere in the internal Affairs of a Foreign Nation, He has never departed from that System of Neutrality which He had adopted.

This Conduct, which the King has seen with Satisfaction to have been equally observed by your High Mightinesses, the good Faith of which all Europe has acknowledged, and which ought to have been respected on many other Accounts, has not been sufficient to secure His Majesty, His People, and the Republic, from the most dangerous and the most criminal Conspiracies.

Committee for expediting the Trial of Mr, Hastings.

Ordered, That the Report from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty, be now received,

Mr. Henry Hobart accordingly reported from the said Committee, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the Housewhich he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as followed; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an additional Number of Twenty thousand Men be employed for the Sea Service, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Ninety-three (including a proportionable Number of Marines) in Addition to the Twenty-five thousand Men already voted.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Four Pounds per Man per Mopth, be allowed for maintaining the said Twenty thousand Men, for Thirteen Months, including Ordnance for Sea Service.

The First Resolution of the Committee being read a Second Time, several Amendments were proposed to be made thereunto, by leaving out the Words, " a proportional Number of," and inserting the Words, " Four thousand," instead thereof.

And the said Amendments were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Resolved, That this House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, so amended, That an additional Number of Twenty-thousand Men be employed for the Sea Service, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Ninety-three (including Four thousand Marines) in Addition to the Twenty-five thousand Men already voted.

The subsequent Resolution of the Committee being read a Second Time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

A Bill for continuing and granting to His Majesty certain Duties upon Malt, Mum, Cyder, and Perry, for the Service of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Ninety-three, was read a Second Time.

Resolved, That the Bill be committed.

Resolved, That the Bill be committed to a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, Tomorrow Morning, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the said Bill.

A Bill for granting an Aid to His Majesty by a Land Tax, to be raised in Great Britain, for the Service of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Ninety-three, was read a Second Time.

Resolved, That the Bill be committed.

Resolved, That the Bill be committed to a Committee of the whole House.

Resohed, That this House will, Tomorrow Morning, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the said Bill.

Resohed, That this House will, upon Wednesday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Wednesday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty.

Ordered, That a Committee be appointed to consider of Means for expediting the Trial of the Impeachment now depending against Warren Hastings, Esquire; and to report the same to the House:

Leed* Cod A Petition of Charles Brandling, Esquire, Lord of Work* Peti- the Manor of Middleton, in the County of York, Owner t,on* and Proprietor of divers Coal Works in the said

Manor and Places adjacent, and the several Inhabitants of the Town and Neighbourhood of Leeds, in the said County, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by virtue of an Act, passed in the Eighteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act " for rendering more beneficial an Act, made in the " Thirty-first Year of the Reign of King George the * Second, intituled, An Act for establishing Agreements made between Charles Brandling, Esquire,

" and other Persons, Proprietors of Lands, for laying u down a Waggon Way, in order for the better supplying the Town and Neighbourhood of Leeds, in the County of York, with Coals, by enabling the " said Charles Brandling to supply annually a larger " Quantity of Coals to and for the Use of the said Town and Neighbourhood," the said Charles Brandling is obliged Yearly, during such Time as he shall continue the said Waggon Way, made for the Purpose of bringing Coals from the Coal Works of the said Charles Brandling, in Middleton aforesaid, to the Repository at a certain Place in the said Act called Casson Close, to bring to the said Repository or‘Cod Yard 40,000 Dozens, or 480,000 Corves of Coals at the least, by Four equal Quarterly Proportions (that is to say) 10,000 Dozens, or 120,000 Corves, in each Quarter of the Year, unless prevented by Fire, Water, or other inevitable Accident; and that the said Act, passed in the Eighteenth Year of His present Majesty, empowers the said Chart Brandling to sell the said Coals brought down to the said Repository from his said Colliery to Persons in the Neighbourhood of Leeds, whereby a very considerable Quantity of the Coals brought to the said Repository are taken and purchased by Persons residing at a great Distance from the said Town of Leeds, and the Inhabitants of the said Town and Parish of Leeds are thereby deprived of a considerable Part of the Benefit and Advantage intended to result to them by virtue of the said last mentioned Act; and that, since the passing of the said last mentioned Act, the Town and Parish of Leeds is very considerably increased in Population, and the Trade thereof very greatly extended, and a great Number of Dyehouses, Engines, and Machines, have been erected therein, so that the Quantity of Coals, stipulated by the said Act to be brought down to the said Repository are found insufficient for supplying the said Town and Parish of Leeds only; and that such Inconvenience hath arisen to the said Town and Parish from the Coal Works of the said Charles Brandling at Middleton aforesaid having been occasionally laid up,

or prevented being worked by inevitable Accidents, and his being restrained by the said Act from bringing any other Coals to the said Repository than such as he should get within the said Manor or Lordship of Middleton, and that such Inconveniences might in future be, in a great Measure, remedied if the said Charles Brandling was allowed, under proper Regulations, to bring Coal from any other Colliery, to the said Repository; and that, since the passing of the said last mentioned Act, the said Charled[Brandling hath been put to a very great Expence in purchasing of Coal, making fresh Winnings in his said Colliery, by laying and making additional Waggon Ways from his said Coal Pits to the said Repository, and by paying much greater Prices for leading and getting the said Coals, and for the Wood and other Materials used therein; and that it would be of great Benefit and Advantage to the Inhabitants of the Town and Parish of Leeds, and the Manufactures and Trade thereof, if the Quantity of Coals stipulated by the last mentioned Act were brought from the Coal Pits and Coal Works of the said Charles Brandling to the said Repository, and there sold to the Inhabitants of the Town and Parish of Leeds only, also, if the delivering the same at the said Repository, and the Manner ana Prices of conveying and carrying the same from such Repository to the Inhabitants within the said Town and Parish were properly regulated and ascertained; and that the Coal got and worked at all the other Collieries or Coal Works in the Neighbourhood of Leeds is very considerably advanced in Price, and it would very greatly distress the Inhabitants of the said Town and Parish, if the said Charles Brandling should discontinue the said Waggon Way and Repository, and also be a very great Loss and Prejudice to the Trade and Manufactories thereof; and that the said Charles Brandling hath proposed, and is willing to continue, to bring down from his said Coal Works at Middleton aforesaid, and deliver at the said Repository, during the Continuance of the Term in the said Act mentioned, or such other Term of Years as may be deemed requisite,

40,000 Dozens, or 480,000 Corves, of Coals, by Weekly Proportions, for the sole Use of the Inhabitants of the said Town and Parish of Leeds (provided Sale can be had for the same) at the Rate of Six Pence Halfpenny a Corf, having Liberty to leave any Quantity of Coals not exceeding 144 Dozens per Week, at any Place near to the said Waggon Way within the said Borough, and also, to take and deposit the Surplus Quantity beyond the Daily Sale or Demand of the said Town and Parish, in any other Coal Yard or Repository within the said Parish, which, by the Petitioners, Inhabitants of the Town and Parish of , is thought a reasonable Price: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Amendment of the last mentioned Act for the Purposes aforesaid, under such Restrictions, and subject to such Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

Sir -Charles Bunbury reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several of the Trustees for carrying into execution an Act of Parliament, of the Thirtieth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for making , and maintaining a Navigable Communication -between Stowmarket and Ipswich, in the County of Suffolk, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the said Petition is not within the Standing Orders of the House relative to Navigation Bills, it not being intended to raise any further or additional - Rates, Tolls, or Duties; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report m his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followed!; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Act was read; whereby it appears that the Trustees were authorized and empowered to raise and borrow any Sum of Money, not exceeding the Sum of Twenty thousand Three hundred Pounds, upon the Credit of the Rates thereby granted: And,

Mr. John Sparke being examined, said, That the Trustees have proceeded in the execution of the said Act, and have borrowed the Sum of £. 20,300, thereby authorized to be raised; which Money has been nearly laid out and expended in carrying the Purposes of the said Act into execution. — Then,

Mr. John Rennie being examined, said, That the said Navigable Communication is not, as yet, near completed; -and that it will require a further Sum of Money to finish and complete the same, so as to afford the Country the several Benefits and Advantages intended to be given to them by the said Act

A Petition of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Commonalty of the City of Coventry: And also,

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Merchants, Manufacturers, and principal Inhabitants of the City of Coventry: And also,

A Petition of the Company of Proprietors of the Coventry Canal Navigation; , N

Were severally presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners are informed a Bill is depending in the House for making a Canal from the Dudley Canal, in the County of Worcester, to the Worcester and Birmingham Canal, now making at, or hear, Selly Oak, in the said County, which is to run in a parallel Direction to the Old Birmingham and Fazeley Canal for near Eleven Miles, the Object of which Bill is to convey Coals from the Netherton and other Mines, lying near to the Line of the Birmingham Canal, into the Worcester and Birmingham Canal, below the Town of Birmingham, instead of conveying them to that Town; and that the Petitioners are also informed that an Application is making to the House for a Bill for making a Collateral Branch or Cut from the said Birmingham and Fazeley Canal, into the said Netherton and

other Mines, to the said Dudley Canal, which is a Distance of Five Miles only, by which Means the Coals from the Netherton and other Mines may be brought immediately into the Birmingham Market at a much less Expence; and the said City, and the several other different Markets in Want of Coals, may be better, cheaper, and more regularly served, than by the proposed Canal to Selly Oak: And therefore praying, That the said Bill for making the said Canal, from the Dudley Canal to the Worcester and Birmingham Canal at Selly Oak, may not pass into a Law, but that the Proprietors of the Birmingham and Fazeley Canal Navigation maybe empowered to extend their Canal, through the said Netherton and other Mines, to the said Dudley Navigation.

Sir John Ingilby reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the several Persons, whose Nam$s are thereunder written, being respectively Owners and Occupiers of Lands within the several Parishes or Districts of Hillingdon, Hartington, Hayes, Southal, Norwood, and Drayton, in the County of Middlesex, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition, and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

A State of the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition is as follows:

It was admitted by Mr, Acton Chaplin, an Agent for the Braunston Canal, that the Name of Mr. Alexander

Mackenzie, One of the Petitioners, is omitted in the List of Land Owners annexed to the original Petition, he not being an Owner of Land through which it is proposed that the Canal should pass. — Then,

Mr. Alexander Mackenzie being examined, said, That he was applied to by the Agents for the Braunston Canal for his Assent; and he related the following Conversation, which passed on the Occasion: Three. Gentlemen called on him about the Middle of November, requesting his Assent to the Canal, with a Declaration that they would pay him for his Land; to which he replied, that was no Indemnification to him, as his Property consisted of Freehold Land, and which ha occupied himself. That these Gentlemen appointed another Meeting on that Day Week, but never came; and he has not heard any Thing to the contrary since that Time, but that the Canal was intended to go through his Land. — He further said. That, it is impossible to ascertain from the Plan, whether his Land will be affected. That his whole Property in Southal Field is about Seven Acres, Four of which he has let — That his Land is dispersed in various Parts of the Field, there not being above an Acre in any One Place. — Then,

The Reverend Thomas Lloyd being examined, said, That he, with Mr. Chaplin, applied to Mr. Mackenzie about the 18th or 19th of October last for his Assent to the Braunston Canal, which was likely to passthrough some of his Property: That much Conversation passed on the Occasion, but Mr. Mackenzie would give no decisive Answer, on which Mr. Chaplin and himself promised to call on him again that Day Week; but understanding, in the mean Time, from Mr. Chaplin, that the Canal was not likely to pass through his Property, they did not call on him again. — The Witness further said. That, subsequent to this, about a Day or Two after the Time appointed to call on Mr. Mackenzie, he (the Witness) was in London, and accidentally met him in the Adelphi — ^That they recognized each other,

and Mr. Mackenzie observed, that they had not called on him — In Reply, the Witness assigned as a Reason, that the Canal was not likely to pass through his Property, and therefore it became unnecessary to- call on him.

Mr. Acton Chaplin being also examined, said, That, previous to the Month of November last, he went over that Part of the Line of the Canal which lies in Southal, with several Farmers of that Place; and'took from those Farmers (many of them the Occupiers of the Land in Question) the Names of the Owners and Occupiers within the Line of the Canal, and it appeared, that Mr. Mackenzie had no Property therein. — That he went over the Line again Yesterday, in Company with John Ossiter, Esquire, Mr. Joseph Fuller, Mr. Joseph Packer, Mr. Barnes (the Engineer) and Mr. William Ncarnan. Mr. Barnes then pointed out

the Line of the Canal; and from the Information of these Persons collectively, it appears, that the Canal does not touch or interfere within the Distance of One hundred and Twenty Yards of Mr. Mackenzie's Property. That the Witness had with him 'a Plan of Southal Field. f Which he produced to your Committee.]

The Witness being asked, How many Yards within each Side of the Line of the Canal did his Enquiries extend the First Thne he went over the Line? he said, From Thirty to Forty, Fifty, or One hundred Yards. — That he, or the Person who attended him, put down in foe Book of Reference, and in the List of Names referred to in that Book, the Owners, or reputed Owners, of Land in Southal Common Field.

John Ossiter, Esquire, being examined, said, That Mr. Mackenzie has no Property in Southal Field within the Line of the Canal — That his nearest Land to the Line was stept off Yesterday by an Husbandman, when it appeared to be One hundred and Thirty

Paces

Paces distant from that Line — That lie has known that Common Field ever since he was a Child — He did not know the Line of the Canal before Yesterday, only in a general Way — He knows the Situation of Mr. Mackenzies Land — No Plan was shewn him, but he went with the Engineer.

And it appeared by the Evidence of Mr. James Barnes, an Engineer, that he stept off the Line with the last mentioned Witness, and shewed him the exact Line: of the intended Canal, from which the original Plan is drawn. — Then,

Mr. William Collison, Surveyor, being examined,

said. That the original Plan was made in September, and he drew it — That the Area of the Common Field is not laid down to a Scale within One hundred Yards of the intended Canal — That when he first took the Survey, he was not able.to get Information sufficient to ascertain the Property — That he afterwards attended Mr. Chaplin, when they procured Information of the Farmers (Occupiers of the Field) stating the particular Lands intended to be cut by the Canal, at which Time they found that Mr. Mackenzie had no Land over that Part of the Field which was to be cut — Those Persons who had Property which would be affected by the Canal, are stated in the Lists annexed to the Original Petition, and he knows of no others.

[It appeared in the List of Land Owners annexed to the Original Petition, Matthew Batt is stated as assenting; and in the said List Fysh Deburgh is stated as applied to, and undecided, but desired to be a Subscriber.]

Your Committee then examined Mr. Matthew Batt, who said, He is both Owner and Occupier of Land in the Parishes of Drayton, Hillingdon, and Harlington, through which the Line of the intended Canal is to pass — That he wras applied to some Time in October by Mr. Chaplin, and another Gentleman, he cannot name, for his Assent; but refused — That with respect to Lands which he occupied of Mr. Deburgh, he said, he should be guided by what he should say: He meant to act as he should advise — No other Application was made to him for his Assent Mr. Chaplin and another Gentleman called on him one Day, and asked him to walk over the Field with them, and shew the Property through which the Canal was to pass — That he told them that he had got a Man who knew the Property as well as he did, and he went — This was after Mr. Chaplin had applied to him, and he did this to oblige Mr. Deburgh — That he conversed with the Man after he went over the Ground, but he never assented at all — That he expressed his Dissent when Mr. Chaplin applied to him at the White Horse — That he considered what he stud with respect to Mr. Deburgh to be a Refusal. Being asked, Whether he, ever more positively refused, than by saying he would do as Mr. Deburgh advised? He replied, Yes: He was determined not to be for th e BraunstonCanal, after he understood

tfrpre was to be another Canal; and he never assented to it before — That he expressed his Dissent to Mr. Brookes, in Uxbridge Street, in December last, but he does oof know who was present: He does not recollect to have conversed with the Reverend Mr. Lloyd on the Subject; but. he has seen him with Mr. Chaplin- — He never authorised them to put down his Name as assenting, never having been asked so to do — That both Parties made him Offers of having Shares in the respective Canals — That with respect to the Canal,

Mr. Chaplin told him at the White Horse, thajt if it went such a Distance of his Land, he was to have a Share; but he made no Reply — That it was in December he first understood there was to be an Opposition to the Braunston Canal, and he joined in that Opposition as soon as he heard of it; because he thought Two Cuts coming across the Common Field would entirely destroy it — That there was a Meeting, of Twp pr Three Parishes at the Magpie, at Hounslow Heath, in Vol. 48.

her, when every Person declared their Intention which Canal they would be for, and he signed for the Hampton Gay Canal; and was told he was a Subscriber, as Mr. Chaplin had told him with respect to the other Canal. — That Notice was given of this Meeting in Drayton Church — That he signed the Petition now before the Committee at the Request of Mr.

That he preferred the Hampton Gay Scheme, because he thought the Braunston Canal would do most Damage. At the Time Mr. Chaplin first applied to him, he aid not know there was any other Canal depending besides the Braunston; it was then said, that Two Ca-

nals were to meet before they came to Uxbridge — That Mr. Deburgh and he both signed the Hampton Gay

Petition — That he never signified to Mr. Chaplin that lie would be glad to take such Shares as his Proportion of Land would entitle him to Being asked, Whether he ever refused to sign the Hampton Gay Petition ? He replied, Yes.

Fysh Deburgh, Esquire, was next examined; who said, He is Landlord to Matthew Batt, who constantly expressed his Design of being guided by him in respect to his Consent to the Braunston Canal — That he was applied to for his Consent to this Canal; and he made no Distinction in that Application between his Right to assent for himself and that of assenting for Mr. Batt, conceiving the y went Hand in Hand, and in the Answer he gave he conceived himself answering for Mr. Batt. Being asked, Whether he did, or did not, assent to the Braunston Canal ? he replied. He could not answer that Question, without an Explanation: He has dissented to the Braunston Canal upon late Grounds, because he was first assured there would be a Coalition, and he now finds there will not — That his Answer, with respect to his Consent to the Canal, was conditional; as follows: Mr. Chaplin, with Three others, in October, called on him at Drayton to solicit his Consent: He replied, that he had previously assented to the Hampton Gay Canal, and had subscribed to it; and hoped there would not be Two Canals — Mr. Chaplin replied, that there was no Fear of that, for there would be a Coalition — That in case of a Coalition, he (the Witness) said, he would give no positive Answer till he had consulted Mr. Hilliard, a very considerable Landholder; and there the Matter rested — He has never seen any of the Parties since — He never gave a positive Opinion, or authorized any Person to put down his Consent — That Mr. Batt applied to him, to know his Sentiments, the very Day Mr. Chaplin called; and he then said, if there was to be only One Canal, he should have no Objection; but this was on a Presumption that there would be a Junction — That as soon as he had heard of the Refusal of the Managers of the Braunston Canal to coalesce with the Hampton Gay, which was in December, he then signified to Mr. Batt his positive Determination to oppose the Braunston Canal; before which Time he had not expressed any Disapprobation — That he had agreed with Mr. Batt to assent to the Braunston Canal, if it went Hand in Hand with the Hampton Gay — That if the Two Canals were made, lie should, have them both go nearly through one Farm Yard — He never expressed any Disapprobation to the Braunston Canal Agents, not having seen them till this Day — That he should not object to One Canal going through his Yard; but he should prefer the Hampton Gay Canal, as he was applied to for that Eight Months before.

Mr. Batt being again examined, he was asked, Whether he ever said to Mr. Hull (hat he was never applied to, but to shew the Premisses ? He replied, he might say so; he could not teU: He does not remember that he said so.

The Reverend Thomas Lloyd and Mr. Edward Oakley Gray, who were both present when the above-mentioned Application was made to Mr. Batt for his Assent to the Braunston Canal, severally corroborated the Testimony of Mr. Chaplin — And Mr. Gray further said, That no Hint whatever was dropt during the Conversation of a Coalition with the Hampton Gay — And that he clearly understood Mr. Bait gave his Consent for his own Land, without intending to consult any Person.

Mr. Thomas Brookes being examined, said, That he had a Conversation with Mr. Batt, about the 17th or 18th of December last, on the Subject of the Braunston Canal passing through his Ground; when Mr. Batt said, he had not any Objection with respect to his own Property; but being a Tenant to Mr. Deburgh, he could not consent without having his Approbation, as to that Land — That Mr. Batt also gave the Witness a Direction to his Tenant, of the Name of Watts, for the Purpose of getting his Assent; but he was not at Home.

[An Obliteration appearing against the Name of Matthew Batt, in the Reference to Horton Field, in the List of Owners and Occupiers (annexed to the Original Petition) and the Word " assenting," written under the said Name, Mr. Edward Oakley Gray, an Agent for the Braunston Canal, explained it thus — That the References were copied by the Clerk, and afterwards revised by the Agents; and the Errors corrected in the Presence of the Witnesses, when Application was made.]

Mr. Robert Edwards, who was next examined, owned. That he signed the Petition now before the Committee — That he never set his Hand to any Canal at all — That he was applied to in November, but does not know by whom: It was not the Braunston Canal Agent — He was applied to for the Hampton Gay Canal, not the Braunston Canal — His Property lies in ton Parish — His Brothers, Benjamin, , and him-

self, are jointly concerned in this Property, as Owners and Occupiers — His Brother Benjamin usually pays the Taxes and Levies — He (the Witness) lives with his Sister, Hannah Edwards, at the lower End of the Town, but has nothing to do with her Property — That the Petition was read over to him when he signed it — The Grievance he complained of was, that he did not like his Land cut in two by any Canal —

That he applied himself to get this Petition brought forward — That when he signed it, he understood that the general Tenor of it went to put a Stop to the Braunston Canal. — Then,

Mr. Acton Chaplin, One of the Agents for the Braunston Canal, -informed the Committee, That Robert Edwards's Name is not entered in the List of Owners and Occupiers; and the Reason he was not so entered was, that Benjamin Edwards told the Witness, that he was the Owner and Occupier of the Property; and he entered it in a Minute Book, which he has in his Hand, and which Minute he made at the Time.

Mr. William CoUison, being examined, said, He was present when Mr. Chaplin applied to Benjamin Edwards, when he |pointed out to Mr. Chaplin and him several Pieces of Land, of which he was Owner and Occupier — He did not mention any Joint Tenants or Occupiers with him.

Hannah Edwards being also examined, said, She signed the Petition — That her Complaint was the Damage that the Canal would do her Land — That she was applied to for her Consent to the Canal passing through her Ground — That she does not recollect the Persons, but thinks Mr. was one — She thinks this Application was made a little after' Michaelmas, but cannot exactly say — That her Answer was. Whether she gave her Consent or not, it was of very little Consequence — That about a Month or Six Weeks afterwards a Gentleman on Horseback asked her to sign for the Braunston Canal, and she refused — That she never gave her Consent to the Braunston Canal, or authorized any Person to put her Name down as such — That she is not an Owner, but Occupier, of Land, through which the Canal is to pass — Her Landlord is Count Desalis — That she is Joint Tenant of Land with her Two Brothers, Benjamin and Robei't — That her Brother Robert has no Property in the House in which she lives. Being asked, Why she thought it was of little Consequence whether she consented or not? She replied, Because she knew nothing about it; but afterwards found out it would spoil a great deal of Land. She was applied to as an Occupier, being Occupier.

Mr. Chaplin being next examined, said, That he applied to Hannah Edwards, as an Occupier, for her Assent to the Braunston Canal, in Presence of the Reverend Mr. Lloyd, Mr. John Hull, and Mr. Joseph Packer. She clearly and decidedly assented, without any Hesitation. Her Words, were, That she had no Objection. She made no further Answer or Explanation.

Mr. John Hull, Mr. Joseph Packer, and the Reverend Mr. Lloyd, being severally examined, confirmed this last mentioned Evidence of Mr. Chaplin.

This was after a Conversation with Mr. Hull. — Philp said, he had been applied to by Lord Berkeley, which caused the Conversation with Mr. Hull.
