he wanted to have his Advice; and he advised him to assent. He then said, he would. — Mr. Chaplin asked Philip, if it should happen that he should be entitled to any Shares, whether he would take them, or no? On this, Philip asked the Witness his Advice; and he advised him to take them; and said, that if he would not, he would for him. Philip then said, he would take them.

— lie said, that Lord Berkeley had been round a few Days ago, and that he did not know what to do. — These Words respecting Lord Berkeley passed before the Conversation respecting the Canal.

Mr. Packer, being also examined, said. He was present on the 9th of November, when Philp's Consent was applied for — That he assented and agreed to take the Shares he was entitled to.

Mr. Richard Philp, being next examined, said; That he never consented to the Bra Canal — He never was asked the Question. He is an Occupier.

The Reverend Mr. Lloyd being examined, said. That, on the oth of November, he applied to a Person, apparently a middle aged Man, who, he understood, was Richard Philp, for his Assent to the Ca-

nal — This was in Harlington Street. He told him, there was a Canal which was intended to pass through some Land which he occupied — He said, he had no Objection. That Mr. Packer was near; but cannot say whether he heard the Conversation: He was near enough to see the Person he was with — That the Witness cannot identify Richard Philp at this present Time.

Mr. Chaplin said, He was at Harlington on the 9th of November — On being told by some Farmers that Richard Philp had just gone up the Street, Mr. Lloyd returned, and went after him.

The Reverend Mr. Lloyd further said. That he applied to Five Persons of the Name of Philp, who all gave their Assent. Being asked, How he was given to understand that the Person he appled to in Harlington Street was Richard Philp? he said. They enquired of several Persons, One of whom pointed to him a Man as Richard Philp — That he believes he addressed him by the Name of Richard Philp — He does not recollect whether he asked him if his Name was Richard Philp. That he understood from William Philp that his Brother was in the Field, and was expected Home very shortly, and it was possible they might meet him; which induced them to make an Enquiry as they passed along. On his being pointed out, he had no Hesitation about addressing him as Richard Pliilp — He is certain he addressed Richard Philp by Name.

Mr. Hull being examined, said, He did not know Richard Philp.

Mr. Richard Philp, being further examined, was asked, Whether any of these Gentlemen ever came to him, and asked his Consent to the Braunston Canal? be said, No: He was out in the Field when his Brother came after him — He did not ask him for his Consent; if be had, he never should have given it. Being further asked, If he ever dissented to the Braunslon Canal? he said, He always did in his own Mind — He never did to any Body else — He never was asked the Question respecting the Braunston Canal at all — He never was asked about it, but in common Talk; and he cannot recollect any Thing about it. He has a Son, named Richard, who is neither Proprietor or Occupier of Land, but lives with him in his Ihisiness. That the Reason he petitioned was, because his Land would be cut in two; and that was the only Reason.

Mr. James Davies was next examined; who said, He did not consent to the Braunston Canal — That Two Gentlemen called on him, and asked him, whether the Canal would not go across some of his Land ? to which he replied, it would cross Two Acres — They then asked his Consent; and he said, he would never give his Consent at all, — Then,

Vol. 48.

Mr. Edward Oakley Gray said. He applied to James Davies on the 14th of November for his Assent to the Braunslon Canal going through his Land — He at first objected, on Account of the small Quantity which he had; otherwise, he said, he had no Objection — That the Witness then left him, and went to John,

his Neighbour, accompanied by Mr. — That

Davies followed them to Raper's; and asked Raper, if he had consented? — That, on Raper saying he had,

Davies' said, they might put him down as consenting —

That the Witness did not tell Davies, when he applied to him for his Assent, that the Canal was to divide the Parishes.

This last mentioned Evidence was corroborated by Mr. James Barnes.

Mr. John Raper, being next examined, said, That he is a Land Owner — That he was asked his Consent; but never gave it. — Then,

Mr. Gray, being again examined, said. That he applied to Raper, on the 14th of November, for his

Assent — That he told him, a Compensation would be made him for what Land was taken for the Canal; and he assented, without any Hesitation.

Mr. Barnes confirmed this Evidence: And further added. That he w as at Harlington on the 4th of this Month, on Business of the Canal — He heard that Mr.

Raper should have said, that he never was applied to — That Mr. Newman went with him to s —

That he asked Raper, if he knew him? He said he did — He asked him, if he had given him and Mr.

Gray his Consent to go through his Land? He said, he had; but he understood it was to cut the Parishes in two.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Pawnbrokers, on Behalf of themselves and others exercisingtbat Business, within the Cities of London and Westminster, and the Bills of Mortality, was presented to the House, and read; Vol. 48.

in pursuance of the several Acts of Parliament for improving the Navigation of the said Rivers Thames and Isis, laid out a considerable Sum of Money in the Improvement and Amendment of the Navigation of the said Rivers, and conceive that, if the Bill for making the said Navigable Canal is passed into a Law, and the said Canal made, it will be injurious to the Navigation of the said Rivers Thames and Isis, by taking into the said Canal several Springs of Water, that for Time immemorial have flowed, and now flow, into 3 A the

the said Rivers, tod, in short Water Times especially, greatly assisted its Navigation: And therefore praying, That there may be inserted in the said Bill sufficient Clauses to prevent the Proprietors or Undertakers of the said Canal from taking the Water in low Water Times from the said Springs, or by any Means diverting the same from flowing into the said Rivers as it usually hath done, and that the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves, or Counsel, against such Part of the said Bill as may affect them, and have such Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet; and that in Default of such sufficient Clauses being inserted in the said Bill, that the Petitioners have Leave to be heard, by themselves, or Counsel, against the said Bill passing into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time.

A Motion was made, and the Question was proposed. That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, That He will be graciously pleased to give Directions, that there be laid before this House, a Copy of any Treaty, or Agreement,' between His Majesty, the Emperor of Germany, and the King of , or either

of those Powers, entered into in January last.

And the said Motion was, with Leave of the House, withdrawn.

The House, according to Order, proceeded to take into Consideration His Majesty's most Gracious Message of Yesterday.

And the same was again read by Mr. Speaker.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, to return His Majesty the Thanks of this House for His most Gracious Message, informing us, That the Assembly, now exercising the Powers of Government in France, have, without previous Notice, directed Acts of Hostility to be committed against the Persons and Property of His Majesty's Subjects, in Breach of the Law of Nations and of the most positive Stipulations of Treaty; and have since, on the most groundless Pretences, actually declared War against His Majesty and The United Provinces: To assure His Majesty that, under the Circumstances of this wanton and unprovoked Aggression, we most gratefully acknowledge His Majesty's Care and Vigilance in taking the necessary Steps for maintaining the Honour of His Crown, and vindicating the Rights of His People: That His Majesty may rely on the firm and effectual Support of the Representatives of a brave and loyal People, in the Prosecution of a just and necessary War; and in endeavouring, under the Blessing of Providence, to oppose an effectual Barrier to the further Progress of a System, which strikes at the Security and Peace of all independent Nations, and is pursued in Defiance of every Principle of Moderation, Good Faith, Humanity, and Justice:

That, in a Cause of such general Concern, it must afford us great Satisfaction to learn, that His Majesty has every Reason to hope for the cordial Co-operation of those Powers, who are united with His Majesty by the Ties of Alliance, or who feel an Interest in preventing the Extension of Anarchy and Confusion, and in contributing to the Security and Tranquillity of Europe:

That we are persuaded, that whatever His Majesty's faithful Subjects must consider as most dear and sacred, the Stability of our happy Constitution, the Security and Honour of His Majesty's Crown, and the Preservation of our Laws, our Liberty, and our Religion, are all involved in the Issue of the present Contest; and that our Zeal and Exertions shall be proportioned to the Importance of the Conjuncture, and to the Magnitude and Value of the Objects for which we have to contend.

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by leaving out from the Words " His most " Gracious Message" to the End of the Question, in order to insert these Words: — "That we learn with the " utmost Concern, that the Assembly who now exercise " the Powers of Government in France have directed " the Commission of Acts of Hostility against the Per*

" sons and Property of His Majesty's Subjects, and " that they have actually declared War against His Majesty and The United ProvincesThat we humbly " beg Leave to assure His Majesty, that His Majesty's " faithful Commons will exert themselves with the " utmost Zeal for the Maintenance of the Honour of " His Majesty's Crown, and the Vindication of the " Rights of His People; and that nothing shall be " wanting on their Part that can contribute to that '

" firm and effectual Support which His Majesty has " so much Reason to expect from a brave and loyal " People, in repelling every Hostile Attempt against " this Country, and in such other Exertions as may " be necessary to induce France to consent to such " Terms of Pacification as may be consistent with the " Honour of His Majesty's Crown, the Security of His " Allies, and the Interest of His People," instead thereof.

And the Question being put, That the Words pro* posed to be left out, stand Part of the Question;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Then the main Question being put;

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to Resolution His Majesty, to return His Majesty the Thanks of f®r Address this House for His most Gracious Message, inform- jJesww* ing us, That the Assembly, now exercising the Powers of Government in France, have, without previous Notice, directed Acts of Hostility to be committed against the Persons and Property of His Majesty's Subjects, in Breach of the Law of Nations, and of the most positive Stipulations of Treaty; and have since, on the most groundless Pretences, actually declared War against His Majesty and The United Provinces: To assure His Majesty that, under the Circumstances of this wanton and unprovoked Aggression, we most gratefully acknowledge His Majesty's Care and Vigilance in taking the necessary Steps for maintaining the Honour of His Crown, and vindicating the Rights of His People: That His Majesty may rely on the firm and effectual Support of the Representatives of a brave and loyal People, in the Prosecution of a just and necessary War; and in endeavouring, under the Blessing of Providence, to oppose an effectual Barrier to the further Progress of a System which strikes at the Security and Peace of all independent Nations, and is pursued in open Defiance of every Principle of Moderation, Good Faith, Humanity, and Justice:

That, in a Cause of such general Concern, it must afford us great Satisfaction to learn, that His Majesty has every Reason to hope for the cordial Co-operation of those Powers, who are united with His Majesty by the Ties of Alliance, or who feel an Interest in preventing the Extension of Anarchy and Confusion, and in contributing to the Security and Tranquillity of Europe:

That we are persuaded, that whatever His Majesty's faithful Subjects must consider as most dear and sacred, the Stability of our happy Constitution, the Security and Honour of His Majesty's Crown, and the Preservation of our Laws, our Liberty, and our Religion, are all involved in the Issue of the present Contest; and that our Zeal and Exertions shall be proportioned to the Importance of the Conjuncture, and to the Magnitude and Value of the Objects for which we have to contend.

Address re- Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer reported from the ported and Committee, appointed to draw up an Address to be agreed to presented to His Majesty, That the Committee had drawn up an Address accordingly, which they had directed him to report to the House j and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, Your Majesty's most dutiful arid loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, beg Leave to return Your Majesty our most humble Thanks for Your Majesty's most Gracious Message, informing us, That the Assembly, now exercising the Powers of Government in France, have, without previous Notice, directed Acts of Hostility to be committed against the Persons and Property of Your Majesty's Subjects, in Breach of the Law of Nations, and of the most positive Stipulations of Treaty; and have since, on the most groundless Pretences, actually declared War against Your Majesty and The United Provinces.

Under the Circumstances of this wanton and unprovoked Aggression, we gratefully acknowledge Your Majesty's Care and Vigilance in taking the necessary Steps for maintaining the Honour of Your Crown, and vindicating the Rights of Your People: Your Majesty may rely on the firm and effectual Support of the Representatives of a brave and loyal People, in the Prosecution of a just and necessary War; and in endeavouring, under the Blessing of Providence, to oppose an effectual Barrier to the further Progress of a System, which strikes at the Security and Peace of all independent Nations, and is pursued in Defiance of every Principle of Moderation, Good Faith, Humanity, and Justice.

In a Cause of such general Concern, it affords us great Satisfaction to learn, that Your Majesty has every Reason to hope for the cordial Co-operation of those Powers, who are united with Your Majesty by the Ties of Alliance, or who feel an Interest in preventing the Extension of Anarchy and Confusion, and in contributing to the Security and Tranquillity of Europe.

We are persuaded, that whatever Your Majesty's faithful Subjects consider as most dear and sacred, the Stability of our happy Constitution, the Security and Honour of Your Majesty's Crown, and the Preservation of our Laws, our Liberty, and our Religion, are all involved in the Issue of the present Contest; and our Zeal and Exertion shall be proportioned to the Importance of the Conjuncture, and to the Magnitude and Value of the Objects for which we have to contend.

The said Address being read a Second Time;

Resolved, That this House dotli agree with the Committee in the said Address to be presented to His Majesty.

Resolved, That the said Address be presented to His Majesty by the whole House. %

A Petition g»f the Owners and Occupiers of Wharfs, in the Port of London, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have observed that a Bill is depending before the House for making a Navigable Canal from Braunston, in the County of Northampton, to Nero Brentford, in the County of Middlesex, which Canal, by Means of Collateral Cuts, is intended to form a Junction with several other Canals, and thereby to open an Intercourse by Water Carriage between the Port of London and the Ports and Principal Places in the Northern, Western, and Eastern Parts of the Kingdom; and that, from Time immemorial, the Inhabitants of this Island have interchanged all Manner of bulky and heavy Commodities by a Coast Navigation, that a large Capital has been and now remains embarked in Shipping, and in the building and maintaining Vessels suitable to the various Branches of the said Navigation, and the Petitioners are interested therein; and that, for the Convenience of the said Trade, large and commodious Wharfs and Warehouses have been erected and maintained at a very great Expence, and the Petitioners are apprehensive of much Injury to their Property from the Decay of the Coasting Trade, which must be occasioned by the Ruin of the Coasting Vessels, and also to their respective Wharfs, in case the Bill for making the said Canal shqpld pass into a Law: And therefore requesting the House to take under their Consideration the Loss and Damage to which the Petitioners Property must be exposed by the Junction of Canals intended by the said Bill, and that they will ordain that such Compensation shall be made to them as the Justice of the Case may require, and as to the House shall seem meet, and that they will allow the Petitioners to produce their Witnesses, and to offer their Objections to the said Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from the Oxford Canal Navigation at Braunston, in the County of Northampton, to join the River Thames at New Brentford, in the County of Middlesex, and also for making and maintaining certain Collateral Cuts from the said intended Canal, is committed.

A Bill for making and maintaining a Navigable Communication from the Junction of the River Foss with the River Ouse, at or near the City of York, to Stillington Mill, in the Parish of Sti/lington, in the North Riding of the County of York, and for draining and improving certain Low Lands lying on each Side of the said River Foss, was read a Second Time.

Resolved, That the Bill be committed to Mr. berforce, Mr. Buncombe, &c.: And they are to meet this Afternoon, at Five of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow

A PETITION of the Company of Proprietors Petition of the Thames and Severn Canal Navigation, w'as ^etherton presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, g£ijy by virtue of several Acts, passed many Years since, a Oak Canal Navigable Caoal, called The Staffordshire and Worcester- Bill. shire Canal, was undertaken and completed from the Grand Trunk Canal at Haywood to the River Severn at Stourport, and Two other Canals, called The Stourbridge Canal and The Dudley Canal, were afterwards made, extending from the Collieries and Iron Manufactories, in the Neighbourhood of Stourbridge and Dudley, to the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal; and that, by virtue of the Powers granted by subsequent Acts of Parliament, passed in the Years 1783 and 1791, the Petitioners have, at a very considerable Expence, made and completed a Canal called The Thames and Severn Canal, by which a Navigable Communication is opened between the River Thames at Leachlade and the River Severn at Framiload, and it was a very material Object with the Petitioners, in making the said Canal, that great Quantities of Coal and Manufactures from the Neighbourhood of Stourbridge and Dudley would be brought along the same; and that an Act w'as passed, in the last Session of Parliament, to enable certain Persons to make a Canal from Birmingham to Worcester, to be called The Worcester Canal, and the same is now making; and that the Petitioners observe that a Bill is depending in the House for making a Canal from the before-named Dudley Canal at or near Netherton, to join and communicate with the

Worcester Canal at or near a Place called Selly Oak, which Canal, if made, will be highly detrimental to the Interest of the Petitioners, without affording (as the Petitioners conceive) any real and substantial Advantage to the Public: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves, or their Counsel, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from the Dudley Canal, in the County of Worcester, to the Worcester and Birmingham Canal, now making at, or near, Selly Oak, in the said County, and also certain Collateral Cuts to communicate therewith, be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by themselves, or Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

I Member And a Member returned upon a new Writ having j utesOaths, taken the Oaths, and made and subscribed the Declaration, and taken and subscribed the Oath of Abjuration, and having delivered in to the Clerk of the House an Account of his Qualification, and taken and subscribed the Oath of Qualification, according to the Laws made for those Purposes;

Warwick Mr. Galley Knight, from the Select Committee, who Hertion de- were appointed to try and determine the Merits of the WBU°t' Petition of the several Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, all legal Voters of the Borough of Warwick, in the County of Warwick, on Behalf of themselves, and many other Electors of the said Borough, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the said Borough, informed the House,

That the Counsel for the Petitioners, having opened their Case to the said Select Committee, delivered in a Statement, upon the Right of Election for the' said Borough, as follows:

" The Counsel of the Petitioners state, that the " Right of Election for the Borough of is,

" according to the last Determination of the House of " Commons concerning the same, made on the 31st " of May, in the Year 1628, " In the Commonalty,"

"that is, according to an Explanatory Resolution of " that House on the 23d of January 1722, and the Vot. 48.

197

u true Construction of such Explanatory Resolution,

" In such Persons only in the said Borough who pay " to Church and Poor."

And that thereupon the Counsel for the Sitting Member also delivered in a Statement of the Right of Election for the said Borough, as follows:

" That the Right of Election of Burgesses, to serve " in Parliament for the Borough of Warwick, is in "such Persons only as pay to Church and Poor in the said Borough."

That, upon the Statement delivered in by the Counsel for the Petitioners, the said Select Committee have determined,

That the Right of Election, as set forth in the said Statement, is not the Right of Election for the Borough of Warwick, in the County of Warwick.

That, upon the Statement delivered in by the Counsel for the Sitting Member, the said Select Committee have determined,

That the Right of Election, as set forth in the said Statement, is the Right of Election for the said Borough of Warwick, so far as the said Right is therein described.

That the said Select Committee, having duly considered the said Statements, and the Evidence adduced before them, touching the Right of Election for the said Borough of Warwick, have determined,

That, pursuant to the last Determination of the House of Commons, the Right of Election of Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Warwick, is in such Persons only as pay to Church and Poor in the said Borough, whether Inhabitants or not.

That the said Select Committee have also determined,

That the Honourable George V is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Warwick, in the County of Warwick.

And also, that the said Select Committee have determined.

That the said Petition did not appear to the said Select Committee to be frivolous or vexatious:

And also, that the said Select Committee have determined,

That the Opposition of the said Honourable George Villiers to the said Petition did not appear to the said Select Committee to be frivolous or vexatious.

And the said Determinations were ordered to be entered in the Journals of this House.

Mr. Speaker reported to the House, That the House attended His Majesty on Thursday last, with their Address; to which His Majesty was pleased to give this most Gracious Answer:

Gentlemen,

I return you My warmest Thanks for this affectionate and loyal Address, and for the cordial Assurances of your firm and effectual Support in the Measures which may be necessary for maintaining the Honour, of My Crown, and for prosecuting with Vigour a just and necessary War, in defence of the dearest Interests of My People.

And therefore praying. Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending -this House, do go into the Places appointed for the Members of this House in Westminster Hall, and clear the same of all Strangers, and summon the Members there, if any, and in the Passages leading thereto, to attend their Service in the House immediately; and, if he find any Strangers in the said Places or Passages, who refuse to go out, that he take them immediately into his Custody.

And the Name of Sir Peter Burrell, Baronet, being drawn, he offered to the House, as an Excuse for not serving on the said Committee, that executing the Office of Lord Great Chamberlain, it is his Duty to attend in Person, at the Trial on the Impeachment of Warren Hastings, Esquire; and the Substance of what was so alledged by him being taken down by the Clerk, and the said Member having at the Table verified the same upon Oath, the Opinion of the House was taken thereon; and he was excused from serving on the said Committee.

Esquire, James Ward, and the several other Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and others, Owners and Proprietors of Estates, and Inhabitants within the said Parish of Paddington, in the said County of Middlesex, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by an Act; made in the Twenty-eighth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for re-building the " Parish Church of Paddington, in the County of dlesex, and for enlarging the Church Yard of the said " Parish," certain Powers were vested in the Trustee# under the said Act for the Time being, to enable them to carry the same into execution; and that the said Trustees, Churchwardens, and Overseers of the said Parish, have made considerable Progress in the execution of such Powers, and have caused the said Parish Church to be re-built, consecrated, and Divine Service performed therein, but the same is not yet complete, nor are the Outside Walls and Fences of the said Church Yard yet finished, although a considerable Sum of Money hath been expended, and is yet due on Account thereof, whereby it is found that the good Purposes intended by the said Act cannot be effectually answered unless the same be amended, and the Powers thereof enlarged; and that the Inhabitants of the said Parish are not capable of raising such further Sum as will be sufficient to completely finish the same without the Aid -of Parliament: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes aforesaid, under such Rules, Orders, and Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

A Petition of the Gentlemen* Clergy, Landholders, Cockerton and Inhabitants of the County of Durham, whose ",m1 s*ain* Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Road leading from the South End of Cockerton Bridge, in the County of Durham, to the Town of Staindrop, through theseve* ral Parishes of Darlington, and High Coniscliffe, Chapelry of Denton, and Parishes of Gai and Staindrop, in the said County, is in a ruinous Condition, narrow in several Places, and from the Deepness of the Soil and many heavy Carriages loaden with Lime and Coal* passing along the same, is become very ruinous, and much out of Repair, and, in the Winter Season, many Parts thereof are so bad that Horses and Carriages canuot pass along the same without Danger, and the said Road cannot be effectually repaired, altered, widened, amended, and kept in Repair by the ordinary Course of Law; but, if the same was properly repaired, altered, widened, amended, and necessary and convenient Bridges, Mounts, and Batteries, erected upon the same, it would be of great Utility and Advantage to the Public, and would facilitate and improve the Communication between many Towns and Places in the said County of Durham: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for repairing, altering, widening, amending, and preserving the said Road, and for erecting, building, and making necessary and convenient Bridges, Mounts, and Batteries, upon the same, with such Provisions as the House shall think lit.

&c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Ordered, That Mr. Burdon do make the Report from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Charles Brandling, Esquire, Lord of the Manor of Middleton, in the County of York, Owner and Proprietor of divers Coal Works in the said Manor, and Places adjacent, and the several Inhabitants of the Town and Neighbourhood of Leeds, in the said County, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred.

Mr. Burdon accordingly reported from the said Committee, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, which they had directed to be reported to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, at} Act, made in the Nineteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for rendering " more beneficial an Act made in the Thirty-first " Year of the Reign of King George the Second, intituled, "An Act for establishing Agreements made " between Charles Brandling, Esquire, and other Persons, Proprietors of Lands, for laying down a Wag-u gon Way, in order for the better supplying the " Town and Neighbourhood of Leeds, in the County " of York, with Coals, by enabling the said Charles " Brandling to supply Annually a larger Quantity of .* Coals to and for the Use of the said Town and " Neighbourhood,"; was read; whereby it appears, that the said Charles Brandling is obliged, Yearly, during such Time as he shall continue the said Waggon Way, made for the Purpose of bringing Coals from the Coal Works of the said Charles Bratidling, in Middleton aforesaid, to the Repository at a certain Place, in the said Act called Casson Close, to bring to the said Repository or Coal Yard, Forty thousand Dozens, or Four hundred and Eighty thousand Corves of Coals, at the least, by Four equal Quarterly Proportions, that is to say, Ten thousand Dozens, or One hundred and Twenty Thousand Corves in each Quarter of the Year, unless prevented by Fire, Water, or other inevitable Accident.

Mr. Joseph Humble, being then examined, said, That Mr. Brandling being empowered to sell the Coals brought down to his Repository from his Colliery to Persons in the Neighbourhood of Leeds, a very considerable Quantity of the Coals so brought are taken and purchased by Persons residing at a great Distance from the said Town of Leeds, and the Inhabitants of the said Town and Parish of Leeds are thereby deprived of a considerable Part of the Benefit and Advantage intended to result to them by the said Acts: That the said Town and Parish of Leeds has lately very considerably increased in Population, and the Trade thereof very greatly extended; and a great Number of Dyehouses, Engines, and Machines, have been erected therein, so that the Quantity of Coals stipulated by the said Act to be brought down to the said Repertory, are found insufficient for supplying the said Town and Parish of Leeds only; which I nconvenience has arisen from Mr. Brandling's Coal Works having been occasionally laid up, or prevented from being worked, by inevitable Accidents, and owing to his being restrained by the said Act from bringing any other Coals to the said Repository than such as he should get within his said Manor of Middleton; and that such Inconveniencies might in future be, in a great Measure, remedied, if the said Charles Brandling was allowed, under proper Regulations, to bring Coal from any other Colliery to the said Repository; that since the passing the said Act, the said Charles Brandling hath been put to a very great Expence in making fresh Winnings in his said Colliery, by laying and making additional Waggon Ways from his said Coal Pits to the said Repository, and by paying much greater Prices for leading and getting the said Coals, and for the Wood and other Materials therein.

That it would be of great Benefit and Advantage to the Inhabitants of the Town and Parish of Leeds, and the Manufactures and Trade thereof, if the Quantity of Coals stipulated by the said Act were brought from the Coal Pits and Coal Works of the said Charles Brandling to the said Repository, and there sold to the Inhabitants of the Town and Parish of Leeds only; and also, if the delivering the same at the said Repository, and the Manner and Prices of conveying and carrying the same from such Repository to the Inhabitants within the said Town and Parish, were properly regulated and ascertained.

That the Coal got and worked at all the other Collieries or Coal Works in the Neighbourhood of Leeds, is very considerably advanced in Price; and that it would very greatly distress the Inhabitants of the said Town and Parish, if the said Charles Brandling should discontinue the said Waggon Way and Repository, and the same would also be a very great Loss and Prejudice to the Trade and Manufactories thereof.

That the said Charles Brandling hath proposed, and is willing to continue to bring down from his said Coal Works at Middleton aforesaid, and deliver at the said Repository, during the Continuance of the Term in the said Act mentioned, or such other Term of Years as may be deemed requisite, Forty thousand Dozens, or Four Hundred and Eighty thousand Corves of Coals, by Weekly Proportions, for the sole Use of the Inhabitants of the said Town and Parish of Leeds, provided Sale can be had for the same, at the Rate of Sixpence Half-penny a Corf, having Liberty to leave any Quantity of Coals, not exceeding One hundred and Forty-four Dozens per Week, at any Place near to the said Waggon Way within the said Borough; and also, to take and deposit the Surplus Quantity, beyond the Daily Sale or Demand of the said Town and Parish, in any other Coal Yard or Repository within the said Town and Parish.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for amending and enlarging the Powers of Two Acts, one . made in the Thirty-first Year of the Reign of His late Majesty King George the Second, and the other made in the Nineteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for the better supplying of the Town and Parish of Leeds, in the County of York, with Coals: And that Mr. Burdon and Mr. Wilberforce do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are thereunto, subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and others, Owners and Occupiers of Estates in the County of Essex, and Merchants, Tradesmen, and Inhabitants of the Town of and the

Neighbourhood thereof, in the said County, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That it appears by Surveys, and Levels, lately made and taken, that a Navigable Communication, for the Passage of Boats, Barges, and other Vessels of heavy Burthen, may be made from the Town of Chelmsford, to, or nearly to, a Place called Colliers Reach, in, or near, the River Blaclcivater, near the Town and Port of Maldon, in the said County, by Means of widening,

deepening, cleansing, straitening, and improving the Rivers Chelmer and Cann, and making Cuts and Deviations by the Sides thereof, w-here necessary, to a certain Part of the said River Chelmer, above, and near to, Beleigh Mill,(which is the nearest Mill upon the said River Chelmer, to the Town of Maldon) and by making a Navigable Cut, or Canal, from thence into, and across, a Stream or River, called the Langford Stream or River, and also by making a Navigable Cut, or Canal, from the said last mentioned Stream or River, into the said River Blackwater, and by widening, deepening, cleansing, and improving the said River Blackwaler, and making Cuts and Deviations by the Sides thereof, where necessary, to, or near to, a certain Mill, called and by

making a Navigable Cut, or Canal, from thence above the said Mill, through the Village of Heybridge, to communicate with the said River at, or

nearly at, the said Place, called Colliers Reach; and that the making of such Navigation will be attended with very great Advantages, not only to the said Towns of Chelmsford and Malden, and the Neighbourhood thereof, but to a great Number of other Towns and Places in the said County of Essex, and will be of general Benefit to the Trade and Commerce of the said County: And therefore praying. Purpose, to which the said Commissioners afterwards readily assented, and, in consequence whereof, the Petitioner began to erect, and hath now completed, a good substantial Brick Bridge, sufficient for the Passage of Carriages as well as Foot Passengers over the said Lake; and that the said Bridge is, and will be, of great Public Benefit and Convenience, particularly to those belonging to the said Hospital, as heretofore the only Mode of Conveyance for Foot Passengers over the said Lake to and from Haslar Hospital and the Parts adjacent has been iu Boats, which are frequently prevented passing the said Lake, sometimes from the Lowness of the Water, and at other Times from bad Weather, and Carriages being at all Times, previous to making the said Bridge, under a necessity of going round from Gosport through the Village of Alverstoke, in order to get to the Hospital, which is a Distance of near Three Miles; and that the building and finishing of the said Bridge hath been attended with a very considerable Expence: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for maintaining the Bridge by him erected across the said Lake, called Stoke or Haslar Lake, from Gosport to the opposite Shore towards Haslar Hospital in the said Parish of Alverstoke, in the County of Southampton, and for enabling the Petitioner to take certain Tolls for passing over the said Bridge, and other Purposes in such Bill to be mentioned.

A Petition of Thomas Baker, J Robert

Allen, William Dawden, James Stevens, Junior, Chrus. Chitty, William Crump, Andrew CoUyer, Thomas Buddie, Robert Trimmer, Andrew Bristow, DanielBristmo, Senior, Bristow Bradley, William Shotter, Caleb Barker, Darnel Walden, Junior, Joseph Brown, Peter Edwards, Andrew Merriott, Stephen Casar, Thomas Knight, John Cullen, John Hughes, John Marriner, Edward Bartholomew, William Mure, Benjamin Nichols, Henry Martin, Ann

Allen, Henry Matthews, Alexander Gilbert, Elizabeth Whittingham, Daniel Bristow, Junior, Thomas Piper, John Walter, John Longhurst, Samuel

Wakeley, John Page, George Alexander, William Taphouse, Charles Restall, George West, Thomas Cooper, John Nowles, Elizabeth Mayo, Samuel Stevens, Mary Manwaring, James Edwards, John Baker, James Nash, William Knight, and Anthony Williams, Inhabitants of, and Hop Planters within, the Parish of Farnham, in the County of Surrey, on Behalf of themselves and the rest of the Hop Planters within the said Parish, was l>resented to the House, and read; Setting' forth, That the Cultivation of Hops in England is, and has long been (as the Petitioners conceive) a Matter of great National Concern, and has, for a considerable Length of Time, been productive of a large Yearly Revenue to Government, and, instead of this Country being supplied with that Commodity from Foreign Parts (as was heretofore the Case) Hops are become an Article of Export, and are likely so to continue, if the Cultivation of them be not checked: That the Cultivation of Hops is also of great Benefit to this Country, from the Employment it affords, and the Money it produces, to the Poor, and from the Improvement it makes in the Land for other Purposes of Husbandry afterwards, and, besides the original and more general Use of Hops in Brewing Beer (in lieu of which no other Bitter can by Law be substituted) they have been found to be an useful Article in Dyeing, and there is a considerable Consumption of them in that Branch of Business, and the finer they are, the better are they suited to that Purpose; and that the first Planting any Ground with Hops is attended with very great Expence, and Hops do not come to a State of Maturity, so as to produce

any Quantity of Crop, until the Third Year, and, after the first Planting, the Annual Expence of keeping the Ground in Order, and training and dressing the Hops, and providing Poles for them is very considerable, so that the Expence of Planting an Acre of Ground, for the first Three Years, cannot Amount to less than loo I.; and that, after Hops are come to Maturity, and tilt they are obliged to be re-planted, the Annual Expence of an Acre of Hop Ground is not less than Thirty-one Pounds, and such Expence is the same; whether there be any Crop or not, no Part of which is paid, or any Allowance made, by the Person entitled to the Tythe of the said Land, and, if the 'Soil be not well suited to them, they will not continue to be productive for any Length of Time: That Yearly Compositions have hitherto been paid by the Planters of Hops, in the Kingdom in general, in lieu of Tythes, which have been a great Encouragement to the Culture of Hops, the Payment of Tythes in Kind being, from the great Expence attending the Cultivation and the Picking, too heavy a Burthen on the Planter, and the setting out the Tythes being in itself a Matter of great Inconvenience, and the Petitioners understand, that the general Compositions that are paid in this Kingdom, in lieu of Tythes of Hops, are from Five Shillings to Twelve Shillings an Acre: That the Inhabitants of the Parish of Farnham were (as it is supposed) Planters of Hops very early after their Introduction into this Country, and from their great Attention to the Business, and the Expences to which they have put themselves, the said Parish is, for its Extent, become one of the principal Plantations in England: That Henry Halsey, Esquire, the present Lessee of the Rectory of Farnham aforesaid (which is an Impropriate Rectory belonging to the Archdeacon of Surrey, in Right of his Archdeaconry, and is, and usually has been, leased out for Three Lives) and who, as such, claims to be entitled to the Tythes in Kind of Hops, planted in the Fields in Farnham, hath lately intimated an Intention of raising the high Composition now paid to him (being Twenty Shillings an Acre subject to Taxes) to Three Pounds an Acre clear of all Assessments to the Poors Rates, which would be equal to Twelve Shillings and Six Pence a Year more, or otherwise of obliging the respective Occupiers to set out their Tythes in Kind; and that, considering the great and increasing Expences of cultivating Hops, and the Uncertainty of the Crops, a Composition of Twenty Shillings an Acre is greater than the Planter can afford to pay, and no Person would undertake to plant and cultivate Hops on the Terms of rendering Tythes of them in Kind, for the Reasons before stated, and, if the Claim of the said Henry Halsey be submitted to, or encouraged by any of the Hop Planters in the said Parish of Farnham, it would probably occasion Demands in other Parishes of high Compositions for Tythes of Hops, and such Demands must necessarily tend to the putting down many of the present Plantations, and prevent the Establishment of others, which would be a great Detriment to the Public; and that there is not, to the Petitioners Knowledge, any other kind of Produce of Land for which a Composition higher than from Two Shillings and Six Pence to Six Shillings an Acre has been paid, and Six Shillings an Acre is considered as a high Composition even for Wheat, the most beneficial of all Grain: That in the Instances of Hemp, Flax, and Madder, the Legislature thought it just and reasonable -to encourage the Cultivation in England, by passing Acts for a Composition in lieu of the Tythes, which, in each Species, was restricted to Five Shillings an Acre, land the Act for regulating the Composition for the Tythe of Hemp and Flax was long since made perpetual, and it is presumed that the Reason, why the Act respecting the Tythe of Madder (which was temporary) has not been revived or renewed, has been

s that

227

that no greater Composition than Five Shillings an Acre has been demanded in lieu of the Tythe; and that the Petitioners conceive it to be both reasonable in itself, and conducive to the Interest of the Planters of Hops and the Persons entitled to the Tythes of them, and to the Benefit of the Public, that Tythes of Hops should not be demandable in Kind, and that the Payment in lieu of Tythes should be ascertained and limited: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that such Bill may be prepared and passed, as, in the Judgment of the House, may best tend to the Relief of the Petitioners, and all other the Hop Planters within the said Parish of ham, and to the Encouragement of the Growth of Hops, with Benefit to the Planters and the Public, and without Injury to the Clergy and other Persons entitled to the Tythes of Hops.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of Alexander Raby, Esquire, one of the Pennygored Proprietors of certain Tin Works, in the County of Tin Work* Pembroke, called The Pennygored Works, on Behalf of Petlllon-himself, and the other Proprietors of the said Works, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth.

That the Proprietors of the said Works are obliged to consume great Quantities of Coals in carrying on their Works, and from the Scarcity of Coal within the said County, they are obliged to import the same from other Counties at a yery great Expence, exclusive of the Duty payable upon such Coals, and The Pennygored Works are the only Tin Works in this Kingdom where the Coals made use of for carrying on the Works are charged with any Duty whatsoever; and that The Pen-nygoi'ed Wotics have, from Time to Time, been improved by different Proprietors at a very great Expence, but, owing to the high Price of Coals, and other Causes, the said Works have frequently been discontinued, to the great Distress of the Poor Persons who were employed in those Works, hut, notwithstanding the Disadvantages which ,the Proprietors of the said Works labour under, in carrying on their Wrorks, they now find Employment for a great Number of Poor Persons, who must otherwise be iu Want of the Means of supporting themselves and their Families, and might therefore become chargeable to their respective Parishes, and that a much greater Number would be employed, if the Duty on Coals was drawn back for the said Manufactory; and that the Petitioners are informed, that, in order to encourage the Working the Copper and Lead Mines in the Island oiAnglesey, an Actwas passed in the Twenty-sixth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for allowing a Drawback of the Duties upon all Coals used in -working those Mines, and, if the like Indulgence was al- . lowed to the Proprietors of the Pennygored Tin Works, for all the Coals used by them in carrying on their Works, it would enable theip to improve and extend their present Works so as to employ a much greater Number of Poor Persons than they will otherwise be enabled to do, if they continue to pay the Duty on the Coals they consume in carrying on the said Works:

And therefore praying the House to take their Case into Consideration, and to give them such Relief in the Premises as the House shall think reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the

Mr. Jervoise reported from the Committee, to

whom the Petition of his Grace the Duke of Marlborough, and the humble Petition of divers Gentlemen, Land Owners, Tradesmen, Manufacturers, and others, residing in the Counties of Oxford, Buckingham, and Middlesex, and in the adjoining Counties, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Navigation Bills, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as foU loweth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Samuel Weston, an Engineer, being examined, said. That, by a Survey he has lately taken, it is practicable to make a Navigable Canal from, and out of, the Oxford Canal Navigation, within the Parish of Shipton, in the County of Oxford, through the interior Parts of the Counties of Oxford, Buckingham, and Middlesex, to join and communicate with the River Thames, at, or near, Isleworth, which will be the Means of ppening a direct Passage, and a safe and expeditious Method of carrying Goods and Merchandize, from the said Oxford Canal to the City of London', and that such Canal, by its respective Communications with the Oxford Canal, and the Thames and Severn Canal, will open a beneficial Intercourse, by Inland Navigation, between the City of London, and the great Commercial and Manufacturing Towns and Places in the Counties of Warwick, Stafford, Lancaster, Chester, Salop, Worcester, Hereford, and Gloucester, the City of Bristol, the Principality of Wales, and other Places in the Northern and Western Parts of this Island; and will also, by going through the said Counties of Oxford, Buckingham, and Middlesex, and to, or near, divers Towns situated therein, increase the Value of Landed Property, facilitate the Conveyance of Goods and Merchandize, furnish Employment for the Poor, and, in many other Respects, will be of great Public U tility.

Mr. Hugh Henshall and Mr. Samuel Simcock, being examined, confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Weston.

Ordered, That Leave be given to , bring in a Bill for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from, and out of, the Oxford Canal Navigation, within the Parish of Shipton, in the County of Oxford, to join and communicate with the River Thames, at, or near, Isleworth, in the County of Middlesex: And that Mr. Jerooise and Mr. Lygon do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of the several Gentlemen, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being of the Committee, for, and on Behalf, of themselves and the rest of the Petitioners for The London and Western Oanal, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That it appears by the Votes, that Two several Applications are now depending in the house, the One for a BUI for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from the Oxford, Canal Navigation at Braunston, in the County of Northampton, to join the River Thames at New Brentford, in the County of Middlesex, intended to be called The Grand Junction Canal, and for making

and maintaining cartain Collateral Cuts from the said intended Canal, and the other of the said Applications for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from the said Oxford Canal at Shipton, in the County of Oxford, to the River Thames, at Isleworth, in the said County of Middlesex, intended to be called The London and Western Canal, and tfre said proposed Canals are intended to commence nt Places very distant from each other, and to open different Communications, and severally appear to have in view Objects of great Public Utility; and that the said Canals, in their Progress through the County of Bucks, approach within the Distance of Six Miles of each other at Mersworth, and, as they advance nearer to the Thames, come at some Places within the Distance of One hundred Yards, and in other Places nearer, and proceed in nearly a parallel Direction to their respective Points of Termination; and the Petitioners conceive it would effectually answer all the good Purposes of the Public, as well as of those interested in the said Two several Schemes of Navigation, and would also be a Matter of great Accommodation to many of the Land Owners, through whose Property the said Canals are intended to pass, if the said Canals were to be united, and tQ form One Canal only, from or near Mersworth aforesaid, and such Junction would

also be a Saving of a very considerable Expence tq the Undertakers of the different Lines of Canal, and in many other Respects tend greatly to their mutual Advantage: And therefore praying. That, in the Bill now before the House for effecting the said intended Canal from Braunston to the said River Thantes, Provision may be made for uniting the Two several Canals, on such Terms and Conditions as shall be deemed reasonable, at or near Mersworth aforesaid, or at such other Place, on the Line of one or other of the said proposed Canals, as may appear best calculated for promoting the Trade and internal Communication from the various Parts of the Kingdom tq the Metropolis, or, that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from the Oxford Canal Navigation at Braunston, in the County of Northampton, to join the River Thames at New Bren ford, in the County of Middlesex, and also for making and maintaining certain Collateral Cuts from the said intended Canal, is committed.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, that they have Power to make Provision in the said Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition.

ble from the 31st Day of December 1774, and the said Company were also thereby empowered to chuse Nine Persons from among themselves, and also Six Persons, Inhabitants of the said Town, not being Members of the said Company, or of either of the said Corporations, which Fifteen Persons, with the Mayor of the said Town for the Time being, and Two of the Aldermen, to be appointed by the Mayor and Aldermen, the acting Warden, one Elder Brother, and one Assistant, of the said Guild or Brotherhood, were, by the said Act, appointed Commissioners for the Purposes therein mentioned, and were authorized and required to make Contracts for the execution of the s.aid Works, to appoint Officers, and make Bye Laws and Orders,

subject to the Contfoul of the said Company, who are; thereby authorized to alter or annul the same, and the said Commissioners were authorized to purchase Lands and Tenements for making Roads, or for making or textending any of the Works, or for laying Soil, Rubbish, Utensils, and Materials, upon, and for other Purposes of the said Act, but for no dther Use, Intent, or Purpose, whatsoever; and if, after the Works, for which such Purchases were made, should he finished, there should remain any Land that should not be used, or should not thereafter be wanted, for the Purposes of the said Act, the same was vested in the said Commissioners, and they were empowered to sell and convey the same for the best Price that could be got, and apply the Money to the Use of the said Company; and that the said Dock Company have made a Bason or Dock for the Reception and Harbouring of Ships and Vessels extending from the River Hull, near to Beverley Gales, as directed by the said Act, and also a Quay or Wharf ranging on the Side thereof, next the Town, which, in the Year 1779, when the same was completed, was thought sufficient for the Reception of the Ships then belonging to the said Port, but which is at present much too small, the Ships resorting to the Port being now more than double the Number they were at that Time; and that, by the said Act all Ships that come to the Port of Kingston upon Hull are liable to pay the Dock Dues, which are much higher than at any other Port, and, the Petitioners conceive, are therefore entitled to receive all the Benefit intended by the said Act, for the Convenience and Accommodation of Trade and Shipping, by being provided with safe and convenient Stations in the Bason or Dock, the very contrary of which is the Case, the Dock Duties having been frequently paid of late Years by many Vessels which could not be admitted into the Dock for Want of Room; and that the Trade of the said Port is of late Years so much increased, and still appears to be in a progressive §tate, and the Ships and Vessels which frequent the same are become so numerous, and of such large Dimensions, that those Advantages, for which more than an adequate Consideration is paid by each Ship, cannot be obtained in the present Dock, which is not capable of properly accommodating Two-thirds of the Ships belonging to, and frequenting, the Port, and those which do obtain Admission into the Dock are in so crowded a State, that the cleansing of the Dock is thereby rendered impracticable, and several Vessels are prevented from going into the same to unlade their Cargoes, and others are detained within it, and retarded from prosecuting their Voyages, to the

Seat Detriment of the Petitioners, of His Majesty's evenue, and of the General Trade and Commerce of the said Port, and, in case of Fire, the total Destruction of the Shipping, and Town of Hull, is almost inevitable; and that, in case the said Bason or Dock should be enlarged and extended, such Losses, Damages, and Inconveniencies, might be prevented, and a safe and commodious Station be provided for the harbouring, lading, and unlading, of the Ships and Vessels resorting to the said Port, which the Petitioners Vol. 48.

submit the said Dock Company are bound to do, for which Purposes their Revenues are amply sufficient, for although, from foe erroneous Estimates and Calculations which were formed before the obtaining foe said Act, the said Company were thereby enabled, in Addition' to the Royal Grant of the said Military Works, and the said Sum of £. 15,000, to raise no less than £. 100,000 for carrying on and completing the said Works, yet the Petitioners are well informed, that the whole Expence attending the whole Undertaking, inclusive of the said ,£.15,000, did not exceed the Sum of £. 50 per Cent, on the Money subscribed, and that, although the said Company have not advanced more than £. 250 upon each Share, from the Profits arising from the Sale of Lands purchased for the Purposes of the Act (such were not then wanted) and the Rates and Duties, from the great Increase of Shipping, they have already divided, several Times, the whole Amount of their Advance, with Interest thereupon; and the Petitioners conceive, that the said Grants of the Military Works, and of the said Sum of £.15,000, were made to the said Company, in Consideration that the Estimates then produced, should be complied with (which the Petitioners are prepared to shew were grossly erroneous) and that the Public have a Right to demand, that they shall, from the Produce of the very great Increase of the Dues, by the Advancement of the remaining Fifty per Cent, on the Shares, extend the present Dock; and that the said Company, on being applied to for the Purposes above-mentioned, have admitted that there is not sufficient Room in the present Dock for the increased Number of Ships, but refuse to provide any additional Dock, or to extend the one already made, unless the said Corporations of the Mayor and Burgesses, and Guild or Brotherhood, and the rest of the Petitioners, can obtain from His Majesty a Grant of Thirty Acres of Land, Part of the Military Works of the Garrison on the East Side of the Harbour, and unless they will comply with other Conditions, which, as the same relates to His Majesty's Revenue, they deem extremely unreasonable, and the more so, as the said Company have already a much larger Portion of the said Military Works granted by His Majesty remaining than they have employed, which adjoins foe said Dock or Bason, and extends from thence towards the River Humber, and is on that Account, and in every Respect, the best situated for the Accommodation and Convenience of the Town, and of the Trade and Commerce of the Port; and that the Profits to which each Subscriber is entitled (being granted without any Limitation) has annually increased, and in the present Year produced £.82. 5 for every Share, which the Petitioners conceive ought to be limited, so as not to exceed a certain Yearly Sum per Cent, the Provision already made for the Purpose of reducing the said Rates being entirely nugatory, as, by the said Act, the Power of doing so is left wholly in the Diseretion of the Parties interested, which Pow'er the Petitioners conceive ought to be vested in some indifferent Person, and that some Limitation should be prescribed to the Extent of the said Rates and Duties, and this the Petitioners think the more reasonable, as, on a careful Examination of foe different Acts of Parliament, enacted for the Purposes of establishing and regulating the Docks and Havens in other Parts of the Kingdom, the Rates and Duties thereby granted to the Persons undertaking the same are invariably limited by some of the following Means, namely, the Rates are eifoer granted for a limited Term of Years only, or, if perpetual, they 4M"e limited not to exceed a certain Sum per Cent. Profit on the Sums advanced, and the Surplus directed to be vested in indifferent Persons, and applied to Public Purposes, which, by a Reference to the Statute Book, will fully appear; and that the said Rates and Duties,

3 Q and

and the Money arising from a Sale of the several Parcels of Ground belonging to the said Company, and of such Parts of the said Military Works as may not be necessary for the Extension contended for by the Petitioners, will form an adequate Fund, not only to produce a just and reasonable Profit to the said Subscribers, but also to defray the Expence of providing sufficient Accommodation for the increased Number of Vessels frequenting the said Port, without which the present flourishing State of the Trade and Commerce of the said Town, and of His Majesty's Revenue, must soon be diverted into some other Channel: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for redressing the said Grievances, and for effecting the several Purposes aforesaid, in such Manner, and subject to such Rules, Oiders, and Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet, or that the Petitioners may receive such other Relief in the Premises as the Nature of their Case may require, and the House shall judge proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Samuel Thornton, Mr. Lygon, See.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Mr. Mudge's Petition.

A Petition of Thomas Madge, Watehmaker, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty's Command, acquainted the House, that His Majesty, haying been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioner hath devoted much of his Attention to the Improvement of Time Keepers, for ascertaining the Longitude at Sea, and having, in the Year 1774, completed One such Time Keeper, it was submitted to a Trial by the Board of Longitude, and the Commissioners, after a competent Trial, requested the Petitioner to prosecute his Invention, that, by having Two Time Keepers of the same Construction, he might become properly a Candidate for the Rewards offered for Inventions of this Kind by Act of Parliament, and granted him 500l. to assist him therein; and that the Time Keeper made by the Petitioner as aforesaid was, in the Years 1784 and 1785, and after the same had been tried by the Board of Longitude, carried Two Voyages to Newfoundland by the late Vice Admiral Campbell, who had then the Command of His Majesty's Ships upon that Station, and Admiral Campbell afterwards declared it had answered every Purpose that could be desired from such an Invention, and that he was convinced the Introduction of such Time Keepers into the Navy would be of great Service to the Public; and that the Principles upon which the Petitioner's said Time Keeper is constructed are so permanent, that it has now gone for more than Eighteen Years, with unequalled Excellence, in the Hands of many different Persons, all of them Men of great Astronomical Knowledge; and that the Petitioner, having, in the Month of June 1789, completed Tjvo more Time Keepers on the same Construction, he placed them in the Hands of the Astronomer Royal, where they remained for upwards Of Twelve Months, to be tried, pursuant to the Act of Parliament passed in the Fourteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, and that, although the Commissioners of Longitude, upon the Report afterwards made by the Astronomer Royal, declared them-

selves of Opinion that the Petitioner's Time Keepers had not gone within the Limits prescribed by the said Act, yet it appears from the Register kept by the Astronomer Royal, and delivered by him to the Petitioner, that, if such Methods of Calculation bad been adopted for ascertaining the going of the Time Keepere as have been approved of by Men of acknowledged Nautical Skill and Abilities, it would have been found that they had gone within them; and that the Petitioner is ready to acknowledge there have been Time Keepers in* vented by other Persons which are possessed of great Merit, but the best of them require an extraordinary Degree of Care to preserve them from Accident, and none of them have ever been brought into general Use, but the Petitioner's Time Keepers, besides their measuring Time with very great Exactness, require no particular Attention to keep them from Injury, have not been found to be affected by the Motion of a Ship at Sea, and are so permanent in their Principles, that they may be relied upon for going with Accuracy for y very considerable Length of Time: And therefore praying the House, upon his making a Discovery of the Principles of his Time Keepers to such Persons as may be appointed for receiving it, to grant him such a Reward for the Invention of them, and for the laborious Employment of great Part of his Life for the Benefit of the Public, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition dp lie upon the Table,

A Motion was made, and the Question being put, Motion for That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, Address to to assure His Majesty, that His faithful Commons, restore animated by a sincere and dutiful Attachment to Hk Peace' Person and Family, and to the excellent Constitution of this Kingdom, a9 well as by an ardent Zeal for the Interest and Honour of the Nation, will at all Times be ready to support His Majesty in any Measures which a due Observance of the Faith of Treaties, the Dignity of His Crown, pr the Security of His Dominions may compel him.to undertake:

That, feeling the most earnest Solicitude to avert from our Country the Calamities of War, by every Means consistent with Honour and with Safety, we expressed to His Majesty, at the Opening of the present Session, "our Sense of the Temper and Prudence " which had induced His Majesty to observe a strict " Neutrality, with respect to the War on the Continent, and uniformly to abstain from any Interference in the Internal Affairs of France," and our Hope, that the Steps His Majesty had taken would have the happy Tendency " to render a firm and ternperate Conduct effectual for preserving the Blessings " of Peace: *

That, with the deepest Concern, we now find ourselves obliged to relinquish that Hope, without any Evidence having been produced to satisfy us, that His Majesty's Ministers have made s&ch Efforts a9 it was their Duty to make, and as, by His Majesty's most gracious Speech, we were taught to expect, for the Preservation of Peace. It is ne less the Resolution, than the Duty, of His Majesty's faithful Commons, to second His Efforts in the- War thus fatally com- ,

jnenced, so long as it shall continue; but we deem it a Duty, equally incumbent upon us, to solicit His Majesty's Attention to those Reasons or Pretexts, by which Hk Servants have laboured to justify a Conduct on their Part, which we cannot but consider as having contributed, in a great Measure, to produce the present Rupture:

Various Grounds of Hostility against France have been stated, but none that appeared to us to have constituted such an urgent and imperious Case of Necessity, as left no Room for Accommodation, and made War unavoidable. The Government of has

We must further remark, that the Point in Dispute seemed to us to have been relieved frotn a material Part of its Difficulty, by the Declaration of the Minister of Foreign Affairs in France, that the French Nation gave up all Pretensions to determine the Question of the future Navigation of the Scheldt: Whether the Terms of this Declaration were perfectly satisfactory or not, they at least left the Question open to pacific Nego-ciation, in which the intrinsic Value of the Object, tp any of the Parties concerned in it, might have been coolly and impartially weighed against the Consequences to which all of them might be exposed by attempting to maintain it by Force of Arms:

We have been called upon to resist Views of Conquest and Aggrandizement entertained by the Government of Franpe, '* at all Times dangerous to the general " Interests of Europe," but asserted to be " peculiarly " so when connected with the Propagation of Principles u which lead to the violation of the most sacred Duties,

" and are utterly subversive of the Peace and Order of " all Civil Society We admit that it is the Interest and Duty of every Member of the Common-Wealth of Europe to support the established System, and Distribution of Power among the Independent Sovereignties, which actually sobrist, and to prevent the ‘Aggrandizement of any State, especially the most powerful, at the Expence of any other; and, for the Honour of His Majesty's Councils, we do most earnestly wish that His Ministers had manifested a just Sense of the Importance of the Principle to which they now appeal in the Course of late Events, which seemed to us to threaten its entire Destruction:

When Poland was beginning to recover from the long Calamities of Anarchy combined with Oppression; after she had established an hereditary and limited Monarchy like our own, and was peaceably employed in settling her internal Government, His Majesty's Ministers, with apparent Indifference and Unconcern, have sfeen her become the Victim of the- moat cm pro -

seriously felt, and might have expressed with greater Justice of the previous Successes of her powerful Adversaries;

vqked and unprincipled Invasion; her Territory overrun; her free Constitution subverted; her National Independence annihilated-; and the general Principles of the Security of Nations wounded through her Side:

With aH these Evils was France soon after threatened, rad with the same Appearance either of supine Indif-streace, or of secret Approbation, His Majesty's Minis- ment of France, appeared' to us neither justified by ters beheld the Armies of other Powers (in evident the Reason of the Thing itself, nor by the Usage of Concert with the Oppressor of Poland) advancing to Nations, nor by any Expediency, arising from the the Invasion and Subjugation of France, and' the March present State of Circumstances. We will not dissemble our Opinion, that the Decree of the National Convention of France, of the 19th of November 1792, was, in a great Measure, liable to the Objections urged against it; but we cannot admit that a War upon the single Ground of such a Decree, unaccompanied by any overt Acts, by which we pr our Allies might be directly attacked, would be justified as necessary and unavoidable, — certainly not, — urdesf upon a regular Demand made try His Majesty's Ministers of Explanation and Security in Behalf of us and oar Allies, the French had refused to give His Majesty such Explanation and Security: No such Demand was made! — Explanations, it is true, have been, received ancj rejected: But it well deserves to be remarked and remembered, that these Explanations were voluntarily offered on the Part of France, not previously demanded on ours, as undoubtedly they would have been, if it had suited the Views of His Majesty's Ministers. tQ have acted frankly and honourably towards „ and

not to have reserved their Complaints for a future Period, when Explanations, however reasonable, might come too )ate, and Hostilities might be unavoidable:

After a Review of all these Considerations, we think it necessary to represent to His Majesty, that none of the Points, which were in Dispute between His Ministers and the Government of France, appear to us to have been incapable of being adjusted by Nepotiar tion, except that Aggravation of French Ambition, which has been stated to arise from the Political Opinions of the French Nation. These, indeed, wo Conceive formed neither any definable Object of Nego-ciation, nor any intelligible Reason for Hostility. — They w ere equally incapable of being adjusted by Treaty, or of being either refuted or confirmed by the Events of War:

We need not state to His Majesty's Wisdom that Force can never cure Delusion; and1 we know His Majesty's Goodness too well to- suppose that Pfe could ever entertain the Idea of employing Force to destroy Opinions by the Extirpation of those who hold them:

And the Counsel for die Bill was also heard.

And then the Counsel on both Sides were directed to withdraw.

And the Amendments made by the Committee to the said Bill, being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrossed.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

and Representing to the House, that, after diligent Enquiry, they are not able to discover that any previous Public Notice has been given of the Application made to the House, for Leave to bring in the said Bill, so far as the same concerns pr relates to the making or improving the Navigation of the River Nen, otherwise called The Northern River, as required by the Standing Orders of the House, made on the 7th Day of June last, or, that this House has given any Leave to bring in the said Bill, so far as the same concerns or relates to the making or improving the Navigation of the said River; and that the Petitioners also observe, that Powers are contained in the said Bill for making certain Navigable Cuts or Canals therein described, materially differing and deviating from the Course or Direction of the Navigable Cuts or Canals described in the Public Notices, which were given in the Month of September last, of the Application then intended to be made in this present Session of Parliament, for Leave to bring in the said Bill, and also materially differing and deviating from the Course or Direction of the Navigations, Cuts or Canals, described in the Petition presented to the House on the 28th Day of January last, for Leave to bring in the said Bill, and in the Map or Plan thereunto annexed, and, that such Maip or Plan also materially differs and deviates from the Course or Direction of the Navigations, Cuts, or Canals, described in such last mentioned Public Notices; and that the Petitioners submit to the House, that, in the several Instances and Particulars above-mentioned, or some of them, the Standing Orders of the House, made on the 7th Day of June last, relative to Navigation Bills, have not been complied with; and that the Petitioners, or some of them, will be materially affected and injured, if the Navigation of the said River, and the said proposed Alterations and Deviations, in the Course or Direction of the said Cuts or Canals, should take Place, inasmuch as One of the Petitioners. is Lord of the Manor, and Owner of the Soil, through which the Navigation of the said River is proposed to be made, and others of them are Proprietors of Estates through which the Line of the said Navigation will be carried, by Means of such Alterations and Deviations as aforesaid, to the great Prejudice of their said Estates: And therefore praying. That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, and that they may be heard, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, against the said Bill, or such Part or Parts thereof as are above-mentioned or referred to, and may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Sir George Cornexvall reported from the Committee,

That they had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be now received.

Sir George Cornewall accordingly reported from the rePorted* said Committee, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That it is highly advisable that the House should take such Steps as may conduce to the most speedy Trial of the several Petitions complaining of undue Elections, or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament, in order that, as far as may be, they should be tried and determined in the present Session of Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That this House should be called over on Wednesday the 6th Day of March next.

Resolved,' That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That such Members as shall not then attend, be sent for in Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the several Petitions complaining of an undue

Election and Return for the Borough of Shaftesbury,

now ordered to be taken into Consideration on Tuesday

next, the 26th Instant, and also, the several Petitions,

complaining of an undue Election and Return for the

Borough or Great Grimsby, now ordered to be taken

into Consideration on Thursday, the 28th Day of this

Instant
