" with a Canal now making between the Rivers Trent " and Mersey," and, so long ago as the Year 1772, the whole of the Money subscribed for making the said Canal, being 50,0001, was expended, and the Petitioners have since that Time, in pursuance of the Powers vested in them by a subsequent Act of Parliament, passed in the Twenty-sixth Year of the Reign of His said present Majesty, intituled, "An Act to enable the " Company of Proprietors of the Coventry Canal Navigation to complete the said Canal to Fradley Heath, " in the County of Stafford, and for other Purposes " therein mentioned," borrowed the further Sum of 40,000/, to enable them to complete the said Undertaking, which last mentioned Sum of Money has been actually expended thereon, and the said Canal was completed in July 1790; and that the Public have long been, and now are, in Possession of very great Advantages by Means of the said Canal, though the Proprietors haye not, since the said 50,000l. hath been

expended (being upwards of TvVerity Years) received more than 3/. per Centum per Annum upon the Average thereon; and that the Petitioners observe, by the Votes of the House, that Leave is given to bring in a Bill for making a Canal from Ashby de la Zouch, in the County of Leicester, to communicate with the said Coventry Canal at Griff, in the Parish of Chilvers Coton, in the County of Warwick, and also to make certain Cuts or Branches from the said Canal, at or near Ashby de la Zouch aforesaid, to communicate with various Lime Works, Lead Mines, and Coal Mines, in different Paris of the Counties of Leicester and Derby, and Repre- -senting to the House, that the making the said intended Canal would be of very great Injury to the Petitioners, but they conceive that, if the same was postponed for the present Session, a Plan might be pointed out by which a Navigable Communication between Ashby de la Zouch and the Coventry and Oxford Canals might be made, which would be equally beneficial and convenient to the Public, and of no material Injury to the Petitioners: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by their Counsel, at the Bar of the House, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law.

Cuts or Branches from the said intended Canal, be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their j Petition, if they think fit.

A Petition of the Persons thereunto subscribing, Burgesses, Heritors, Traders, Manufacturers, and Inhabitants, of the Royal Burgh of Kirkcaldy, in behalf of themselves and others, Burgesses and Inhabitants of the Royal Burghs in Scotland, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by the ancient Constitution of the Royal Burghs, and by the express Words of their Charters, the Magistrates and Common Councils were elected Annually by the free Suffrage of the Burgesses, but, by Acts of the Scottish Parliament, passed in the Years 1469 and 1474, it was ordained, that the old Council should choose the new, that the new and old Council should choose the Officers, and that four Persons out of the old should be chosen Yearly into the new Council, and the local Usages founded upon the Principle of Self-election, introduced by those Statutes, have established Systems of Government in the Royal Burghs by which Men, once in Possession of Power, are enabled to retain it for ever by successive Re-elections of themselves, or their Friends and Dependents, and Persons without Residence, without Property, without Trade, without Interest of any Kind in the Burghs, may, for any Length of Time, enjoy the important Offices of Magistrates and Councillors, and to those Institutions, m direct Opposition to the original Rights of the Burgesses, the Courts of Justice, even in the last Resort, have given the Force and Authority of Laws: Under the Name of Setts, dr Constitutions, these unjust and arbitrary Systems have fundamentally overturned the ancient Government of the Burghs, and invaded the Rights and Privileges of the Burgesses; fluctuating, and uncertain in every Thing, except the Principle of Self-election, some of these Setts have been created, others have been repeatedly altered within the last Hundred Years: The Statutes prescribe one general uniform Constitution, or System of Self-election, for all the Royal Burghs, but from that Constitution the Setts have deviated in numberless Instances, and they are maintained in direct Violation of Charters granted so recently as in the Course of the last, and at the Beginning of the present Century, which give in general the Right of Election to the Burgesses: The pernicious Consequences of these Establishments have not only affected the Liberties and Political Government of the Burghs, they have contributed to prevent, or render fruitless, the Execution of Statutes, made for the Protection of the Revenues, and have extended their baneful Influence to every Branch of the Administration: By gross Misapplications and Dilapidations of the Common Property, and by enormous Contractions of Debt, the Burghs are reduced to Poverty and Distress; Police, and the necessary Accommodations of the Inhabitants, are neglected; Taxes are imposed and levied without the Authority of Parliament; and, for these, and many other enormous Grievances, there is no Judicature, from which it is practicable to obtain any effectual Relief. In the Year 1784, the Burgesses were impelled, by the common Feeling of the Evils which they so universally endured, to appoint Delegates to meet in Convention at Edinburgh, and to prepare an Application to the Constitutional Authority of the Legislature few: Redress: After the most serious and mature Deliberation in successive Conventions, after repeated Communications with the Burgesses of the individual Burghs, Petitions were presented to this House, in the Year 1788, from a very great. Majority of Bur-Vol, 48.

gesses, Heritors, Traders, or Manufacturers, Inhabitants of the Royal Burghs, praying, that their present , Systems of Government should be altered,' corrected, or amended, as to the House should appear proper, for removing the Evils complained of Actuated by no light and trivial Considerations, the Burgesses have continued to assemble Annually, by their Delegates in Convention, at Edinburgh, and to pursue the moderate and Constitutional Measures which they originally adopted for obtaining the important Object of their Associations: Complaining of no imaginary Grievances, they deemed it. incumbent upon them to establish the actual Existence of the Abuses in the internal Government of the Royal Burghs, by the clearest Evidence; by the indisputable Authority of Statutes, and of Public Records; by the Admissions of the Magistrates in the Returns on the Table of this House, and by the Oral Testimony of Witnesses to Facts daily passing before their Eyes: From such Authorities the Petitioners think themselves entitled to affirm, and to represent to this House, that they labour under very great and intolerable Grievances, not only in relation to the Election of the Magistates and Common Council of the Royal Burgh of Kirkcaldy, to the Management of the common Property and Revenues, and to the whole Administration of that Burgh, but likewise as being materially interested in the Prosperity of all the other Royal Burghs in Scotland. Impressed with the warmest Attachment to the Person and Family of their Sovereign, and to the Constitution of their common Country, the Petitioners are seduced by no speculative Opinions, they seek the Establishment of no new or untried System, they have recently seen their ancient Constitution restored, in a great Measure, to the Burgesses of the Burgh of Stirling: Limiting their Request to a similar Restoration of their ancient Rights, ascertained by their most ancient Laws, and defined by their Charters, the Petitioners trust that they shall receive, from the Wisdom and Justice of the Legislature, that Relief which the Nature of their Case so loudly demands, and which, by an accidental Concurrence of Circumstances, the Burgesses of Stirling have been enabled already to obtain from the Beneficence of their Sovereign; and, in order to shew that this Demand is understood to be consistent with the Public Utility, the Petitioners observe, that, in every new Election of Burghs of Barony, the Election of the Magistrates is granted to the Burgesses, agreeably to the Principle of their present Application: And therefore praying, That the Abuses complained of in the internal Government of the Royal Burghs in Scotland may be enquired into, and, being

enquired into and proved, that the present System of Government may be altered, corrected, or amended, not only in the said Royal Burgh of Kirkcaldy, but in all the other Royal Burghs in Scotland, and that such other Relief may be given in the Premises as to the Wisdom and Justice of the House shall appear proper for removing the Evils complained of; ana likewise praying, that Counsel may be allowed to be heard in Support of this Petition.

A Petition of the Persons thereunto subscribing, Burgesses, Heritors, Traders, Manufacturers, and Inhabitants of the Royal Burgh of in be-

half of themselves and other Burgesses and Inhabitants of the Royal Burghs in Scotland, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That by the ancient Constitution of the Royal Burghs of Scotland, the Magistrates and Common Council were elected by the free Suffrage of the Burgesses; and it appears, by the Scottish Acts of Parliament, of the 20th of November 1469, and the 20th of November 1475, that the old Council shall choose the new Councillors and Office Bearers, and that Four Persons out of the old should be chosen Yearly to the new Council, but, by Usage, those Laws have gone into Disuse, and Systems of Government established in every Royal Burgh by those in Power, which has now introduced the baneful Influence of Self-election, by which the Principles laid down by the Legislature, for the good Government of Burghs, are entirely departed from, and the Laws made by the Subjects, known by the Name of Setts, are introduced, by which the Power, Management, and Direction of the Burghs is thrown into the Hands of One or Two leading Men, and the Burgesses, Traders, and those that pay the Public Burthens, are deprived of the Choice of their Managers and Rulers, which, by the Laws and good Government of our Country, they are entitled to; and that the pernicious Consequences of those Innovations as now established, which have so affected the Liberties of the Subject, and Political Government of the Burghs, is no where so severely felt as in the Burgh of Inverkeithing, the Particulars of which the Petitioners beg Leave shortly to lay before the House: The Sett of the said Burgh is to consist of a Provost, Two Baillies, Dean of Guild, and Treasurer, and Fifteen or more Inhabitant Burgesses, as Councillors, who; when once elected, continue for Life; the Election of new Councillors is made by the old, and when so made, the Government and Prosperity of the Town and Common Good is not the Object, but entirely to strengthen the Political Party then in Power; therefore the Councillors, as elected by (and in Addition to) the old Council, are very seldom fit Objects for the Trust or Charge reposed in them; the principal Inhabitants, Merchants, and People of Trade, have not the smallest Voice or Vote in the Choice of their Rulers, far less in the Management of the Affairs of the Burgh, although they and their Properties are liable for every Transaction of the said Council and Rulers: It is true, the Five incorporated Trades have each One Vote in Council by their Deacon, chosen by them Annually for that Purpose, and for the Management of the Affairs of their respective Incorporations, but unfortunately these Five Deacons are Deacons and Councillors by Name, their Representation is nothing, especially when any Political Contest happens, and People of Ambition get the Power, the Good and Interest of the Burgh is not then their Object, except in Words upon their Canvas; their Principle is to give out, and attempt to make it be believed, that the Good of the Town is their solff Object, till they model themselves into what is called, in this baneful Sett, a Majority — when this is done, the Ball is at their Feet, and, for their Preservation, they Fee it, and their grand Stroke is a lasting Majority of Councillors (for Life) independent of the Trades, Deacons, ex officio — for that Purpose they fly to the extreme and unconstitutional Plan of making a great Number of Councillors, and, as they are for Life, the great Study is to have them obedient and ready at a Call to receive Directions — such Means being used, and Men introduced as Rulers, the Mercantile and Trading Part of the Community and principal Inhabitants feel the Effects of their horrid and unconstitutional Practices 2 introduced

Inverkeith

ing.

Dumbarton*

introduced by what is called a Sett, never made nor confirmed by the Legislature, but has crept into the Petitioners Police by Practice, introduced by Act of what is called the Convention; but it must be observed, that those at present in the Political Career do not stick at the general baneful Rule; they have of late fallen short to find Inhabitant Burgesses obe-. dient to their Call — a Point is therefore stretched — they have called Councillors from the Eastmost Corner of Fife and Town of Leith, neither of them having Property within the Burgh, carrying on no Trade, but elected entirely to attend when their Votes are wanted, and of Course to deprive those of having a Choice of their Rulers, who in all Justice ought to have it, the Inhabitants and Traders of the Place, whose Properties are amenable for the Conduct and Transactions of those their Rulers, by the Junto of Council in Power: The above State of Facts the Petitioners hope will be so far satisfactory, and shew to the House the Grossness and Illegality of the present Mode of Self-election, and Oppression the Petitioners labour under, they being entirely deprived of having any Choice in the Election of their Rulers; but that the Councillors being for Life, when once elected into that Office, continue there, and, however tyrannically or improperly they act, the Petitioners are deprived of the Power of making a new Choice; and the present Councillors and Rulers, by the Custom established, being sensible of their Durability, generally indict Hardships upon the Petitioners, which are intolerable to bear: This is the Fate of the Petitioners — at the same Time the Petitioners are actuated by no trivial or Political View; their entire Study and Wish is to have it in their Power to be of Use to the Good and Welfare of the Burgh, and to preserve their Liberty as free-born Britons: Their Royal Sovereign and

their happy Constitution they adore, and will support - — they do not ask nor look for any System speculative or untried; all they wish to have in their Power, and which they apprehend they are entitled to, is a free and fair Choice in their Representation, and particularly in their Council and Rulers: And therefore praying, That the Abuses and Grievances, complained of in the internal Government of their and all the other Burghs in Scotland, may be enquired into, and, being so found out and proved, that the present System of Government may be altered, and corrected, or amended, and that such other Relief in the Premises will be anted, as to the Wisdom and Judgment of the ouse shall appear proper for removing the Evils, complained of.

A Petition of the Persons thereunto subscribing, Burgesses, Heritors, and Traders, or Manufacturers, being Inhabitants of the Royal Borough of Dumbarton, in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the ancient Constitutions of the Royal Boroughs of Scotland possessed a very high Degree of Freedom, the whole Magistrates, such as the Mayors, otherwise called Provosts, and the Baillies, otherwise called Aldermen, and also the Town Councils, having been elected Annually by the free Suffrage of- the Burgesses, otherwise called the Honest Men of the Borough; but, by several Acts, passed in the Parliament of Scotland, in and posterior to the Year 1469, the ancient Constitution of the Royal Boroughs was fundamentally overturned, the Freedom of the Burgesses invaded, and Systems of Government established in the Boroughs of Scotland, which enabled Men, once in Possession of Power, to retain it for ever, by repeated Re-elections of themselves, or their Friends and Dependants: Local Usages, likewise altogether inconsistent with the Rights of the Burgesses, have established Institutions whereby not only Persons thus self-elected, but also Persons without Residence, without Property, without Trade, without Interest of any Voi. 48.

kind in Boroughs, may, for any Length of Time, enjoy the important Offices of Magistrates and Councillors, and to those local Institutions, created by Usage, in direct Opposition to the inherent Rights of me Burgesses, the Decisions of the Courts of Justice, even in the last Resort, have given the Force and Authority of Laws: Evident Violations therefore of the Liberties of the Burgesses created by Statutes and local Institutions, consisting in nothing but Abuses and Deviations from Law ana Right, pervade throughout the Governments of Boroughs. Those direct Infringements of Liberty, and these gradual Corruptions of Time and of Usage, now matured into Systems, compose those partial and absurd Establishments in Bo-, roughs, which have become not only the Subjects of the best-founded Complaints, but also the Objects of very general Reproach: They are only veiled and protected by a popular Name, for they are called the Constitutions of the Royal Boroughs of Scotland; of this' Corrupt Formation, particularly, is the Sett or Constitution of the said Borough of Dumbarton: The pernicious Consequences of these unjust and illiberal Systems have not only affected the Liberty and Political Government of Boroughs, their baneful Influence has also extended to every Branch of the Administration, and has contributed to prevent, or render fruitless, the Execution of Statutes made for the very Protection of the Revenues of Boroughs, reducing them to Poverty and Distress by gross Misapplications and Dilapidations of their Revenues and Property, and by enormous Contractions of Debt: Impressed as the Petitioners.. are with t>>e warmest Attachment to the Constitution of their common Country, and to the Person and Fami: - */ ‘heir Sovereign, it is with deep Regret, but \vi?h a 1'vely Hope of obtaining Redress of their Grievn. tha* they find themselves under the Necessity of app: t aching the House in the Language of Complaint: In conveying their Sentiments on Subjects so important, they have deemed it incumbent on them, and becoming the Dignity and Wisdom of the House, to support their Assertions by Authorities derived from the indisputable Evidence of Statutes, the Constitution of their Borough, or notorious Usage: From these Authorities the Petitioners conceive themselves entitled to affirm and to represent to this House, invested as it is with a Constitutional Power of affording Redress, that the Petitioners labour under very great and intolerable Grievances, not only in relation to Election of the Magistrates and Common Councils of the said Borough, and the Administration of the Property and Annual Revenues of the same, but as being materially interested in the Prosperity and Independence of all the other. Royal Boroughs of Scotland; and the Petitioners rely with the firmest Confidence on the Wisdom and Justice of the House, that for those very deep and intolerable Grievances they shall receive that Redress which their Nature and evil Tendency so loudly demand, and which it is natural for them to expect from the Spirit and and Liberality of Men whose Dignity and Power confessedly originate in the Consent and Authority of the People; and therefore the Petitioners having, by fatal Experience and daily Observation, been impressed with the deepest Sense of the pernicious Effects of the present Systems of Borough Government, in relation to the Liberty, Police, Revenue, Trade, and whole Administration of the Affairs of Boroughs, particularly of the said Borough of Dumbarton, are thereby impelled

to make the present Application to the House, in order to have those Systems altered, corrected, or amended, in all the Royal Boroughs of Scotland, in such Way and Manner as to the Justice and Wisdom of the House shall appear proper for removing the Evils complained of; and requesting that the House will allow Counsel to be heard in Support of the Subject Matter of this Petition.

James Edwards, John BakerJames Nash, William Knight, and Anthony Williams, Inhabitants of, and Hop Planters within, the Parish of in the County of Surrey, on behalf of themselves and the rest of the Hop Planters within the said Parish, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read^ and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, John Stevens, of Farnham, Esquire, being examined, said, That the Cultivation of Hops is a National Concern, and productive of a large Revenue to Government, being upon an Average upwards of £. 100,000 per Annum.

And he produced to your Committee an Account of the Total Net Produce, paid into the Exchequer, of the Duties of Excise in England, in the Four Quarters next preceding the *ioth of October 1792; from which it appeared, that the neat Duties on the Article of Hops, amounted to £. 82,776. — Then,

Henry Dyson, Esquire, of Sundridge, in the County of Kent, Being examined, said, That he is a Hop-Merchant and Planter, and has, for upwards of Thirty Years past, dealt largely as a Merchant, in buying and selling the same, and that, during that Period, he has imported as well as exported various Quantities, to answer the Demands of the Consumers of the Article.

And to prove that Hops were formerly imported, he produced to your Committee the following Statutes, viz. Second William and Mary, Chapter 4; Ninth Anne, Chapter 12; and First George the First, Chapter 12. — Then,

Mr. John Stevens being again examined, said. That he is resident within the Parish of Farnham, and has been an Inhabitant there for upwards of 68 Years, and that till within these last Six Years he has been largely concerned in the planting and Cultivation of Hops — that during the Season for the picking of Hops, exclusive of the Poor Inhabitants within the said Parish, who are very numerous, and in general all constantly employed in picking Hops, he computes the Number of Strangers, who attend to be employed during the Season of Hop gathering, amounts to upwards of 5,000.

Mr. Henry Dyson being further examined, said, That, from his own Observations at the Pickings, ne can corroborate the Evidence of Mr. Stevens as to this Subject — only, that he believes the Number of 5,000 is far short of the Number employed.

And the Witness further said, That the Cultivation of Hops greatly benefits the Poor, by finding Employment for Women and Children, in tying the Vines to the Poles, and in the Winter Time also in shaving the Poles — that it gives Employment to the Poor People for Eight Months at the least out of the Twelve: And, that in Kent, the Poor Rates have been reduced very considerably, in consequence of the Hop Plantations increasing.

And both the said Witnesses being further examined, said, That the Utility of Hops in the Brewery is very great, and cannot be dispensed with, as no other Bitter can be used in lieu of it.

And, in Confirmation of this Part of their Evidence, they produced to your Committee, an Act made in the Ninth Year of Queen Anne, intituled, "An Act " for laying a Duty upon Hops," wherein it is stated, That " it is found by Experience, that Hops used in the making of Malt-drinks are more wholesome " for those that drink or consume the same, and of " greater Advantage to the Drink itself, than any other bitter Ingredient that can be used instead thereof."

And the said Two Witnesses being further exa-Vol. 48.

mined, said, That the planting Ground with Hops, is, attended with very great Expence; and after the first planting, the keeping the Plantation in a proper State of Cultivation is also attended with a very great Annual Expence. — Then,

Mr. John Stevens informed your Committee, That Three Years are required to bring a Hop Plantation into a State of Maturity:

That the planting an Acre of Ground with Hops the first Year, will cost £. 29 6 —

For the Second Year 22 8 9

And for the Third - 64 8 —

And to keep the Plantation in a proper State of Cultivation and Management, including Poles, will Annually cost £. 30. — And,

Mr. Henry Dyson being again examined, said, The Expences of the Hop Planters in Kent are about'Two-thirds of those at Farnham, as near as can be, and that Difference arises from Rent and Manure chiefly.

And being further Examined, the said Two Witnesses informed your Committee, That the Comparative Expence of planting an Acre of Hops with that of planting any other, the most productive Article of Grain, exceeds more than Six or Seven to One. — Then,

Mr. Henry Dyson being again examined, said, That a Hop Plantation is subject to various Accidents, which frequently destroy the whole Crop; and he stated to your Committee the following Instances; — In

1778 the Amount of the Duty was £. 160,000, but in the Year 1782, it only amounted to £. 12,800, with an Addition even of £.15 per Cent, upon the latter, which was not upon the former: And that, on the 6th of September 1785, there happened a violent Wind, which destroyed, moderately speaking, not less than

15,000 Bags of Hops — many People, he said, estimated the Loss at 25,000, but he thought the former Quantity was certainly within the real Loss.

And being further examined, he said, That if the Soil is not well suited, the Plantation will not be long productive, but new Ground must be employed, and a new Plantation made: And he further said, That in Kent they generally change their Ground Once in Twelve or Fifteen Years, unless near, the large Towns, where they get great Plenty of Manure, and where the Ground, in consequence of that extraordinary Quantity of Manure, is more kindly. — Then,

Mr. John Steoens informed your Committee, That he has paid a Composition for the Tythe of Hops in Kind, growing within the Parish of Farnham, for upwards of 37 Years past, and that he has been informed by various old Persons, resident within the said Parish, and Hop Planters, That a Composition in lieu of the Tythes of Hops, has been paid for Time immemorial, and that the Tithe has never been paid in Kind.

The Witness further informed your Committee, That the Payment of Tythes in Kind of Hops, is incompatible with the Culture of them, by reason of the great Expence attending the Cultivation, by the Delay and Inconvenience occasioned by the Interfere ence of the Tythe Gatherer, in respect of the measuring and ascertaining his Right; because, if obliged to measure, it would be the Means of bruising and discolouring the Hops, and, by the Delay, subject the Produce to Rain and other Stofms, which, if wet before dried, will greatly lessen the Value of them, besides the great additional Expence of the Pickers being prevented going on with their Business, for which they will have an additional Allowance on Account of Loss of Time; otherwise the Planter will lose their Labour. — That in large Plantations the Pickers are divided into different Companies, at great Distances from each other, and if there are not as many Tythe Gatherers as Companies picking, great Inconvenience and Delay will arise.

Mr. Henry Dyson confirmed the foregoing Evi-5 E dence,

" Sir,

" In Answer to a Letter, dated Yesterday, and " signed by the Committee^ requesting me to state " to them- the Proposals I made to the Meeting of u the Owners and Renters of Hop Ground, on the " 24th Ultimo: My Proposals then were, and which " I now repeat, that for the Tythe of Hops by Composition, I require Sixty Shillings per Acre, and " the Planters subject themselves to all Tenants " Taxes; but in Case it should be preferred, on Account of the disproportionate Goodness of Hop " Grounds in the Parish of Farnham, as well as unfruitful Years, I am ready to accept my Proportion by the Excise Account, allowing the Planter " a fair Deduction for Drying, Bagging, Duty, and " any other reasonable Allowance that may be determined on between us for Trouble — With respect to " the Tythe of Arable and Grass Lands, if it is " agreeable to the Tenants, I am ready to compromise with them upon an equitable Medium on the " Calculation of Crops. When I stated the above on " the 24th Ult, I then declared, that upon a Committee being appointed to meet and settle, that in " case they could point out any other Mode of settling with me that might be more agreeable to themselves, reserving my Dues without Vexation to me,

" that I was not so determined on my Propositions,

" but to be open to Conviction and Reason.

was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for paving and repairing certain Streets, Lanes, and other Public Passages and Places, in the Parish of Saint Matthew, Bethnal Green, in the County of Middlesex, and for paving and regulating such Parts of Old Cock Lane and York Street as are in the Parish of Saint Leonard, Shoreditch, and for removing Obstructions and Annoyances therein; and Setting forth, That several of the Powers and Provisions contained in the said Bill will be very prejudicial and oppressive to the Petitioners and other Inhabitants of the said Parish, the greatest Part of whom are poor working People: And therefore praying,

Benwick, Chatteris, Whittlesea Saint Mary's, Whittlesea Saint Andrew, and Wisbeach, within the Isle of Ely, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative'to Navigation and Drainage Bills, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followed); viz.

A. 1793.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Robert Myfne being examined, said. That he is an Engineer: That the River Ouze, in the County of Norfolk, between Saint German's Bridge and King's Lynn, id the said County, which River is the great Outfall for the Waters from the Middle and South Level of the Fens, the Country of Marshland, and divers other Lands, which drain to Sea thereby, through the Harbour of King's Lynn, is in a State very insufficient for the Purposes of a complete Drainage and safe Navigation, Occasioned, principally, by the Channel or Bed of the said River being too wide, and bending very considerably between the said Place celled

Saint German's Bridge and King's Lynn aforesaid, by reason whereof the Drainage of Barge Tracts of Land lying in the above-mentioned Parishes is greatly impeded, and the Trade and Navigation to and from the Port of Kings Lynn are materially injured. And being asked to state some instances to prove that the Navigation is not safe, or the Drainage complete? he said, The First Cause is, the Passage Way of the Water from the Land to the Sea is blocked up entirely by Sand Banks and Shallows: And that again, is a Second Instance, or Cause, arising from the tod great Width of the Channel: A Third Instance, or Cause, is, that the Channel goes round abQut instead of going straight forward; all which is better to be understood from the Map which represents the exact Relation and Size of the Port. — Being asked to state the Instances of the Unsafeness of the Navigation? he said, There are Two Causes in which it is dangerous to Navigation; the One, in the' going down with Gangs of Boats, and the Difficulty of passing the Line of Navigation during Ebb Tide: The other Instance of Danger is, in going up the River, when there is any thing of a Fresh of Wind, the Channel being so very wide, a Surge or Swell of the Water is raised by that Means; and if the Boats are deep loaded they are apt to sink, by the Water getting over the Gunwale. — Being asked. Whether they employ Pilots between Lynn and German's Bridge? he said. The Instances of Danger and Difficulty which he has stated is the Cause that a certain ClasS of Men are employed for no other Purpose than as Pilots from Lynn to German's Bridge, and are not employed higher up or lower d,own. — Being asked, If Pilots will be required in the new Cut? he said, He should apprehend not at all, because it is to be made of a Breadth or Width proportionably with the River Ouze, immediately above it. — Being asked, Whether he knows any Instance by which he is led to think that the Navigation is unsafe ? he said, He cannot, from his own personal Knowledge, state any Instance, because he did not live there himself, and there are other Witnesses who may answer that Question; but viewing and examining the present State of the River at Low Water, and comparing that with other Rivers, he has no Doubt but that it must, in the Nature of Things, be highly productive of Danger and Difficulty to Navigation. — Being asked, Whether any other Part of the River between German's Bridge and Denver Sluice is in a bad State for the Purpose of Drainage or Navigation? he said, The Whole of it is in a very bad State, but that is caused by the Impediments the River Ouze meets with in the District below, from Eau Brink to take

away these Impediments, and there will be very little Trouble to cleanse out the Whole of that District; from Denver Sluice to Eau Brink: There are some other Difficulties of a small Nature at all the Bridges cross the Ouze, between Denver Sluice and Eau Brink: There are more or less Obstructions in the Water Way under the Bridges: There are some Points of; Land to be rounded off and there are some Shoals below those Points of Land which require to be removed, and which may be easily so done, when the Velocity of the Current is increased. —

Being

393

Being asked, Whether he has any Reason to think the Navigation is in a worse State now than it ever was before? he said, I think so, and it is the general Opinion of the Country. — Being asked, By what Means he collects that general Opinion ? he said, By the satpe Means which every Man takes to collect Facts, and state the Opinion of others; by Inspection of Maps, Drawings, Paintings, Soundings, and the voluminous Treatises which have been published on the Subject for 200 Years past — Being asked, Whether he believes the Navigation to be better or worse than it was between 20 and 30 Years ago? he said, I think it has been gradually growing worse for a long Succession of Time, and that Increase seems to have a Relation to the Increase of the Width between Eau Brink, and the Width of the River as far as The Crutch, below Lynn: I was at Lynn about 30 or 32 Years ago, and viewing the then State of the River, and of the Harbour, as a Matter of Curiosity in my Profession, and comparing, as far as J can recollect, the then State of the Navigation with that of my own View in 1791 or 1792,1 think I can safely say, from my own Knowledge, it has grown worse; and I think that I can rest my Opinion, truly, upon this Point, although what I have said upon the Subject may be called, by some Persons, ex parte Opinions. — Being asked, Whether he collected the Opinion of the Country relative to the State of the Navigation from Persons conversant in, and used to, navigating that River and Channel? he said, Some Part of it was collected from Persons who get their Bread, by navigating upon the Channel. — Being asked, Whether the Sill of Denver Sluice is not higher than the natural Bed of the River above and below the Sluice ? he said, The Sill of the Floodgates of Denver Sluice, opening downwards, is as low as the Bed of the River above it, and much lower than the Bed of the River Three, Four, or Five Miles above it. — Being asked. If he means the original Bed, or the Bed as it is now silted up ? he said, lie does not admit the Fact that it is silted up; the most egregious Falsehoods have been published on that Head, arising from the Parties who published them not ascertaining Low Water Mark at the Sea by some fixed Object that was not to be altered; One Instance of which is, that the Denver Sluice of the present Day is not the Denver Sluice that is represented in s Representation.

— Being asked, What was that represented in s

Representation, and when? he said, By the Inspection of Badslade's Book it will appear. — Being asked,

Whether he means that the present Denver Sluice is not in the same Situation as that represented by Badslade? he said, It is in the same Situation. — Being asked, Whether it is not the same as the old Sluice was? he said, No; it is almost the same in point of Figure, but it is not so in point of Level, compared with the Sides and Lands: More than that, it is a Representation of a Sluice and Bridge, which could not have been passable if it had been made so. — Being asked, If the Sill of this Sluice is higher or lower than the old one? he said, as he has said, That his Representation is false, he thinks the Level of the present Sill has always been the same compared with the Lands adjoining, but not compared with the Tide, for Low Water is considerably higher now than it was formerly, and that for the Reasons he had already given. — The Question being repeated to the Witness, he said, He means to say directly, that it is neither higher or lower. — Being asked, What is the Width jof the Water Way at Denver Sluice? he produced to your Committee a Plan and Section, whereby it appeared, that the Three Arches of Denver Sluice appropriated for draining, amounts to 1,005 Feet and 9 Inches superficial for the Section of the Water Way.

Mr. Henry Haines being then examined, said, That he knows the Channel from Lynn to Saint German's Bridge, having navigated it several Times, and lie Von. 48.

believes it is a very dangerous Navigation. — Being Eau Brink asked. Whether he has known of any Boats being lost and King'* by the Badness of the Navigation ? he said, Yes, both ^"pJtition coming to and going from Lynn; he has seen it several age e 1 lon* Times — The Navigation is so wide that he has been detained several Days waiting for still Weather, and more than Once or Twice has been obliged to turn back — that Pilots are very necessary, and they are now obliged by Act of Parliament to have them. The Boats that go up the Country may not return, perhaps, in a Month, during which the Channel , is frequently altered, which makes Pilots necessary, who, by going backwards and forwards every Day, are acquainted with it — the Expence of the Pilots and of additional Assistance is very heavy, besides Delay — it is worth One per Cent. Insurance. ..He has known Scores of Boats sunk. — Being asked, if he ever knew of any Boats lost above German's Bridge? he said, He had heard there have been some sunk, but never saw them — it is very seldom it does happen. — Between Lynn and German's Bridge he attributes the loss of the Boats to the Winds and Waves, which is owing to the Width of the Channel — he has not navigated the Channel these Ten Years — he is sure that the Channel is worse now than formerly, except that he navigated it last November or December Twelvemonth for the Purpose of inspecting it.

Mr. George Maxwell being then examined, said,

That the Drainage of the Tracts of Land mentioned in the Petition is greatly impeded by the State of the Ouze, between Saint German's Bridge and the Town of King's Lynn; and the Trade to and from the inland Parts and Lynn is prejudiced by the Defects and Impediments in the River between German's Bridge and Lynn — that a very large Tract of Country that formerly traded with Lynn is now generally cut off from any . Communication with the Port of , owing to the present State of the Navigation between Germans Bridge and Lynn — the Parts of the Country he means is from Whittlesea, Peterborough, and Northampton — the.

Trade of the Country is impeded by the bad State of the River Nene; and the bad State of the River Nene is occasioned by the bad State of the River Ouze between Eau Brink and Lynn — he does not think that any other Means exists of improving that Navigation except the Means proposed by making the Cut in the Petition, and he is confident, as he can be of any Thing, that it will be of Benefit to the Drainage of the Lands, and that it would tend to promote the Commerce of King's Lynn, and upwards. — Being asked, Whether he has formed any Opinion respecting the Means by which the Expences of executing the necessary Works might be provided for? he said, Yes, by referring to the Estimate, Four Pence per Acre upon the Lands, and Four Pence per Ton upon the Goods, for Ten Years, will raise more Money than the Estimate amounts to.

— Being asked, What Quantity of Land he has made the Calculation upon ? he said, He made it upon the South Level of the Fens 120,000 Acres, Middle Level of the Fens 143,000 Acres, Marshland 40,000 Acres, Bardolph and Dawham 7,000 Acres, Lands bordered on the Fens and on the East Side of the Ouze 10,000, making together 320,000 Acres. His Calculation of the Means to provide for the Expences is made upon the Tonnage as well as upon the Lands:

He has also made some Calculation of what would be produced by a Tonnage; upon Information as to the Amount of the Tonnage, which has been given me by Mr. Creasy, Three Pence per Ton on all Goods navigated through the new Cut, except only those that are meant to be excepted, will produce 1,428/. 3s. and that, added to a Tax of Four Pence per Acre on the Land, will produce an Annual Income of 6,765/. jo,j. and a Fraction; and that, for Ten Years, is worth, reckoning Interest at 5/. per Cent. 52,297/. 6 s. —

not know that the Corporation of Bedford Level can. keep what Quantity of Water in the River Nene they please ? he said, He knows they have a Power of taking in Water into the River Nene, and that they do, at some Times, exercise that Power. — Being asked, Whether he has not the Total Power over the Regulation of the Sluices? he said, He believes they have over Standground Sluice and Salter's Load. — Being asked, In what State are the Banks of the River Nene ? he said, They are, in general, as good as can possibly be made. — Being asked, If they are not now broken down ? he said. There is a Breach in One of them. — Being asked, If he does not know that the Corporation of the Bedford Level are obliged by Act of Parliament to keep up the Drainage of the Country, and to keep the Rivers in a proper State for Drainage, so as not to be injurious to Navigation ? he said, The Banks he has been giving Evidence about are, in general, taken out of the Hands of the Corporation, by particular Acts of Parliament, obtained from Time to Time, for throwing the Country into Districts, in order to enable it to attempt to drain by the artificial Means of Water Engines; and those Engines have been obliged to be increased from Time to Time in point of Size and Strength, inso much, that they throw against a Head of Water in the internal Rivers of not less than about Five Feet on an Average; and those Waters, instead of going to the Outfall through the River Ouze, are overridden by the Waters of the Ouze, and the Consequence is, that the Waters thrown from the Engines are found to recoil the contrary Way, and being always impregnated with the Soil of the Fens, that Soil is deposited in the Beds of the internal Rivers, which are, generally speaking, considerably higher than the Surface of the adjacent Lands; and no Act of Drainage, except that of improving the Outfall of the Ouze (which Outfall, he has before given an Opinion, can only be improved by the intended new Cut) or can be carried into Effect either by the Corporation, or by any other Person, so as to enable them to form any better Banks to resist the Waters in those internal Rivers — And the Witness added, That, so far as he understands, the Bank which has lately given way, is not a Corporation Bank, but a District Bank.

Mr. William Creasy being then examined, was shewn the Paper produced by Mr. Maxwell, and said. That that Paper contains an Account of the Tolls of Three Pence per Ton on all Goods navigated for Twelve Months, ending with December last, going into and coining from Lynn, amounting to 1,428/. 2 10 £</.

which Paper he received from Mr. William Forster of Lynn, the Officer appointed to collect the Haling Dues under the Act of Parliament: And the Witness said, That the Name Wm Forster, thereto set, is his Hand Writing.

Mr. Robert Mylne being then further examined, said, That in consequence of his Survey of the River, he assisted in making the Plan annexed to the Petition, and is of Opinion that the Cut, as laid down in that Plan, is very easy of Execution, and that it is a Design not merely laid down upon Paper; but being in the Company of Two or more Engineers upon this District, we laid there the Design, such as it is represented in the Map, and upon a full Consideration of all the Matters that occurred to our Minds. — Being asked. What are the other Works stated in the Petition, and where are they to be made ? he said. The

mere making of this Cut, and toe digging it out, will not answer the End alone; the present Bed of the old River must be banked out by a Dam made across the Mouth of it, to prevent the Waters of toe River going that Way, after a new Bed is provided for k; Two new Cuts must he made in the District named Marshland, One to empty a Quantity of the Waters into the River Ouze, further up than the present Exk of Knight's G00U, and the other to empty another Part

of the Marshland Waters, below the lower End of the new Cut, which, at present, empty their Waters at Cleackwartm Goole; of other Works I have stated the Particulars on that District, which extends from Eau Brink to Denver Sluice: Another Work to be done, in Addition to these, is to run a Bank across the lower End of the old River, and form a Sea Wall or Bank to preserve the Quantity of Land which is now occupied by the extreme Breadth of the Ouze, and which will be silted up in a very short Number of Years; toe Position of this last Bank which he has mentioned, is proposed to be set down in such a Direction, as to be a great Improvement of the Navigation to the Port of Lynn, and a Protection to the Sea Wall or Bank of that Psut of Marshland opposite to the Town and Harbour of Lynn. — Being asked, Whether, in the Description he has given, he includes all the Works that are to be made for this Purpose ? he said, With respect to the Remainder of the Works, he begs Leave to refer to the Estimate which details them; as to the Works for the Improvement of the Navigation, he begs Leave to refer to the Estimate; whatever Title is given to the Estimate* it i3 certainly for the Improvement of the Navigation, as well as the Preservation of it. — Being asked, Whether any Works are necessary to be erected for the Protection of the Navigation of toe Mildenhall River, or River Lark? he said, The Particulars of this Estimate are collected and formed by Two Engineers, resident in the Country, and are particularly conversant in the several Branches of Drainage into the River; and, so far as he had Occasion to consider their Labours, he gave them his hearty Approbation: The Question being repeated to the Witness; he said, He expected from this Undertaking, if it is performed, that the Water of the River Ouze, above Denver Sluice, will be considerably lowered, especially in Time of Flood, to the Advantage of the Country in point of Drainage; and if, by doing so, any of the Navigable Branches, such as the Mildenhall, should have the Waters in them lowered to a Level, that would make them less capable of Navigation than they are at present, then his Proposition is to place a small Lock at the Mouth of such Navigable Branch, to maintain the Waters up to their usual and present Level, and in such a Manner as to be consistent with the Drains age of the Lands above it. — Being asked, If he thinks a Lock of this Kind would be a sufficient Security to the Proprietors of the River ? he said, Undoubtedly; and he thinks it would be an Improvement upon it, because that Length of it, which extends from tbs Tail of the lowest Lock upon it to the River Out*, is liable to all the Fluctuations of the Ouze itself; the same Observation will apply to all such Cases as the Mildenhall River. — Being asked, whether he conceives the Brandon Rimer to be One of those Cases ? he said. He does not apprehend that any such. Thing is necessary at the Mouth of the Brandon River, because there is a good Depth of Water for a considerable Way up that River, and that toe Waters will bear lowering, for the Benefit of Drainage, without injuring the Navigation. — Being asked to explain what are the Works necessary to be done to preserve the Drainage of that Part of Swaffham and Bottisham District, lying above Swaffham Road, and lip by the Hat'd Lands of Clay Hithe? he said, There is a particular Article in the Estimate to that Head, to wit, a Pound Lock to

for the Purposes of Navigation, the extensive Commerce carried on by the said Canals will, in all Probability, be much impeded, if not altogether, at different Times, wholly obstructed; and that, as the Canals already made are abundantly adequate for all the Purposes of Trade and Commerce within their respective Districts, the Canal now proposed appears to the Petitioners wholly unnecessary, and if it takes Effect, will furnish a Precedent dangerous to the Petitioners, and to the Property of every Person who has embarked in the Works of inland Navigation, on the Authority of Parliament, without affording the Prospect of any additional public Benefit: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, and that they may be heard, . by their Counsel, at the Bar of the House, against the said Bill, if they shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for making and maintaining a Navigable Communication between the River Trent Navigation, at, or near, the Town of Burton upon Trent, and the Coventry Canal at Fradley Heath, in the County of Stafford, be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Petition from the Inhabitants of Coventry to suspend the Ashby de la Zouch Canal Bill.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Tradesmen, Manufacturers, and others, Inhabitants of the City of Coventry, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Bill is depending for making a Navigable Caual from certain Coal Mines at, and in the Neighbourhood of, Ashby Woulds, in the County of Leicester, to join the

C&oentry Canal at Griff, in the Parish of Chilvers Coion, in the County of Warwick', and that the Petitioners are informed, that the Distance by Land between the said Collieries and Coventry is about Twenty-four Miles, and, by the Course of the said intended Canal to Griff, and from thence to Coventry by the Coventry Canal, will be a circuitous Course of near Forty Miles; and that the Petitioners are informed, that it is practicable to make a Canal from the said Collieries at Ashby Woulds aforesaid, to join the Coventry Canal at, or near, Grendon, in the said County of Warwick, within the Distance of Eleven Miles, or thereabouts, and that the Distance by the Coventry Canal from Grendon to Coventry is only Nineteen Miles, making in all only Thirty Miles; and that, by making the Communication at Grendon instead of Griff, the Promoters of the said Canal will have the same Advantages of a Communication with the Coventry and Oxford Canals, as if the same was to be made at Griff, and the Distance will be about Ten

Miles shorter between the said Collieries, the Oxford Canal, and the City of Coventry, than by the Line to Griff, and thereby about Twenty Miles of cutting will be saved, and consequently near One Hundred and Fifty Acres of Land will be preserved; and that the Petitioners are also informed, that, if the said Canal to Griff is suspended for the present Session, it is intended to propose the said Line of Canal from Ashby Woulds to Grendon, in the next Session of Parliament; and the Petitioners submit to the House, that the shortest Line of Canal, and such as will be the Means of furnishing Coals to the City of Coventry, and upon

the Line of the Oxford Canal, upon the most reasonable Terms, should be preferred: And therefore praying, That the said Bill for making the said Canal from Ashby Woulds aforesaid, to Griff, may not pass in the present Session, in Order that an Opportunity may be given to propose, in a future Session, such Scheme as may embrace the greatest Advantages to the Petitioners and the Public.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from Ashby de la Zouch, in the County of Leicester, to join and communicate with the Coventry Canal, at or near Griff, in the Lordship of Chilvers Coton, in the County of Warwick, and also certain Cuts or Branches from the said intended Canal, be read a Second Time.

An ingrossed Bill to indemnify such Persons as have Omitted to qualify themselves for Offices and Employments, and to indemnify Justices of the Peace, or others, who have omitted to register or deliver in their Qualifications within the Time limited by Law, and for giving further Time for those Purposes; and to indemnify Members, and Officers in Cities, Corporations, and Borough Towns, whose Admissions have been omitted to be stamped according to Law, or, having been stamped, have been lost or mislaid, and for allowing them Time to provide Admissions duly stamped; to give further Time to such Persons as have omitted to make and file Affidavits of the execution of Indentures of Clerks to Attornies and Solicitors; and for indemnifying Deputy Lieutenants and Officers of the Militia, who have neglected to transmit Descriptions of their Qualifications to the Clerks of the Peace within the Time limited by Law, and for giving further Time for that Purpose, was read the Third Time.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: And that the Title be, An Act to indemnify such Persons as have omitted to qualify themselves for Offices and Employments, and to indemnify Justices of the Peace, or others, who have omitted to register or deliver in their Qualifications within the Time limited by Law, and for giving further Time for those Purposes; and to indemnify Members and Officers in Cities, Corporations, and Borough Towns, whose Admissions have been omitted to be stamped according to Law, or, having been stamped, have been lost or mislaid, and for allowing them Time to provide Admissions duly stamped; to give further Time to such Persons as have omitted to make and file Affidavits of the execution of Indentures of Clerks to Attornies and Solicitors; and for indemnifying Deputy Lieutenants and Officers of the Militia, who have neglected to transmit Descriptions of their Qualifications to the Clerks of the Peace within the Time limited by Law, and for giving further Time for that Purpose.

Ordered, That Mr. Henry Hobart do carry the Bill to the Lords, and desire their Concurrence.

A Petition of the several Owners of Lands between Burton upon Trent and Fradley Heath, in the County of Stafford, through which a Navigable Canal is intended to be carried, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed Application is intended to be made to Parliament, for an Act to make a Navigable Canal from Burton upon to the Coventry Canal on Fradley Heath, in the County of Stafford, through the Lands of the Petitioners; and that such Canal, in the Opinion of the Petitioners, is no ways necessary for any Public Purposes, there being already a Communication by means of a Canal Navigation

Vol. 48.

between the above Places, in a parallel Direction, and very near, to the Line or Course of that now proposed, but such Canal will, if executed, be a wanton Destruction of many Acres of valuable Laud, and highly injurious to the Petitioners and others whose Estates are to be intersected by this needless Project: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by their Counsel, against the Bill for making such Canal, if the same should be brought into the House.

A Petition of the Company of Proprietors of the Navigation from the Trent to the Mersey, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by virtue of various Acts passed in the present Reign, the Petitioners have made and completed a Navigable Canal from the River Trent at, or near, in

the County of Derby, through the Counties of Stafford and Chester, to the River Mersey at Runcorn, in the said County of Chester, and that from the said Canal, at a Place called Fradley Heath, near to the City of Litchfield, other Canals have been extended to Coventry, Oxford, Birmingham, and many other Towns and Places; and that the Canal of the Petitioners was near Twenty Yearn in completing, and in the execution was attended with great Risque, Hazard, and Difficulty, and the Benefits it has afforded, and now daily affords to Trade and Commerce, the Petitioners submit, render it an Object of Public Concern; and that the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that Application is making to the House, for a Bill to make a Navigable Canal from the River Trent, at Burton upon Trent, in the County of Stafford, to the said Place called Fradley Heath, there to be cut into the Coventry Canal, near its Junction with the Canal of the Petitioners, and that the said proposed Canal is to be formed in a parallel Course with the Canal of the Petitioners, the Whole of its Length being about Ten Miles, and in many Places not more than Five hundred Yards distant from its Banks; and that, as the River Trent, at Burton aforesaid, is near Seventy Feet lower than the Canal of the Petitioners, and the said Coventry Canal at Fradley Heath aforesaid, Water for the Supply of the said proposed Canal and its numerous Locks must, as the Petitioners apprehend, be wholly, or in a great Measure, drawn and taken out of the Canal of the Petitioners, and the said Coventry Canal, the extensive Communications effected by the said Canals must necessarily be impeded, and may eventually be entirely obstructed; and that, as the Canals already made are abundantly sufficient for all the Purposes of Trade and Commerce, the Canal now proposed is, in the Opinion of the Petitioners, wholly unnecessary, and under all its Circumstances wholly unprecedented, and will, if it takes Effect, be highly injurious to the Petitioners, and to the Public: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill.

A Petition of Arthur Lord Baron of

Fishenvick, in the County of Stafford (Marquis of Donegal!, in Ireland) was likewise presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner observes, by the Votes, that a Bill has been brought into the House, for making a Navigable Canal from Burton upon Trent, to join the Coventry Canal on Fradley Heath, in the County of Stafford, for the Supply of which the Petitioner is informed Water is intended to be diverted and taken out of the Brooks or Streams which now run near to the Mansion House of the Petitioner, called Fisherwick Park, in the said County, some of which flow into the Pools and Reservoirs from which the said Mansion House, and the several Offices thereunto belonging, afre supplied with Water; and that, should any Part of such Waters be turned out of their present Course, it will be productive of real Injury to the Petitioner, and the said Bill, if it passes* will be injurious to many other Persons as well as the Petitioner, without affording any material Benefits to the Public, there being already Communications by

Water

Little Tew A Bill for dividing and inclosing the Open and Inclosure Bill Common Field, and other Commonable Lands and committed. Grounds, lying within the Hamlet and Liberties of Little Tew, in the Parish of Great Tew, in the County of Oxford, was read a Second Time.

above-mentioned Restriction in particular, the Trade of the Hawkers and Pedlars, who are a very industrious and useful Body of Men, is nearly annihilated, whereby great Numbers of them are brought to Poverty and Distress, and those who, from Circumstances, are enabled to continue their Business, suffer the utmost Inconvenience; and that, at the Time of passing the said Act, the Trade of the Hawkers and Pedlars was very considerable and extensive, and highly beneficial to the Kingdom at large, and to the Town and Neighbourhood of Manchester in particular, especially in the Sale of Silk Handkerchiefs, in Imitation of India Handkerchiefs, and other Goods, which pay a great Duty to Government, but, since the said Act, such Sale has very greatly decreased, and large Quantities of India Handkerchiefs, and other Goods, have been imported and sold, which before were, in a great Measure, prevented by the Industry and Vigilance of the Hawkers and Pedlars; and that, as the Restriction above complained of is so very injurious in its Consequences, not only to the Revenue, but to the Trade of the Kingdom at large,

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they have Power to make Provision in the said Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition.

THE Hour appointed for taking into Consideration the Petition of Nathaniel Newnham, Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the Borough of Ludgershall, in the County of Wilts, being come;

The House proceeded to the Appointment of a Select Committee, to try and determine the Merits of the said Petition.

Vol. 48.

The Serjeant at Arms was directed by Mr. Speaker to go, with the Mace, to the Places adjacent, and require the Attendance of the Members on the Business of the House.

And he went accordingly.

And being returned;

.The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and One hundred and Thirteen Members.being present;

The Counsel and Agents were called in to the Bar.

And the Door of the House being locked;

The Order of the Day, for taking the said Petition into Consideration, was read.

And the Names of the Members were taken out of the Box (before prepared) put into Six Glasses, and drawn and read in the usual Manner.

And the Names of Ten Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the . Name of James Baillie, Esquire, being drawn, he was nominated to serve on the said Committee by the Counsel for the Petitioner.

And the Name of the Honourable Robert Banks Jenkinson being drawn, he was nominated to serve on the said Committee by the Counsel for the Sitting Member.

And the Names of Thirty-nine other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

Note, That in the Course of drawing the said Names, the Names of Alexander Popham, Esquire, and Sir Charles Morgan, Baronet, were drawn, who, having sworn that they were Sixty Years of Age, or upwards, were excused from serving on the said Committee; and the Names of Thirty-seven other Members, then present, were drawn, and set aside; Eleven on Account of their being Sixty Years of Age, or upwards (before sworn); Two against whose Election Petitions were depending; One as being a Petitioner complaining of an undue Election and Return; Seven as then serving on Select Committees; Fifteen on Account of having, in this Session, served on Select Committees; and One on Account of his Return to serve in Parliament not having been brought in Fourteen Days.

And the whole Number of Forty-nine Names being complete, Lists of the said Names were delivered to the Counsel; and the Door of the House being opened, the Counsel and Agents withdrew.

The Counsel and Agents being returned to the Bar, the Clerk appointed to attend the said Select Committee delivered in to the House One of the said Lists, which had been struck by the said Counsel in his Presence, together with a new List of the Names of the Thirteen Members then remaining unstruck; to which last mentioned List the Names of James Baillie, Esquire, and the Honourable Robert Banks Jenkinson, being added, the same was called over; and is as follows:

The Honourable Henry Hobart, Charles Yorke, Esquire, Sir George Jackson, Baronet, Lord Viscount Slopford, Sir John Call, Baronet, Ewan Law, Esquire, Joshua Smith, Esquire, William Praed, Esquire, Charles Pierrepont, Esquire, William Egerton, Esquire, George Templer, Esquire, the Honourable Cropley Ashley, William Clive, Esquire, James Baillie, Esquire, the Honourable Robert Banks Jenkinson.

And the said Fifteen Members, being the Select Committee for trying the Merits of the said Petition of Nathaniel Newnham, Esquire, were sworn, by the Clerk at the Table, in the usual Manner.

And thereupon the Counsel and Agents withdrew.

Ordered, That the said Select Committee do meet forthwith, in One of the Committee Chambers

The Lord Arden reported from the Select Committee, appointed to try and determine the Merits of the Petition of the Honourable William Wesley Pole, and Robert Wood, Esquire; and also, the Petition of Christopher Clayton, the Reverend William Smelle, and William Bell, Electors of Members to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Great Grimsby, in the County of Lincoln, on Behalf of themselves and many other Electors of the said Borough, severally complaining of an undue Election and Return for the said Borough, that the said Committee met this Morning, at Ten of the Clock, pursuant to their Adjournment of Yesterday, when the Committee received an Account from Thomas Master, Esquire (One of the Members of the said Select Committee) that, being very much indisposed, he was confined to his House, and unable to attend his Duty on the said Select Committee this Day; and that the said Select Committee then adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

And the House being informed that Mr. Blackett (Apothecary) attended at the Door, who could give the House Information, respecting the present state of Mr. Masters Health; he was called in; and, at the Bar, examined upon Oath, and acquainted the House, That he had attended Mr. Master this Morning, and found him much indisposed with a Pain in his Stomach and Bowels, which made it impossible for him to have attended the Committee this Day; and that he thought Mr. Master could not attend his Duty upon the said Select Committee Tomorrow, without great Danger to his Health.

And then he was directed to withdraw.

Ordered, That the said Thomas Master, Esquire, be excused for his Non-attendance this Day on the said Select Committee; and that he have Leave to absent himself from any further Attendance on the said Select Committee.

A Petition of the Merchants, Manufacturers, Shopkeepers, Land Owners, and others, Inhabitants of Manchester, and of the several other Trading Towns in the Vicinity thereof, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, as a Bill is now depending in the House for the Establishment of a Canal from Manchester, through Rochdale, to Sowerby, and which is intended to communicate with his Grace the Duke of Bridgewater's Canal at, or near, Manchester aforesaid, the Petitioners beg Leave to observe, that such Communication cannot be commodious, or of any considerable Utility, unless it is free and uninterrupted, and, for that Purpose (which is necessary to facilitate Carriage, and prevent the Delays and Damages otherwise arising) it is evident that the said intended Canal must be capable of admitting Vessels of, at least, Fourteen Feet wide and Forty Tons Burthen; and therefore soliciting the Attention of the House to the important Object before stated, and that such Measures for securing the same may be adopted as in the Discretion of the House shall seem expedient, and also that the Petitioners may be heard, by their Counsel, in respect to the Necessity thereof.

I®Mr. Bastard reported from the Committee, to whom iitite it was referred to consider of the Report which, upon touching tie Friday last, was made from tire Select Committee, ap-imstof pointed to try and determine the Merits of the Peti-Jlr.Petrie. tj0Q of Samuel Petrie, Esquire; and also, the Petition of the Inhabitants possessing Houses within the Borough of Crick lade, in the County of Wilts, who, by immemorial Custom and Usage, have a Right to vote at all Elections for Members to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, severally complaining of an undue Election and Return for the said Borough, and which Committee were directed to enquire into the Matters contained in the Report made from the said Select Committee, and to examine Precedents relating thereto, and report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House; that the Committee had examined the Matters to them referred, and had searched Precedents for that Purpose, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the same, together with an Appendix thereunto, in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Report was read; and is as followed; viz.

Your Committee having, in Obedience to the Commands of the House, carefully examined the whole of the Matter referred to them, beg Leave to report; That they find by the Examination of Mr. Thomas Wright, an Officer of the Sheriff of Middlesex, who appeared before this Committee, and was examined, That he had had Two Warrants against the j said Samuel Petrie, Esquire, for some Time in his j Possession, previous to the Arrest herein after mentioned, one of which Warrants had been granted by

Ithe said Sheriff, in pursuance of a Writ issued out of His Majesty's Court of Common Pleas at Westminster, at the Suit of William Williams, for 3451. 1 6d.

and upwards, which Warrant was dated the 6th Day of March 1793; and the other of which Warrants had been granted by the said Sheriff in pursuance of a Writ issued out of His Majesty's Court of King's Bench, at the Suit of James Palmer, for 6501, and upwards, w'hich Warrant was dated the 5th Day of March 1793; and that Mr. Jaynes , the Plain-

tiff in One of the Actions before-mentioned, called upon the Witness on Thursday, the 14th Day of this Instant March, about Three of the Clock in the Afternoon, and desired the Witness to go with him to arrest Mr. Petrie, whoqi he w'ould point out to the Witness,

That the Witness, thinking it his Duty to do so, accordingly went with Mr. Palmer on the same Day, and was introduced by him to Mr. Petrie, at N° 22, in Pall Mall (which House the Witness then understood, and now believes, to have been the Place of Residence of the said Mr. Petrie) about Five Minutes past Four of the Clock in the Afternoon; whereupon Mr. Petrie shewed the Witness a Notice, signed by the Right Honourable the Speaker of the House of Commons, and also an Order of the House of Commons, signed by John Halsell, Esquire, Clerk of this House, requiring the said Mr. Petrie to attend the House, by himself, his Counsel, or Agents, on Tuesday the 12th Day of this Instant March, at the Time when the Petition, complaining of an undun Election and Return for the Borough of was ordered to be taken into Consideration; by virtue of which Notice and Order, Mr. Petrie claimed the Privilege of Exemption from Arrest. The Witness desired to observe to the Committee, that as it was not mentioned in those Papers, that Mr. Petrie was required to attend on any other Day than the said 12th Day of March, the Witness did not think that he should be justified in not making the Arrest; but thought himself bound to attend the Select Committee on the next Morning to inform them of it, which lie accordingly did.

The Witness said, That he did thereupon, at the Time and Place aforesaid, arrest the said Mr. Petrie, and has him still in his Custody under the said Arrest, by virtue of the Two several Warrants before mentioned; and that there are several other Detainers in the said Sheriff's Office against Mr. Petrie, to the Amount in the whole of 402 /. and upwards, exclusive of the Two several Sums contained in the Warrants before-rmentioned.

A Member present (being a Member of the said Select Committee) informed your Committee, That the said Select Committee met for the first Time to do business, on Wednesday the 13th Day of this Instant March, at Eleven of the Clock in the Forenoon, and having sat till Three of the Clock in the Afternoon of the same Day, adjourned till the next Morning, Thursday, at Ten of the Clock, at which Time the said Select Committee met, and then continued to sit till Half an Hour past One of the Clock in the Afternoon, w hen they adjourned till Friday Morning, Ten of the Clock; such Adjournment having been made at the Application of Mr. Petrie, on account of the Absence of Two material Witnesses, whose Names he delivered in, and who had been summoned, but were not yet come to Town.

The said Member further informed your Committee, That Mr. Petrie, the Petitioner, attended the said Select Committee during the whole Time of their sitting on the Wednesday and Thursday, as a Party in the Cause, and did besides, in all Respects, act as his ow n Agent in the Course of the Cause, in assisting his Counsel, and furnishing them with Instructions; and that although he did deliver in to the Clerk of the said Select Committee, in the usual Manner, the Name of Mr. Sleigh, as the Agent for his Petition, yet that the said Agent was present only for a very short Time,

Privilege A rrest of Mr. Petrie.

424 20° Martii . 1795.

and did not appear to take any Part in the Conduct of the Cause, the whole being managed by Mr. Petrie himself as the only effectual Agent.

Your Committee have also, according to the Order of the House, examined the Precedents of various Cases entered in the Journals of the House, respecting the Subject referred to them.

By these Cases, some of which are contained in an Appendix to this Report, it appears that the House have from the earliest Times, exercised the Right of giving the Protection and Privilege of the House, to the several Persons who were ordered to attend the House, or its Committees, or who, either on private or public Concerns, were attending the Service or the Business of the House; and that, in many of such Cases, the House have given Orders that such Persons, having been arrested by Process from the Courts of law, should be delivered out of Custody. But your Committee, in the Course of their Enquiry into the Subject referred to them, having found it connected with several Circumstances of the highest Importance to the Privileges of the House, have not presumed to give an Opinion thereon, but desire to submit the whole Matter to the Wisdom of the House.

Veneris, 24* diejanuarii, Anno 23° Georgii 3'" Regis, 1783.

The Earl of Surrey reported from the Committee, who were' appointed to examine the Matter of the Complaint of the Breach of Privilege set forth in the Petition of Samuel Petrie, Esquire, and to search for Precedents of Persons taken in Execution, and in Custody, who have been Petitioners claiming a Seat as Members of this House, and desiring to be allowed the Privilege of this House to be delivered out of such Custody, and to report the same to the House; That the Committee had examined the Journals accordingly; and had directed him to make a Report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Your Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Journals, and find many Precedents where the Privilege of the House of Commons has been allowed to Members taken in Execution, and in Custody for Debt; the greater Part of which are recited in the Reports made upon the 15th of November and the 16th of December 1707, from the Committee appointed to examine the Matter of the Complaint of Mr. Asgill, then a Member of the House, and to search Precedents, what had been done for the Discharge of any Members upon Execution and Mesne Process. — But your Committee, upon the most accurate Search, have not been able to find any Precedent, where a Person, being a Petitioner, and claiming a Seat as Member of this House, has at any Time desired to be allowed the Privilege of the House, upon any Account whatever; much less do your Committee find any Instance of the Privilege of this House being granted by the House to Persons under that Description.

The House was moved. That an Act, made in the Tenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for the further preventing Delays of " Justice, by reason of Privilege of Parliament," might be read.
