ORDER for the Surveyor 'j

General and Mr. Scrope to AFTER our hearty Commendations: Whereas we are given to understand, consider of a Way to pass \ that the great Charge of passing Exchequer Leases makes it impracticable Leases of small Estates at j for several Crown Tenants, whose Holdings are of small Yearly Value, to an easy Expence. J renew their Leases; so that they continue their Possessions after their respect

tive Terms are expired, paying only their old reserved Rents, which,' for the most Part amount to no more than bare Acknowledgments; whereby the Fines that might arise from those Estates are lost to the Crown: Now, to the End this Grievance to the Subject, and Loss to the Crown, may be remedied, as in Justice and Reason we conceive it ought to be, We do hereby order and appoint you, calling to your Assistance every His Majesty's Officers having Concern herein, or so many of them as you shall think necessary, to consider, consult, and agree, by what Means, and in what Manner, such small Estates (every of which shall not exceed the Yearly Value of 2o /. per Ann. on the Rack) may be leased in Possession, or in Reversion, with little Charge to the Lessees; and we do hereby charge and require all His Majesty's said Officers, or such or so many of them as you shall think necessary as aforesaid, to attend your Summons, and to be aiding and assisting to you in consulting, advising, and agreeing the Means of effecting this Service, as often as you shall think fit to call on them for that Purpose; and you are to lay before us, in Writing, the Result of your Consultations and Agreements hereupon with all convenient Speed, for our further Orders therein; and for so doing this shall be your sufficient Warrant.

Whitehall, Treasury Chambers,

20th May 1724. R. WALPOLE,

GEO. BAILLIE,

To our very loving Friends John Pulteney, Esq. His WILL. YONGE,

Majesty's Surveyor General; and John Scrope, Esq. GEO. DODINGTON.

One of the Secretaries attending this Board.

Summons. — The Lords Commissioners of His Majesty's Treasury having, by Warrant, dated the 20th of this Instant May, ordered and appointed us, calling to our Assistance every His Majesty's Officers having Concern in the passing Exchequer Leases of Crown Lands, &c. or such or so many of the said Officers as we shall think necessary, to consider, consult, and agree by what Means, and in what Manner, such small Estates in the Premisses (every of which shall not exceed the Yearly Value of 20/. per Ann. on the Rack) may be leased in Possession, or in Reversion, with little Charge to the Lessees; and we being thereby likewise directed to lay before their Lordships, in Writing, the Result of our Consultations and Agreements, touching the aforesaid Matter, with all convenient Speed, for their Lordships further Pleasure therein, we do therefore hereby appoint you in that Behalf to attend us at the Surveyor General's Office, near St. James's Palace, on Tuesday the 2d Day of June next, at Ten o'Clock in the Forenoon.

St. James's, 22d May 1724. J. PULTENEY, S. G.

J. SCROPE.

venteenthReporl Land Revenue.

Minutes. — 2d June 1724. At a Meeting of John Pulteney, Esqr, Surveyor General of His Majesty's Lands, &c. and John Scrope, Esqr, One of the Secretaries of the Treasury, with the several Officers concerned in passing Exchequer Leases who were summoned thereto.

PRESENT,

John Pulteney, S. G.

John Scrope.

Mr. Auditor Jett, and his Deputy.

Mr. Audr Godolphin's Deputy. The Deputy Clerk of the Pipe. The Clerk of Exchequer Leases.

The Order of the Treasury, dated the 20th of May last, relating to the Charge of passing Exchequer Leases, being read, and the said several Officers having declared what Fees were payable in their respective Offices, for Exchequer Leases, it appeared thereby that the Charge of passing every such Lease, of what Yearly Value soever the Premisses might be, and though the same consist of no more than One Parcel, nor the Lease of more than One Skin of Parchment, does amount to Thirty-one Pounds, including the Sum of Four Pounds for the Double Stamp Duty.

N- B.At the Second Meeting-! this Part was revoked, and limited 1 But if the Lease be of or more Parcels, the Auditors do respectroely to several Properties, instead of se- claim a several Fee for each Parcel; or if there be Two or more Skins of veral Parcels. J Parchment, though containing One Parcel only, they claim a several Fee for each Skin; however they said, that they very often moderated their respective Fees, according to the particular Circumstances of the Case.

And the Deputy Clerk of the Pipe said, that when the Lease contains a Grant of Two or more several Terms, having different Commencements, or different Determinations (which are distinct Estates) or when Two or more several Rents are reserved on such Lease, he takes a Double Fee for such additional Term or Rent, over and above the Fee payable to him only.

In each of the other Offices (if the Premisses are the sole Property of the Lessee) no more than One Fee is paid for any Exchequer Lease, be the Parcels never so many, or though such Lease contain several Habendums or Reddendums.

The Order of the Treasury, dated the 31st of December 1716, relating to the inrolling with the proper Auditor all Assignments of Crown Leases, being read; after some Discourse thereon (touching the Charge it occasioned in the passing such Leases) Mr. Auditor Jett said, that while the same continued in Force, he was bound in Duty to obey it; but he had no Objection to the revoking it, if the Lords of the Treasury shall so please.

Then Two Precedents were read out of the Entries in the Surveyor General's Office, to shew in what Manner Leases of small Estates belonging to the Crown had been formerly granted, viz*.

Anno 1702. — A General Lease to John Latton, Esquire, for the Tenants of His Majesty's Manor of Richmond, in Surrey.

1716. — Another of certain small Parcels in His Majesty's Manor of Rosedale, in the County of York.

And a Sign Manual of the late Queen, dated the 12th Day of August 1705, w>as likewise read, whereby the then Lord 'treasurer was impowred and directed to authorize and require the Auditor of Wales to grant Leases of small Estates within that Principality, in the Manner therein mentioned.

But after some Discourse about the several foregoing Precedents, a Second Meeting was appointed to be on Saturday next, the Sixth Instant, at Ten in the Forenoon; and the several Officers were desired, in the mean Time, to consider by what Means and in what Manner such Leases may be granted with little Charge to the Lessees; and the Auditors are then to deliver in Tables of their respective Fees, duly attested, in such Manner as that which the Deputy Clerk of the Pipe had delivered in.

6th June 1724. — Pursuant to the Appointment above, the aforesaid several Officers (except the Clerk of the Pipe) met together, and the Auditors produced Tables of their Fees; after which Mr. Scrope produced a Copy of a Warrant from the Treasury, impowering the Auditor of Cumberland to let Leases to the several Tenants of the late Lord Preston, of their respective Holdings, &c. in that County; and after some Discourse concerning the Matters in Question, the several Officers being asked if they had thought of any Method for passing small Estates at an easy Charge; but they had nothing to propose more than what had been mentioned at the former Meeting, other than that, if the Lords of the Treasury should think fit, they were willing to abate of their respective Fees, upon the Renewal of such small Estates.

ANNE

Sign Manual Whereas Our trusty and well-beloved Sidney Godolphin, Esq', Auditor of ouf Revenues of Wales, hath by

his Memorial set forth, that among the Leaseholders of Our Revenue of North and South Wales there are several small Tenements, and other Improvements, that formerly were, and now might be, made by Cottages that are built upon our Wasts, most of which Tenements are of and under the clear Yearly Value of Fifty Shillings, and which, as he is informed, have antiently been leased by the Auditor of Wales, at a small Rent reserved to the Crown, many of which Leases being long since expired, and the Value so very small that the Tenants do not think it worth the Charge of renewing by Exchequer Leases, whereby We do not only loose the antient Fine and reserved Rent, but oft the said Tenements and Wasts are enjoyed by the adjacent Inhabitants as their Freeholds; and is therefore of Opinion, that it will very much improve Our Interest to authorize and impower the Auditor of Our Revenues of Wales, for the Time being, to renew and grant Leases for all sdeh small Tenements and Cottages, so that the Annual Rent do not exceed Fifty Shillings, for such Term or Terms of Years as shall be thought fit, w-hereby not only Our present Revenue will be increased, but also the antient Right of the Crown secured: All which We having taken into Our Royal Consideration, Our Will and Pleasure is, that you forthwith issue your Warrant to the Auditor of Our Revenues of North

33 Geo. III. 280 Mariii. 595

and South Wales, now and for the Time being, authorising and impowering him, from Time to Time, to Seventeenth Report

renew and grant Leases for all such small Tenements and Cottages, where the full Annual Value thereof 011 L3H(i ^eveilue-

shall not exceed Fifty Shillings, for such Term or Terms of Years as you shall think fit, not exceeding in v ' J

any One Case the Term of One-and-Thirty Years, and for the most that can be got for the same; in which

Leases you are to direct the said Auditor to insert a Clause, that the said Rents be made payable to the respective Receivers or Bailiffs of the Premisses for the Use of Us, Our Heirs and Successors; and that he take

Care all such Leases be duly inrolled in his Office, and that the reserved Rents be, from Time to Time,

delivered in Charge to the respective Receivers of North and South Wales, and such other Clauses for keeping

the Premisses in Repair, and paying the reserved Rents, as are usual in Leases of the like Nature; and you

are to direct the said Auditor, at Michaelmas in every Year, to transmit to you, or to the High Treasurer or

Commissioners of the Treasury for the Time being, to certify under his Hand of what Leases he shall have

made in pursuance thereof in the Year preceding (to wit) of what Lands or Tenements, for what Number of

Years, under what Rents, and to whom he hath made the said Leases; and for so doing this shall be your

Warrant. Given at Our Court at Windsor Castle, the 12th Day of August 1705, in the Fourth Year of Our

Reign.

By Her Majesty's Command.

GOD O L P IIIN.

To Our right trusty, and well-beloved Sydney Lord Godolphin, Our High Treasurer of England, and Treasurer of Our Exchequer.

In pursuance of her Majesty's Pleasure signified to me by the foregoing Warrant, these are to authorize and empower you, from Time to Time, to renew and grant Leases for all such small Tenements and Cottages as are therein mentioned, where the full Annual Value doth not exceed Fifty Shillings, for such Term or Terms of Years as you shall think fit, not exceeding, in any One Case, the Term of Thirty-one Years, and for the most that can be got for the same; and you are to insert in the said Leases the several Clauses for enrolling the said Leases, keeping the Premisses in Repair, and paying the reserved Rents, as are directed by her Majesty's said Warrant, and such other as are usual in Cases of the like Nature; and you are also, at Michas in every Year, to transmit to me, or the High Treasurer or Commissioners of the Treasury for the Time being, a Certificate under your Hand of what Leases you shall have made in the Year preceding (to wit) of what Lands or Tenements, for what Number of Years, under what Rents, and to whom made, according to her Majesty's Pleasure signified as aforesaid; and for so doing this shall be your Warrant. Whitehall Treasury Chambers, 15th August 1705.

GODOLPHIN.

To my very loving Friend Sidney Godolphin, Esq1, Auditor of her Majesty's Revenues of North and South Wales, and to the Auditor thereof for the Time being.

AFTER our hearty Commendations: Whereas it hath been represented unto us, that the several Persons hereafter named, who were Tenants to the late Lord Viscount Preston, and had Leases which expired the 2d of February 1690, of Part of his Estate in the County of Cumberland (which became forfeited to their Majesties by Reason of the Attainder of the said Lord Preston) have since been turned out of their Farms, Lands, or Tenements, by his Agents, because of their ready Submission to their Majesties Title, and paying their respective Rents to the Crown: And whereas it is necessary, for their Majesties Services, and to prevent the Lands from being unoccupied, that good Tenants may be continued or put in Possession of the said Farms or Lands, without being put to the great Charge and Trouble of Leases under the Great or Exchequer Seals: These are therefore to authorize and require you to enter into Contracts, or make Leases, for and on the Behalf of their Majesties, to the respective Persons hereafter named, of the several Farms or Tenements hereafter mentioned, and to put them into the Possession thereof; to hold the same of their Majesties for the like Term of Years, at the former Rents and Services, to be payable to their Majesties, and under the like Provisoes and Covenants as were contained in the former respective Leases, which they respectively had of the Premisses; viz. To Richard Story of the Messuages, I.ands, Tenements, and Hereditaments of Howend, the Lands of Chappel Town, and all that was in his former Lease, to Richard Grimston the Messuage and Lands called the Field, the Mill Hill, and the Mill Town, the Kiln there, the Water Corn Mill called the Field Mill, at the Mill Town, and all other the Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, demised by the former Lease to Stephen Grimston his Father [and so of several others}; and that you cause to lie inserted in such Contracts or Leases any new Covenants or Agreements, as you may think necessary for their Majesties Service; and for so doing this shall be your Warrant. Whitehall Treasury Chambers, January 17th 1692.

R. HAMPDEN,

To our loving Friend their S. FOX,

Majesties Auditor of the C. MONTAGUE.

County of Cumberland.

May it please your Lordships, Seventeenth Report

IN Obedience to your Lordships annext Order of the 20th of May last, requiring us to consider and report^0® Lawl Revenu*y to your Lordships by what Means and in what Manner small Estates belonging to the Crown (every of which shallV

not exceed the Yearly Value of Twenty Pounds on the Rack) may be leased in Possession or in Reversion, with little Charge to the Lessees; and impowering us for that Purpose to call to our Assistance such of His Majesty's Officers, having Concern therein, as we should think necessary, we have conferred with the Auditors of His Majesty's Land Revenue, the Deputy Clerk of the Pipe, and the Clerk of Exchequer Leases, touching the aforesaid Matter; and having considered the same,

Do humbly report, That by the Tables of Fees claimed by the respective Officers, as their antient legal Fees, payable in the several Offices through which such Leases do pass, it appears that the Charge of every Exchequer Lease, of how small Yearly Value soever the Premisses may be, does amount to Thirty-one Pounds, or thereabouts.

Which Charge having been found a great Discouragement to the Crown Tenants, and others, in the taking Leases of small Estates, in 1701 Mr. Latton, then Steward of the Manor of Richmond, in Surrey, having by virtue of a Royal Sign Manual contracted with several Tenants and others, for Leases of small Parcels of Land or Tenements within the said Manor, particular and distinct Constats thereof were made forth, and separately rated, by the then Surveyor General, in order to the passing a gener Lease of all those several Parcels; which Lease in 1702 passed under the Exchequer Seal to Mr. Ayloff, the then and now Deputy Steward of the said Manor, in Trust for and to the Use of the several Persons so contracted with for their particular and respective Premisses. And we find that in or about the Year 1717, alike general Lease was passed of several small Estates within His Majesty's Manor of Rosedale, in the County of York; which Manner of leasing small Estates, in Ease of the several Tenants, may be practicable when the Premisses lie contiguous, or in the same County (as in the afore-mentioned Cases); but we apprehend 'twill be very difficult, if not impracticable, when such Estates lie scattered in different Counties: Therefore do think that this Way of leasing them will not fully answer the Intent of your Lordships Order.

We also find, that in 1692, the then Auditor of the County of Cumberland, was by Warrant of the then Lords Commissioners of the Treasury, reciting as therein is recited, and to avoid the Charges of Exchequer Leases, authorized and required to contract with or make Leases for and on Behalf of their Majesties, to the several Persons therein named, who had been Tenants to the late Lord Preston, of the several Farms or Tenements therein mentioned, and which were then vested in the Crown by His Lordship's Attainder.

We likewise find, that in 1705, the then Lord Treasurer Godolphin did, by virtue of her then Majesty's Royal Sign Manual, impower the Auditor of Wales to grant Leases of small Tenements and Cottages within that Principality, each Estate or Holding not to exceed the full Yearly Value of Fifty Shillings; Copies of which Sign Manual, and of the aforesaid Treasury Warrants, are annexed.

But notwithstanding these last mentioned Precedents, we cannot advise the granting Leases df any Crown Lands or Tenements whatsoever, by virtue of a Royal Sign Manual, which we conceive not to be warranted by the Civil List Act, wherein the several Ways of leasing are particularly specified; (that is to say) under the Great Seal, the Exchequer Seal, the Seals of the Duchy and County Palatine of Lancaster, or by Copy of Court Roll.

We find that the Order of the Treasury, dated the 31st of December 1716, for inrolling all Assignments of Crown Leases with the proper Auditor (a Copy whereof is annexed) has very much increased the Charge of passing Exchequer Leases, particularly with respect to the divided small Parcels of the Bailiwick of Saint James's, great Numbers of the Under Tenants having purchased their respective Holdings for the Residue of the several and respective Terms, which were granted therein by the Crown to the late Earl of Saint Albans. Whereupon the Auditors being asked. Whether that Order was of any Use or Benefit to His Majesty's Land Revenue ? they said, That while it continued in Force, it was their Duty to obey it, but gave no, Reason for its being continued:

So that if your Lordships shall please to revoke the same, it will very much lessen the Charge of Crown Leases, without doing any Prejudice to His Majesty's Land Revenue; in which Case the Auditors propose, that instead of the inrolling all mesne Assignments, as by that Order is required, every Tenant applying to renew his Lease be obliged to inroll with the proper Auditor the last Assignment only, whereby he is become the Crown's immediate Tenant of the Premisses.

As to which, we presume it may sufficiently ascertain the Tenancy, according to the Intent of the aforesaid Order, if a Memorial only of such last Assignment be recorded with the proper Auditor, containing the Day and Year of the Date, the Names and Additions of the Parties, the Description of the Premisses assigned, the Habendum, and the Rent or Rents reserved; which is agreeable to the Form prescribed by the Act for the public registering of Deeds, &c. of Lands in Middlesex.

Upon the Whole, if the said Order for inrolling mesne Assignments with the respective Auditors be revoked; if the several Officers having Concern in the passing Exchequer Leases take no more or other Fees for every such Lease (though the Premisses shall consist of different Parcels, so as the same be the sole Property of the Lessee) than what are mentioned in their respective Tables of Fees, herewith laid before your Lordships; and if such small Estates as separately do not exceed the clear Yearly Value of Twenty Pounds, nor do together exceed One hundred Pounds per Ann. on the Rack, be granted by One general Lease, in such Cases, where it may be practicable, we hope that the Charge of passing Exchequer Leases, in Possession or Reversion, will so far be lessened in Ease of the Crown Tenants, as may effectually answer the Intent of your Lordships afore-mentioned Order in thqt Behalf.

All which is humbly submitted to your Lordships Wisdom.

J. PULTENEY, Surv' Gen1.

25th June, 1724. J. SCROPE.

A true Copy of the Entry in the Office of His Majesty's Surveyor General.

W" Harrison,

Acting Surveyor General.

AN ingrossed Bill for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from the River Severn, at or near Shrewsbury, in the County of Salop, to the River

Mersey, at or near Nether Pool, in the County of Chester, and also certain Collateral Cuts, from the said intended Canal, was read the Third Time.'

An ingrossed Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, by Way of Ryder, to empower the Proprietors of the Ellesmere Canal to take the Waste Water from the Chester Canal.

And the said Clause was Thrice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill, by Way of Ryder.

Then the Amendments following were severally proposed to be made to the Bill; viz.

Pr. 184. 1.3. At the End of the Line to add " which shall not be wanted for " the Purposes of the said Canal, or of the said Ellesmere " Canal, or either of them,"

Pr. 194. 1. 34. To leave out from "required" to " at," in 1. 36. and insert " within Two Years next after the " Commencement of this Act" instead thereof.

And the said Amendments were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House; and the Bill was amended at the Table accordingly.

Vo t. 48.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: And that the Title be, An Act for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from the River Severn, at Shrewsbury, in the County of Salop, to the River Mersey, at or near Nether-pool, in the County of Chester; and also for making and maintaining certain Collateral Cuts from the said intended Canal.

Ordered, That Mr. Kynaston do carry the Bill to the Lords, and desire their Concurrence.

A Petition of the Merchant Manufacturers, Traders, Petition from and other Inhabitants, of the Town of Nottingham and Nottingham its Neighbourhood, was presented to the House, and respiting read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners approach 1 e ar‘ the House as the Guardian of the Public Peace and Welfare, and pray, That, by the Interposition of their Wisdom and Patriotism, the Petitioners and their Country may be rescued from the Evil of an impending War, singular in its Character, not founded on the usual Causes of War, which has no specific Object in View, no definite Prospect of Termination, unless in the absolute Conquest of a numerous and powerful People, a most arduous, if not impracticable Attempt, and which, in the present Circumstances of Great Britain, must be attended with heavy Suffering, without the Probability of any Gain or Acquisition to compensate for this Suffering: That to a Series of Wars, many of which with National Dignity might have been avoided, is owing to the immense Load of Debt, which bears with the most oppressive Weight on every Individual, and which nothing but the singular Prosperity of our Foreign Commerce could enable these Kingdoms to sustain: One principal Source of this Prosperity is Peace; the Petitioners pray, therefore, That the House will not suffer this

Source

.. i

8° Aprilis.

611

Source to be destroyed, nor this Country to participate in the Misery by participating in the Folly of other Nations: To add to a Debt which the Petitioners fear is irredeemable, and to an Amount which no one can calculate, ought to be justified by the last Necessity; nothing but the very Being and Preservation of our Country could reconcile it to the National Will; every Thing in our present Circumstances is adverse to War, the Dearness of Provisions, and of all the Necessaries and Comforts of Life, every Day advancing, and hardly supported by the utmost Exertions of Industry and Ingenuity; the alarming Progress of the Poor Rates; a wide Range of Taxation, which embraces every Form of Property, and cramps very Movement of the Subject; together with that delicate Balance between the Excellence and the Price of our Manufactures, on which our Foreign Commerce depends, all with One ominous Voice repel the Thought of War — War will increase every one of these internal Burthens, and co-operating with them diminish or ruin that Trade on which all depends, the Enjoyments as well as the Resources of this Country; And therefore also praying the House, That in their Goodness they will attend to the Supplications of their Country, and in their Wisdom avert an Evil which has but barely commenced, and which a pacific Disposition in the House cannot fail to dispel: To the-House, and to the Protection of the God of Peace, the Petitioners recommend themselves, their Fellow Citizens, and the impending Fate of Britain.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the

Table.

A Petition of several Merchants and other Inhabi- petition from tants of the Parish of Blakeney, in the County of Nor- Blakeney folk, and of several other Persons who are Owners of agan, st Stiff-Messuages, Lands, and Tenements, within the said I'tonTnclo-0^ Parish of Blakeney, and in the Neighbourhood thereof, £ure and interested in the Preservation of the Harbour of Blakeney, in the said County, was also presented to the House, and read; likewise taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth. That the said Harbour lies on the North Coast of the said County, and is well situated for the general Purposes of Navigation and Commerce, and the Petitioners, and the Public in general, are interested in the Preservation thereof; and that there are within the Parishes of Stiffkey and Morston aforesaid, or one of them, certain large Tracts of Commonable Land called Salt Marshes, near, or adjacent to, the said Harbour, over which Marshes the Tide and Water of the Sea hath, for Time immemorial, flowed and reflowed, and the said Harbour of Blakeney hath been, and is now, kept open, and fit for the Purposes of Navigation and Commerce, chiefly by Means of the natural Operation of the said Tidal Waters flowing and re-flowing the rein; and that if the said Bill, in its present Form, should pass into a Law, and the said Salt Marshes should be inclosed and -embanked from the Sea, the Petitioners apprehend, that, for Want of the Tidal Water flowing and reflowing thereon in its usual and accustomed Manner, the said Harbour would be soon choaked up with Silth, and the Navigation therein would thereby be rendered difficult and dangerous, to the great Injury of the Petitioners and of the Public: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves, their Agents, or Counsel, against such Part or Parts of the said Bill as may affect their Property or Interests, or tend to the Injury or Obstruction of the said Harbour, and that some Provision may be made in the said Bill for preventing any Damage to the said Harbour by embanking or inclosing the said Salt Marshes, or that the Petitioners may have have such other Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

And the Amendments made by the Committee to the said Bill, as far as the Amendment in Fo. 28. 1. 4. being severally read a Second Time, upon the Question severally put thereupon, some of them were disagreed to, and the rest were, with an Amendment to One of them, agreed to by the House.

The Amendment in Fo. 28. 1.4, which was after " Realm," to insert, " and that any Offence against " this Act, committed within that Part of Great " tain called England, may be alledged, and be laid, " enquired of, and tried, in the County where such " Offence shall have been committed, or in the " County of Middlesex; and that any Offence against " this Act, committed within that Part of Great Britain " called Scotland, may be alledged, and be laid, enquired of, and tried, either before the Court of " Justiciary at Edinburgh, or in any of the Circuit " Courts in that Part of the United Kingdom," being read a Second Time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the said Amendment, by leaving out the Words " and " that any Offence against this Act, committed within " that Part of Great Britain called England, may be " alledged, and be laid, enquired of, and tried, in the County where such Offence shall have been " committed."

And the Question being put, That the Words proposed to be left out stand Part of the said Amendment;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Then the said Amendment was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Two of them were disagreed to, and the other-was, with several Amendments thereunto, agreed to by the House.

Setting forth, That the Petitioners having, a few Days since, procured a Copy of the said Bill, and having duly deliberated thereon, conceive that, should the same, as it now stands, pass into a Law, certain Clauses thereof, affecting the American Trade, and the Insurances thereunto relating, will most essentially injure the Interests of this Country, and of Justice, without, in any adequate Degree, distressing the Enemy; and that the Petitioners have since been busily occupied in holding sundry Public Meetings of their own Body, and in obtaining Information respecting the same, especially from His Majesty's Ministers, and have in no respect whatever lost any Time therein, but on the contrary have been most busily employed to that End: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, Tomorrow, by Counsel, at the Bar of the House, touching the Tendency of the said Clauses in the Bill so pending, not being able earlier to prepare the proper Materials respecting the same, and therein duly to instruct their Counsel.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Walker and Mr. Spranger:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for repealing Part of an Act, passed in the First Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, intituled, "An Act for preventing Frauds in the Duties upon Salt, " and for the better Payment of Debentures at the " Custom House," which may relate to the refining and making of Salt at certain Works intended to be erected at Garston, in the County Palatine of Lancaster,

instead of the present Salt Works at Liverpool; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for continuing the Term, and altering and enlarging the Powers, of an Act of Parliament, of the Twenty-ninth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for repairing and widening the Road from the Town of Wakefield to the Town of Abberford, in the West Riding of the County of York-, without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for incorporating the Company of Free Fishers and Dredgers of Whitstable, in the County of Kent, and for the better ordering and Government of the Fishery; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for the better preventing Forgeries and Frauds in the Transfers of the several Funds transferrable at the Bank of England; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for dividing allotting, and inclosing, the Open Fields, Meadows, Pastures, and Commonable Heath Grounds, within the Parish of Normanton, in the County of Rutland; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for naturalizing John Anthony and John

Isaac CharretiS; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act for naturalizing Peter Benezech; to which the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

Mr. Blackburne reported from the Committee, to Carnarvon whom the Petition of the Mayor, Bailiffs, Burgesses, Harbour Pe-and other Inhabitants of the Town of Carnarvon, or ^lon report‘ trading to the Port thereof, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's *

Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;' viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, a Member present informed your. Committee, That the Harbour of Carnarvon, and the several Channels leading thereto, have of late Years, by the Flux and Reflux of the Tides, been greatly choaked and filled up with Mud, Sand, and Dirt, whereby Vessels are prevented from getting up to the Quays, Wharfs, and Landing Places, within the said Harbour, and the Shipping lying in the Harbour are exposed to Inconvenience and Danger — That the present Quays and Piers are not sufficient for the Preservation of the Harbour, and the Reception of Vessels resorting thereto, and for the requisite and convenient Dispatch in loading and unloading — That it would therefore be a great Benefit and Advantage to the Merchants, and others, living in, or trading to and from, the said Town and Port, and of Public Utility, if the said Harbour, and the several Channels leading thereto, were properly enlarged, deepened, cleansed, scoured, improved, and regulated, and if new and additional Piers and Quays were constructed and built for the Preservation and Protection of the Harbour, and the Accommodation of the Trade thereof.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging, deepening, cleansing, improving, and regulating the Harbour of Carnarvon, in the County of Carnarvon: And that Mr. Blackburne, the Lord and Mr. Thomas Williams, do prepare and bring in, the same.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr,

William Griffith being examined, said, That the Harbour of Amlwch, in the Isle of Anglesey, is inadequate to the Occasions of the Trade now carrying on there, and in certain Winds does not afford Safety for Vessels lying the re, for Want of a Pier, and other necessary Works — And the Witness further said, That the said Harbour is capable of being rendered safe and commodious, and that if the same were effectually improved and regulated, it would not only be beneficial to the Trade and Commerce of the said Isle, but would, in Cases of strong North and Westerly Winds, be very useful as a Retreat for Ships and Vessels navigating the North, the English, and the Irish Channel.

Petition of A Petition of Susannah Brown, was presented to the Ma Brown jjouse> an(j reafj; Setting forth, that the Petitioner is ioVown's0" Defendant in a Bill of Divorce now before the House, Divorce Bill, instituted by Edward Brown; and that the Petitioner, in the Year 1776, married with the said Edward Brown, who wa3 at that Time involved in great Difficulties, having contracted various large Debts which he was totally unable to pay, and on this Account, soon after their Marriage, it was thought necessary by the Friends and Relations of the Petitioner (the said Edward Brown being entirely abandoned by his own Friends and Relations) that the said Edward Brawn should go Abroad, and accordingly, through the Means of the Husband of the Petitioner's Aunt, Jackson,

of Brompton, in Kent, he was fitted out and enabled to go to the East Indies as a Cadet; and that it was settled, between the sard Edward Brown and the Relations of the Petitioner, that the Petitioner should reside with her said Uncle and Aunt at Brompton till her said Husband's Return, and that, meanwhile, her said Husband should remit her Money for her Maintenance and Support; and that, for the Space of Se-wen Years, the Petitioner never received more than the Sum of £. 20, although both the Petitioner and her Relations wrote to her Husband, stating, that unless he sent her Remittances for her Support, she could mot live with them any longer; and that the said Edward Brawn was well able to send her Remittances, although he neglected so to do, notwithstanding the IRemonstrances of the Petitioner and ' her Relations; and that in the Year the Petitioner's said Aunt

(who was her only Protector) dying, she was obliged by her Uncle to leave his House at Brompton, where she had resided, and, being thereby reduced to the greatest Distress, she was compelled to the Necessity of accepting a Proposal, made her by Lieutenant James Dodd, to live and cohabit with him as his Wife, or starving, which Offer her miserable Situation compelled her to accept and that till that Time the' Character of the Petitioner was unimpeached, and, had she met with that Protection from her Husband which he was both enabled and bound in Honour to grant, the Petitioner would have behaved as a virtuous and dutiful Wife, and would not at this Time, through such unnatural and ungrateful Conduct of her Husband, the said Edward Brawn, be a Prisoner in the Gaol of Newgate, where she has been confined Three Years for a Debt of about ,£.51; and that the said Edward Brawn is uow a Captain in the Service of the India Company, and has long held several lucrative Appointments s And therefore praying the House to take Compassion on her unhappy Case, and, as all the Fortune now enjoyed by her Husband has been derived to him solely by the Means of herself and her Relations, that some Provision may be made in the said Bill for her Support and Maintenance.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the ingrossed Bill from the Lords, intituled, An Act to dissolve the Marriage of Edward Brown, Esquire, with Susannah Solley, his now Wife, and to enable him to marry again, and for other Purposes therein mentioned, is committed.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Owners and Proprietors of Houses and Lands within the Borough of Stock-bridge, in the County of Southampton, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Borough of Slockbridge, in the County of Southampton, is an

ancient Borough, and a Borough by Prescription, and the Right of Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the said Borough is in Householders paying Scotland Lot, and not receiving Alms, and the Petitioners, if not solely, principally because the Right of Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the said Borough was confined within the Limits of the said Borough, have invested their Property in the Purchase of Houses and Lands in the same Borough, and are now Proprietors and Owners of the same; and that the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Bill has been brought into the House, and is now depending,

o

by which, should it pass into a Law, the Value of their Property will be very much depreciated, the usual and ancient Mode of Election in the said Borough being intended, by the Provisions of the said Bill, to be essentially altered; and that, by the Minutes taken before a Select Committee, appointe to try and determine the Merits of the last Election of Members of Parliament for the said Borough, it appears that some of the Voters at such Election, but all of whom were in One Interest, and voted for John Color and John Scott, Esquires, were alledged to have been guilty of Bribery and Corruption, yet the Petitioners submit to the House, that their Rights, Franchises, and Interests ought not to be so materially affected, as they will be, should the said Bill pass into a Law, for the Crimes of which others have been guilty, and to the Commission of which the Petitioners were neither directly nor indirectly privy, but, that if any Punishment has been incurred, and is fit to be inflicted, it should fall only on the Guilty, and should extend only to the Personal Disability of such of the Electors as can be proved to have made an improper Use of their Franchise: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, and that the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, against the said Bill, and upon the Matters contained in this their Petition.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being proposed, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for the preventing of Bribery and Corruption in the Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Stoclcbridge, in the County of Southampton, be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit;

The House was moved, That the Entry in the Journal of the House, of the 26th Day of April 1775, of the Proceedings of the House, in relation to the Bill to incapacitate certain Persons, therein mentioned, from voting at Elections of Members to serve in Parliament; and for preventing Bribery and Corruption in the Election of Members to serve in Parliament, for the Borough of Hindon, in the County of Wilts, might be read.

taking the Ground, are liable to receive Damage in blowing Weather. — And being asked. Whether there are Interruptions and Delays in delivering the Coals in blowing Weather? he said. Very great, from the strong Easterly Winds preventing the light Craft from coming down the River. — And being asked, What was the longest Time he ever was without Craft coming down the River from Maldon he said. Seven Days; but he has delivered a Cargo in Three Days. — And being asked, Whether a Canal leading from Colliers Reach to Potman's capable of receiving Ships drawing 15 Feet Water, would remedy the Evils he has stated arising from the Anchorage in Collier''s Reach ? he said, Yes; and would considerably reduce the Expence in Wear and Tear, Anchors, Cables, and Hawsers, and the Hull of the Vessel. — And being asked, If Cables are not, in some Instances, parted in Collier's Reach he said, He was on board a Ship that broke her Cable last Year from the Strength of the Tide. — And being asked, If Vessels ever navigated from Collier's Reach to the Town of Fullbridge? he said. Yes; Vessels of 50 or 60

Tons Burthen, but only at Spring Tides. — And being asked, If Vessels of more than 50 or 60 Tons can navigate to Fullbridge? he said, Not with Safety. — And being asked, If a Canal was formed from Collier's Reach to Maldon, of Depth equal to the Water at Collier's Reach, would it admit Vessels at ordinary Tides up to Maldon? he said, Yes; Vessels of 200 Tons Burthen, if a Shoal at Collier's Reach was taken away. — And being asked, Whether he knew of any Vessel being lost in Colliers Reach? he said. No. — And being asked, If he knew of any material Damage being done there which might not have happened elsewhere in the same Weather? he said Yes; from the breaking of Anchors and Hedges by the rapid Tides.

Mr. John Rennie, an Engineer, being examined, was asked, What Means he has in Contemplation to remedy the Grievance complained of at by

Mr. Barnard ? he said, By making a Cut from the Canal to the River Blackwater, and from thence scouring out the River to Heybridge Mill, and also to make a Cut from the Tail of Heybridge Mill, to near Fullbridge, under the Line of the proposed Canal, which will cross the same by an Aqueduct under which the Barges may navigate, except in Spring Tides. — And being asked, If the present Navigation to Heybridge is not an Open Navigation? he said, Yes. — And being asked, At what Part of the Spring Tides it is that Barges will be prevented from passing up to the Mill at Heybridge? he said, At the Height of the Tide, and for a Day or Two before and after, but that depended, in a great Measure, on Winds; if the Wind blew down Channel, the Water would not rise so high. — And being asked, If he did not suppose that the Navigation of the River Blackwater to Heybridge would be injured ? he said, The Navigation of the River Blackwater to Heybridge will certainly be injured, but the additional Accommodation arising from the new Cut will be more than adequate to the Injury it may receive. — And being asked, In what Manner? he said, The Interruption that Vessels meet with in navigating the River,

prevents them from going, except in Times of Tide, and consequently confines them to that Space only, whereas by the proposed Cut they will be able to navigate at all Times, whether Tide is up or not. — And being asked, If the Coal Wharf at Heybridge will have any Communication by Water with the Potman Cut ? he said, It will have no Communication with the Potman Cut, except by a Road being made; but when the Cut from the Tail of the Mill to Fullbridge is navigated, the Barges may then come alongside the Wharf* — And being asked, If it will be of the same Use to the Proprietors of Mills and Wharfs to navi-

gate the Tail Cut at Neap Tides at Heybridge Mill, as it is now ? he said. He was informed that the present Tail Water of Heybridge Mill was only navigable in Spring Tides, but the proposed Cut will be navigable at Neap Tides, and in that Case will be an equal Accommodation to the Proprietors of the Wharfs. — And being asked, If there is the same Convenience of loading and unloading of Vessels in Neap Tides at Fullbridge, as in Spring Tides? he said, If the Vessel has got to Fullbridge during the Spring Tide, and is to be loaded or unloaded against the Time of next Spring, it will certainly be most advantageous to navigate with Neap Tides; but if the Vessel is to be loaded or unloaded during a Spring Tide, it certainly would be less advantageous. —

And being asked, What is the Depth of Water at Collier's Reach ? he said, To the best of his Recollection, 13 Feet on the Bar. — And being asked, If there was 13 Feet Water in the Reach, how could there be 15 Feet Water in the Bason? he said, By raising it Two Feet. — And being asked, How that Water is to be obtained? He said, By locking down from above, from the Chelmer. — And being asked,

What Locks there are to be on the Potman Cut from Beleigh Mill? he said, One at Colliers Reach, One at Heybridge Causeway, and probably One at Beleigh Mill.

— And being asked. If there is to be any Lock between Heybridge Mill and Wharf, and the Cut? he said, None; but there will be a Stop Gate. — And being asked. Where the Potman Cut is meant to enter into the Chelmer at Beleigh Mill ? he said, Between Beleigh Mill and the Flood Gates. — And being asked, If that would not be a Hindrance to the Proprietor of Beleigh Mill to enlarge and extend his Mill, if it could be done ? he said, It does not appear it would; but he does not see any Objection to carrying the Cut higher if that is made an Obstacle. — And being asked. How far higher ? he said, That will depend on the Extent of the Accommodation the Proprietors mean to give.

Sir George Jackson accordingly reported from the said Committee, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, which they had directed to be reported to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the same, together with an Appendix thereunto, in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Report was read; and is as followed; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Edward Falkner, Esquire, being examined, said, That the Trade and Commerce of the Town of Liverpool, and the various Manufactures in its Neighbourhood, have of late Years greatly increased, and were continuing to do so, till the Stagnation of Credit, which has lately taken place, both there, and in other Parts of the Kingdom, checked the same, and occasioned serious Alarms of further Inconvenience.

And being further examined, he said, That in the Event of such a Want of Credit being even of a short Duration, there is great Reason to apprehend the Town of Liverpool will be greatly injured thereby, and that the Manufacturers and Traders throughout the County of Lancaster will feel the Effects of it to a very great Extent, by which the Interests of the Public and of Individuals will be materially affected. — Then,

Mr. Henry Brown, Attorney, being examined, said, That he officiates for the Town Clerk, and is acquainted with the Estate of the Corporation, and he thinks it will be much lessened in its Value if such a Want of Credit should take place as is mentioned by Mr. Falkner.

And being further examined, he said, That this alarmfog Evil may, he conceives, be remedied by

Authority being given to the Corporation of the said Town to issue Negotiable Notes for different Sums of Money, in the Whole considerably below the Value of their Estates, after making Allowance for their present Debts, the Notes to be payable, with lawful Interest thereon, or otherwise, at a Time to be limited; Provision being made that the Estate of the said Corporation shall be subjected, after paying the existing Debt due, to the Discharge of such Notes at the Period at which they shall become payable. — Then,

Clayton Tarleton, Esquire, Mayor of Liverpool, produced to your Committee,

A General Account and Valuation of the Estate and Revenue belonging to the Corporation of Liverpool, taken the 21 st of March 1793: And also,

An Account of Money received by the Corporation of Liverpool for Fines for the Renewal of Leases, from 3783 to 1792; specifying the Average for that Period, and also the Average for the last Seven Years: And also,

A Statement of the Town's Duties, Fines for the Renewal of Leases, Graving Dockage, Anchorage, and Ground Rents, received by the Corporation of Liverpool, from 1783 to 1792:

Which Papers are annexed in the Appendix to this Report, Numbers 1, 2, and 3.

Mr. John Foster, Surveyor to the Corporation of Liverpool, was then called; and being asked, What is the Nature of the Fines received for the Renewal of Leases? he said, It is a Fine which the Corporation charge for the Renewal of those Lives which drop in the Leases. — And being asked, For what Term the Corporation Leases are usually granted ? he said, The Leases are granted for Three Lives, and Twenty-one Years after the Death of the last Life. — And being asked, What is the Nature of the Ground Rents received by the Corporation? he said, Upon the taking up of any Lease under the Corporation, they charge an Annual Ground Rent, which is generally One Shilling per Yard, for the Front of any Building erected on their Land; and this is invariably the same, whether the Houses are good ones or bad ones; it is valued from the Front of the House. — And being asked, Whatsis the Nature of the Rents for Buildings in Possession let to Tenants at Will? he said, They arise from Buildings, and other Premisses; Dwelling Houses, Warehouses, Stables, Shops, Ac-compting Houses, and Offices; they are let free of Taxes, and generally free of Repairs; the great Bulk of this Property has lately been purchased by the Corporation for the Purpose of public Improvements, and the Tenants of many of the Premisses are permitted to enjoy their Leases (for several of them have Leases in them) at the old Rents, which are the low Rents, till the Premisses are actually wanted to carry on the Improvements; many of them are not taken down, because the Corporation have bought so much Property, as to take the Advantage of their own Improvements. — And being further examined, he said, That he does not conceive the Repairs' upon this Property exceed too/, a Year, or the Insurance more than 50/. — The Witness further said, That at least Three Parts of the Whole are kept in Repair by the Tenants, and the other Fourth Part has been built within the Space of Five Years. — And being asked, What is the Nature of the Rents for Land in Possession let to Tenants at Will ? he said, It is Land belonging to the Corporation, let for the Purpose of Timber Yards and Ship Carpenters Yards. — And being asked, If there are any Charges upon that Property? he said, None; the Tenants pay all Taxes. — And being asked, What is the Nature of the Town's Duties ? he said, He don't think himself perfectly competent to answer that Question, but as he understands it, it is a Toll paid at the Custom House upon Goods imported and exported, and accounted for to Von. 48.

the Town; the neat Income is 12,180/. 75, — And Report on being further examined, he. said. He has heard; that Liverpool the Right of the Corporation to the Collection of some FetlUon* Part of those Duties is disputed. — Then,

Mr. Henry Broum was again called, and being asked,

Whether the Right of the Corporation to collect the Town's Duties was disputed? he said, The Title itself to the Duties is not disputed; but a certain Description of Persons claim an Exemption from the Payment of those Duties — that Description of Persons is the Eree-men and Citizens of London, and the Claim to this Exemption is now in a Course of Litigation. — And being asked, What would be the Difference in the Amount of those Duties, supposing the Privilege claimed by the Citizens of London should be established? he said, He could not pretend, to say.--Then,

Mr. John Foster was again called, and being asked;

What is the Nature of the Income arising from the Graving Docks? he said, Every Vessel entering those Docks for Repair, pays a certain Tonnage for the Benefit they receive from the Use of them. — And being asked, Whether there are any Charges upon this Article ? he said, Some very trifling Repairs to the Graving Docks. — And being asked. What is the Nature of the Income arising from the Anchorage? he said, All Vessels, he believes, pay a Toll for anchoring in the River. — And being asked, What is the Nature of the Small Tolls, called Ingates and Outj-gates ? he said, It is a Duty that is paid to the Corporation for various Articles brought into, and carried out of, the Town of Liverpool. — And being asked,

Under what Title this Duty is collected ? he said, It is a Manerial Right; every Cart the Property of a Non Freeman is liable to a Duty of Four Pence, but it is very loosely collected. — And being asked, What is the Nature of the Income arising from the Weighing Machine? he said, It arises from the Profits of a public W'eighing Machine in the Hands of the Corporation. — And being asked, Wrhat is the Nature of the Rents of Seats in Saint George's Church he said.

The Rents are received for Pews in that Church, which belong to the Corporation. — And being asked,

What is the Nature of the Arrears of Interest received from the Parish of Liverpool? he said, It is Annual Interest upon a Sum of Money borrowed by the Parish from the Corporation; the Parish now stand indebted to the Corporation in the Sum of 4,000l., which, at Five per Cent, amounts to 200 per Annum. —

And being asked, Whether there are any Arrears of Interest due upon the Annual Interest of the Bond Debts ? he said, None that he knows of, nor to the Annuitants. — And being further examined, he said,

The Annuities are principally, if not all, upon One Life. — And being asked, What are the Annual Outgoings to be paid by the Corporation of Liverpool? he said, Salaries to the following Officers, viz. The Mayor 500 Guineas, the Treasurer 500 /., the Secretary 150/. Two Surveyors 2,50/., the Sword-bearer 80/., Five Head Constables 50 Guineas a Year each, Recorder 40/., Deputy Recorder 30/.,

Two Chaplains at 200 Guineas each, and the Gaoler 80 /. — And being asked, What is the Annual Expence of paving? he said, It has for several Years past been very considerable (but he can't state the Amount) the Corporation having opened several Roads and Avenues into the Town, and paved them; the Pavements of the Town are now in very great Order and good Repair; the Corporation are not bound to the Repair of more than a very small Part of the Town, though they have been in the Habit of doing it; they are only bound to repair (as he understands it) the ancient Highways and Streets of the Town, which are very few indeed.

Mr. Charles Eyes, Surveyor of the Pavements of the Town of Liverpool, was then called; and being asked,

What

Report on ^Liverpool Petition.

What is the Annual Expence of paving the Town to be paid by the Corporation ? he said, It is a very difficult Matter to state, as the Corporation have, for the last Five Years, laid out a great Sum of Money, in the Repair of the Pavements and Sewers, to the Amount of 20,000l. but the Pavior employed by the Corporation has offered to contract to keep the Pavements in Repair for the Sum of 3001, Annum; he being allowed to collect a small Toll of Four^Pence per Annum from each House in Addition to that Sum: There aTe about Seven or Eight Thflu-sand Houses in Liverpool, but they don't all pay the Four Pence, as some of them are poor. — And being asked, Whether there is any Annual fcxpence incurred by keeping the Sewers in Repair? he said, About 30 /. per Anrtum. — Then,

Mr. Henry Brawn was again called, and being asked, Whether the Corporation is bound by Charter, or otherwise, to pay any of the Salaries specified ? he said, Not that he knows of — And being asked, Whether the Corporation Cash Book is in Town, or any other Document, by which the Annual Income and Expenditure of the Corporation will appear? he said, No'. — Then,

Mr. John Foster was again called, and being asked, How the Calculation was formed of the Value of the Reversionary Interest of the Houses and other Buildings erected upon Land held in Lease under the Corporation? be said, At Five Years Purchase upon the Annual Rent of those Buildings erected upon the Corporation Estate, being, as he conceives, a low Computation on the Difference between Leasehold and Freehold; and that lie is confirmed in this Opinion, from his Official Situation as Surveyor to the Buildings: That he has had repeated Offers for a greater Allowance (by which he rneans more Years Purchase than Five) from Persons who were in full Lease; and he is confident that he has had Offers sometimes for as much as Eight Years on New Buildings. — And being further examined, he said, That the Rents amount to 84,280/. per Annum, which he states from a Schedule of the Property taken by himself and Mr. Eyes; and he is of Opinion, that if the Reversionary Interest bad been brought to Market Six Months ago, it would have fetched its Valuation, namely 421,000l.

The Witness then produced to your Committee, a Valuation of Houses, Warehouses, and other Buildings, upon the Estate belonging to the Corporation of Liverpool, and leased out by them for Three Lives and Twenty-one Years; which is annexed to this Report, Appendix N* 4.

And the Witness being asked, What was the Quantity of Land leased, but not built upon? he said, About 350 Statute Acres. — And' being asked, What was the Annual Value thereof? he said, The Corporation charge about a Shilling for each Statute Acre, which amounts to 17/. 10s. per Annum: This is a reserved Rent exclusive of Fines, and the Land is let upon Three Lives. — And being asked, Upon what Principle he formed this Calculation? he said, At 250/. per Acre; the Difference between Lease-

hold and Freehold *Tt is let at present in Herbage, but he is of Opinion, from its lying so contiguous to the Town, that it is of the Average Value he has mentioned. — That at the greatest Distance from the Town, he estimates the Land to be worth 150/. per Acre, but nearer the Town, from 600l. to 800l. per Acre; and he has known an Instance of 900 /. per Acre being asked. — And the Witness added, That he means this for the Reversionary Interest in the-Land. — And being asked. How the Calculation was formed of the Value of the Annual Ground Rents ? he said, at Thirty Years Purchase; and that those Ground Rents are for Buildings and Lands. — And being asked, Upon what Principle the Calculation was formed of the Value of the Buildings in Possession let to Tenants at Will? he said, At Twenty Years Purchase upon the Nett Rent. — And being asked, Upon what Principle the Value of the Land in Fee Simple let to Tenants at Will was calculated ? he said. At Thirty Years Purchase. — And being asked, From whence the Amount of the Money owing for Land sold, was collected? he said, From the Corporation Books: And he added, That the Corporation are in Possession of the Land, and there are many Buildings erected upon it. — And being asked. How the Value of the Land in Fee Simple unoccupied, and intended to be sold, was calculated ? he said, In proportion to the Land already disposed of in similar Situations for the Purposes of Building. — And being asked, Upon what Principle the Value of the Strand of the River, to low Water, was calculated ? he said, At a less Rate than Land in a similar Situation, which was purchased by the Corporation. — That the Part purchased was intended for the Extension of the Docks, and the other Part lies adjoining to it, and is equally convenient for the Purpose. — And being asked, How the Calculation was formed of the Value of the Town's Duties? -he said, At Twenty Years Purchase, subject to the Observations formerly stated. — And being asked, Upon what Calculation the Value of the Graving Docks is estimated? he said, At Twenty Years Purchase. — And being further examined, he said, That the Value of the Anchorage, and also of the small Tolls, Weighing Machine, and Seats in Saint George's Church, are likewise calculated at Twenty Years Purchase. — And being asked, From whence the Amount of the Money due from the Parish of Liverpool, was stated ? he said, From the Treasurer's Books. — And being asked, Whether, in the Evidence he had given with respect to the Value of the Corporation Estate, he had not formed his Computation with a View to the late Increase, and probable further Increase of the Prosperity of the Town ? he said, In his Judgment it would have sold Six Months ago for what he had estimated it at; and, that he calculated upon the past Increase, and not upon the future. — And being asked, Whether the Annuities are included in the Sum of 355,159/. stated, in the first Account delivered in by the Mayor, as the Money due upon Bond from the Corporation of on the

21 st of March 1793? he said, No.

to be made, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for making and maintaining a Navigation from, or nearly from, the Town of Chelmsford, in the County of Essev, to a Place called Collier's Reach, in or near the River in the said County; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners find that their Rights, Interests, and Property, will be materially ana essentially injured, if the said Bill should be suffered to pass into a Law as it now stands, the Clauses in the said Bill not having provided adequate Compensation for the great Injuries the Petitioners are likely to sustain in respect to their Lands, Mills, Wharfs, Quays, Granaries, Store Houses, and other Property: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves, or Counsel, against such Parts of the said Bill as may be injurious to their several and respective Rights, Interests, and Property.

Mr. Samuel Thornton reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor and Burgesses of the Town of Kingston upon Hull, the Guild or Brotherhood of Masters and Pilots Seamen of the Trinity House of Kingston upon Hull, under their respective Common Seals, and of the Merchants, Ship Owners, and principal Inhabitants, of the Town and Port of Kingston upon Hull, and others interested in the Trade and Shipping of the said Port, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's' Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the Fourteenth Year of His present Majesty's Reign, intituled, "An Act for making and establishing " Public Quays or Wharfs at Kingston upon , for " the better securing His Majesty's Revenue of Customs,

" and for the Benefit of Commerce in the Port of " Kingston upon Hull; for making a Bason or Dock,

" with Reservoirs, Sluices, Roads, and other Works, for " the Accommodation of Vessels using the said Port,

" and for appropriating certain Lands belonging to His Majesty, and fcr applying certain Sums of Money " out of His Majesty's Customs at the said Port, for " those Purposes, and for establishing other necessary " Regulations within the Town and Port of Kingston " upon Hull," was read: And,

Hugh Ker, Esquire, being examined, said, That the Trade of the Port of Hull has of late Years so much increased, and still appears to be in a progressive State, and the Ships and Vessels which frequent the same are become so numerous, and of such large Dimensions, that the Advantage proposed by the New Dock cannot be obtained in the present Dock, which is not capable of properly accommodating Two Thirds of the Ships belonging to and frequenting the Port, and those which do obtain Admission into the Dock, are in so crowded a State that the cleansing of the Dock is thereby rendered impracticable, and several Vessels are prevented from going into the same to unlade their Cargoes, and others are detained within it, and retarded from prosecuting their Voyages, to the great Detriment of all Persons concerned in the Trade and Commerce of the said Port, and of His Majesty's Revenue; and, in case of Fire, the total Destruction of the Shipping and the Town of Hull is almost inevitable.

That in case the said Bason or Dock should be extended, such Losses, Damages, and Inconveniences might be prevented, and a safe and commodious Station be provided for the harbouring, lading, and unlading of the Ships and Vessels resorting to the said Port.

That the Revenues of the Dock Company are amply sufficient for making a necessary Extension of the present Dock; and that great Part of the Land, for making the said Dock, and also the Sum of 15,000 /. have been given to the said Company by the said Act; but the said Company have not advanced more than 250 /. upon each Share, and by the Profits arising from the Sale of Lands purchased for the Purposes of the Act (which were not then wanted) and the Rates, from the great Increase of Shipping, they have already divided more than double the Amount of their Advance, with Interest thereupon at Five per Centum per Annum.

Vol. 48.

And the Witness further said, That it is conceived the said Company ought, from the increased Produce of the Rates, to make the necessary Extension of the said Dock for the Accommodation of all the Shipping coming to the said Port; and on being applied to for that Purpose, they have admitted that there is not sufficient Room in the present Dock for the increased Number of Ships, but refuse to provide any additional Dock, or to extend the one already made, but upon Conditions which relate to the Lands and Revenues of His Majesty, and which do not seem reasonable, as the said Company have already a large Portion of the Land granted by the said Act remaining, which adjoins the said Dock, and extends from thence towards the River Humber, and is on that Account, and in every Respect, the best situated for the Accommodation and Convenience of the Tow n, and of the Trade and Commerce of the Port.

And the Witness added, That the Profits upon the Shares in the present Dock, have for some Years been Annually increasing, and in the Year 1792 produced 82/. 5 s.for every Share; and that the said Rates and Duties will form an adequate Fund, not only to produce a reasonable Profit to the said Company, but also to defray the Expence of providing sufficient Accommodation for the increased Number of Vessels frequenting the said Port, without which the present flourishing State of the Trade and Commerce of the said Town, and of His Majesty's Revenue, may soon be diverted into some other Channel: — Then,

Mr. Edward Anderson, one of the Auditors of the last Years Accounts of the Dock Company: And,

Mr. Thomas Robinson, a Merchant at Hull, being examined, confirmed the Whole of Mr. Ker a Evidence: — And,

Mr. John Green, a Ship Owner at Hull, and Mr.

Thomas Gleadon, a Ship Builder at Hull, confirmed such Part of the Evidence of Mr. Ker as respects the confined State of the Dock, and the Necessity of extending the same.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging the Bason or Dock of the Port of Kingston upon Hull: And that Mr. Samuel Thornton and Sir Adam Fergusson do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A MESSAGE from the Lords, by Mr. and Mr. Graves:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for granting to His Majesty the Sum of Two hundred thousand Pounds, to be issued and paid to the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, to be by them placed to the Account of the Commissioners for the Reduction of the National Debt; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to explain and amend an Act, made in the Sixth Year of the Reign of His late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, "An Act for erecting Piers in, and " for repairing, and keeping in Repair, the Harbour of " Littlehampton, called Arundel Port, in the County of Sussex," and for empowering the Commissioners acting under the said Act to improve the Navigation of the River Arun, from the said Harbour to the Town of Arundel, in the said County; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for altering the Provisions of an Act, passed in the Twenty-second Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for repealing the Duties payable for Beer and Ale above Six Shillings the Barrel, exclusive of the Duties of Excise, and not exceeding Eleven Shillings the Barrel, exclusive of such Duties, and for other Purposes therein mentioned, so far as respects the Quality of Table Beer, brewed by Common Brewers; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for amending, widening, and repairing, the Road from Clay Hill, in the Turnpike Road between stone and Chipping Norton, in (the County of Oxford, over Heyford Bridge, to the Water Lane, in the Town of Bicester, in the said County, and from Bicester aforesaid to the Turnpike Road in Weston on the Green, in the said County; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for repairing, widening, and altering the Road from the Turnpike Road between Gateshead and near Lobley Hill, in the Parish of Whickham, in the County of Durham, to Burtry Ford, in the Parish of Stanhope, in the same County, and a Branch from the said Road, near Bryans Leap, in the County of Durham, to the Corbridge Turnpike Road near Black-hedley, in the County of Northumberland, and another Branch from the said Road at Wolsingham, in the County of Durham, to Crosgale, near the City of Durham; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for dividing and inclosing the Open and Common Fields, Meadows, Common Fens, and other Commonable Lands and Waste Grounds, in the several Parishes of Covenham Saint Bartholomew and Covenham Saint Mary, in the County of Lincoln; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for dividing and inclosing certain Commons or Waste Lands within the Townships of Moreton and Wil-brighton, otherwise Wilberton, in the Parish of Gnosall, in the County of Stafford; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from, or nearly from, the Town of Grantham, in the County of Lincoln, to the River Trent, near Nottingham Trent Bridge, and also a Collateral Cut from the said intended Canal at or near Cropwell Butler, to the Town of Bingham, both in the County of Nottingham; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from the Oxford Canal Navigation at Braunston, in the County of Northampton, to join the River Thames, at or near Brentford, in the County of Middlesex, and also certain Collateral Cuts from the said intended Canal; with some Amendments; to which Amendments the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House: And also,

And then the Messengers withdrew.

A Petition of John Taylor, Devisee in Trust of the real Estate of John Walker, deceased, within the Manor and Township of Armley, in the West Riding of the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner is informed, that certain Owners of Lands and Tenements, within the said Manor and Township of Armley, have presented a Petition for Leave to bring in a Bill for dividing and inclosing a certain Parcel of Waste Ground, called Armley Moor, and other Waste Ground, within the said Manor and Township, w'hich Bill has been read a Second Time; and that the Petitioner conceives that an Inclosure of the said Moor and Waste Ground would be productive of no Advantage to any of the Proprietors claiming a Right of Common thereon, but, on the contrary, would very materially injure and prejudice their respective Estates in the said Township, by laying upon the Township the Burthen of making, maintaining, and repairing, the necessary new Roads, which must be set out to a considerable Extent over the said Moor and Waste Ground, and also by increasing the Poors Rate, in as much as the Petitioner conceives that the Inhabitants of the said Town of Armley, who are very numerous, and principally poor Manufacturers of Broad Woollen Cloth, receive considerable Benefit and Advantage from the present Open State of the said Moor and Waste Ground, particularly in having Tenters and Frames, to stretch and dry their Cloth Warps and Wool, after it has been dyed, put up and fixed, upon the said Moor and Waste Ground, which Privileges and Advantages have hitherto conduced to alleviate the Distresses and Hardships of the said poor Manufacturers in the said Township of Armley, and which, if the said Inclosure takes place, they will be totally deprived of, and reduced to Poverty and Want: And therefore praying, That he may be heard by his Counsel and Witnesses against the said Bill, or that the Petitioner may have such further Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

and that the Petitioners, and particularly the poorer Manufacturers in the said Township, who are very numerous, have received great Comfort and Benefit from the Privileges they have hitherto enjoyed of fixing Tenters and Frames, to stretch and dry their Cloth Warps and Wool, after it has been dyed, upon the said Common and Waste Ground, and from many other Advantages resulting to them from the present Open State of the said Common and Waste Ground, and the Petitioners conceive an Inclosure of the said Common and Waste Ground will not only totally deprive them and the said poor Manufacturers of the said Privileges and Advantages which they and their Ancestors have hitherto enjoyed, but also be it further very material Injury to the Petitioners, by laying upon them, and the other Inhabitants of the said Township, the Burthen of maintaining and upholding the necessary new Roads which must be set out to a considerable Extent over the said Common, and by depriving the said Inhabitants of Armley of the necessary Materials for repairing as well the same new Roads, as those which they are now obliged to maintain, and also by increasing the Poors Rate, which is at present very high, inasmuch as it will deprive the said poor Manufacturers of the said Privileges and Advantages, and also of that Pasturage upon the said Common which they have hitherto much depended upon: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by their Counsel and Witnesses, to oppose the said Bill, and that the Petitioners may have such further Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee, to whom the Bill for dividing and inclosing the Common and Waste Grounds within the Manor or Township of Armley, in the Parish of Leeds, in the West Riding of the County of York, is committed; and the Petitioners are to be then heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petitions, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petitions.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. John Thompson, an Engineer, being examined, said. That, by Surveys lately taken, it appears that a Navigable Canal may be conveniently made from the River Dunn Cut, near Stainforth, in the County of York, through the several Parishes mentioned in the Petition, to join and communicate with the River Trent, at or near Keadby, in the County of Lincoln; and also, that another Navigable Cut may be made, branching from the said first-mentioned Canal upon Thorne Common, near the Sluice, to join and commu-, nicate with the said River Dunn, at or near a Place called Hangman Hill, in the said County of York: — And the Witness further said, That the making and maintaining of such navigable Canals, together with such Collateral Cuts as may be found necessary, and also proper Railways communicating the rewith, together with necessary Roads and Towing Paths on the Banks thereof, will be the Means of opening a Communication with several considerable Iron Works, and other Manufactories, and several Mines of Coals and other Minerals, and will, in other Respects, be of great Public Utility.

And that Mr. Wilberforce and Mr. Duncombe do prepare, and bring in, the same.
