in Great Britain shall have been reduced to One Million Five hundred Thousand Pounds, the Surplus of the said Net Proceeds, after such Provisions made as aforesaid, and after Payment of a Dividend after the said Rate of Ten Pounds per Centum per Annum on the said Capital Stock, and the said Annual Sum of Five hundred Thousand Pounds into the Exchequer, and after making good all former Deficiencies in the said Annual Payments (if any such shall happen) shall be applied and disposed of in Manner following'(that is to say) One Sixth Part of the said Surplus shall be reserved and retained by the said Company for their own Use, and applied in Augmentation of the Dividends on their said Capital Stock, and the Residue of the said Surplus shall be set apart, and, from Time to Time, paid into the Receipt of His Majesty's Exchequer, to be applied as Parliament shall direct, without any Interest to be paid to the Company in respect or for the Use thereof, but nevertheless to be considered and declared as a Collateral Security to the said Company for the said Capital Stofck," and for the Dividend of Ten per Centum per Annum in respect thereof, not exceeding the Sum of Twelve Millions of Pounds Sterling, and that the Excess of such Payments (if any) beyond that Amount, shall be deemed and declared the Property of the Public, and at the Disposal of Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, Th^t, if the Company's Debts in India, after the same shall have been reduced to Two Crores of Current Rupees, or Two Millions of Pounds Sterling, shall be again increased beyond that Amount, or if their Bond Debt in Great Britain, after the same shall have been reduced to One Million Five hundred Thousand Pounds, shall be again increased beyond that Sum, then, and so often as either of those Cases shall happen, there shall be reserved and set apart, out of the said Net Proceeds, next after Payment of the said Dividend of Ten Pounds per Centum on the said Capital Stock, but in Preference to any other Application thereof, the Sum of Five hundred Thousand Pounds per Annum, to be appropriated to the Reduction of such

new Debts respectively, until the Debts in India shall be again reduced to Two Crores of Current Rupees, and the said Bond Debt in Great Britain to One Million Five hundred Thousand Pounds.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, to secure to the Company at all Times the Means of carrying on their Trade with Credit and Advantage, it is expedient to make Provision for so arranging the Payment into the Exchequer, of the aforesaid Proportion of any Annual Balance, or Surplus of the said Net Proceeds becoming due and payable there, as to authorize the Company to retain a Sum, not exceeding Two hundred Thousand Pounds, for their Current Cash for so long Time, after the End of each Year, as may be reasonably deemed sufficient for their receiving new Monies in the Course of their Trade to replace the Sums so retained; and, for the like Purpose, that a Power should be vested in the High Treasurer, or Commissioners of the Treasury, upon the Requisition of the Company, to postpone any of the said Half Yearly Payments into the Exchequer for a reasonable Time to be limited in that Behalf, on its being satisfactorily shewn to him or them that the Affairs of the Company require such Postponement.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, during the further Term in the exclusive Trade, the Company shall be restricted from making any other Distribution of the Sum of Money and Stock now standing upon their Books, under the Title of " The Company's Separate Fund," (the said Sum now amounting, with Interest thereon, computed to the 1st Day of March 1793, to Four hundred and Sixty-seven

A. 1793.

thousand Eight hundred and Ninety-six Pounds Seven Shillings and Four Pence, and the said Stock being East India Stock, to the Sum of Nine thousand Seven hundred and Fifty Pounds) or any future Interest or Dividends arising the reby, otherwise than as hereafter is mentioned (that is to say) That, after Payment into His Majesty's Exchequer of the Two first Instalments of Two hundred and Fifty thousand Pounds each, which will accrue due to the Public on the 1st Day of July 1793, and the 1st Day of January 1794, or otherwise, after setting apart a sufficient Sum for such Payment, it shall be lawful for the said Company, out of the said separate Fund, and the growing Income thereof, to make and declare a Dividend, or Dividends, after the Rate of Ten Shillings per Centum per Annum, on the present, or any future Amount of their Capital Stock, which said Dividend, or Dividends, shall be paid and payable to the said Company, over and above any other Dividend or Dividends, which shall become due in respect to the said Capital Stock.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it is proper to make Provision for so limiting the granting of Pensions, or increasing the Salaries of Officers, or creating any New Establishments at Home as may effectually protect the Company's Funds in Great Britain from any unnecessary Charges.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Court of Directors of the said Company shall, within the first Fourteen Sitting Days next after the 30th Day of March in every Year, lay before both Houses of Parliament an Account, made up according to the latest Advices, of the Annual Produce of the Revenues of the British Territories in India, distinguishing the same under the respective Heads thereof, at their several Presidencies or Settlements, with the Amount of their Sales of Goods and Stores within the Limits of their exclusive Trade, and of all their Annual Disbursements within' the said Limits, distinguishing the same under the respective Heads thereof, and the Amount of their Debts Abroad, with the Rates of Interest they respectively carry, and the Annual Amount of such Interest, and the State of their Effects at each Presidency or Settlement, and in China, consisting of Cash and Bills in the Treasuries, Goods and Stores, and Debts owing to the Company, according to the latest Advices, together with a List of their several Establishments Abroad, and the Salaries and Allowances payable by the said Company at each Presidency or Settlement, and in China; and also, another Annual Account, made up to the 1st Day of March next preceding the Delivery thereof to Parliament, containing the Amount of the Proceeds of the Company's Sales at Home, and of their Commercial and other Charges and Payments in Great Britain, under the several Heads thereof, and of their Bond Debts, and Simple Contract Debts, with the Rates of Interest they respectively carry, Rnd the Annual Amount of such Interest, and the State of the Cash remaining in the Treasury, and other Effects appertaining to the Company at Home or a-float.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in the present Circumstances of the East India Company, they should be enabled to raise a Sum of Money, by adding One Million Pounds Capital Stock to their present Capital of Five Million Pounds, so as to make their whole Capital Stock in future Six Millions, and that such Addition be made by opening a Subscription to the Amount of the said One Million Pounds Capital Stock, at a Rate to be fixed for every One hundred Pounds of such Capital Stock, or at such Rate as the Court of Directors of the said Company, with the Approbation of the Commissioners of the Treasury, shall direct; and that the Subscribers to the same be declared entitled to the like Profits, Benefits, and Privileges, in respect thereof, as the Proprietors of

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Richard Bowsher being examined, said, That the several Streets, Lanes, Ways, Passages, and Places, within that Part of the Parish of Walcot which is not within the Jurisdiction of the City of Bath, are very insufficiently paved, cleansed, lighted, and watched,

tion, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followed; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, William Wheeler, Esquire, being examined, said, That the Branch of Road leading from Bradford Brook, through Cursley Lane, to Mustatd Green, in de County of Worcester, is at present in a ruinous State, and that if

Present,

The KING'S most Excellent MAJESTY in Council*

1

It is this Day ordered by His Majesty in Council, That so much of the Order made at this Board on the 6th of this Instant February, as permits all Bye Boats, whether British or French, employed in the Conveyance of Letters and Passengers between Great Britain and France, or the Countries occupied by the Armies of France, to pass and re-pass, as heretofore, with their respective Complements of Men, be, and the same is hereby revoked and made void; and that no Ship or Vessel whatsoever belonging to any of His Majesty's Subjects, except such as are or may be emplpyed by His Majesty's Post Master General, in such Number as shall be approved of by One of His Majesty's Principal Secretaries of State, between the Ports of Great Britain and France, or between the Ports of this Kingdom and the Ports of the Countries occupied by the Armies of France, for the Purpose of conveying the Mails, and except such Ships or Vessels as are or may be employed by the Directors of the Post Offices in France, or in the Countries occupied by the Armies of France, in such Number as shall be approved of by One of His Majesty's Principal Secretaries of State, in consequence of any Agreement which has been or may be made for that Purpose, for conveying the Mails between the Ports of Great Britain and France, and the Countries occupied by the Armies of France, be permitted to clear out or sail for any of the Ports of France, or of the Countries occupied by the Armies of France, until further Order. — And His Majesty, with the Advice of His Privy Council, is hereby further pleased to order, That no Person or Persons whatever be permitted to embark on Board any of the before described Ships or Vessels employed in Carrying the Mails from this Kingdom to France, or the Countries occupied by the Armies of France, or to land in this Kingdom from any of the Ships or Vessels before described employed in bringing the Mails from France, or from the Countries occupied by the Annies of France, without such Person or Persons, being furnished with a Passport from One of His Majesty's Principal Secretaries of State. — And the Right honourable the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty's Treasury, the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty, and the Lord Warden of the Cinque Ports, are to give the necessary Directions herein as to them may respectively appertain.

(Signed)

W.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, An Act passed in the Twenty-sixth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for allowing a Drawback of the Duties upon Coals, used " in smelting Copper and Lead Ores, and in Fire ""Engines for draining Water out of the Copper " and Lead Mines, within the Isle of ," was

read, by which it appeared that the Amount of the Duty allowed to be drawn back by virtue of the said Act is limited to 1,5001, per Annum: And,

A Member present informed your Committee, That in Consequence of the said Drawback, which was granted on Account of the Want of Coals in the said Isle, Ores have been smelted with Coals brought there, the Drawback of the Duties on which has amounted to the Sum limited by the said Act.

Mr. George Pengree being examined, said, That there are still very large Veins of Copper Ore in the said Isle, capable of yielding great Quantities of Fine Copper, and which might be worked, if the Duty on all Coals imported into the said Isle for the Purpose of calcining or smelting such Copper Ore, and used in Fire Engines for draining Water out of the Mines of Copper and Lead in the said Isle, were drawn back without Limitation; but the said Ores are of so poor a Quality, that they will not bear the Expence of being carried to be smelted in Countries where Coals pay no Duty, nor can they bear the Expence of being smelted there with Coals, chargeable with the Duty for which no Drawback is allowed: That the Demand for Fine Copper is daily encreasing, on Account of the great Advantages arising from the Use of Copper in the Fastenings and Sheathing of Ships, and the Consumption is greater than what this Country produces.

Mr. Wilberforce reported from the Committee, to whom the Bill for making and maintaining a commodious Carriage Road from the Town of Bazvtry to the Town of Selby, in the West Riding of the County of York, was committed; That the Committee had examined the Allegations of the Bill, and found the same to be true; and that the Committee had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto, which they had directed him to report to the House, and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Amendments were Once read throughout, and then a Second Time, One by One; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, w'ere, with Amendments to several of them, agreed to by the House.

A Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, that the Mortgagees shall not be entitled to Principal or Interest till the Road is certified to be in good Repair.

And the said Clause was Twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, that Persons shall not be subject to more than One Third of the Tolls for passing through any One Turnpike, and that the Turnpikes shall not be nearer than Six Miles to each other.

And the said Clause was Twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrossed.

A Message by'Mr. Quarme, Yeoman Usher of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty's Commission, for declaring His Royal Assent to several Acts agreed upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate Attendance of this Honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;

Petition from A Petition of the there-undersigned Merchants,

Romsey Traders, and Inhabitants, of the Town of Romsey againstSouth- Infra, in the County of Southampton, and its Neigh-bour^&c r" bourhood, was presented to the House, and read; Bill,' Taking Notice of the Bill for abolishing certain Dues called Petty Customs, and for improving the Trade and Navigation of the Port of Southampton, for making a convenient Dock for the Security of Ships, for extending the Quays and Wharfs, and making Docks and Piers in the Harbour there, for regulating the Wharfage, and for imposing certain Duties for those Purposes, and for enabling the Corporation of the said Town to exchange certain Lands and Hereditaments; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners conceive the Accomplishment of the Objects of the said Bill would prove injurious to the Commercial Interests of the said Town of Southampton, and its Neighbourhood, by enhancing the heavy Duties already imposed on all Articles of Trade, by which the Petitioners, amongst others interested therein, would be materially affected, without receiving any adequate Advantage: And therefore praying. That the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

Petition from A Petition of the Merchants, Traders, Ship Owners,

Southamp- and Inhabitants of the Town of Southampton, Isle of a'ainu D* Wight, and Places adjacent, whose Names are there-pMt undersigned, was also presented to the House, and read; likewise Taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth, That by far the greatest Part of the Vo i, 48.

Merchants and Tradesmen of the Town of Southampton, who are unquestionably the best Judges of iheir own Interest, and who will, with others of the Petitioners, be most materially affected by the said Bill being passed into a Law, are, and have been for some Years past, entirely deprived of those Privileges, Immunities, and Advantages, originally intended them by the genuine Spirit of the Corporate Institution, by an impolitic and unjust Exclusion from any Share or Participation therein, contrary to those wise and ancient Maxims of Commercial Polity which have invariably produced the Affluence of Individuals, and the Wealth of Nations; and that the said Bill is brought into the House on the Petition of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Burgesses only of the said Town, a great Majority of whom are Persons wholly unconnected with any Kind of Trade or Commerce, and who are very incompetent to judge what will best tend to the Increase of Navigation, and Improvement of Trade, within the Town and Port of and that,

of late Years, the Promotion of Trade, and the Aggrandizement of the Merchant, the great Source of National Prosperity, has been the least Consideration of those who compose the Body Corporate of the said Town, by whose Protection and Succour they were originally designed to flourish, and, for these and the foregoing Reasons, it is seriously apprehended, that the Object of the said Bill, though colourably prefaced, cannot in Reality be intended to promote the Commercial Grandeur of the said Town, but to secure to the Members, composing the Corporation, Emoluments distinct and independent of the Interest of the Trading Inhabitants, and thereby effectually, and by the Legislative Authority, to bereave the Public of those Rights originally granted by His Majesty's Progenitors, Kings of England, for the Encouragement and Protection of Trade, to the Emporium of which the Town of Southampton, has, from its Situation, a just and natural Claim; and that it is the Opinion of the best and most experienced Navigators, that the Plan intended by the said Bill, for making a Bason for the Security of Ships at the said Port of Southampton, is chimerical and absurd, the present Harbour being the best possibly adapted by Nature for the safe Repose and Anchorage of the largest Ships coming to the Port, and which, by a very trifling Improvement, may be made to answer all the Purposes of a Bason, without any additional Burthen on Trade and Shipping: and that, besides the enormous, uncertain, unnecessary, and lasting Expence, which will be inevitably incurred by the making of such Bason, no Benefit or Advantage will be derived equivalent to the Imposts to be raised for making the same, forasmuch as Ships of considerable Burthen will not lay within the said Bason with the same Ease and Security as they now do on their natural Beds of Mud; and that the Quays and Wharfs of the said Town are not, as is pretended by the said Bill, the sole and exclusive Property of the Corporation, but the same are only holden in Trust by them for the Benefit and Advantage of the Inhabitants in general, and the Wharfage and Profits of the said Quays and Wharfs are appropriable not only to the Repairs of the same, but, if expedient or necessary, to their En-tension and Enlargement; and that the Corporation of the said Town have, for many Years past, received and possessed themselves of very considerable Sums of Money by their Receipts for Wharfage, sufficient to form a Fund for enlarging and improving the present Quays, and thereby to answer all the Purposes of an extensive Trade, without the Imposition of any additional Burthens; and that the Petitioners, Inhabitants of the said Town, understanding, from undeniable Testimony, that the Rents and Profits of the said Quays and Wharfs haye beep misapplied by the said

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Commonalty, Merchants, Traders, and Inhabitants, of the City of Winchester, in the County of Southampton, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for abolishing certain Dues, called Petty Customs, and for improving the Trade and Navigation of the Port of Southampton, for making a convenient Dock for the Security of Ships, for extending the Quays and Wharfs, and making Docks and Piers in the Harbour there, for regulating the Wharfage, and for imposing certain Duties for those Purposes, and for enabling the Corporation of the said Town to exchange certain Lands and Hereditaments; and Setting forth, That, if the said Bill be passed into a Law, the Trade of the City of Winchester, and of the Towns adjacent, will be greatly injured, as the Prices of all Articles will be considerably enhanced: And therefore praying, That they may not be burthened with any Rates or Taxes on such vessels as come within the River Itchin, it having ever been a free River unconnected, and at a considerable Distance from Southampton Quay, and, as the Petitioners cannot in the least be benefited by the Alterations proposed to be made in the said Bill relating to the Town and County of the Town of Southampton, that such Part of the said Bill as relates to them may not pass into a Law.

A Petition of the thCre-Undersigned Merchants, Petition from Traders, and Inhabitants of Stockbridg in the County Stockbridge of Southampton, was also presented to the House, and ®8a|nst read; likewise taking Notice of the said Bill; and t.^itar'bour, Setting forth, That the Petitioners, amongst other &c. Bill. Traders and Persons importing Goods into the Port of Southampton, and being obliged to have the same therefrom when imported, will, if the said Bill be passed into a Law, be most heavily aggrieved by the great Enhancement of the Prices of such Goods, which must inevitably proceed from the additional Imposts intended to be made payable, at the Said Port, for Purposes which will eventually prove ruinous instead of beneficial to the Trade of the Town of Southampton and its Neighbourhood: And therefore praying, That the sard Bill.may not pass into a Law.

A Petition of the there-undersigned Merchants, Ship Petition from Owners, and Inhabitants of Lymington, in the County Lymington of Southampton, was likewise presented to the House, ®8ainst and read; also taking Notice of the said Bill; and B '

Setting forth, That the said Bill contains Clauses repugnant to the true Interests of Trade and Commerce, and the Purposes for which the same is really intended will, if carried into Effect, not only prove burthensome to Trade, but likewise extremely dangerous and incommodious to Shipping in general; and that, if the said Bill be passed into a Law, the Trade of Southampton will be diminished, the Prices of all Articles brought into the said Port enhanced, and the Petitioners, amongst other Traders and Persons interested therein, be heavily affected, without receiving any equivalent Benefit, or Advantage: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, and that they may have Leave to be heard against the same, by themselves, or their Counsel, and to produce Evidence in Support of their Allegations, at the Bar of the House.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time; and the last mentioned Petitioners are to be then heard, by themselves, or Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

A Petition of the Company of Proprietors of the Union Canal, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for limiting, regulating, atod applying, the Produce of the Tolls imposed by Acts of Parliament for making Navigable Canals and Aqueducts; and Setting forth, That, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, the Petitioners conceive that it would greatly depreciate the Property in Navigations in general, the Shares in some of which have been sold at very high Prices, the Parties presuming that the Tonnages heretofore given by Act of Parliament would not be varied or reduced, and that, in consequence of the said Bill, many deserving Men would sustain great Losses, which they could by no Means have avoided but by reposing less Confidence in Acts of Parliament: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Beaufoy, according to Order, reported from the'

Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of the Government and Trade of India, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as followed*; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it is the peculiar and bounden Duty of the Legislature to promote, by all just and prudent Means, the Interests and Happiness of the Inhabitants of the British Dominions in India; and that, for these Ends, such Measures ought to be adopted as may gradually tend to their Advancement in useful Knowledge, and to their Religious and Moral Improvement.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That sufficient Means of Religious Worship and Instruction be provided for all Persons of the Protestant Communion, in the Service, or under the Protection of the East India Company in Asia, proper Ministers being, from Time to Time, sent out from Great Britain for those Purposes; and that a Chaplain be maintained on board every Ship of Seven hundred Tons Burthen, and upwards, in the East India Company's Employ; and, moreover, that no such Ministers, or Chaplains, shall be sent out or appointed until they shall first have been approved of by the Archbishop of Canterbury, or the Bishop of London, for the Time being.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

A Petition of the Merchants, Traders, Fullers, Dyers, Pressers, and others, concerned in the Preparation and finishing of Woollens of the Devonshire and Exeter Fabrics, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the principal Article of Devonshire Manufactory is Long Ells, distinguished by a Variety of Denominations; that the Annual Exports of the said Article to China, through thd East India Company, have increased in a few Years, from an inconsiderable Amount, to nearly £. 400,000, and the Directors represent the Consumption to be still progressive: That this increased Demand of the East India Company for Long Ells (a Fabric peculiar to Devonshire) has so enhanced the Price of the Article at Home, that the Countries of Europe, whither it has usually been exported, either substitute other Articles in its stead, or obtain a Supply of the same from their own Fabrics on bettor Terms than England can now furnish it: That this is particularly the Case with regard to Spain, hitherto the principal Mart for Long Ells; the Manufactories of that Country, especially those of Guadalajara and St. Fernando, have supplanted, in great Measure, those of Devonshire since the Exports to China have so astonishingly increased, and a similar Effect is prevailing in Germany from the same Cause: That the East India Company procures this Article, in the Raw State, through the Factors resident in London, where it is prepared, dyed, and finished, and consequently that the Labour arising from these Processes, which amounts to about a Fifth Part of the entire Value of the Article, is lost to the Establishments of Exeter and other Towns of Devonshire, which have hitherto been

supported by those Processes of Preparation exercised on the Long Ells exported from thence to every Part of Europe: That the Merchants, Traders, Dyers, Pressers, Packers, and Workmen, of Exetcj',. and such other Places of Devon, w hose Industry consists . Vol. 48.

in the Preparation, dying, pressing, and Exportation of Long Ells, derive no Advantage directly or indirectly from the China Trade, the Merchants being restrained, by the exclusive Privilege of the Company, from Access to the Markets of China, and the Dyers, Pressers, Finishers, Packers, and Workmen of every Description, being equally deprived, by the prevailing System of purchasing the Long Ells through Factors in London, and preparing them there, of any Employment or Advantage whatever from the Exports of the Company: That the Consequences of this System are, 1st, an Exchange of European Markets near Home, of free Access, and familiar to the Traders, for the remote Markets of China, which are said to be so precarious, that the chief Argument advanced for confining the Trade to a Company is the Danger of Offence, from the Approach of Individuals, to the capricious Government of that Empire; 2dly, a Removal from Devonshire to London of the Industry derived from the Preparation of Long Ells, hitherto the chief Support of Exeter, and other Towns of the County, in Establishments for which Branch of Industry immense Fortunes are embarked, and from the Employment of which the Bread of a most numerous Body of Labourers is derived; and 3dly, the accustomed Trade of the Merchants of Exeter, is transferred to the East India Company, and their Shipping, hitherto employed in transporting the Fabrics of-Devon to the Countries of Europe, is deprived of Employ: That the Petitioners, though unable, after the maturest Investigation of the Arguments adduced in Defence of the Measure, to comprehend the Necessity or the Expediency of confining the China Trade to an exclusive Company, do not presume, under the present Circumstances, to solicit the Change of a System which apparently meets the Concurrence of Parliament, but they hope the Wisdom and Humanity of Parliament-will be equally interested in favouring their Application for preserving a Part, at least, of the Employment on which their Support, and that of a most numerous Body of Workmen, already without Labour, depends, and which their Situation and Resources enable them to perform with great Advantage to the Company itself: That the Petitioners are the more urgent in their Claim from the Circumstance, that, being confined by their local Situation to the few Objects which form the immediate Commerce of their District, no Resource w'ill remain if their Application fail: That no Injury can accrue to London from a Compliance with the Petitioners Request, since the Woollen Export to China is a Trade of very recent Acquisition to that Metropolis, where an Infinity of Objects is ever at Hand to employ the Talents and Capitals of the industrious: That the Rate of Labour, the Supply of Water, the Compactness' of the Establishments for preparing, dying, and finishing Woollens, the Vicinity to the Fabrics, and a Variety of other Causes, afford to the City of Exeter such Advantages over that of London in the Preparation of Long Ells, as to enable the Petitioners to serve the Company with the Article in a finished State at least as well as they are now served, and with more Oeconomy. — On these Grounds the Petitioners pray, That such Provisions be made in the New Charter, as to the House shall appear expedient, for conveying to the Petitioners the Right of supplying the East India Company, during the Term of their Charter, with a certain Portion, at least, of their Long Ells for China in a finished State, provided the Supply be made by the Petitioners in as perfect a Manner, and on as advantageous Terms, as the Company at present procures them through the existing System, and that such Arrangements be made for giving Effect to the Measure as may meet the Approbation of Parliament, and of the Directors of the East India Company, to whom the Petitioners are prepared . to submit Propositions for that Purpose:

That

That the Petitioners disclaim die Attempt of injuring the various Classes of Traders accustomed to prepare the Long Ells in London; that Trade, as has already been stated, is of recent Acquisition to London, it has been removed thither from Devo not by a fair Competition, but by the exclusive System under which it is deemed expedient to conduct the China Trade: The Petitioners only solicit a Part of the Business; and that Part only on the Ground of serving the Company at least as well, or at least as advantageously, as they are served in London: That the Petitioners have the Means of so serving the Company is evinced by the Circumstance that all the Consumers of the World, who have the Choice of the Two Markets, London and Exeter, for the Purchase of Long Ells, in the finished State, almost exclusively prefer Exeter, and that the Countries beyond the Cape of Good Hope, where the Consumers have not the Choice, are alone supplied with Long Ells prepared and finished in London: That the Petitioners are aware of the Objection, that their Prayer relates to an internal Regulation of the Company's Trade; and their Reply is, that they can substantiate the Grievance, and establish their Assertions, by incontrovertible Facts: That they have in vain solicited the Company for Relief; and that no Resource is left but to throw themselves on the Wisdom and Justice of Parliament, for procuring such Arrangements with the Directors as may preserve, in some Degree at least, their Fortunes and their Trade, preclude the Necessity of emigrating in Quest of new Employment, and save their Workmen and Artizans from becoming Pensioners of the Poors Rate, or Victims to Famine.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty1, entreating, that His Majesty would be graciously pleased to take into His Royal Consideration the Advantages which might be derived, by the Public, from the Establishment of a Board of Agriculture and Internal Improvement:

Humbly representing to His Majesty, that, though in some particular Districts improved Methods df cultivating the Soil are practised, yet that, in the greatest Part of these Kingdoms, the Principles of Agriculture are not yet sufficiently understood, nor are the Implements of Husbandry, or the Stock of the Farmer, brought to that Perfection of which they are capable:

That HiS faithful Corntftoris are persuaded, if such ah Institution were to take place, that such Enquiries might be made into the internal State of the Country, arid a Spirit of Improvement so effectually encouraged, aS must naturally tend to produce tnany important National Benefits, the Attainment of which His Majesty has ever shewn a riiost Gracious Disposition to promote; and, in particular, that such a Measure might be the Means of 'uniting a judicious System of

Husbandry to the' Advantages* of domestic manufacturing Industry, and the Benefits of Foreign Commerce, and consequently, of establishing, on the surest and best Foundations, the Prosperity of His Kingdoms:

And, if His Majesty shall be1 graciously pleased to direct the Institution of such a Board, for a limited Time, to assure His Majesty, that His faithful Commons will chearfully defray any Expence attending the same, to the Amount of a Sum not exceeding £. 3,000 per Annum;

Mr. Henry Hobart, according to Order, reported

from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of an Act, made in the Thirty-first Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for regulating the Importation and Exportation of Coni, and the Payment of the Duty on " Foreign Corn imported, and of the Bounty on British " Corn exported," the Resolutions which the Committee bad directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, whenever the Price of middling British Oatmeal shall be under Thirteen Shillings per Boll, there be allowed upon the Exportation thereof a Bounty of Eighteen Pence per Boll.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, whenever the Price thereof shall be at or above Fourteen Shillings per Boll, the Exportation thereof shall be prohibited.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, whenever the Export of any Sort of Corn, with Bounty, is stopped in any one District, because the Price thereof is above' the Price at which Bounty is allowed. Corn of the same Sort should not be allowed to be carried from thence Coastwise to any other District, the Ports of which are open for the Exportation thereof with Bounty.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That His Majesty be empowered, with the Advice of His Privy Council, to prohibit, generally, for a limited Time, the Exportation from England and Scotland respectively of any Sort of Coni, whenever the Average Price thereof, taken from the Returns of England and Scotland respectively, is at or above the Price at or above which Corn is allowed by Law to be imported from Ireland, Quebec, and the British Plantations, at the first low Duty, and in like Manner to permit, generally, the Importation, or the taking out of Warehouse, at the lowest Duties, of any Sort of Foreign Corn, whenever the Price thereof is at or above the Price At or above which Corn is allowed by Law to be imported from other Foreign Countries at the first low Duty.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in upon the said Resolutions: And that Mr. Henry Hobart and Mr. Ryder do prepare and bring in, the same.

A Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, for regulating the Exportation of Copper to the East Indies.

And the said Clause was Twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause being offered to be added to the BiH, for empowering the Court of Directors to send out Schoolmasters, and Persons approved by the Archbishop of Canterbury, or the Bishop of,

&c. for the Religious and Moral Improvement of the Native Inhabitants of the British Dominions in India;

The House was moved, That the Resolutions which, upon Tuesday last, were reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of the Government and Trade of India, and were then agreed to by the House, might be read.

And the same were, as agreed to by the House, read accordingly; and are as followeth;

" Resolved, That it is the peculiar and bounden " Duty of the Legislature to promote, by all just fnd " prudent Means, the Interests and Happiness of the " Inhabitants of the British Dominions in India; and " that, for these Ends, such Measures ought to be " adopted as may gradually tend to their Advancement

in useful Knowledge, and to their Religious and " Moral Improvement.

" Resolved, That sufficient Means of Religious

" Worship and Instruction be provided for all Persons of the Protestant Communion, in the Service, " or under the Protection of the East India Company " iu Asia, proper Ministers being, from Time to " Time, sent out from Great Britain for those Purposes; and that a Chaplain be maintained on Board " every Ship of Seven hundred Tons Burthen, and " upwards, in the East India Company's Employ; " and, moi^over, that no such Ministers, or Chaplains, shall be sent out or appointed until they shall " first have been approved of by the Archbishop of " Canterbury, or the Bishop of London, for the Time " being."

Then the said Clause was Twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill. r

Another Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, requiring the Court of Directors to settle the Destination, ana provide for the decent Maintenance of the said several Persons.

And the said Clause was Twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, directing the Removal of such Persons, in certain Cases.

And the said Clause was Twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, for sending out and maintaining Chaplains at the principal Garrisons and Factories, and on Board Ships, of a certain Burthen, in the Service of the Company.

And the said Clause was Twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, for the Protection of Tea Brokers.

And the said Clause was read the First Time; and, with Leave of the House, withdrawn.

Another Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, prescribing the Oath to be taken by Persons who shall hereafter be elected Directors of the East India Company.

And the said Clause was Twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Then several Amendments were made, by the House, to the Bill.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Graves and Mr. Eaines:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for dividing and inclosing Part of the Moors and Wastes within the Manor of Masham and Mashamshire, in the North Riding of the County of without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to allow the Drawback of the Duties of Customs and Excise upon Wines consumed by Admirals, Captains, and other Commissioned Officers, on board Ships of War in actual Service, and to allow such Ships to be supplied with Tobacco Duty free; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for the more easy raising Money upon the Hundred of Hemlingford, in the County of Warwick, for paying

the Damages and Costs incurred on Account of the late Riots within the said Hundred, than is authorized to be done by the Laws now in being; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have commanded us to acquaint this House, That their Lordships will proceed further in the Trial of Warren Hastings, Esquire, Tomorrow Morning, at Ten of the Clock, in Westminster Hall, precisely.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

A Petition of Messieurs George Bishop and Argles Bishop, of Maidstone, in the County of Kent, Distillers, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That an Act was passed in the Twenty-seventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for repealing the several Duties of Customs and " Excise, and granting other Duties in lieu thereof, " and for applying the said Duties, together with " other Duties composing the Public Revenue; for " permitting the Importation of certain Goods, " Wares, and Merchandize, the Produce or Manufacture of the European Dominions of the French " King, into this Kingdom; and for applying certain " unclaimed Monies, remaining in the Exchequer, for " the Payment of Annuities on Lives, to the Reduction of the National Debt," whereby certain Regulations were established with respect to the Method of making Geneva at the Distillery then carried on by Mr. George Bishop, of Maidstone, lately deceased, and certain Rules were prescribed for the Payment of the Duties on such Geneva for a limited Time; and that the Petitioners were in Partnership with the said George Bishop at the Time of his Decease, which happened in the Month of March last, and the said Distillery hath been since carried on by by the Petitioners and Sir William Bishop, of Maidstone aforesaid, Knight, for their joint Account; and that the Petitioners are informed, that a Bill is depending in the House to continue certain Duties of Excise on Foreign Spirits imported into this Kingdom for a Time to be limited, and also for continuing certain Laws of Excise therein mentioned, whereby the Provisions and Regulations respecting the said Distillery of the said Mr. George Bishop, deceased, are to be further continued for a limited Time; and that Doubts have arisen, whether the Provisions, Regulations, and Exemptions, contained in the said Act of the Twenty-seventh Year of His present Majesty's Reign, and proposed to be continued by the said Bill as above-mentioned, were not personal with respect to the said George Bishop, and were therefore to cease at his Death: And Representing to the House, that the said Distillery has been carried on many Years with the strictest Regularity and Propriety, according to the Regulations and Exemptions established and grant-

Mail A. 1793.

A Petition of John Tarleton, John Barnes, and Petition Richard Miles, on behalf of themselves and the Mer- th* chants of Liverpool, was presented to the House, and hshiuetoT* read; Taking Notice of the Bill for abolishing the Trade for Trade carried on for supplying Foreign Territories supplying with Slaves; and Setting forth, That the said Bill, if ^ore,8n passed into a Law, will be attended with the most fatal Wl Effects, not only to the African and West India Trade, but to the Manufactures, Commerce, and Navigation of this Country: That the Supply of Negro Labourers to the Foreign Colonies in the West Indies and America has been always considered as one of the Branches of the African Trade the most beneficial to this Country, the Merchandize employed in the said Trade being chiefly British Manufacture, the Navigation British, and the Returns generally in hard Specie, inso much that Government has always given every possible Protection and Encouragement to that Commerce, and, in particular, used very great Exertions to secure it exclusively to this Country at the memorable Treaty of Utretcht, and the Petitioners have, under such Protection and Encouragement, embarked very large Capitals in the Prosecution of that valuable Commerce, and they submit it to the Justice of the House, whether they ought not to receive a reasonable Compensation for the heavy Loss which they must sustain if they should be deprived of it: And Representing to the House, that an Attack upon so valuable a Part of the African Trade, at this late Period of the Session, is a very great Hardship, as the Petitioners can neither have sufficient Time to defend their Interests, nor can they benefit by the Deliberation of many of the Members of the House who have already left Town; and the Petitioners finally beg Leave to observe, that, while the present Bill would deprive this Nation of a most important Branch of its Commerce, it would not at the same Time have any Effect in the Attainment of that particular Object for which it is intended, it being utterly impossible, by any Law of this Country, to hinder the Foreign Settlements in the West Indies from obtaining Negro Slaves, the certain Consequence then would be the Transfer, not only of the Trade, but of the Traders, and their Capital, together with the Navigation, to Foreign Countries, who are ready with open Arms to receive them, and who hold out every Species of Allurement and Encouragement to settle in their Ports: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves, and their Counsel, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law, or that they may receive such Compensation and further Relief, as to the Justice and Wisdom of the House may seem reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by themselves, or Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petitions, if they think fit.

And the Members being equal, Mn Speaker said, That as the Original Motion appeared to have been made in Conformity to the Wishes of the Managers appointed to conduct the Impeachment against Mr. Hastings, he thought it entitled, in a peculiar Degree, to the Attention of the House. — In Consequence of some Observations which had been made with respect to the Proceedings on the Trial, they had desired Permission to lay before the House an Account of those Proceedings, together with such Remarks as they might judge necessary to explain them: He concurred with those who were of Opinion that such a Request should be edmplied with, particularly as in the Conduct of the Managers, the Honour of the House was materially involved. That whilst the Managers enjoyed the Confidence of the House in their present arduous and important Trust, they might justly consider themselves as entitled to its Protection and Support, and they might therefore reasonably hope for the Concurrence of the House in a Motion, the immediate Object of which was to state all the Circumstances of the Trial, upon which alone a proper Judgment could be formed of their Conduct in the Course of it; and therefore he declared himself with the Yeas.

So it was resolved in the Affirmative.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Annual Duty of Nine Pounds per Gallon be charged upon the Contents of every Still used in distilling Worts, Wash, or Low Wines, from Malt, Corn, Grain, or British Materials, in the Low Lands of that Part of Great Britain called Scotland.

.Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Annual Duty of Nine Pounds per Gallon be charged upon the Contents of every Still used in distilling Worts, Wash, or Low Wines, from Malt, Corn, Grain, or British Materials, in that Part of Great Britain called England, to be exported to that Part of Great Britain called Scotland.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Annual Duty of Nine Pounds per Gallon be charged upon the Contents of every Still used in rectifying or compounding Spirits in that Part of Great Britain called England, to be exported to that Part of Great Britain called Scotland.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Annual Duty of Fifteen Pounds per Gallon be charged upon the Contents of every Still used in distilling Worts, Wash, or Low Wines, from Melasses or Sugar, in that Part of Great Britain called England, to be exported to that Part of Great Britain called Scotland.

Resolved, That it is . the Opinion of this Committee, That an Annual Duty of Eighteen Pounds per Gallon be charged upon the Contents of every Still used in distilling Worts, Wash, or Low Wines, from Foreign Materials (except Melasses or Sugar) in that Part of Great Britain called England, to be exported to that Part of Great Britain called Scotland.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Three Shillings and Two Pence Halfpenny per Gallon be laid upon all Spirits brewed or made from Malt, Corn, Grain, Melasses, or Sugar, or British or Foreign Materials, of the Strength of One to Ten over Hydrometer Proof, which shall be imported into England from that Part of Great Britain called Scotland.

Petition from A Petition of the Merchants, Traders, and Vic-

Gloucester tuallers, of the City of Gloucester, was presented to the Pennhe"8 House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners feel themselves aggrieved by the Refusal of the Officers of the Excise to grant sufficient Time in Permits for the Removal of Goods, whereby their Property is exposed to frequent Seizures, and they involved in much Trouble and Expence to regain it: That the Time generally granted for the Water Conveyance of Goods from Bristol to Gloucester, Fifty Miles, is Two Days, more than which-i? positively refused, although it rarely happens that the Voyage is accomplished in less than Three Days, and it is frequently not possible to compleat it in less than a Week: That the 26th of George the Third, Cap. 59. Sect. 36. in Cases of Seizure by the Officers of the Excise, where the Goods are not delivered within the Time limited by the Permit, hath prescribed a summary Mode of Procedure for the Adoption of the Petitioners, equally calculated for the Protection of the Revenue and the Redress of the injured fair Trader, but the Benefit of the said salutary Clause cannot be extended without the Aid of the House to investigate Seizures made by Officers of the Customs i and that a Difficulty hath arisen with respect tq the Computation of the Time granted by Permits, that is to say, Whether the Time specified, i£ for Instance, Two Days, is to be deemed inclusive or exclusive of the Day upon which the Permit is granted, and if jt be deemed exclusive, whether the Point of Computation, as in otjher Cases legally decided, does not commence immediately after Twelve o'Clock of the Night of the Day of the Date of the Permit; and that the present Practice of the Officers of the Excise is to subdivide the Days into Hours in the Permit, notwithstanding Hours are not mentioned in the Grant of Time for conveying the Goods, in doing of which it is respectfully submitted that they impose a Fetter upon Trade, invert the Maxim, that Penal Laws should receive a liberal Construction in favour of the Petitioners, and oppose the Common Law of the Kingdom, which admits not of the Fraction of a Day: And

W Mail 4- 1T93,

therefore praying. That the House will take Jfteir Petition into Consideration, and frame such Measures for redressing the Evil as their Wisdom shall suggest Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of Arthur Strother, Agent on Behalf of his Catholic Majesty, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, in or about the Month of February last, a Cargo of Tobacco, the Produce of West Florida, was brought, on Board a Spanish Ship called the San Juan Bauptista, from New Orleans into the Port of Plymouth; and that Application was made to the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty's Treasury, stating, that the said Cargo was originally intended for Nantz, in the Kingdom of France, but the same was brought into the Port of Plymouth on Account of the Hostilities between Spain and that Country, with a Request that the said Cargo might be admitted to an Entry in this Kingdom as Tobacco imported from the Countries belonging to the United States of America, and the Lords of the Treasury directed that the said Cargo should be admitted to Entry on the Payment of the Duty of One Shilling and Three Pence per Pound Weight, being the Duty payable on Tobacco of the Growth or Production of His Majesty's Colonies in America, or the United States of America, on Condition that Security should be given to His Majesty for the Payment of the Duty of Three Shillings and Six

Pence per Pound Weight on the said Tobacco, unless Provision should be made by Parliament for admitting the same on the lower Duty: And therefore praying, That he may have Leave to present a Petition for admitting the said Tobacco to Entry on Payment of the lower Duty, notwithstanding the Time limited for receiving Petitions for private Bills is elapsed.

Ordered, That, in Consideration of the particular Leave given. Circumstances set forth in the said Petition, Leave be given to present a Petition as desired by the said Arthur Strother.

Then a Petition of Arthur Strother, Agent on Behalf Mr. Stro-of his Catholic Majesty, was presented to the House, tiler's Ped-and read j Containing the same Allegations as the last tion* preceding Petition: And praying, That Provision may be made in the Bill now depending for the better Regulation of Warehoused Tobacco for admitting the said Tobacco to Entry on Payment of the lower Duty, or that such other Relief may be given in the Premises as 'to the House may seem proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Rose, Mr. Henry Hobart, kc.: And they are to meet upon Monday Morning next, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber.

A Petition of Sir John Henderson, of , in the Petition of County of Fife, Baronet, William Wemyss, of Wemyss, Sir f°bn Esquire, and John Campbell, Esquire, Writer to the Signet, was presented to the House, and read; Set- against the ting forth, That the Petitioners are Proprietors of cer- Scotch Coals tain Coal Mines in that Part of Great Britain called SpinJ?„ Scotland, and are informed, that a Bill has lately been Llceuces 1 brought into the House, for repealing the several Duties on Coals carried Coastwise, from any or certain Ports or Places of Great Britain, to any or certain Ports or Places in Scotland; and that the Petitioners (though not insensible of the Expediency of repealing the said Duties'in such Manner as the Wisdom of the Legislature may see best, either on all Coals carried from Port to Port in Great Britain, or to such Places and Districts in Scotland or England, respectively, as from the immoderate Price or constant Scarcity of Fuel, labour under any peculiar or uncommon Hardship) conceive the Mode of Repeal proposed by the said Bill to be injurious to their private Interests, and not necessary for the Public Good, and they also conceive, and are advised, that the Bill would, in its Consequences, infer a manifest and flagrant Violation of the Treaty of Union, inasmuch as, notwithstanding that English Coals would, according to the Tenor of the Bill, be admitted Duty free into all Ports of Scotland, yet Scotch Coals would not be thereby allowed the reciprocal, and therefore (in the Petitioners Apprehension) just and due Advantage of, in like Manner, passing Duty-free into all, or even into any Ports of England: And therefore praying to be heard, by Counsel, against the said Bill passing into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for repealing the Duties on Coals, Culm, and Cinders, brought or carried Coastwise into Scotland, and for granting other Duties on Licences to sell certain distilled Spirituous Liquors, in lieu thereof, be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That the said Bill be read a Second Time upon Friday Morning next.

Mr. Bramston, according to Order, reported from the Committee, who were appointed to enquire into the Matter of the Complaint made to the House, by a Member in his Place, of an Omission having been made in the ingrossed Bill for making and maintaining a Navigation from, or nearly from, the Town Of Chelmsford, in the County of Essex, to a Place called Collier's Reach, in or near the River in the said County, of the Name of One of the Commissioners, which was inserted on the Report of the said Bill, and also, that the Names of Two Proprietors, inserted by this House, appeared to have been erased from the said ingrossed Bill; That the Committee had enquired accordingly, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

It appeared to the Committee, That the Name of John Strutt was clearly wrote in the Amendment received by the House upon the Report of the said Bill, Voi. 48.

and that the said Name is the Third upon the List1, which List is not taken Alphabetically.

It also appeared upon the ingrossed Bill, thfet the Commissioners Names are inserted Alphabetically, and that the Name of John Strutt is omitted;

Your Committee then called Mr. David Jones, the Ingrossing Clerk; who was asked, Whether he ingrossed the Chelfner Navigation Bill? he said, He did not — That the customary Way of doing Business in the Ingrossing Office, after a Bill is ordered to be ingrossed, is, to put the Bills in Harid by Rotation, as they are reported to the House. This Bill, for thie Convenience of the Agents, was sent out to be ingrossed; and on its Return was delivered tb Mr. White, the Agent for the Bill, to be exaihined.

And being asked, Whether hie (the Witness) exaihined the ingrossed Bill with the House Bill and Amendments? he Said, No. That the Examination of Bills, by the IngrosSing Clerk, has been dispensed with for near Thirty Years past. Thdt Bills formerly were examined by the Ingrossing Clerk, and the Agent for the Bill; and when Mr. Onslow was Speaker, he always asked the Chairman, whether he had examined the Bill; it being at that Time customary for the Chairman to examine the Bill. — And being asked. Whether the Bill was re-delivered to him by Mr. White? he said, It Was, by him, or One of his Clerks — It was delivered into the Office to be prepared for the Third Reading in the usual Way. That he does not know the Person who actually ingrossed the Bill; but Part of it was done at Messrs. Richards and Watt, Stationers, in Wych Street, and the other Part at Messrs. Hughes and Walsh, Stationers, in the Temple — It was divided into different Parts for the Sake of Expedition, on Account of its Length — it is the usual Practice to ingross from a printed Bill — they pay no Regard to the written Copy, if they can get a printed Bill. — And being asked, Was this the only private Bill sent out to be ingrossed this Session ? he answered, No; not by many. That he received the printed Bill from the Agent, Mr.; — Then,

Mr. John White being examined, tvas asked, How it happened that the Name of John Stt'Utt is omitted in the ingrossed Bill ? he replied, That in the Bill, as reported from the Committee, is a long List of Commissioners Names, arranged in Alphabetical Order. When the Report was considered in the House, there were about Twenty more Commissioners added by the House — These were not arranged Alphabetically; but were either fastened in the Bill, or left loose; he knows not which. The Bill so amended was ordered to be ingrossed, and taken into the Ingrossing Office. It is not usual for the Ingrossing Clerks to ingross from the House Bill and Amendments, but from a printed and altered Copy given them by the Solicitor for the Bill — Those Bills the Clerks in his Office usually prepare; but, in this Instance, they being exceedingly hurried, he prepared the Bill himself. He had before him a Bill, with the Amendments, as it passed the Committee — In this was a Manuscript Copy of the First Set of Commissioners. He wrote into that, from the additional List added upon the Report, those Names, placing them Alphabetically, ticking them off, as he believes will appear from (the Paper; upon that Paper were the Names of John Strutt and Joseph Holden Strutt, at the Distance of Two Names from each other: That he, by Mistake, wrote John Holden Strutt; and also, by Mistake, omitted the Name of John Strutt; and so the Bill was ingrossed; as also were the Proof Acts prepared. That he meant to say, that he had not to copy the additional Names one immediately following the other, but to select them, and mix them in their Alphabetical Order with the others. — Being asked, Who examined the Ingrossment, and where it was examined r he said, It is never customary

for the Ingrossing Clerks themselves to examine the Ingrossment — They give it to the House Solicitor for that Purpose; some of whose Clerks examine it. — It is the constant Practice of their Office to make the Country Agents examine all Ingrossments; most particularly because neither they, nor their Clerks, can be competent to decide upon the Spelling of Names. This Ingrossment, 'according to the Practice of their Office, was, in the first Instance, examined by Three of their Clerks, with the Proof Act, and the House Bill and Amendments. Their Clerks would find the Ingrossment and Proof Act agree; and, as they also had, in the reading of the Commissioners Names, to select into Alphabetical Order the additional Commissioners Names, they, he supposes, fell into the same Error as he had done. The Ingrossment and the Proof Act yere again examined in the Ingrossing Office by One. of their Clerks, and Mr. the Country

Agent. — Being asked. What was become of the Paper which lie transcribed from the original List of additional Commissioners ? he said, That Paper was in the Bill which he had in his Hand, which went to the Press for a Proof Act: Such Bills, when returned from the Press, are considered in their Office as Waste Paper, and thrown about as such; by which Means such Papers as are loose in them are frequently lost, and he had, in fact, great Difficulty in finding any Pqrt of this Bill; the List of Commissioners Names so transcribed by him, and put into the Bill, he cannot find — -He means to say, that he was the original Cause-of this Error; but he had no Motive for leaving out Mr. John Strutt's Name, as it must be a Matter of total Indifference to him who were, or who were not, Commissioners. — Being then shewn the Paper of additional Commissioners, ne was asked, Whether the Ticks therein were made by him ? he said, They were — He meant them for his Guide in inserting those additional Names among the others, putting the Tick over each Name as he selected it, and wrote it into the other Copy. — Being asked, Why these being ticked, did he imagine they were omitted to be copied ? he said, In the Proof Act, which was printed from his Manuscript, stands John Holden Strutt; and because he has some time since seen the Paper which is now lost, iq which he saw, in his own Hand Writing, John Holden Strutt, and neither the Name of John Strutt or Joseph Holden Strutt; and because he has been told by Mr. Leapinguell that he found it so in the Ingrossment; and that, knowing the re was no such Person as John Holden Strutt, he so far corrected the Mistake, in his Examination of the Ingrossment, as to alter the Name of John to Joseph — That he never looked to this Part of the Ingrossment till the Error was discovered.

It appearing upon the Face of the additional List that there are Ticks at the End of the Names of John Q/mius, Sir George Jackson, and John Strutt, and of those Names only, he was asked, How he accounted for that ? he said, He cannot account for it; but he wishes the Committee to observe, that there are other Marks at the End of other Names — That One of the Names has Two Ticks above it, and that One of the Names has no Tick at all — How these additional Ticks came lie cannot account for; but he should wish to inform the Committee, that that List has not been in his Custody, but has been in no less than Three different Offices in the House of Commons, as he has' been informed; meaning the Ingrossing Office, Mr. Benson the Clerk of the Papers Office, and Mr. Rosiers Office — The Marks at the End of the Three First Names he does not believe are of his making. — And being asked, If he can recollect when he first discovered the Omission of Mr. John Strutt's Name? he said, It was on one of the Days on which the Committee on the Bill sat at the House of Lords, when Mr. Bramslon asked him, If he knew of the Omission of any Name? to which he replied, No.

He immediately mentioned Mr. Strutt's Name; upon which he looked in the Report at the House of Commons, where he found the Name — That he looked into the Ingrossment at the House of Lords, where he found the Alteration from John to Joseph — He looked at that Paper in his Hand Writing, which is now lost, in which he found the original Mistake. — And being asked, Whether that Paper was then in his Custody? he said, He then found it, after some considerable Search, lying with other Waste Paper in the Office in which his Clerks write: Not considering the Matte* to be of much Consequence, he left the Paper where he found it; and never enquired for it again till last Night, or the Night before. — And being asked. Whether he informed Mr. Bra, or any other Per-, son, that the Mistake was owing to himself? he said.

He does not know. — And being asked, What Impression he meant to convey to the Committee, by saying, that he did not consider the Matter to be of much Consequence? he replied, That he meant to say, that he did not suppose any further Notice would be taken of it; especially as Mr. Bramston had authorized him to say that his Son, and Mr. Baker that his Brother, should instantly resign, that Mr Strutt, might be elected a Commissioner, and which he immediately told to Mr. Joseph Holden Strutt, his Son. — -And being asked, What was the Reply of Mr. Strutt to him ? he said, The Conversation passed in the Lords Committee Room, he believes; and he believes, in rather a low Voice; and he thinks Mr. said,

that he should not be satisfied unless his complete List, or the Whole of his List, was inserted, or Words to that Effect — To this Conversation he cannot speak positively. — And being asked, Whether the Offer of Two (Commissioners to resign, and the Answer of Mr. Joseph Holden Strutt, did not impress him with an Idea of the Importance of the Subject in Question ? he replied, It did not; because he supposed Mr. Strutt would have been satisfied by being made a Commissioner, and so no Person would have Reason to complain; but if not so, he supposed that, upon his Com-, plaint, the Lords Committee would have amended the Bill, by inserting his Name; and that when the Bill come back to this House so amended, this House would; agree to the Amendment, as his Idea was, that they . would consider the Matter as a clerical Mistake; it apr pearing that the Lords had only corrected their Error, they having in one Stage of the Business constituted Mr. Strutt a Commissioner, and they, the House, not having themselves left him out. — And being asked. Whether it was not represented to him by the Gentleman who made an Offer for a Commissioner to resign, to be of Consequence ? he said, He is almost positive not: He thinks the only Conversation that ever 'passed upon the Subject was, as to the Matter of Fact, whether the Name was in or out; and whether, if the Lords did so amend the Bill, it was such an Amendment as the Commons could agree to — And being asked, What Answer did he make to those Gentlemen? he said, It is impossible for him to recollect the Particulars of such Conversation, which passed a long Time since, and which he never thought he should be questioned about. He begged to add, to all that he has said, That the Commission of so great an Error, if done intentionally, must have been extremely prejudicial to him in his Situation; and he cannot but be extremely concerned, that he has even unintentionally omitted the Name of Mr. Strutt. — And being asked, In what Stage of the Bill did Mr.

or his (the Witness's) Clerks, having examined the Ingrossment, tell him of the Alteration made from John to Joseph ? he said, The Ingrossment has never been in the Power of his Clerks, or Mr. Leapingwell, since it was read the Third Time, and passed, in the House of Commons; and he believes Mr. Leapingwell told him of the Discovery and Correction of the.

Mr. John Leapingwell was called in, and asked, What does he know of the Alteration of the Name of Joseph Holden Strutt in the Ingrossment of the Chelmer Canal Bill? he said, The Name was , and as he knew Mr. Holden Strutt's Name to be , he altered it from John to Joseph. — And being asked, At what Time did he alter it? he said, Upon examining the Bill (at Mr. White's Request) the Day before it was read the Third Time, in the House of Commons, and in the Ingrossing Office. — And being asked, What Connection he had with the Bill? he said, He was one of the Country Agents for the Bil). — And being asked, When did lie first see that Ingrossment? he said, On the Day he examined it. — And being asked, With what did he examine it? he said, With a printed Bill. — And being asked, Had he no other Document whatever ? he said, Not as far as concerned his Examination. — And being asked, Whether he examitied the whole Bill ? he said, He believes he examined the whole Bill, from Beginning to End, except the Commissioners Names, and those he corrected, many of them being wrong spelt. — And being asked, When did he correct those Commissioners Names as to their Spelling? he said, Immediately afterwards. — And being asked, How many of the Commissioners Names did he correct in the Spelling? he said, He. could not recollect — And being asked, Why did he alter the Name of John, to that of Joseph he said, He had answered that Question before. — And being asked, Whether he did never see a List of Commissioners, wherein the Name of John Strutt was inserted? he said, No. — And being asked, Whether he (being in the Gallery of the House of Commons) did not hear Mr. Joseph Holden Strutt read the Name of John Strutt, from that List to the House? he said, He really does not recollect. — And being asked, Whether lie did not hear Mr. Joseph Holden Strutt read' a List of Commissioners proposed by him, and rejected in the Chelmer Navigation Committee on the Bill? he said, He did. — And being asked, Whether he did not, when he saw the Name of John Holden Strutt, hesitate in his Mind, whether it might be Mr. John Strutt, or Mr. Joseph Holden Strutt? he said, No. — And being asked, What determined him to know, that John Holden Strutt was intended for Joseph Holden Strutt? he said, Upon seeing Holden Strutt, he knew Joseph ought to precede Holden, and did not think of John Strutt. — And being asked, Whether he referred to any Document to see how the Mistake in the Name of Joseph arose ? he said, He did not, as he was merely correcting the wrong spelt Names. — And being asked, Whether he informed any Person, and when, of this Alteration he made? he said. The Clerk with whom he examined the Bill at the Time. — And being asked, Who was that Clerk ? he said, He did not know. — And being asked, Was he a Clerk of Mr. White to his Knowledge ? he said, He believes so. — And being asked, Whether he informed anybody else, and when ? he said, He informed Mr. White that Evening, that he had corrected the wrong Spelling of the Commissioners Names, who said, That was One of the Purposes, for which he was desired to examine the Bill. — And being asked, Whether he (having heard the Name of John Strutt read over in the Committee Room on the Bill) ever mentioned that he did not see that Name in the List of Commissioners in the ingrossed Bill ? he said, He does not recollect that he did; or if he did, it must have been from some Person having mentioned it to him. — And being asked, Whether he did not know that the Name of John Strutt was rejected in the Committee upon the Bill ? he said. He knew that the List proposed by Mr. Joseph Holden Strutt was rejected by the Committee. — Vo l, 48.

Yes. — And being asked, Having then heard Mr. Joseph Holden Strutt say, that there were Three additional Names to his List, was not that List in his Opinion the same as was offered to the Committee on the Bill, and rejected? he said, Yes. — And being asked, Whether he has any Doubt that Mr. John Strutt was appointed by the House a Commissioner? he said, He has no Doubt. — And being asked, Whether he understood, when he was called upon by Mr. White (the Solicitor for the Bill) to compare the ingrossed Bill with the printed Bill, that it was for the Purpose of correcting, in point of Spelling, the Names inserted therein? he said, Certainly. — And being asked, Whether he had, at the Time of his Examination of the Ingrossment, any other Copy of the Bill, by which he did actually examine the Ingrossment, than that which was delivered to him by Mr. White, together with the ingrossed Bill? he said, No. — And being asked. Whether he did, in all such Alterations which he made, make. them with the sole View of having the Bill more conformable to the Truth, and to the Intention of the Parties interested ? he said, Most' certainly he did. — And being asked, Whether he knew, while he was correcting the Names in the Ingrossing Office, that the Name of John Strutt was omitted in the Ingrossment? he said, No, he did not; if he had he would have instantly inserted it. — And being asked. Mr. leapingwell being called in, and asked, Whether

he knew anything of the Erasures of the Names of Betyamin Folkes and John Rennie from the ingrossed

Bill? he said, He made the Erasures. — And being asked, When he made them ? he said. At the Time of the examining the Bill the Day before it was read the Third Time in the House of Commons. — And being asked, How he came to make them ? he said, Upon finding their Names in the Ingrossment, he left the Ingrossing Office, where he had been examining the Bill, and went with a printed Bill in his Hand to Mr. White's Office, and told Mr. White that the Names of John Rennie and Benjamin Folkes should not have been in the Ingrossment, as they bad long since sold their Shares, upon which he said " We must leave them out " or take them out," or some such Words,-by which he understood he was to take them out; he returned to the Ingrossing Office, and took them out accordingly. — And being asked, Whether any Person was present when he erased the Names? he said, The same Clerk with whom he examined it, was he believed there at that Moment. — And being asked, Whether he communicated to any Person whatsoever that he had erased those Two Names? he said, He did to Mr. White.

— And being asked, When? he said, After the examining the Whole of the Bill on the Evening he did it. — And being asked. When he first knew Mr. Rennie had sold out? he said, It was in the Month of he thought the Ninth. — And being asked, Whether he prepared any Transfer of the Share of Mr. Rennie? he said, He filled up a a printed blank Agreement for a Transfer. — And being asked, Whether it was for an immediate Transfer, or for a future Day ? he said, A Transfer he believed to take place after the Act should be obtained. — And being asked, When J Folkes informed him that be had sold his Share ? he said. Some Months ago. — And being asked. If he knew whether any other of the Proprietors now standing upon the Bill had sold their Shares ? he said, He believed some of them had.

Mr. John Rennie being called, was asked, Whether he was a Proprietor of the Ch Navigation? he said,

He had been, but was not now — Ana being asked. If he had sold his Shares ? he said, He had absolutely sold them; that he sold them on the Eighth of last March, and was paid for them on the Ninth. — And being asked, Who he sold them to? he said, Mr. Wedge sold them for him to Mr. Clacker; they were in fact sold in January, but some Dispute prevented the Transfer 'till March.

Mr. Benjamin Folkes was called iu, and asked. Whether he was a Proprietor of the Chelmer Navigation ? he said, He had been, but disposed of his Shares near Five Months ago, and received the Money for them instantly; they were sold to the Reverend Mr. Maynard, Brother to Lord Maynard.
