Mr. Henry Hobart, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of proper Bounties to be allowed, in certain Cases, to Masters and Surgeons of Ships employed in the Conveyance of Slaves from the Coast of Africa, the Resolution which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read, and is as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Bounty of One hundred Pounds be allowed to each Master, and Fifty Pounds to each Surgeon of every Ship employed in conveying Slaves from the Coast of Africa, upon Proof being made that not more than Two Slaves in each Hundred that shall have been taken on board such Ships have died, and of

Vol.48.

Fifty Pounds to each Master, and Twenty-five Pounds to each Surgeon, where not more than Three Slaves in each Hundred have died within a certain Period.

The said Resolution being read a Second Time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Gentlemen who are appointed to prepare, and bring in, a Bill to continue, for a limited Time, and to amend, several Acts of Parliament for regulating the Shipping and carrying Slaves in British Vessels from the Coast of Africa, That they do make Provision in the said Bill pursuant to the said Resolution.

Mr. Henry Hobart reported from the Committee, to Mr. Stroth-whom the Petition of Arthur Strother, Agent on behalf er'8 Potion of his Catholic Majesty, was referred; That the Com- reporte mittee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, It appeared by the Memorial of Morgan and presented to the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty's Treasury, that to or about the Month of February last, a Cargo of Tobacco, the Produce of West Florida, was brought on board a Spanish Ship called The San Juan Bauptista, from New Orleans, into the Port of Plymouth; and stating that the said Cargo was originally intended for Nantz, in the Kingdom of France, but the same was brought into the Port of Plymouth, on Account of the Hostilities between Spain and that Country, with a Request that the said Cargo might be admitted to an Entry in this Kingdom as Tobacco imported from the Countries belonging to the United States of America.

And it further appeared, That by a Warrant to the Commissioners of His Majesty's Customs, the said Lords of the Treasury directed that the said Cargo should be admitted to Entry, on the Payment of the Duty of One Shilling and Three Pence per Pound Weight, being the Duty payable on Tobacco of the Growth or Production of His Majesty's Colonies in America, or the United States of America, on Condition that Security should be given to His Majesty for the Payment of the Duty of Three Shillings and Six Pence per Pound Weight on the said Tobacco, unless Provision should be made by Parliament for admitting the same on the lower Duty.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for the better Regulation of Warehoused Tobacco, is committed.

That they have Power to receive a Clause to permit certain Tobacco of the Spanish Dominions to be admitted to Entry on Payment of the British Plantation Duties.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put, That a Message be sent to the Lords, to acquaint their Lordships, That the House of Commons, taking into Consideration the State of the Impeachment now depending against Warren Hastings, Esquire, together with the advanced Period of the Session, are convinced that it is not only impossible to obtain Judgment on their several Charges, but to complete their Reply to the Defence on more than One principal Head thereof, and even that with great Inconvenience; and being of Opinion that it would be prejudicial to the Cause of Justice, in any Point of view, that the Course of the Reply should be broken, and the Attention of the Court divided on the Matter of the said Impeachment, the Whole of which their Lordships have considered as One Cause, they desire the Lords to postpone any further Proceedings on the same till the next Session of Parliament, when the Commons will be ready and desirous to attend from Day to Day, if their Lordships think fit, to make good their Charges;

Sir William Dolben reported from the Committee, appointed to inquire into a Method of making the Approach to both Houses of Parliament more convenient, by removing the Building at the End of the Court of Exchequer which extends into the Street between New Palace Yard and Saint Margaret Street, or such Part of the said Building as shall be found necessary for the Purpose before mentioned, and the Sheds and Buildings thereunto annexed; and, also to prepare a Plan of such Work, and an Estimate, of the Expence thereof, and report the same, with their Observations and Opinion thereupon, from Time to Time, to the House; That the Committee had made a Progress in the Matters to them referred, and had directed him to make a Report thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the same, together with an Appendix thereunto, in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Report was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Your Committee, having inspected, in the First Place, the particular Situation and Position of the Building referred to, in the Order appointing this Committee, are clearly of Opinion, that it will be extremely expedient for the House to adopt some Measure, by which the great Inconvenience occasioned by this Building may be removed as speedily as the Circumstances after mentioned will permit. This Incon-

venience and Obstruction proceeds not only from the Passage between New Palace Yard and Saint Margaret Street being so much contracted as it is at present, but from the particular Inclination of the Line passing through the Building, and the Deviation of the said Passage by the North-West End of the Building, from the direct Line leading out of Parliament Street towards Saint Margaret Street, which renders that Place extremely incommodious and dangerous both to Carriages and Persons passing that Way. These Circumstances would be noticed as producing great Inconvenience in Situations much less frequented; but the Matter seems to require particular Attention, when it is considered that this is tire only Way to both Houses of Parliament, ana much frequented as an Approach to the Courts of Justice in Westminster Hall. Your Committee think it unnecessary to say mote to induce the House to take such Steps for the Removal of this Inconvenience as to them shall seem proper: And your Committee have also, for the same Reason, thought it unnecessary to receive any Evidence respecting Accidents which have happened at this Place from the Circumstances before mentioned, although your Committee have been informed, that Persons living near the Spot, and others, would have been able to have laid before them very material Evidence on that Head.

Your Committee, in the next Place, inspected the Inside of the said Building, and they find, that it consists of a Ground Floor, of a First and Second Floor, and of Garrets in the Roof

On the Ground Floor there are Apartments claimed by John Wtalter Heneage, Esquire, as Hereditary Chief Usher of the Court of Exchequer: These Apartments are now occupied by Devereux Davis, Esquire, his Deputy, and have been so for upwards of Forty Years last past, and by the Chief Ushers themselves, or their Deputies, for more than a Century past.

On the First Floor there are Two Rooms, both of them appropriated to the Office of King's Remembrancer. The First Room, called The Long Room, and the Inner Room at the North-West End of the Building, called The Seizure Room, both of which are furnished with Shelves and Presses, and contain valuable and important Records.

On the Second Floor there is a Room divided into Three Compartments, also furnished with Shelves and Presses, Two of them containing very important Records belonging to the Augmentation Office, and One of those Compartments containing Records belonging to the Pipe Office.

The Two Garrets situated towards the Southern Side of the said Building, contain Papers belonging to the Office of King's Remembrancer; and a small Garret, situated at the North-West End of the Roof, contains Papers belonging to the Augmentation Office, and in a Portion of a Garret on the North-East Side of the Building, there are Papers belonging to the Pipe Office.

Your Committee, in considering of the Measures proper to be taken to remedy the Inconvenience complained of, required John Thomas Groves, Esquire, an Architect, to prepare Plans, descriptive of the Situation and present State of the said Building, and the proposed Alterations.

Mr. Groves accordingly laid before your Committee,

A General Survey of the Line of the Streets, lead- Appendix, ing from the Middle of Parliament Street to the End of Abingdon Street: And also,

A Plan of the Apartments on the Ground Floor of (B) the said Building, which extends into the Street between New Palace Yard, and Saint Margaret Street, now occupied by Devereux Davis, Esquire: And also,

preserved With respect to the present State and Condition of with the the Records and Papers in the said several Offices, your Report. Committee, having been appointed for a different Purpose, do not think it would be proper for them to make any Report to the House relative thereto; but, upon Inspection, it occurred to your Committee, that the Records and Papers there deposited (which appear to be of very considerable Importance) might be preserved and arranged in a Manner more convenient to the Officers who have the Care of them, and to the Public, if proper Places and Accommodations were provided for that Purpose.

Before your Committee took any further Steps in the Matter referred to them, they thought it proper and respectful to communicate on the Subject with the Right honourable the Lord Chief Baron of His Majesty's Court of Exchequer; and several Members of your Committee wraited on him for that Purpose; when his Lordship was pleased to express his entire Concurrence in whatever might tend to the Convenience of the Public in this Respect, provided that Care was taken for the due Preservation and Arrangement- of the Records of that Court, and the same were not removed to any Place detrimental to them, or inconvenient to the Officers or Suitors of the Court.

John Walker Heneage, Esquire, (a Member of this House) having attended your Committee, informed them, That he is Hereditary Chief Usher of the Court of Exchequer, and derives his Office under a G rant" originally made in the Time of King Henry the Second; and that, as such Officer, he has an Interest in Part of the Premisses which are the Subject of this Enquiry; and that he has always understood it to be Part of the Duty of his Office, that either he as Principal, or his Deputy, should reside in this Building, which contains the Records before mentioned; all of which are in the Charge of himself, as such Officer, or his Deputy; and that for this Purpose, the whole of the Ground Floor of the said Building had been allotted for the Residence of himself, or his Deputy, as above mentioned.

Mr. Heneage also stated. That if a Residence could be provided for his Deputy at a small Distance from the Offices before mentioned, he conceived that no material Inconvenience would happen from it, and that if it was necessary for the Public Accommodation to remove this Building, he was ready to part with the Interest claimed by him therein for a reasonable Compensation.

Mr. Heneage further stated to the Committee, That a Public House fronting towards New Palace , known by the Sign of The Coach and Horses, bad been built upon Part of the Premisses annexed to the said Apartments in which his Deputy lives, which Public House had been leased by himself and his Predecessors to divers Tenants for more than an Hundred Years last past.

And, upon the Whole, Mr. Heneage desired to leave the Consideration of the Value of his Interest in the Premisses to be ascertained by his Solicitor, Mr. Thomas Marsh Hughes, and such Person as the Committee would be pleased to appoint, to confer with Mr. Hughes on the Subject: Whereupon the Committee determined, that Mr. Grover, before mentioned, should confer with Mr. Hughes, as to the Value of the Interest claimed by Mr. in the Premisses, and

Appendix reP°rt the same to the Committee. In consequence of "(E) ' which Mr. Groves, by his Report, dated the 23d Day Vot. 48.

of May, 1793, informed your Committee, That in Report od Obedience to their Order, he had conferred with Improving Mr. Hughes, and having viewed the Premisses, and the Ap-considered the Value of the Interest claimed by [J[eHoi»et0 Mr. Heneage, as above stated, he was of Opinion, that the same would amount to the Sum of Fifty Pounds per Annum, clear of all Deductions: Which Report, made by Mr. Groves, is contained in the Appendix hereunto annexed, marked (E).

Although it is not immediately applicable to thd Matter now in Consideration, your Committee cannot refrain from stating in this Place to the House, by Way of Observation, and as an additional Motive to the House to provide for the better Security of these Records, that the Apartments in which the Deputy Usher resides, have in them a large Kitchen Chimney, at the South-West End of the Building, and Two or Three other Chimnies besides, the Flues of which pass to the Top of the Building, close to the Parts where the Records are deposited; and that the Public House has Chimnies built up in the same Manner, the'

Smoke of One of them being conveyed by a slight Tin Funnel, which ends near One of the Window^ of the said Building; and that Part of the same House is constructed with Weather Boards, covered with I^itch, and is in immediate Contact with the Outer Wall of the said Building. — The Danger arising from these Circumstances is too obvious to require any Observation.

Subsequent to Mr. Groves's Report, Mr. Heneage further informed your Committee, That there are certain Officers in the Court of Exchequer, who are appointed by the Chief Usher for Life, and are entitled to certain Fees for Searches amongst the Records contained in the said Building; and Mr. Heneage requested, that the Committee would consider o making some Compensation in respect thereof, in case it should be found expedient to remove any of the Records contained therein to another Place. Your Committee thereupon called Mr. Samuel Baker, One of the Ushers of the Court of Exchequer; and he informed your Committee, That the Court Keeper of the said Court, who is also one of the Ushers,-receives Thirteen Shillings and Four Pence a Term,-in lieu of Fees for Searches in the Augmentation Office, from the Keeper of the Records therein, and certain Fees, for Searches made amongst the other Records belonging to the Court of Exchequer out of Term Time; and the Witness stated to your Committee, That he conceived, if the Sum of Three Pounds per Annum was to be allowed for every Loss to be sustained by the Removal or other Disposal of the Records proposed to be deposited at Somerset Place, from under the Care'of the Usher, the same would be an adequate Compensation.

That there are several Chests m it, containing a Variety of unsorted Papers, which, it Is apprehended, do not at all concern or relate to the Court of Exchequer; and that these Papers are noticed in a Report of the Deputy Remembrancer to a Committee of this House, made on the 21st of March 1731. — That there, are no Indexes or Calendars to the Records in the Seizure Room, and they do not appear to be in a regular State; but the Depositions

And Sir Richard Heron being further examined, on a> subsequent Day, informed your Committee, That since his last Examination, he had been at Somerset Place, when Sir William Chambers shewed him certain Parts of the arched Record Rooms not yet appropriated, which are sufficiently spacious for the Records, in the Custody of the Treasurer's Remembrancer, now remaining near the Court of Exchequer; and that the Rooms were light, and Sir William Chambers assured him that they were dry.

Your Committee then inquired. Whether there were any other Places, in or near the Court of Exchequer, which might be cleared for the Purposes before-mentioned. And,

Allatson Burgh, Esquire, being again called, informed your Committee, That he is Deputy Foreign Apposer in the Court of Exchequer, which Office he has held about Ten Years: That his Office is at Somerset Place, where the Records belonging to it, for the greatest Part of the present Century, are deposited; and that the rest are in Presses in the Court of Exchequer, which he thinks might be removed to Somerset Place, without any Inconvenience to the Public, and with more Convenience to himself in the Execution of his Office.

He further said, That there are other Records and Papers, kept in the Presses in the Court of Exchequer, belonging to the Clerk of the Estreats, and Comptroller of the Pipe: That the Two last mentioned Offices are now kept at Somerset Place, and he thinks that those Records and Papers might be removed from the Court of Exchequer to Somerset Place, without any Inconvenience to the Public: And the Witness said, That as there was much Connection between those Offices and the Office of Deputy Foreign Apposer, he conceived himself enabled, from his long Experience, to give the Committee competent Information on this Head.

Mr. William Harris, Deputy Clerk of the Estreats, and Joint Deputy Comptroller of the Pipe, and Mr. William Marner, Joint Deputy Comptroller of the Pipe with Mr. Harris, confirmed the Evidence given by Mr. Burgh.

Then George Barker Devon, Esquire, the Remembrancer of the First Fruits, and John Bacon, Esquire, Senior Clerk in the same Office, were called in, and examined with respect to such Part of the Records belonging to that Office, as are kept in a Press in the Court of Exchequer; but it appearing from their Evidence, that those Records are placed in a Situation not necessary to be disturbed by the proposed Alterations, your Committee forbear from stating it to the House.

Your Committee next examined Roger Jortin, Esquire, who said, That he is Senior Attorney in the Office of Pleas, in the Court of Exchequer, which Office is kept in Lincoln's Inn Old Buildings; and that some of the Records and Papers belonging to that

Office are kept there, and some in Thirteen Presses, in a Passage to the Back Way of the Court of Exchequer; which Records consist of Rolls, Posteas, and Writs, returned and filed: That they are of very ancient Date, none of this Century being the re: That it is very seldom there is any Occasion to refer to them, and that they might be removed either to Lincoln's Inn, or to any vacant Chamber near the Court of Exchequer, without Inconvenience to the Public; but there is no Room for them in the Office of Pleas.

The next Place near the Court of Exchequer in which the Records proposed to be removed from the said Building may be deposited, is the Residue of that Building, after so much of it is taken down as shall be thought proper for the Purposes before mentioned; and after the fullest Consideration, your Committee have determined, That the best Method will be to take down so much thereof as lies to the North-West of the Blue Line, described in Mr. Gracs Plan, marked (A), which Line ranges sufficiently well with the Eastern Sides of both Parliament Street and Saint Margaret Street, to afford a spacious Opening, and give an Opportunity of completing the Stone Building in Saint Margaret Street, if at any Time hereafter a Plan should be thought of for that Purpose.

Upon the Evidence above referred to, your Committee conceive. That the following Places may be appropriated to the receiving the Records to be removed; viz.

The Long Gallery, in the Court of Exchequer: ' '

The Record Rooms at Somerset Place.

Your Committee therefore, in the first Place, called Robert Leete, Esquire, One of the Deputy Chamberlains of the Tally Court j who informed them, That the only Records or Papers of Consequence which are now in the Tally Office, are Books of the Tallies, but these are not considerable in Number. — And he further said, That there is a Quantity of old Tallies, the greater Part of which it is impossible to refer to, as they would moulder into Touchwood if meddled with: That the Office is very much crowded at present, on Account of the old Tallies before mentioned; but, if they should be removed, he conceives there would be Room sufficient. The said Mr. Heneage claims also a Right to the Ground occupied by the Building referred to in the above Order, and to a Residence acyoining the Court of Exchequer for himself or Deputy, according to an ancient Paper signed John IVulker, wherein his Residence is mentioned as a Duty of his Office. In lieu of all those separate Claims, I humbly offer it as my Opinion; that the Sum of Fifty Pounds per Annum, clear of all Deductions, will be a sufficient Compensation.

Appendix (I) -

To the Honourable the- Committee of the House of Commons, appointed to survey the old Buildings adjacent to the Court of Exchequer.

I beg Leave to certify, That, if the Records of the Augmentation Office are removed from their present Repository, into the Rooms over the King's Bench Treasury, that it will be necessary that Presses should be made to receive them; and as the Arrangement now in use is found, with some few Exceptions, to be a proper one, I -humbly propose that the Presses for their Reception should be well seasoned, and free from Wormp; that they be made not so deep as the present ones, but with more Shelves and Partitions; and as there are a great Quantity.of small Deeds, of considerable Value, called Chartoe Antiques, now disposed inconveniently in Bundles, marked with the Letters of the Alphabet, and liable to be lost out of the Bundles to which they respectively belong, that there may be made a Number of Drawers for the Purpose of receiving them, as also several Boxes, in which may be placed such other Deeds as may be too large for Admission into those Drawers.

It having been suggested, that Racks for the Rolls would be better than inclosed Presses with Folding Doors, I have taken the Opinion of several Gentlemen conversant with ancient Records, who join with me in thinking that Mode not so convenient, the Rolls being infinitely more liable to be injured by Dust, which from their great Antiquity they are already too apt to gather; but this I submit to the Disposal of the Honourable Committee.

As the Removal of these Records, which are exceedingly numerous, though eventually of Benefit to the Public, by their being placed in a more commodious Situation, and less in Danger of Fire, will be of some present Inconvenience and Loss of Time to me, who as Keeper of these Records enjoy no Salary whatever, and will require likewise a great Portion of Attention in the subsequent Arrangement of them, I hope that the Sum of One hundred Pounds will be considered a moderate Recompense for the same. And lastly, as the Removal

Appendix (M)

To the Honourable the Committee of the House of Commons, appointed to consider of taking down the Buildings adjoining the Court of Exchequer.

In Obedience to your Order of the 1st Instant, I have estimated the Expence that would be incurred by the general Repair of, and fitting up for the Use of the Augmentation Office and King's Remembrancer, all me old Presses now standing in the several Apartments; and adding thereto such a Quantity of new as is necessary for the Deposit of all the Records displaced by the intended Alterations; namely,

In the Five Rooms over the King's Bench Treasury, in the Two Stories, in the Residue of the Building, Part of which is to be taken down; in the Garrets of the same; in the Long Gallery in the Court of Exchequer; in the Three Balcony Rooms, and Garret over the Treasurer's Remembrancer's Office, would amount to Six hundred and Twenty-one Pounds Sixteen Shillings and Six Pence.

5 June 1793*

All which is humbly submitted by

J. T. Groces.

To Lath and Plaster the Floor of the Five Rooms above-mentioned, as a Security against Fire, would cost, in Addition to the above Sum, Fifty-three Pounds.

ltoyal Assent A Message by Mr. Yeoman Usher of the

to Bills. Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty's Commission, for declaring His Royal Assent to several Acts agreed upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate Attendance of this Honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House, at the Desire of the Lords authorized by virtue of His Majesty's Commission afore-mentioned, had been at the House of Peers, where a Commission under the Great Seal was read, giving, declaring, and notifying, the Royal Assent to the several Public and Private Bills therein mentioned; and also impowering His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, His Royal Highness the Duke of York, His Royal Highness the Duke of Clarence, His Royal Highness the Duke of Gloucester, the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, and several other Lords, to declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills; and that the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, the Earl Graham, and the Lord Amherst, named also in the said Commission, did accordingly declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills: Which Bills are as followeth; viz.

An Act for placing the Stock, called East India Annuities, under the Management of the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, and ingrafting the same on the Three Pounds per Centum reduced Annuities, in Redemption of a Debt of Four Millions Two hundred Thousand Pounds owing by the Public to the East India Company, and for enabling the said Company to raise a Sum of Money by a further Increase of their Capital Stock, to be applied in Discharge of certain Debts of the said Company:

An Act for vesting in His Majesty certain forfeited Estates in Ireland, subject to the Disposition of the Parliament of Ireland:

An Act for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from the River Dun Navigation Cut, at or near Stainforth, in the West Riding of the County of York, to join and communicate with the River Trent at or near Keadby, in the County of Lincoln, and also a Collateral Cut from the said Canal to join the said River Dun, in the Parish of Thorne, in the said Riding:

An Act for making effectual the Statute Labour in the Shire of Inverness; and for levying Conversion Money in Lieu of Labour; and for otherwise regulating, making, and repairing Highways and Bridges in the said Shire; and for improving, widening, and lighting the Streets within the Royal Burgh of Inverness:

An Act for repairing and widening that Part of the Road, leading from Kelso towards the Town of Selkirk, which lies to the Eastward of the Turnpike

Road leading from Jedburgh to Lauder, which crosses the River Tvoiot near the Town of Kelso, and the Road leading from Kelso towards Coldstream, to the Place where it joins the Turnpike Road leading from Greenlaw to Coldstream, and from Kelso, through Ednam, to Orange Lane, in the Parish of Ecdes, in the County of Berwick, and from the Ford at Newton Mill, through Ednam, to Edenfoot, and from Kelso to Cornhill, in the County of Durham:

An Act for enlarging the Term and Powers of an Act, passed in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act to continue and " render more effectual Two Acts, passed in the " Twelfth Year of the Reign of King George the " First, and the Nineteenth Year of the Reign of his " late Majesty, for repairing the Road from Market " Harborough to Loughborough, in the County of " Leicester, and for repairing, widening, turning, " and altering, the Road branching out of the aforesaid Road at a Place called Filling Gate, to a " Road called The Foss Road, and from thence to " the Turnpike Road leading from Melton Mowbray "to the Guide Post in Saint Margaret's Field, " Leicester:"

An Act for repairing, widening, altering, and improving, the Road from Heage, in the County of Derby, through Belper, to Duffield, in the said County:

An Act for empowering the Committees, or. Committee, for the Time being, of the Estate of the most Noble Anna Eliza Dutchess of Chandos, a Lunatic, to make Leases of her Estate during her Lunacy, and for other Purposes therein mentioned:

An Act for confirming and rendering effectual a Partition and Division between William Thomas Darby, Esquire, and Saint Andrew Saint John, Esquire, of divers Manors, Lands, and Hereditaments (heretofore the Estate of Richard Jackson, Esquire, deceased) in the several Counties of Norfolk, Essex, Surrey, Middlesex, and the City of London, and for limiting and settling the specific Parts thereof, which, upon such Partition and Division, were allotted to each of them, to the several Uses therein mentioned:

An Act to enable Sir Henry Bridgeman, Baronet, and, after his Death, other Persons, to grant Building Leases of his settled Estates at and near Bolton in Lee Moores, in the County of Lancaster, for long Terms of Years >

An Act to enable James Lever, of Hindley, in the County of Lancaster, Esquire, to make Grants iu Fee, and also to grant Building Leases of certain Estates in the Township of Bolton le Moors, in the said County:

An Act to dissolve the Marriage of the Reverend Calverley John Bezvicke, Clerk, with Mary Elisabeth, otherwise Mary Eliza Vaughan, his now Wife, and to enable him to marry again, and for other Purposes therein mentioned.

Mr. Bramstm, according to Order, reported from Report on rt-the Committee, to whom the Report was re-oom- committed minted, which was made from the Committee, who Complaint were appointed to enquire into the Matter of the Com-, ^gp^^g plaint made' to the House, by a Member in his Place, Chelmsford of an Omission having been made in the ingrossed Navigation Bill for making and maintaining a Navigation from, B,u' or nearly from, the Town of Chelmsford, in the County of Essex, to a Place called Colliers Reach, m or near the River Blackzcater, in the said County, of the Name of one of the Commissioners, which was-inserted on the Report of the said Bill, and also, that the Names of Two Proprietors, inserted by this House, appeared to have been erased from the said ingrossed Bill; That the Committee had considered the said Report, and had directed him to make a further Report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place;

12 and

and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

vis.

It appeared to the Committee, That the Name of

John Strutt was clearly wrote in the Amendment re* ceived by the House upon the Report of the said Bill, and that the said Name is the Third upon the List, which List is not taken Alphabetically.

It also appeared upon the ingrossed Bill, that the Commissioners Names are inserted Alphabetically, and that the Name of John Strutt is omitted.

Your Committee then called Mr. David Jones, the Ingrossing Clerk, who was asked, Whether he ingrossed the Ckelmer Navigation Bill? he said, He did not.

That the customary Way of doing Business in the In- grossing Office, after a Bill is ordered to be ingrossed, is, to put the Bills in Hand by Rotation, as they are reported to the House: This Bill, for the Convenience of the Agents, was sent out to be ingrossed; and on its Return was delivered to Mr. White, the Agent for the Bill, to be examined.

And being asked, Whether he (the Witness) examined the ingrossed Bill with the House Bill and Amendments? he said, No. That the Examination of Bills by the Ingrossing Clerk has not been usual for near Thirty Years. That Bills formerly were examined by the Ingrossing Clerk, and the Agent for the Bill; and that he hath heard it was formerly customary for the Chairman of the Committee to whom the Bill was committed, to examine the Ingrossment. — And being asked, Whether the Bill was re-delivered to him by Mr. White she said, It was, by him, or One of his Clerks — It was delivered into the Office to be prepared for the Third Reading in the usual Way. That he does not know the Person who actually ingrossed the Bill; but Part of it was done at Messrs. Richards and Watt, Stationers, in Wyth Street, and the other Part at Messrs. Hughes and Watsh, Stationers, in the Temple — It was divided into different Parts for the Sake of Expedition, on Account of its Length — it is the usual Practice to ingross from a printed Bill — they pay no Regard to the written Copy, if they can get a printed Bill. — And being asked, Was this the only private Bill sent out to be ingrossed this Session ? he answered, No; not by many. That he - received the printed Bill from the Agent, Mr. White. — Then,

Mr. John White being examined, was asked, How it happened that the Name of John Strutt is omitted in the ingrossed Bill ? he replied, That in the Bill, as reported from the Committee, is a long List of Commissioners Names arranged in Alphabetical Order; tvhen the Report was considered in the House, there were about Twenty more Commissioners added by the House; these were not arranged Alphabetically, but trere either fastened in the Bill, or left loose, he knows not which — the Bill so amended was ordered to be ingrossed, and taken into the Ingrossing Office. It m not usual for the Ingrossing Clerks to ingross from the House Bill and Amendments, but from a printed and altered Copy, given them by the Solicitor for the Bill — Those BiHs the Clerks in his Office usually prepare; but, in this Instance, they being exceedingly hurried, he prepared the Bill himself: He had before him a Bill, with the Amendments, as it passed the Committee; in this was a Manuscript Copy of the First Set of Commissioners — he wrote into that from the additional List added upon the Report, those Names, placing them Alphabetically, ticking them off, as he believes will appear from the Paper; upon that Paper were the Names of John Strutt and Joseph Holden Strutt, at the Distance of Tw'o Names from each other: That he, by Mistake, wrote John Holden Strutt, and also, by Mistake, omitted the Name of John Strutt, and so the Bill was ingrossed; as also were the Proof Acts prqiarcd: That he meant to say, that he

V ol. 18.

had not to copy the additional Karnes one immediately following the other, but to select them, and mix them in their Alphabetical Order with the others. — Being asked, Who examined that Ingrossment, and where it was examined ? he said. It is never customary for the Ingrossing Clerks themselves to examine the Ingrossment — They give it to the House Solicitor for that Purpose; some of whose Clerks examine it. — It is the constant Practice of their Office to make the Country Agents examine all Ingrossments; most particularly, because neither they, nor their Clerks, can be competent to decide upon the Spelling of Names. This Ingrossment, according to the Practice of their Office, was, in the First Instance, examined by Three of their Clerks, with the Proof Act, and the House Bill, and Amendments. Their Clerks would find the Ingrossment and Proof Act agree; and as they also had, in the Reading of the Commissioners Names, to select into Alphabetical Order the additional Commissioners Names, they, he supposes, fell into the same Error as he had done. The Ingrossment and the Proof Act were again examined in the Ingrossing Office by One of their Clerks, and Mr. Ltapingwdl, the Country Agent. — Being asked, What was become ‘of the Paper which he transcribed from the Original List of additional Commissioners? he said, That Paper was in the Bill which he had in his Hand, which went to the Press for a Proof Act: Such BiHs, when returned from the Press, are considered in their Office as Waste Paper, and thrown about as such, by which Means such Papers as are loose in them are frequently lost, and he had, in fact, great Difficulty in finding any Part of this Bill; the List of Commissioners Names, so transcribed by him, and put into the Bill, he cannot find — He means to say, that he was the original Cause of this Error, but he had no Motive for leaving out Mr. John Strutt's Name, as it must be a Matter of total Indifference to him who were, or who were not, Commissioners. — Being then shewn the Paper of additional Commissioners, he was asked, Whether the Ticks therein were made by him? he said. They were; he meant them for his Guide in inserting those additional Names among the others, putting the Tick over each Name as he selected it, and wrote it into the other Copy. — Being asked, Why these being ticked, did he imagine they were omitted to be copied ? he said, In the Proof Act, which was printed from his Manuscript, stands John Holden Strutt, and because he has some Time since seen the Paper, which is now lost, in which he saw, in his own Hand Meriting, John Holden Strutt, and neither the Name of John Strutt, or Joseph Holden Strutt, and because he has been told by Mr. Lcapingtoell, that he found it so in the Ingrossment; and that, knowing the re was no such Person as John Holden Strutt, he so far corrected the Mistake, in his Examination of the Ingrossment, as to alter the Name of John to Joseph — That he never looked to this Part of the Ingrossment till the Error was discovered.

It appearing upon the Face of the additional List that there are Ticks at the End of the Names of John Otmius, Sir George Jackson, and John Strutt, and of those Names only, he was asked, How he accounted for that ? he said, He cannot account for it; but he wishes the Committee to observe, that there are other Marks at the End of other Names — That One of the Names has Two Ticks above it, and that One of the Names has no Tick at all — How these additional Ticks came he cannot account for; but he should wish to inform the Committee, that that List has not been in his Custody, but has been in no less than Three different Offices in the House of Commons, as he has been informed; meaning the Ingrossing Office, Mr. Benson the Clerk of the Papers Office, and Mr. Rosiers Office — The Marks at the End of the Three First Names he does not believe are of his making. —

rif the Importance of the Subject in Question ? he replied, It did not; because he supposed Mr. Stnitt would have been satisfied by being made a Commissioner, and so no Person would have Reason to complain; but if not so, he supposed that, upon his Complaint, the Lords Committee would have amended the Bill, by inserting his Name; and that when the Bill came back to this House so amended, this House would agree to the Amendment, as his Idea was, that they would consider the Matter as a clerical Mistake; it appearing that the Lords had only corrected their Error, they having in one Stage of the Business constituted Mr. Strutt a Commissioner, and they, the House, not having themselves left him. out. — And being asked, Whether it was not represented to him by the Gentleman who made an Offer for a Commissioner to resign, to be of Consequence ? he said, He is almost positive not: He thinks the only Conversation that ever passed upon the Subject was, as to the Matter of Fact, whether the Name was in or out; and whether, if the Lords did so amend the Bill, it was such an Amendment as the Commons could agree to — And being asked, What Answer did he make to those Gentlemen ? he said, It is impossible for him to recollect the Particulars of such Conversation, which passed a long Time since, and which he never thought he should be questioned about. Mr. John Leapingwell was called in and asked, What does he know of the Alteration of the Name of Joseph Holden Strutt in the Ingrossment of the Chelmer Canal Bill? he said, The Name was John, and as he knew Mr. Holden Strutt's Name to be Joseph, he altered it from John to Joseph. — And being asked, At what Time did he alter it? Mr. Leapingwell being called in, and asked, Whether he knew any thing of the Erasures of the Names of Benjamin Folkes and John Rennie from the ingrossed Bill ? he said, He made the Erasures. — And being asked, When he made them? he said, At the Time of the examining the Bill the Day before it was read the Third Time in the House of Commons. — And being asked, How he came to make them ? he said, Upon finding their Names in the Ingrossment, he left the Ingrossing Office, where he had been examining the Bill, and went with a printed Bill in his Hand to Mr.

White's Office, and told Mr. White that the Names of John Rennie and Benjamin Folkes should not have been in the Ingrossment, as they had long since sold their Shares, upon which he said " we must leave them out " or take them out," or some such Words, by which he understood he was to take them out — he returned to the Ingrossing Office, and took them out accordingly. — And being asked, Whether any Person was

Eresent when he erased the Names ? he said, The same Ilerk with whom he examined it, was he believed there at that Moment. — And being asked, Whether he communicated to any Person whatsoever that he had erased those Two Names? he said, He did to Mr.

White. — And being asked, When? he said, After the examining the whole of the Bill on the Evening he did it. — And being asked, When he first knew Mr. Rennie had sold out ? he said, It was in the Month of he thought the Ninth. — And being asked, Whether be prepared any Transfer of the Share of Mr. Rennie? he said, He filled up a printed blank Agreement for a Transfer. — And being asked. Whether it was for an immediate Transfer, or for a future Day ? he said, A Transfer he believed to take place after the Act should be obtained. — And being asked, When Benjamin Folkes informed him that he had sold his Share? he said, Some Months ago. — And being asked. If he knew whether any other of the Proprietors now standing upon the Bill had sold their Shares ? he said, He believed some of them had.

Mr. John Rennie being called, was asked, Whether he was a Proprietor of the Chelmer Navigation? he said,

He had been, but was not know. — And being asked.

If he had sold his Shares ? he said, He bad absolutely sold them; that he sold them on the Eighth of last March, and was paid for them on the Ninth. — And being asked. Who he sold them to? he said, Mr.

Wedge sold them for him to Mr. Clacker; they were in fact sold in January, but some Dispute prevented the Transfer 'till March.

Mr. Windham reported from the Select Committee, Report from to whom it was referred to consider of the Report which f

was made from the Committee td whom the Petition of Mr. Madge's Thomas Mudge, Watch-maker, was referred, and who Petition, were directed to examine the Matter thereof, and also to make Enquiry into the Principles on which Mr.

Mudge's Time-keepers have been constructed, and to report their Opinion thereupon to the House; That the Committee had considered the said Report, and made Enquiry accordingly, and had directed him to report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House; and he read {he Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the same, together with an Appendix thereunto, in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Report was read; and is as followed); viJs.

Your Committee having met accordingly, were of Opinion, that the latter Object of their Enquiry would be best attained by calling in the Assistance of Persons, eminent either for Mathematical and Meehan nical Knowledge, or practical Skill in Arts connected with the Subject before them, who might be desired to receive confidentially from Mr. Mudge the Principles of his Machine, and report thereon their Opinion to the Committee. The Persons chosen on this Occasion, and who consented to undertake the Examination referred to them, were,

The Bishop of Saint David's, Mr. and Mr.

Atwood; Messrs. Ramsden and Troughlon, Mathematical Instrument makers; Messrs. Holmes, Haley, and Howells, Watch-makers.

Your Committee in the mean Time proceeded in the other Part of the Enquiry, and received Evidence of various Sorts, tending to shew what had been done by Machines made on the Construction in Question, what had been done by the Machines of other Artists, and what was the Inference to be derived from the Whole, as to the Merit or Demerit of the supposed Invention of Mr. Mudge.

It appears to your Committee, that Three Watches only have been made on the Construction that is now the Object of Enquiry, of which Watches, One was made in the Year 1774, and the other Two in the Year *777-

That of these Watches, the First has been at different Times in the Possession of . Doctor Maskelyne, Doctor Hornsby, his Excellency Count Bthe late Admiral Campbell, Doctor Zach, Astronomer to His Serene Highness the Prince of Saxe Gotha, and again of Count Bruhl, with whom it still remains.

That tile Second and Third, except at Times when they were returned to the Maker, were on Trial at the Royal Observatory till the Year 1790, when they were finally delivered to Mr. Dutton, Mr. s

late Partner, with whom they have remained ever since.

Preparatory to any Statement derived from thence, either in favour of, or against the Merit of the Invention in Question, your Committee wish to state to the House a few general Remarks, by which the Nature and Value of such Statements may be better understood and appreciated.

It appeared early to your Committee, that the Methods commonly pursued for comparing Machines constructed for keeping Time, were not very exact, even for ascertaining the comparative Accuracy of their going in any past Trial, and still less for the Purpose of judging, with Precision, of the Excellence of the several Constructions, so as to say how much of their Irregularity was chargeable to accidental Causes, and how much inherent in the Machine itself. If such, at the Outset, was the Opinion of your Committee, the same was greatly confirmed in the Progress of their Enquiry.

The common Mode in Cases of this Sort is, from a Trial during a certain Period, to take a Rate, and then, in a future Period or Periods, to try the Watch by its Conformity to that Rate.

On each of these Operations, the Conception of which it is very necessary to keep distinct, your Committee observe great Difference of Opinion; proceeding, as they conceive, from considerable Difficulty in the Operations, which it seems impossible to reduce to any certain Rule, or not to leave as Matters in great measure discretionary and experimental.

The Question of finding a Rate is, in the Opinion of your Committee, the finding, from any Number of Trials (what is called a Period of Trial, being in Fact a Succession of several Trials) that Rate from which the Deviation of the Watch, during any future

Period, is likely to be least Previous to which Enquiry, it is necessary to determine what shall be the Measure of the Deviation of the Watch during any Number of Trials, from such Rate as shall be assigned to it

With respect to this last Question it is apparent that neither the Sum of the daily Errors, considering Excess and Defect as Quantities of the same Kind; nor the Sum of the greatest Excess and greatest Defect on any Two Days; nor the Result of the Whole, considering Excess and Defect as destroying each other, will fonn any Thing like an adequate Criterion. It may be said indeed, that the Sum of the Errors made each Day, and called in Doctor s Register,

" Errors of the Watch," will be a Measure of the whole Quantity of Error for which the Watch will have been chargeable during the Course of the Trial; but though this Method may be as accurate as any single One that can be chosen for that Purpose, yet it is altogether defective as a Measure of the Irregularity of the Watch, for the Purpose of estimating the Reliance to be placed upon it in any future Trial.

In like Manner, no general Rule is laid down, nor seems capable of being found, for assigning, from any Number of Trials, that Rate which the Watch shall be most likely to observe in any Trial in future.

The common Way, of dividing the Whole that the Watch has done during a given Period, by the Number of Days, and applying the Quotient as a daily Rate to be used in any Period succeeding, is certainly not a Method that can pretend to any extraordinary Exactness.

It seems indeed not to be well agreed what is the Object and Purpose which the taking a Rate is intended to answer. One of the Witnesses has said, that " the Meaning and Use of taking a Rate, is to find " whether the Watch goes vegularly or not." But your Committee are of Opinion, that the Witness, in giving this Answer, did not distinguish between the Application of a Rate for the Purpose of finding the Deviation of the Watch from itself (which Purpose may equally be effected by one Rate as by another) and the final Choice of a Rate from which if the Watch deviates, its Deviation shall be imputed to it as Error; such a Rate can only be that which, after competent Trial, may be concluded to be a Rate from which the Watch is least likely to deviate in future.

Accordingly your Committee have found that, among Persons likely to be best informed upon such Subjects, great Diversity of Opinion prevails, and that even the same Persons fluctuate at Times between Opinions widely different from each other.

An Example may be seen, P. 49 of the Minutes*, See thi* where One of the Witnesses, who had stated his Opinion, Journal, that a Rate taken from any Month, was as likely to be *8&

true in a Period of Six Months commencing at several Months Distance, as in the Period immediately succeeding the Month from which the Rate was taken; declares afterwards, that for a Period of Six Months, commencing from the present Time, he should always take a Rate from the Month last past.

From this apparent Diversity of Opinion in Persons so well instructed, your Committee can only infer considerable Uncertainty in the Subject itself; of which indeed no better Proof need be given than what occare in Pages and 45 of the Minutes \, where in the same f See this Trial, by a Rate applied in Doctor Maskelyne'& Method, Journal, the Watch Green has the Advantage, while by a Rate taken from the Month preceding, which Doctor Hutton declares to be a very proper Method, the Advantage is found to lie on the Side of the Watch Blue.

It is apparent, therefore, that between Watches nearly equal, no Reliance can be placed on a Judgment formed by any single Comparison, even with respect to their Merit in any past Trial: Much more uncertain must the Judgment be, where the Question is, not as

9 to

879

to their actual Performance, but u to the Merit of the Principles oo which they may be supposed to be constructed.

Your Committee therefore think k safer, under this Head, to lay before the House the Results of the Comparisons, such as they have been submitted to them, rather than to offer on the Whole any general Judgment of their own.

Mr. Mudge's Petition respecting his Watches.

On a view of the whole Evidence, were your Committee called upon to declare which of the several Watches had gone best, they should be inclined to say that both Mr. Arnolds, N° 36 and N# 68, had gone with a Degree of Accuracy greater than could be shewn on any corresponding Trial of Mr. Madge's, more especially if in giving this Judgment they were to include a Circumstance, not admitted generally by those who deny the Merit of Mr. Madge's Watches; viz. that a Rate applied in Doctor Me-

thod is less likely to be true, or in other Words less favourable to the Watch, than a Rate taken from the Period preceding that to which it is applied; but wCre your Committee required further to state the Presumption thence arising, as to the Merit of their several Constructions, with a view to the Reliance to be placed on others of the same Sort, or to the Ad-vahtages to be derived from thence in the general Improvement of Time-keepers, they should confess their Inability to offer any Opinion that could be at all deserving of Attention. They are of Opinion, that though the Merit of the Construction of Timekeepers can be finally decided only by Experience, yet that nothing could be more fallacious than the Judgment to be formed in that Respect from Experience so limited and imperfect as that which must make the Basis of their Judgment in the present Instance.

They entertain this Persuasion, not only from general Consideration of the Nature of the Subject, but from Facts appearing on the Face of the Evidence now sabmftteu to them. It is said by some of the Witnesses, that Watches made on the same Construction, end with the same Care, can hardly fail to go with nearly the same Exactness. If this be so, they are at a Loss to account why the Maker of such a Watch as Mr. Arnolds N° 36 or 68, should not have possessed himself long since of the Whole of tire Reward assigned under thre Act of Longitude, -especially as 13 Years have elapsed since tire YYiai Of N° 36 wa3 completed.

They are equally at a loss to account for thwt Provision in the Act of Longitude which requires that, before the Reward can be Obtained, Two Machines, conforming each to the Conditions of the Act, shall be made on the same Constructions; a Provision that must be wholly superfluous, could it be inferred with Certainty that what was done with one Machine might, by employing equal Care, be repeated always in another. The Fact they conceive to be, that Watches -formed on the best Principles will, either for Want of Care'or "Skill in the making, from Defects in some of thfe Parts, from Failure in the Adjustment, or finally from some of those mumerouste and fortuitous Causes which disturb the going of Time-keepers, and of whose Existence and Operation no Account can be given, nor any Estimate be formed, be found occasionally to go very ill; while others, made oh very defective Principles, will, from accidental Success in the Workmanship, or accidental Exemption from 'Some of the Causes of Error above -enumerated, be found -at Times to go with great Exactness. Mere Trial therefore, Urfless carried 4o great Extern, and multiplied through Variety of Instances, will Id! but little as to the Merit of the Principle on which a Watch is 'constructed. At all Events, where an Inference is to be drawn as to the probable going of a Time-keeper, from Experience of others of the same Sort, Consideration must be had of those of that Sort which -have -gone ill, as well as of those which have gone well; nor can your Committee be of Opinion, with one of the Gentlemen examined on this Occasion, that in comparing the Watches of Mr. and Mr. Arnold, and reasoning from thence to their respective Constructions, little Stress was to be laid on the Circumstance of Mr. Madge's Watches being

12

the only ThrCe which he had ever made, While those of Mr. Arnold were Two or Three selected out of near a

Thousand.

It may be observed of Mr. s Watches, that they afford one Ground of judging beyond that of any of the others, from the Length of Time during which their going is known. The First Watch is known from a Period so distant as the Middle of the Year 1776, and for the greater Part of the intervening Time. Of the Two remaining Watches, the earliest Register possessed by the Petitioner is in the Year 1779; but both of the Watches have been made since the Year 1777, and the going of all is not at this Moment less perfect, as appears by the Registers of Count Bruhl and Mr. Dutton^ than at any Time since they were first made.

From this Fact, joined to the Remark of the late Admiral Campbell, that the Watch which he had, seemed to possess the Property of changing its Rate less, after being stopped or let down, than any other he had known, your Committee cannot help thinking, as far as an Opinion may be hazarded on a Matter of so much Uncertainty, that there appears in these Watches, whether compared with each other, or with themselves at different times, such an Equality of going as would lead to a favourable Judgment, on the Truth and Permanency of the Principles of thrfr Construction. They are far however, from relying with Confidence on this Observation, or on any other of the Kind, or from asserting more of the Watches in Question than that they are Machines of great and indubitable Excellence. Of this they conceive abundant Confession is made, when of so many Timekeepers as have been produced of late Years, so few are brought whose going is said to be superior. The best Foundation for deciding the Question, which makes the proper Object for the consideration of the Committee, viz.What is the originality and Value of the Improvement alledged to be made by Mr. Mudge in the Construction of Time-keepers ? must, they apprehend, he sought for in the Report of the Gentlemen who have examined the Machines in Question, and know what the Nature of the Contrivance is. Whatever Doubt may be thought to attend even this Mode of judging (and its Uncertainty will vary through nearly all Degrees, according to the Nature of the Circumstances) it is, they conceive, far preferable to a Judgment from Experience, where the Experience is of no greater Extent than that furnished by the present Instance. It is» urged in Proof of the Demerit of these Machines, that they were very ill adjusted against the Effects of Heat and Cold. If such is the Fact, the Inference must be, that with abetter Adjustment, their going would have been still more exact. It is said that the Application of the Part used for Adjustment, and the Form of One of the Springs, is less advantageous than in other Watches; if that be se^ these Watches, by the Use of those Methods, will become capable of still greater Excellence. No Proof has been glveh to your Committee, nor have they any Reason to believe, that the Contrivance which contains the supposed Invention, is of a Nature to be incompatible with either of the Improvements above-mentioned. Were the Watches therefore already made ever so defective In their going, there is no reason for concluding (nor. cttn It be known but by those acquainted with their Construction) that with the Addition of Methods now geneially understood and practised, they may not give Birth to Machines far superior to any at this Time in Use; should it be thought necessary by the House, this Question might be put to the Gentlemen who acted rs a Sub-Committee. As far as your Committee believe and are informed, there is nothing in the present Contrivance that is not perfectly consistent with the Me-tltods above referred to The Merit and Value of this Contrivance, as far as the same can be stated on Theoretical

In virtue of this Report, and of such other Evidence as the Enquirythas furnished, your Committee have no Difficulty in declaring, that they consider the Improvement in Question sufficiently ascertained, and as likely to conduce to Advantages sufficiently important to at-traet the Notice of ‘Parliament. As a further-Ground of such Notice, it may be right to state to the House certain Circumstances relating to the Inventor, as well as the.Merit of the Invention itself. It is admitted on all 'Hands, that Mr. Mudge was One of the First Watch-makers which this Country has produced. 'It is- hardly1 less admitted, by all who have had an Opportunity of enquiring into the Fact, that at the End of this . Period, Mr. Mudge is closing his Life with a very scanty "Pittance, while many of the Profession, with no Pretence to Genius, nor any extraordinary Industry, by the mere Application of their Talents in the Way of Report on Trade, regardless of any Improvement in their Art, Mr* Madge'* have amassed splendid and independent Fortunes. Mr. J>ee^l"n Mudge, acting on other Principles, and withdrawing WatehS. from Business while his Powers were yet entire, devoted Twenty Years of a Life, which his former Inventions, freely communicated to the T^de, forbid to be considered as of no Value, to the laudable Hope of benefiting the World, and Ip the same of himself and

his Country, by Improvements made in the higher Branches of his Pxofpssipn. It would be much to be lamented if Endeavours like these, though only tolerably successful, should he left wholly without Reward.

There is in this Instance good. Reason to hope, that they may have hpen successful to the full Extent of the most sanguine Wishes. But other Considerations, approaching nearer to a Pfpq ef Right, may contribute to mark out Mr. Mudge as a proper Object of the Public Bounty. Three Years after Mr. Mudge had quitted Business, with a View to become a Candidate for the Reward under the Act of Longitude, and when he had actually completed his First Time-keeper, the Legislature thought it necessary to pass a new Act, wholly changing the Terms of Trial, and increasing, in a great Proportion, the Difficulty through which Ae Reward was to be obtained. It is not contended, that every Hardship suffered under Ae Operation of public Acts, can confer on the Sufferer a Claim to Comr pensafion: but your Committee conceive, that where such an instance happens to be distinctly made out, it will strongly recommend the Party to Ae Consideration of the Legislature, and insure a liberal and indulgent Reception of any oAer Plea which he may have to their Favour. It is a Fact, Aat in Ais Instance,

Ae Terms of the Act subsisting when Mr. Mudge engaged in this Undertaking, and applied by the Mode of Trial adopted by Ae Astronomer Royal in the Case of Mr. Harrison, would have been fulfilled, so far as Ae Trial went, by Mr. Mudges Watches; and, if the Performance of these Watches, in Ae further Trials required by that Act, may be judged of by Trials nearly similar, in Voyages to Newfoundland, Aere is nothing to prevent the Belief that he would finally have been in a Situation to claim, as a Matter of Right, Ae whole of the Reward granted by that Act, being double the Reward granted by the Act at this Time subsisting. The present Act does indeed impose Conditions so difficult, and so impossible to be surmounted, if enforced to the full Extent of which they are capable, Aat it is to be feared that.few Artists will engage in an Undertaking so discouraging and precarious, or quit Ae certain Gains of their Profession, for the Hope of Rewards, which must at last depend for their Attainment on the Discretion of those by whom Aey are to be dispensed.

For Aese. Considerations, joined to those above set forth, your Committee think Aemselves authorized to recommend the Petitioner to Ae Attention of Ae House; conceiving that Ae Circumstances attending his Case, give him a strong Plea to Favour; and, that the Invention of which he is the AuAor, contains an important Improvement in Ae Art of constructing Timekeepers, such as the House might well wish to secure to the Public, as.well as to Reward Ae Person by whom it was produced.

Have you made any Calculation of the going of Mr. Mudge s Two Time-keepers in their late Trial at the Royal Observatory ?

Yes.

What Method of Calculation do you think most proper and agreeable to the Terms and Intent of the Act of the 14th of His present Majesty, to calculate their going by ?

By taking the mean daily Rate of the Watches in the First Month of the Trial, and applying it to the several Periods of Six Months each comprized in the Twelve Months Trial, to any Number of Periods of Six Months each.

Is this the Method, which was used by the Astronomer Royal, and approved of by the Board of Longitude, and upon which they decided that the Watches had not gone within the Limits of the Act?

I believe it is, by the Publications of Doctor Mas-kelyne and Mr. Mudge.

What were the Errol's of Mr. Mudge's Watches by this Method of Calculation ?

Are these Errors beyond the Limits of the Act ?

They are.

What do you think of the Method of taking the mean daily Rates of the Watch in the several Months, and applying them to the several Periods of Six Months, immediately following each Month?

I think it a very proper Method, when it is practicable, which however can seldom be the Case during a Voyage.

What were the Errors of Mr. Madge's Watches by this Method ?

On a Medium, upon Six Periods of Six Months each, as in the former, were as follows:

Watch Green,

Watch Blue,

3'. 31''; but the Errors were much greater than these in some of the Periods, and in One amounted as high as 9. 28'.

What do you think of the Method proposed by Mr. Madge, namely, to find the mean Rate of the Watch in the First Six Months, and apply it to the going in the Second Six Months?

I think it a very improper Method on all Accounts, whether for a First Trial of a Watch at the Observatory, or for a Trial to get the Rate before going a Voyage to Sea; for with respect to a Voyage, this Method would seldom be practicable, as a Six Months previous Trial to a Watch before going to Sea could seldom be attained; and at any Rate the Method must be very fallacious on Account of Heat and Cold, whether the Half Yearly Periods contain equal or unequal Portions of the hot and cold Seasons of the Year; for in the first Place, if these Periods should contain unequal Portions of it, so that the one of those Periods should fall all on the Six Summer Months, and the other on the Winter Months, and if the Watches were not most exactly regulated for Heat and Cold, then the greatest Difference would fall on the Result, and if the Watches should be addicted to accelerate or retard their daily Rates of going, then in Process of Time a considerable Error must arise, when the Period from which the Rate is taken, and that to which it is applied, comprize so great a Compass of Time; on the other Hand, should those Two Half Yearly Periods contain equal Portions of the hot and cold Months, and should the Watches have a Periodical Return in their Rates of going, as to Heat and Cold, which is commonly the Case, then the medium Results of these Two Half Yearly Periods would probably be equal, or very nearly so, from whence it would seem as if the Watches had kept their Rate of going all that Time very accurately, and yet nevertheless they may have deviated by enormous Errors backward and forward in the interior Parts of these Two' Half Yearly Periods.

What are the Errors by this Method of Mr. Report on Mudge'sr MrMudge't

They were various, as might be expected, sometimes more and sometimes less; but according to the his Watches! most favourable Way for the equal Portions of hot and cold Seasons, and according to Mr. Madge's Mode of Computation, the Error upon Six Months amounted to 4'. 2" I; but by the unequal Portions of Heat and Cold, the Error amounted to almost 9', using still Mr. Mudge's Computation.

Do the Watches appear to be well regulated with respect to the Effects of Heat and Cold ?

No.

How does this appear ?

By comparing the Rates of the Watches in the several Periods of Six Months in Summer, with the like Periods in Winter; for in the Six Winter Months, the Watches went considerably faster than in the Six Summer Months: The Watch Green, by the Quantity 8'. 56", and the Watch Blue 5'. 5"; and these might, in Reality, have been the Errors of the Watches, as reported from an Observatory, if the Trial of them' had commenced in the Middle of Spring, or in die Middle of Autumn, instead of commencing, as it did, in the Middle of Summer, using Mr. Madges Mode of Calculation.

Do you think the Goodness of a Watch can be better ascertained by an Examination of its Constroc--tion and Principles, than by an Examination of its going?

Certainly not; in every Machine whatever, we always try Experiments in order to judge of its Accuracy, and we rate its Value and Goodness, in Proportion to the Accuracy it seems to possess from that Result.

Don't you think that it is an Objection to Doctor Maskelyne's Method, that the Period from which the Rate is taken, becomes gradually more and more removed from that to which it is applied ?

I think quite the contrary; and think that Circumstance a particular Part of its Excellence.

Do you think the Rate, so taken, equally good for all the successive Periods?

It has an equal Chance to be equally good for all; it is a Method which does not seem to militate against one Period more than another.

In taking a Rate for a Period of Six Months, commencing from the present Time, do you think it indifferent whether the Rate be taken from the Month terminating at the present Time, or from a Month beginning Six Months antecedent to the present Time?

I think it might be material, on account of the Difference of Seasons, not otherways; it does not occur to me at present that there is any other material Difference, unless the Watch should have a continual Pro-

gess in altering its Rate of going — there may be other ircumstances that don't occur to me at present.

To what Extent would you carry the Principle, that the Distance of the Period from which the Rate was taken, from that to which it was applied (the going of the Watch in the intermediate Time being supposed not to be known) was of no Consequence i

In the Course of Twelve Months Trial, I would take each Month, or every single Month, and compare it with every Period of Six Months, during that Twelvemonth.

In order to obtain a Rate for the next Six Months, would it be indifferent, in your Opinion, whether the Rate was taken from the last Month, or

On the same Principle, on which you would prefer the nearest Month to one a Year off, why should you not prefer the nearest Month to one Six Months off, the Consideration of Seasons being supposed to be out of the Question ?

Upon what Principle d? you consider it as no Excellence in Doctor s Method, that the

Period from which the Rate is taken, is removed from all the Periods, except to which it ia applied?

It is removed to all the different Distances from the Periods to which it is applied, and the greatest Variety of Results, really differing from each other, will be obtained in this Way, it being by this Means removed to the several Distances of l. 2. 3. 4. 5. &c. Months, and the Medium of the Whole will he the most likely tp he nearest the Truth.

Will a greater Variety of Results be obtained this Way, than in the same Number of Periods, each tried by a Rate taken in any other Way ?

I think it likely there will.

Js it not meant by taking a Rate, to find that Rate to which the Watch is most likely to eon-form ?

I conceive that the Meaning and Use of taking a Rate, is to find whether the Watch goes regularly or not.

Won't one Rate do that as well as another ? I think not.

Was not Doctor Maskelyne s Method particularly necessary to be used by the Commissioners of Longitude, in judging whether the Watches came within the Limits of the Act, because that Act requires a Method generally useful and practicable ?

I think it was.

Do you mean to say, universally, that every Judgment that can be formed of a Machine by the Knowledge of its Construction, is inferior to that whch can be derived from the Experience of its Effects, however limited and imperfect that Experience may be?

The universal Way of judging Machines is by trying their Effects.

Do you mean to say that no Knowledge can be formed by Means of their Construction i

I do not.

Do you mean to say more than this, that the Properties of Machines, as of all other Things, must be judged of partly by Theory and partly by Experience, and that the Value of the Opinion derived from each, will be regulated by the Means by which each is formed, and by the Nature of the Subject ?

I don't mean to say more.

Don't you think, that by how much Machines are more complex, by so much they are more difficult to be judged of by their Principles ?

Certainly I do.

Don't this Opinion particularly apply to Timekeepers?

Yes, very particularly.

Do you mean to imply more, than that Timekeepers are complex Machines?

No.

Adjourned till Tomorrow.

Committee on Report of Mr. Petition met,

Sir Gilbert Elliot in the Chair.

Sir George Shuckburgh,

Mr. Gregor,

Mr. Windham,

Mr. Ryder, and Mr. Bragge.

Sir Joseph Banks, Baronet.

Are you not deputed by the Board of Longitude to oppose Mr. Madge's Petition in Parliament ?

I am.

What are the general Grounds the Board go upon in opposing the Petition ?

They are of Opinion that Mr. Madge's Allegations in his Petition, respecting the Superiority of his Watches over the Watches of other Artists, is not founded in Fact; and this I learn from their Proceedings: From Conversations from many of their Members I am of Opinion, that the Majority, if not the Whole of the Board, will coosder a Reward given by the House of Commons, in direct Opposition to their Opinion, as a Censure upon their Conduct in the Execution of the Trust devolved on them by Parliament, and that they had far rather the House of Commons would make an Enquiry into their Management of Public Money, if they suspect them to have done wrong, than to thus cast an oblique Reflection upon them.

Did the Astronomer Royal, when he gave in his Report to the Board, upon the going of Mr. Mudge's Time-keepers on their late Trial, explain to‘them at the same Time the Grounds and Principles of the Calculation which he used, to shew whether they had gone within the Limits prescribed by the Act of Parliament?

He explained to them the Rate he made Use of and his Mode of applying it. I apprehend the Commissioners were well competent to judge of the Remainder.

Did the Board thereupon determine that the Timekeepers had not gone within the Limits of the Act, and that they were not authorized to order further Trials of them ?

They did; and, to the best of my Knowledge, unanimously.

Has the Board of Longitude ever shewn any Disinclination to encourage the Improvement of Timekeepers ?

Certainly not, since I have belonged to it, which is more than Fourteen Years.

Does not the Board of Longitude, in determining Rewards to be given to Artists, consider itself as acting under the Authority, and confined within the Provisions of an Act of Parliament ?

Yes.

Withdrew'.

Doctor Maskelyne.

Did you try Mr. Madge's Time-keepers at the Royal Observatory ?

Yes; his First Time-keeper between the Year^ 1774 and 1778, at Two several Times. His Second Time-keepers, Green and Blue, Three several Times; the First Time in 1779 and 1780, the Second in 1783 und 1784, the Thud in 1789 and 1790; the First, between 1774 and 1778, for the Space of 18 Months, in 1779 and 1780 for 15 Months, in 1783 and 1784 for 14 Months, and 1789 and 1790 for 12 Months.

887

How came the First Time-keeper to be sent by the Board of Longitude to the Royal Observatory to be tried there at all, as the Act of Parliament of the 14th of the King requires Two Time-keepers to be tried together?

This was done at the Desire of Mr. Mudge, and is a strong instance as well of the Indulgence of the Board as of myself to him, since I was not obliged by the Act to admit a single Time-keeper to the Royal Observatory.

How did his First Time-keeper go ?

It went pretty regularly from Day to Day, but it gradually accelerated its daily Rate of going, till, at the End of the Three Months Trial, it went 4" a Day faster than at the Beginning. It stopt One Day however soon after winding up, which Mr. Mudge attributes to the Motion in carrying it back from the Transit Room (where it was compared with the Clock) to the Great Room, where it was kept; this however I have much Doubt of, as Mr. my Assistant

at the Time, who managed the Watch that Day relates in a Letter to Barton Masseres that he carried the Watch back from the Transit Room to the Great Room uncovered before him, and thinks it highly probable that if the Watch had stopt in consequence of the horizontal Motion it received in his Return with it, he should have seen it. The Watch was set going again in a few Days, and Three Weeks after the main Spring broke, and then it was taken away to be repaired. 'It was brought again the 1 ith Ac-vember 1776, and tried for 15 Months, till February 26th 1778, successively, when the main Spring broke again; at the End of this Time the Watch had accelerated its daily rate of going by 8"f above that of its going at the Beginning of the 15 Months. This is the most pernicious Error to which a Watch can be subject, since by going always the same Way it never compensates itself, but continually accumulates Error. — The First Trial of the First Time-keeper commenced on the 14th of December 1774.

Did the Commissioners of Longitude, after a competent Trial of the First Time-keeper, request Mr. Mudge to prosecute his Invention, that by having Two Time-keepers of the same Construction he might become properly a Candidate for the Reward offered for Inventions of this Kind by Act of Parliament?

No, he was not requested by the Board to prosecute his Invention. It was his owm Proposal to do so, provided he could receive some Assistance from the Board; the Board in Consequence gave him 500l.

When did the Three Trials of Mr. s

Two Time-keepers, called Green and Blue, commence at the Royal Observatory ?

The First began April 20th 1779, and was continued 15 Months: the Second 21st July 1783, and lasted nearly 14 Months; the Third began 24th June 1789, and continued 12 Months.

How did they go in the First Trial ?

But indifferently: The Watch Green having accelerated its daily Rate at the End of the Trial 11", and the Watch Blue 18".

How did they go in the Second Trial ?

The daily Rates of each varied by 9" f, and at the End of the Trial the daily Rate of Green was accelerated near 3", and that of the Watch Blae by 4" |, and the Watch Green erred 1' 25' in the First Period of 6 Months, and 7'. 6" in the Second Period of 6 Months; and the Watch Blue erred 5'. 43". in the First Period of 6 Months, and 11'. 4". in the Second Period of 6 Months. AH which Errors (except the first) of the Watch Green, are considerably above 4', the Limit of Error prescribed by Act of Parliament.
