What were the Errors of the Watches in 6 Months in their late Trial ?

In Two of the Periods of 6 Months the Error of the Watch Green was less than 4', and in Four of the Periods more than 4', or beyond the Limits of the Act; and the Error of the Watch Blue in One Period was less than 4', and in Five of the Periods more than 4'.

Did you give an Account of these Errors of the Watches, m your Report of their going, to the Board of Longitude?

Yes.

What Resolutions did the Board come to upon this Report?

They resolved unanimously, that as the Time-keepers had not gone upon the 12 Months Trial with the Exactness required by the Act of the 14th of the present King, the Board was not authorized to order further Trial of them.

What Method of Calculation did you use in computing these Errors of the Watches ?

I took a Mean of the Daily Rates of each Watch in the First Month of the Trial, which I applied to correct its going in several Periods of 6 Months comprized in the 12 Months Trial, and I accounted the Errors remaining (after the said Corrections were made) to be the Errors of the Watches in 6 Months.

What do you think of a Method which has been proposed of computing the going of Watches, namely, by taking the several mean daily Rates of the Watch in each Month of the First Half Year, and applying them respectively to the several Periods of 6 Months immediately following each Month?

It is a very proper Method to be used when it can be put in Practice, but Ships do not always stay long enough at a Place to admit of it.

What were the Errors of the Watches in 6 Month#, according to this Method ?

Two of the Errors of Watch Green were under 4', and Four of the Errors were above 4', and One of them amounted to 9'. 28"; and Three of the Errors of Watch Blue were under 4', and Three of the Error# were above 4'.

What are your particular Reasons for preferring your Method of Computation, namely, that of correcting the going of the Watches, in the several Periods of 6 Months, by the mean daily, Rate taken from the First Month of all ?

That as the Act of Parliament requires a Method of finding the Longitude, which shall be generally useful and practicable, the Method of Calculation employed to judge of the Agreement 01 Disagreement of Watches with the Terms of the Act. should be of such a Kind- as ean be practised in every V oyage; and as one cannot be sure that a Ship shall stay long enough at every Port which it shall touch at, to get a fresh Rate of going by Observation, and therefore it may often be necessary to keep on the Use- of the daily Rate of the Watch, with which it first went to Sea, so in like Manner one should calculate the Errors of the Time-keepers at Land, by using the Rate of the first Month, to judge whether they would probably always go within the Limits of the Act in 6 Months.

What Authority is there for this Account of the going of Mr. Arnold's Watch, N® 36 ?

It was tried at the Royal Observatory in 1779 and 1780, and I and Mr. George Gilpin, my Assistant at that Time, do certify to the Truth of it.

What do you think of this Method ?

That it would seldom be practicable, as a 6 Months Trial of a Watch before it went to Sea could seldom be obtained; and if One of the Periods of 6 Months should fall in the Summer, and the other in the Winter Parts of the Year, and the Watches were not most exactly regulated for Heat and Cold, the greatest Difference that could arise from the imperfect Correction, would fall upon the Result; and if the daily Rates of the Watches were subject to accelerate or retard, in Process of Time a considerable Error would arise, when the Period from which the Rate is taken, and that to which it is applied, comprize so large a Compass of Time.

What are the Errors of the Watches by this Method?

The Error of the Watch Green was a few Seconds above 4', and the Error of the Watch Blue a few Second under 4'; so that both Watches did not go within the widest Limit of the Actj by this Mode of Computation.

Do the Watches appear to have been well regulated with Respect to the Effects of Heat and Cold ?

No.

How does this appear?

The Watch Green went faster in the 6 Winter Months than in the 6 Summer Months by near 9'; and the Watch Blue went faster in the 6 Winter Months than in the 6 Summer Months by more than 5'; and these might have been actually the Errors of the Watches, according to Mr. Mudge's own Method of Computation, if the Trial of them had commenced in the Middle of Spring, or the Middle of Autumn, instead of Midsummer.

What Authority is there for this Account of the going of Mr. Arnold?s Watch, N® 68 ?

It was tried by Mr. Everar of Lynn, the Owner of the Watch, who communicated the Account of its going to Mr. Arnold, by whom it was printed and published; and Mr. Everard, in a Letter to me, dated " Lynn, 4th March 1792," certifies the going of the Watch, as stated in this Publication, to be very accurate. The Error of this Watch in 6 Months, was computed from the said Publication by the above-mentioned Mr. George Gilpin, who is ready to certify to the Truth of it.

The daily Rate of its going, as published by Count Bruhl in a Pamphlet and Printed Sheet, were given away by Count Bmhl to his Friends, and among them to myself, and the Errors in 6 Months were computed both by myself and by Mr. George Gilpin.

What Voyages?

Port Jackson, in New South Wales, and to the South West Coast of America.

Does it often happen, during those Voyages, that the Ships do not touch at some Place, the Longitude of which is known, or which they may have Means of ascertaining ?

I believe it often happens that they do not touch at any Port at all, or not long enough to get a fresh Rate of the Watch by Observation.

What Length of Time is necessary for that Purpose ?

A Month.

Cannot a new Rate be obtained for the Watch, whenever the Longitude of the Place is ascertained ?

Yes.

Cannot the Longitude of the Place be ascertained in less than a Month ?

Sometimes it may.

Must it not be a particular Combination of Circumstances that can prevent the Longitude of a Place at which a Ship may Stop, from being ascertained in less than a Month ?

I think it may often happen — it is sometimes cloudy both at the Cape of Good Hope and Port Jackson for a Fortnight or three Weeks.

From your own Trials, and those of others, of the going of Mr. Mudge's and Mr. Arnold's Watches, which do you think to be made on the best Construction and Principle ?

I think it a right Principle to judge of the comparative Merits of Two Constructions, by the best Specimens of the going of each, or those of each which have gone best; 1 judge of the Goodness of Mr. Madge's Construction, from the Performance of his Two Watches in the late Trial, after they had been made 12 Years, and repeatedly corrected and improved in the intermediate Time; in like Manner I judge of the Goodness of Mr. Arnold's Construction, from the going of the best Watches he has made, which is incontestably superior to the going of Mr. Madge's.

In following the above Mode of judging of the comparative Merit of the Construction of Two Watches, from the best Specimens from each, don't you think it necessary to take into Account the Number of those Specimens, and the Proportion of each Sort that are good, to those that are otherwise ?

I should judge from the best Specimens of each, without requiring a considerable Number of Specimens.

If one Watch has gone better than another, do you think that you can conclude confidently that the Watch that has gone best is of the better Construction ?

Yes, if each Artist has used his utmost Care and Pains in making and adjusting his Watch.

Does it always happen that Watches made with the same Care, and upon the same Construction, go with equal Excellence ?

Nearly so, if sufficient Time is taken to correct and adjust them.

To multiply the Experiments of the Watches, by which Means a more sure and speedy Judgment might be formed of their Agreement or Disagreement with the Terms of the Act.

I think it might, from a competent Number of Trials.

Mr. William Wales.

Don't you think that the Causes of the Irregularity in the going of a Time-keeper, may be of such a Nature, and so small, as totally to escape ah Discovery by Inspection?

In all those I have seen I think it is.

Can any Thing very conclusive be drawn as to its going from the Examination of its Mechanism?

I think not, without Trial, and I think Mr. A fudges Watches have shewn it; because if the Principles of the Watches had been good from the Beginning, they would always have gone well, which they have not; and from what I know of Mr. I

think his Principles are as likely to be as good as any.

In case of Oil being used, may not the Quality of the Oil be changed by Heat or Cold, or other Causes, so as to produce a sensible Alteration in the going of the Watch, although the Change in the Quality of the Oil, as to its Tenacity, should be wholly insensible to the Eye ?

I don't know whether to the Eye of a Person used to looking at Watches, it may or may not; but the Rate of Time-keepers has been much altered, and it was supposed to have arisen from an Alteration in the State of the Oil, when I could see none.

May not similar Changes and Irregularity take place, or originally exist in the main and balance Springs, which shall equally elude Discovery by the Eye, but be very discernible in the Irregularity, of its going ?

Certainly.

Is it not preposterous to attempt to judge of the Merit of a Time-keeper by Inspection of its Mechanism ?

I think nothing certain can be gained from it, without a Trial of its going.

Are not the Causes that disturb the going of Timekeepers, many of them of such a Sort as will as well affect Time-keepers of a good Construction, as those of an inferior one ?

As the best Time-keepers are not perfect Machines, they may be liable to be affected in a small Degree, by the same Causes that affect inferior Time-keepers in a greater Degree.

Are there not many Causes that will operate in disturbing Time-keepers, without any certain Proportion to the Excellence of their Construction ?

There may be some, but that would arise from the Carelessness of the Watchmaker, in adjusting and putting the Watch together; such as bad Oil, making

use of bad Metals, and putfipg the Watch together carelessly.

Are there not Causes of Disturbance against which the Workman can make no adequate Provision, and which will happen irregularly and fortuitously f

There may be some which will affect a had Timekeeper considerably, hut which will not affect a gppd one, so as to be of any material Consequence.

all

No.

Does not this Consideration render the Judgment to be formed of foe Construction of Time-keepers, from their Performance in Trials, unless such Trials shall have been very numerous, in a seat Degree uncertain ?

I think not, in the best Time-keepers that have been produced.

Though it be true that Experience is ultimately the Test of Merit in eh practical Concerns, mast not that be meant of Experience continued to an indefinite Extent, so as to insure, that between Two Objects so tried, the Operation of casual and extraneous Causes may be presumed to be equal ?

No; for I suppose the extraneous Causes wiH affect the best Machines in an inconsiderable Degree, and that a moderate Number of Trials is sufficient

Are there not Mechanical Contrivances of a Nature so simple, that their Effects may be determined with Certainty beforehand ?

When used separately by themselves they may; npt when combined together, as in a Watch,

Does not the Judgment to be formed of the Operation of Mechanical Contrivances, according to the Nature of the Contrivance and the Subject to which it applies, pass through nearly all Degrees of Certainty, from the greatest Doubt to the most thorough Conviction ?

Through great Variations of Certainty.

Is not the same true, that of a Judgment formed by Experience, namely, that according to the Extent and Nature of the Experience, jt may pass through all Degrees of Certainty from the least to the greatest?

According to the Degree of Experience.

Must it not happen then, that some Judgments formed a priori, or by reasoning from Causes to Effects, must be better than some formed the contrary Way, vis. by Experience?

That may sometimes happen.

Is the Question, therefore, whether Machine# are to be best judged of by Knowledge of their Construction, or by Experience, a Question liable tP be answered by a simple Affirmation or Negation, that is such a one as is universally true either Way?

It is pretty generally true, but not universally.

That it is a very good Contrivance.

' Is not the Helical Spring more likely than the common Spring, to cause the long and short Vibrations to be performed in the same Time ?

It is more likely and more easy to make it.

Mr. John Arnold.

Do you apprehend your Correction Piece for Heat and Cold differs from Mr. Mudge's, either in the Construction or Application ?

In both — the Correction Piece of my Time-keeper is in the Balance itself, which Mr. Harrison says in his Book, would be the greatest possible Perfection could it be obtained — we have made those Corrections so perfect now that they may be adjusted to any possible Degree of Perfection, to Half a Second in Twenty-four Hours for 60' of the Thermometer, which I believe is the greatest Variation in this Climate; but we usually adjust them from 32 % or below, to 112*: but we find if they are well adjusted to 6o*, they answer for all others — the other Method of Adjustment for Heat or Cold, is by shortening or lengthening the Balance Spring which was Mr. Harrison's, and is incorrect and impossible from its Nature to be made perfect.

What Objections do you see to the Correction Pieces which clip the Balance Spring in different Places, according to the Heat or Cold of the Weather?

That the Increase and Decrease of the Motion of that Piece cannot be made to correspond with the different Lengths of the Spring; for Example, suppose the Spring to be 40 Inches long, and it is necessary to shorten tfint Spring One Inch for 10* of Heat, the

That it is never a Spiral, but when it is at rest; for the Instant it begins to move, it assumes a Figure that is not a perfect Spiral, both when the Spring opens and closes by the contrary Vibrations.

What is the Advantage of the detached Escapement ?

Less Oil, and that the Balance is less impeded by the Change of the Oil of Pallot.

Have you any Method of adjusting your Watches, so as to make the Balance describe large and small Arcs in the same Time ?

Yes, perfectly; so much so, that 180° Difference in the Length of the Vibration of the Balance, shall have no sensible Effect on the Time shewn by the Chronometer.

Mr. George Gilpin.

Do you know any thing of the Trial of Mr. Mudge's First Time-keeper at the Royal Observatory ?

Yes, I assisted in the Trial of it 15 Months.

Were those Trials conducted with Care?

Yes, very great, both on the Part of Doctor Maskelyne, as well as on the Part of myself; except by being let down once, if that may be thought an Accident.

Do you use any Remontoire to your Watch ?

None.

Is there no Advantage in the Use of the Remontoire ?

Only as a Help to bad Workmanship, or to those that don't understand the Helical Spring.

Do you apprehend that the best Time-keepers made by other Persons require any particular Care or Attention to preserve them from Accident ?

Not more than common Watches.

How many Time-keepers have you made?

Upwards of 900; but never made Two exactly alike, while I was able to improve the Principles; I have Twenty N° Ones.

What Knowledge have you of the going of your Time-keepers and of the Number?

From those who have had them — upwards of 50 we have got Account of.

From what Prices do you sell your Watches ?

From 25 to 120 Guineas.

Did you ever hear how many Time-keepers Mr. Mudge made ?

Four or Five.

Did any Accident happen to it during the Time ?

No Accident to the Watch, but it stopt on a sudden, without any apparent Cause, before it was taken from the Observatory.

Was any Cause assigned for its stopping?

Mr. Dutton, who came to the Observatory to take it away, attributed its stopping to the breaking of the Main Spring.

How did the Watch go before it stopped?

Indifferently; it altered its Rate 8"J per Day in the 15 Months. I mean that on some Day during the latter Part of the Time, it went 8"J faster than it had gone on some Day at the Beginning.

Do you know any thing of the Trial of Mr. Mudge'& Two Time-keepers, called Green and Blue, at the Observatory in 1779 and 1780?

Yes; I also assisted in the Trial of them for 15 Months.

Was that Trial conducted with Care, and did any Accident happen to the Watches during the Time ?

The Trial was conducted with very great Care, both on the Part of the Astronomer Royal, as of myself, and no Accident happened to either of them.

What is the Disadvantage of this Kind of Error in a Watch, namely, its continually accelerating its daily Rate?

It is the most pernicious of all Errors incident to ft Watch, because going always the same Way, it never compensates itself, but continually increases with Time. Thus, if the Watch gradually altered its daily Rate till it was increased only by 2" -rVhs at the End of 6 Months* this would occasfon the Watch to differ from the Calculation of its going, made from the Rate of the preceding Month, by 4', or beyond the Limits of the Act. What Method of Calculation did you use in finding the Errors of the Watches in 6 Months?

By taking the Mean of the first Month's Rate, and applying it to the succeeding Periods of 6 Months, each Period beginning a Month later than the preceding.

Is this the Method which was used by the Astronomer Royal, and approved of by the Board of Longitude, and upon which they decided that the Watches had not gone within the Limits of the Act?

It appears so from Doctor Maskelyne's Publication.

Did Doctor Maskelyne appear to wish well to Time-keepers in general, and think them useful Machines ?

Yes, — he not only wished well to them in general, but actually gave the Makers of them great Encouragement, not only by taking upon himself the Trouble of giving their Watches private Trials, but of rendering pecuniary Aid to some who would not have been able to have prosecuted the Business of making Timekeepers so long as they did, had it not been for his Assistance.

Did Doctor Maskelyne ever uste any Expression that shewed his Satisfaction or Dissatisfaction at Mr. Mudge's Watches going well?

I never knew him express any Dissatisfaction at his Watches going well; on the contrary, I have frequently heard him express great Satisfaction when they went well, and a Regret when they shewed Signs of going ill.

Whether what is stated by you as an Error, and an Error of the most pernicious Kind, is not consistent! with the going of a Watch which might be considered as perfect?

They have not all done so.

Will nqt a Watch, whose Variations conform to a constant and known Law, be as good, or nearly as good, as One which does not vary at all ?

Yes, if you can be certain that it will always go so; but I apprehend that is not the Case — when a Watch begins to accelerate its Rate, we can never tell when it will stop-.

Can you tell for certain what a Watch will do that is sometimes accelerated, and sometimes retarded ?

That may depend upon its not being adjusted for Heat and Cold.

Does not the true Merit of a Watch consist in being subject to a constant and known Law, whatever' that Law may be ?

Yes;

May hot a Watch, therefore, which has constantly accelerated during the Course of its Trial, afford as good a Presumption of its possessing that Merit, as One that has occasionally compensated itself?

No; ft Watch will very frequently accelerate for a considerable Time, and then cease to do so; therefore, nothing can be determined from that: but ft Watch that sometimes accelerates, and sometimes retards, if it depends upon its not being sufficiently

Did Doctor Maskelyne appear to wish well to Time-keepers in general, and think them useful Machines?

He certainly did; and did every Thing in his Power to encourage the Construction of Timekeepers.

Did he ever use any Expression that shewed his Satisfaction or Dissatisfaction at Mr. Mudge's Watches going well?

Many of Satisfaction, when they went well; but none of Dissatisfaction.

Did Mr. Emery shew you Mr. Mudge's Escapement applied to a Watch?

He did, which he said was Mr. Mudge's.

What Observation did you make on it ?

I told him there was a great deal of Work, and a great deal of Oil. I never apply Oil to my detached Escapement, and it will wear less than any other Part which is subject to wear, because it has no Friction whatever.

What is the Detriment of Oil to other Escapements ?

Because it alters its Tenacity, and in frosty Weather a Watch that has a great deal of Oil will almost stop with it. The President de Scarron, who has a Watch made by Mr. Emery with Mr. Mudge's Escapement, as he told me, actually stopped on being put in the Ice to try the Rate of its going, but in temperate Weather it went very well. — The balancing Spring was of my Construction.

Do you know any Thing of the going of Mr. Mudges first Time-keeper, in Two Voyages to Newfoundland in 1784 and 178.5, during which it was tried by Vice Admiral Campbell, who had the Command of His Majesty's Ships on that Station?

I have been enabled to compute the Longitude of Newfoundland, from the going of the Watch, in its Voyage out to Newfoundland, as well as in its Return

to England, in the Year 1784, from the Account of its going in that Voyage, placed at the End of a Pamphlet published by Count Bruhl, which he formerly made me a Present of As Count Bruhl had not mentioned any Rate of the Watch settled from Observation made in England before the Voyage, and in fact allowed none himself, without giving any Reason for the Omission, I w-as constrained to take the Rate deduced from Observations made by Admiral Campbell at Newfoundland, by which I found the Longitude came out 10 f Miles greater than the true Longitude, by the Watch in the Voyage out, and Miles less than the true Longitude in the Voyage home — the mean Error of these Two Determinations is therefore Miles. I was not able to make any Inference with respect to the going of Mr. Madge's Watches in the Voyage to Newfoundland in 1785, for Want of having been furnished with proper Details for that Purpose.

What is the Length of the Voyage to Newfoundland, or back?

About a Month.

Has any One a Right to conclude from the near going of a Watch in a Month, that it would probably, go within the Limits of the Act in the larger Time of Six Months, as required by the Act ?

No; because the Errors of Watches in giving the Longitude will be apt to increase in a greater Proportion than that of the Time, if the Watches are not rightly regulated for Heat and Cold, or if they are liable to gradually accelerate or retard their Rates of going.

When you touch at any Port whose Longitude is known, in the Course of a Voyage, cannot you get a new Rate of going of the Watch from its going during the Voyage?

By no Means, for it is impossible to know on whit Vol. 48.

What are the general Grounds the Board go upon in opposing the Petition ? *

The Board of Longitude, being appointed by Act of Parliament, with competent Powers to reward Mr.

Mudge as far he shall be found deserving, and having made a great many Trials of his Time-keepers a long Course of Years, and having passed several Resolutions about the going of them, to the best of their Knowledge and Judgments agreeably to thte Act, cannot but feel it as an Imputation of Blame thrown upon them by this Honourable House, if it shall disregard, all their Trials and Examinations, and bring in a fresh Bill, which will virtually repeal the old Act under which they have proceeded, without (as they flatter themselves) any Proof having been given that they have abused their Trust, or not done Justice to Mr.

Mudge under it. The Trials of Time-keepers, and the Calculation of their going, being Matters of a scientific Nature, the Commissioners of Longitude hope they have been properly appointed by the Act to take Cognizance of these Matters, for many of their Members, being chosen from their Offices as attached to Science, and others from their Offices under Government or in the Navy, which Committee probably no better can be appointed. The Board of Longitude entertain serious and well-grounded Apprehensions, that if this Honourable House should give Countenance to Mr. Mudge, which he solicits, future Watchmakers will be thereby encouraged, if they can't get rewarded by the Board of Longitude according to their Expectations, however unreasonable, to fly to and trouble Parliament with their pretended Claims, and after the Example set before them in this Instance, publish scandalous and abusive Invectives against the Persons who shall officially try their Watches, and calculate their going, with a View of preparing the Way for their Petitions to this House, and to the Rewards which they would then see may be obtained by Patronage and Solicitation, without a strict weighing and examining of Merits. Thus the Appointment of the Board of Longitude might be rendered nugatory, and much Pains taken by them in the Execution of their Office would prove useless; or they might on the other Hand be tempted to be lavish of the Public Money, through the Apprehension of being accused by a dissatisfied Watchmaker before this Honourable House, which very Thing might eventually bring them under the Censure of the House; not for Oeconomy of the Public Money, but for Profusion of it.

When a Rate is taken from a Trial of any Extent on Shore, as from the First Month, for Example, in your Method, is any Account taken of the Times, during that Period, when the Watch has changed its Rate?

No; the Mean of the daily Rates of the First Month is taken in Calculation at the Observatory, for judging of the Watches going within the Limits of the Act.

Does the taking of a Rate from the Result of a Period passed at Sea, differ from taking a Rate on a Period of the same Extent passed on Shore ?

We obtain the Mean of several Days Rates on Shore, but only the Rate deduced from the first and last Day in its going from one Port to another, and

In addition to my Answer to the former Question, I would observe, that if the Watch should be found to vary its Rate considerably during the first Month, I should think that a sufficient Objection to the conti* nuance of the Trial.

The only Difference therefore between taking a Rate from a Period passed at Sea and one on Shore is, that in the former Case the Opportunity will be lost of rejecting such Rate, in case any great Change in the going of the Watch should have happened during that Period ?

This is not the only Difference, for we may take a Rate from the Observations made on Shore, from the Time it has become stationary, if that should be the Case, and that has been my Practice at the Royal Observatory.

But if, in Point of Fact, the Rate is taken, such Rate will be the same wherever the Period has been passed ? Yes.

Are you acquainted with the Principles of Mr. Time-keeper ?

From what has been mentioned in Conversation from his Friends, and from his Pamphlet, I am acquainted with the principal Particulars of his Watch, and on which the going of Watches chiefly depends — never seen any formal Description of it. I derive my Information from the Publication of his Pamphlets.

Whether the Opinion which you have given of the comparative Merit of Mr. Mudges Watches, is formed not solely from their Effects, but partly from what you conceive yourself to know of their Construction ?

My Opinion is formed from each Method, taken separately, and is the same from both.

Mr. Josiah Emery.

Might not the Watch which you made for Count Brukl have gone as well as it did, if it had been fitted with some Escapement which you know, and which is not of the Invention of Mr. Mudge?

No Watch can go so well as with a detached Escapement. I have made some with Escapements different from Mr. Mudge's, which I conceive to have gone well, but of which I have no accurate Accounts.

Has not this Watch a Spiral Balance Spring?

No; it was made with a Spring of the same Sort as that which is called by Mr. Arnold an Helical Spring, and of which I read an Account in an English Paper, under the Name of a Cylindrical Spring, about a Year or two before Mr. Arnold took out his Patent. The Account was contained in an Advertisement from Bow Street, relative to a Number of Watches that had been stolen in France and brought to England.

At what Time did you see this Account ?

In 1775 or 1776 I believe it might be, but I can't tell precisely.

When do you apprehend Mr. Arnold took out his Patent for his Helical Spring ?

I can't speak precisely.

ot

How do you know this Advertisement was before Mr. Arnold took out his Patent?

I am sure I read the Advertisement before he took out his Patent, and I never heard of that Invention of the Cylindrical Spring till I read the said Advertisement.

Might not Mr. Arnold have taken out his Patent some Time before you knew it, and therefore before you saw the Advertisement ?

He might have taken out his Patent before I knew it, perhaps a Month or two, but am sure it was not before I saw the Advertisement, which was at least a Year or two before I knew of the Patent

Is the Compensation for Heat and Cold applied upon the Balance Spring, or upon the Balance, in your Watch ?

Upon the Balance.

Is there any Contrivance in this Watch to cause the long and short Vibrations to be performed in the same Time ?

Yes.

Might not then this Watch have gone equally well if nothing in it had been borrowed from Mr. Mudge's ?

It is possible — but I have not had the same Oppor tunity of knowing, as Observations had not been made with the same Exactness on other Watches which I made with different Escapements.

To what Degree are those other Escapements which you have mentioned, different from those of Mr. Mudge's ?

In having single Pallets instead of Two — I mean for Pocket Watches — -1 have made some large Watches with Escapements of double Pallets, which have not yet appeared, and that are quite unlike Mr. Mudge's.

Had you made either of these Escapements previous to Mr. Mudge's having been communicated to you ?

No.

Withdrew.

Mr. Wales.

Do you know the Method that was used by the Astronomer Royal, in calculating the Errors of Mr. Mudge's Two Watches in 6 Months, during their late Trial, and upon which the Board of Longitude decided, that the Watches had not gone within the Limits of the Act?

Yes — Doctor Maskelyne took the Rate of its going during the First Month, as the Rate which it ought to go at during the whole Year's Trial, and calculated by that Means, what the Watches ought to have gained or lost during the Periods of 6 Months; he then took the Difference between these Results, and what they actually gained or lost in the same Period, for the Errors of the Watches.

Do you know for what Reason it was adopted ?

Because the Act of the 14th of Geo. III. requires that the Method proposed for determining the Longitude at Sea, should not only be practicable but general.

Have not other Methods been proposed of computing the going of Watches, to determine whether they went within thp Limits of the Act?

Yes, there were Two other — one is to take the Rate of the Watches going during each of the first 6 Months, and apply it to the 6 Months next following that from which the Rate was taken — the other was to take its Rate during the first 6 Months of its Trial, and compare it with its going in the latter 6 Months,

Have

Have Mr. Mudges Watches gone within the Limits of the Act, by any of these Methods of Calculation ?

Neither of them have by either of the Two first Methods of Comparison — by the latter, the Watch Blue has gone within a few Seconds of the Limits of the Act, and Watch Green a few Seconds beyond.

What were the Errors by the First Method ?

In Four of the Periods the Watch Green was without the Limits of the Act, and Two within: and in some of them, the Errors were 6 and 7 Minutes; the Watch Blue went within the Limits but in One Period, and in Five were beyond it; and in Three of the Periods the Errors were somewhat more than 6'.

What were the Errors by the Second Method ?

The Watch Green went within the Limits Two Periods, and in Four Periods were beyond, and in One the Error was near 9' J; the Watch Blue was within the Limits in Three Periods, and in Three beyond, and the greatest Error did not amount to 6'.

What were the Errors by the Third Method ?

At the End of the Trial, the Error of Watch Green was under 2', but at one Time, during the latter Period, the Error was 4' and a few Seconds; the Error of Watch Blue was greatest at the End of the Trial, and was a few Seconds under 4'.

Were the Watches rightly adjusted for Heat and Cold?

No.

How does this appear ?

It does not appear.

On what do you found your Opinion ?

: By comparing the Rates the Watches went at during the o Summer Months, with the Rate they went at during the 6 Winter Months; the Watch Green lost in the 6 Summer Months j'. 47", and gained in 6 Winter Months 7'. 8", the Error is therefore 8'. 55''; the Watch Blue lost in the 6 Summer Months, 4'. 45", and gained in the 6 Winter Months 20", its Error therefore is 5'- 5"-

Whether do you think a better Judgment may be formed of the Goodness of a Time-keeper, from examining the Principles of its Construction, or its Exactness in keeping Time P

Certainly from its Exactness in keeping Time.

Do you think that every Judgment formed of the Goodness of a Time-keeper from a Knowledge of its Construction, is inferior to that which can be formed from Experience of its Effects, however imperfect that Experience may be ?

No — but I conceive the Question to be unlimited.

If by unlimited is meant universal, is not your former Answer equally unlimited P

In my former Answer, I supposed that in either Case the best Moans of judging were resorted to.

Then you only mean to say, that Experience is the best Test, provided the Experience can be had to a sufficient Extent?

Certainly.

Are not the Causes described by you in a former Part of your Evidence as escaping Observation, yet greatly affecting the going of Watches, sufficient to shew, that Watches of equal Merit in the Construction may occasionally go very differently ?

So far as relates to the Effects of Oil, or Foulness of the Machine, I think they may — but if the Watches are equally well constructed, which the other Causes of Change seem to refer to, I think not.

Vol. 48.

Is it not true, in Point of Fact, that Watches made on the same Construction, and apparently with the same Care, do not go with the same Exactness either one with another, or each with itself, at different Times ?

Yes; but the Maker may not have sufficient Time to adjust them properly, which may cause different Watches of the same Construction to go differently; and the same Watch may go better at one Time than another, either from its being in a fouler State, or from an Alteration in some of its Parts ?

Is not this in Fact to say, that Watches may occasionally go worse from Causes not connected with their general Merit, and must not a Judgment therefore formed in these Instances of their Construction from their Effects, prove erroneous ?

Yes, if the Watch is tried when it is in an improper State for Trial, or when improperly put together or adjusted.

When I am pronouncing on a Watch from its Effects in Trial, am I not supposed to be ignorant whether it has or has not been completely prepared with respect to those Causes of Error ?

If it has not been properly adjusted, it will appear from Trial that it has not — and it is supposed a Watchmaker would not send a Watch out of his Hands for Trial in an improper State; but in this latter Respect, the Person who tries it cannot be supposed to be a Judge.

Is not the Judgment pronounced upon Mr. Madge's Watches from their Effects in Trial, given without any Allowance for such Causes of Error as have been above described, and which are independent of the Merit of its Construction ?

Certainly, I think.

If a Ship sails from England, and after a Voyage of a Month or more touches at a Port where the Longitude is known, cannot a new Rate of the Watch be obtained ?

No; it may be determined by that Means whether the Watch has altered its Rate or not, but if it has, the Quantity of that Alteration cannot be determined, because it cannot be known when the Alteration in the Rate took Place.

In taking a Rate of a Month on Shore, is an Account taken in general of the Time or Times when the Watch altered its Rate ?

It would be, or ought to be, if the Watch altered its Rate in the Course of that Month.

Withdrew.

Doctor Maskelyne.

Have the Watches in which you have Reason to think the Construction the same, gone with equal Excellence ?

I apprehend not, as more Time and Care may have been employed in making and adjusting some than others, particularly a Watch adjusted for Heat and Cold, in Summer, with the Use of artificial Cold, cannot be so well depended on in that Respect, as one adjusted in Winter, with the natural Cold of the Season.

Will the Inference then, from the going of a Watch, to the Merits of its Construction, hold in those Instances ?

No.

Were the Three Watches of Mr. Mudgcs of equal Excellence ?

The Two Watches Green and Blue, at their First Trial, were inferior to the First Time-keeper as tried by me; at the Time of their Second Trial they may have been of equal Merit; and in their Third Trial they were much superior to the First Time-keeper.

Was not that Watch (whether better or worse) made upon a Construction of Mr.

Only with respect to the Escapement- — Mr. Emery has stated in his Evidence, that he has used a cylindrical Spring, and put the Compensation for Heat and Cold upon the Balance, and that he had a Contrivance in it to make the large and small Vibrations to be performed in equal Time.

Ib not the Construction of some Watches such, as to depend more than others on the Nicety of the Work* mans hip, and on Methods of which the Workman cannot be sure beforehand ?

Yes

May not Watches, depending on such Contrivances, go occasionally (when the Execution has been successful) , better than others that are upon the Whole more to be relied on ?

Yes, to a certain Degree.

Is it not notorious that Watches, professedly of the same Construction, and sold at the same Price by the same Makers, have some of them gone with great Excellence, and some so ill as to be good for nothing ?

I believe some have gone much better than others, but don't know of any that have gone very ill; and I think most of the Difference has been owing to the Want of-Time and Care in putting the Watches out of Hand.

Would it not be true, in general, that a Watch varying within certain (even not) very small Limits, but that might be depended upon not to exceed those Limits, would be better than One which, though sometimes going with singular Exactness, was liable at others to fall into great Irregularity ?

Yes.

How many Days of going of the Watch Green, intervened between the 29th December 1789, and the 29th June 1790; considering that the Watch was let' down Five Days in January 1790 ?

One hundred and Seventy-seven.

Is not this less than Six Months ?

Yes; but in calculating the going of the Watches for the Two Periods of Six Months, by applying a daily Rate deduced from the preceding Month of each Period, I have taken Care to compensate son the Loss of those Five Days, by adding Five others immediately succeeding the lost Days in the First Period, and the like Number immediately preceding in the Second Period — the Calculation alluded to, is in the Paper delivered in by me Today.

Had you made the Compensation for those Five

Days, in the Calculation on which you grounded your Evidence before the former Committee?

No; but having done so now, the Results of the Calculations delivered in, justify the Declaration I then made. *

Will 177 Days make Six Months, reckoning by-weekly Months?

More than Six Months — I use the Calendar Months in my Calculation.

Have you made any Calculations of whet would be the Errors of the Watches in Six Months, supposing them to have gone to Sea at the End of the 2*, 3* 4", or 5,fc Month respectively ?

I have not.

On this Part of his Evidence, Mr. Graham desires to observe, that though the Paper, which he delivered in in Support of the Assertion {here contained, appears upon Examination to be erroneous (for which his Excase must be, that the Calculation was made by him while attending at the Hooae of Commons, and engaged with the Business of another Committee, as well as of the present) and that the real Emit is what was afterward* given in by Doctor MaskWyns, yet that the Assertion is still true, if for the Five Days during which the Watclw* wen let down, a Rate be taken, which shall be the Mean of the Rates of the Two Days immediately preceding and following; such a Rate Mr. Graham conceives to be a very proper one to be assumed, particularly as against those by whom the Watches were let down.

If either of the Watches have erred trrore then 4' in any Period of Six Months, after being corrected by the Rate taken from the preceding Month, is not this a Proof, that it has not gosse within the Terms of the Act?

By no means--the Act does not prescribe any parti* cular Mode of taking the Rate.

Supposing that Method of taking a Rate had been prescribed by the Act, what then would have been your Answer to the former Question?

I should have answered, No; for according to the Construction I had put upon the Act when I gave the Answer alluded to before the former Committee, I am of Opinion that if the Watches, upon a Trial of 12 Months, had at the Expiration of Two Periods consisting of Six Months each, the Second beginning at the End of the First, gone within 4', they would have gone within the Limits prescribed by the Act.

Do you mean to give the same Answer, on the Supposition that the Errors of the Watches may have been greater than 4' in some intermediate Periods of Six Months ?

If it had been expressed in the Act, that an Error of more than 4', in any Period of Six Months within the 12 Months Trial, should determine it not to be entitled to the Reward, then a Watch, shewing an Error of more than 4' in any of these intermediate Periods, could not be said to have gone within the Limits of the Act — but the Act directs a Trial of »2 Months to be made, and that the Results in that Trial shall be within 4' upon a Voyage of Six Months, and as there can only be Two such Voyages made in 12 Months, I think, if at the Expiration of each Voyage the Error is not greater than 4', that then the Terms of the Act would be complied with.

Could the Commissioners of Longitude declare and determine under the Act, that the Method afforded by the Watches is generally practicable and Useful, and sufficiently exact to determine the Longitude at Sea within the Limits of the Act, if the Watclie9 have erred 4' in any Period of Six Months Comprized in the Twelve Months Trial?

According to the Construction I have put upon the Act, I think they could.

Doctor Maskelyne.

In the last Question, what Rate do you suppose to be adopted by which the Error is to be estimated ?

I meant a general Question, and suppose no particular Rate, but relative to that Rate which should be thought most reasonable and proper, in the Judgment of the Commissioners of Longitude.

REMARKS by Mr. Graham, on his Letter sent to Doctor relative to the going of

Mr. Arnold's, and Mr. Haley's Watchesy in 1790.

When I received Mr. Arnold's, Watch from Doctor Maskelyne, on the 28th July, 1790, it was 23', 9, fast of mean Time; and its daily Rate (or gaining upon mean Time) was +9*,374; the Thermometer being 62*. 4'. I was informed in Writing by the Doctor, that an Increase of Ten Degrees in the Height of the Thermometer, occasioned an Acceleration of 4?, 9 on the daily Rate of the Watch. This Account of the Effect of the Thermometer upon the going of the Watch, was true; as appeared by the following Observations made at Portsmouth, previous to the Watch being carried to Sea.

The Reason of my sending the last Account, in preference to the one which had been depended on for the use of the Ship, I really and conscientiously believe to have been (for at this distant Period I cannot undertake to speak positively upon the Subject) that when I had the Watch in my Possession, I was informed the Astronomer Royal, and Mr. Arnold, were upon very bad Terms; therefore in making out my Report (which at that Time I had no Idea would ever be made a Public u$e of) I did not care to give the latter Gentleman an Opportunity of complaining that I had arbitrarily adopted a Rate of my own, in order to shew an Error in his Watch, which the Rate to be deduced from the Portsmouth Observations would (and as the Thing turned out did) free it from. This, however, does not serve to shew the Goodness of the Watch, which was evidently affected by the State of the Thermometer; for the Rate (lo",72) that had been so favourable to it when the mean State of the Thermometer was 63°, in the course of Five Weeks (the Thermometer falling to 52) changed to 8', 8; and if, instead of carrying the Watch to the Observatory at Portsmouth, I had sailed from England, depending upon its Rate as given me by Doctor Maskelyne, it would, so far from shewing the Degree of Accuracy which appears upon the Face of my Letter, have erred in the course of the Voyage (consisting of 59 Days) upwards of Two Minutes; viz.

As to the Statement on the Passage Home, I need only soy, that the Observations were made on board a Ship, in squally and cloudy Weather, with a great S|ea, and the Distance of the Ship from the Land obliged to be estimated, in order to determine the Accuracy of the Watch by. This might have done (as it was intended) very well for the private Satisfaction of Mr. Arnold, rand fee Astronomer Royal, and to shew them of what Use the Watch had been to the Ship; but when real Accuracy is required, I cannot allow that such should be the Method of proving it; and I should haw *f any Error had

appeared in consequence of such Observations, and such estimated Distance, to have brought it forward as Vot. 48. a Proof

Therefore allowing that the Doctor may be right in rejecting my assumed Rate, and trying Mr. Arnolds Watch by the Rate deduced from the Portsmouth Observations, yet surely he must be wrong in rejecting the Portsmouth Rate and accepting my assumed Rate for the Trial of Mr. Haley's Watch only, because the same Rate applied to both will not answer his Purpose.

I offer no Comment upon the Conduct of Doctor Maskelyne in producing a private Letter of mine, without my Consent; which, if I had not by mere Accident had in my Possession such Proofs as (I trust) account reasonably for my writing it, would not only have deprived an ingenious Artist of my Evidence, but have impeached my Veracity upon every other Occasion. I have studiously avoided unnecessary Prolixity, but hope in so doing 1 have.not been too concise to render my Meaning intelligible.

Appendix, N° 7.

LETTER from Mr. Edward Everard to the Reverend Doctor Maskelyne, Astronomer Royal, &c. &c.

Dear Sir,

Since I had the Pleasure of writing you, Mr. Arnold has sent me his Publication, and the going of my Watch, as there stated. I have examined, and I believe it very accurate. At Foot I send you the different Comparisons at Greenwich and Lynn, made with my Watch: I do not recollect whether you have them all or not. — I have not yet seen Mr. Mudge's Pamphlet, but expect it within a few Days; and am,

Dear Sir,

Your obliged and obedient Servant,

The Periods used in the above Comparison are taken, without any Selection, as they naturally present themselves in the Order of Time; except that the Trial by the Astronomer Royal, not admitting of a sufficient Number of Days from the First Period, Mr. Dutton's Trial was had Recourse to in order to supply it; afterwards each Trial is pursued regularly on Doctor Maskelyne's Register, as long as it will afford a sufficient Number of Days for the respective Periods, and if it leaves a small Remainder, not sufficient for the next Period, but

large enough for some of the subsequent Ones, it is resorted to again as soon as the Lengths of them will admit of the Whole being made Use of The Periods marked D. M. are taken from Doctor Maskelynes Register, and those marked with a single D. from Mr. Dutton's. Some of them will appear to consist of a greater Number of Days than the Number set against them, which is occasioned by the Time-keepers having been sometimes let down.

Appendix, N° 17.

REMARKS on Mr. Graham's Account of some Errors in Doctor Maskelyne'$ Table, N° XVI. of Appendix

of his Answer to Mr. Madge's Pamphlet, by Dr. Maskelyne.

THE principal Errors shewn in the foregoing Account, namely, the 1st, 3d, 8th, 9th, and 10th, which are all that exceed One Minute, were occasioned by the Mistake of an Amanuensis, who in making a Copy of the Original Register, which was deposited with the Board of Longitude, set down 3'. 33",39, instead of 4', 33",39 for the Sum of the daily Rates of the Watch Green to March 15th 1790. This Copy, with the Error here mentioned, I submitted to the Inspection of the Select Committee. This Error of One Minute being multiplied by Six, produced an Error of Six Minutes in one Instance. The other Errors are to be attributed to the Haste with which I wad obliged to put out my Answer to Mr. Madges Pamphlet, in order to make it in Time for the taking up of Mr. Madge's Business in the House of Commons last Year. It is to be remarked, that the Purpose with which I introduced these Calculations, which was to show that a Rate taken from Six Weeks and applied to Six Weeks was not more favourable to the Watches than the Rate taken from the preceding Week, is better answeted by the Account corrected by Mr. Graham, than as it stood Originally in my Pamphlet; for the Sum of the Errors of the Watch Green with the Rate of Six Weeks is now, 33'. o", and with the rate of a Week is 33'. 14", whereas they were before 40'. 55", and 37'. 45".

I desire to observe, that these Errors of the going of the Watch in Periods of Six Weeks, do not in the least affect my Calculations of the going of the Watch in Periods of Six Months (the Term required by the Act) which have beeir re-computed and certified to be just by the concurrent Evidence of Doctor Hutton and Messrs. Wales, Gilpin, and Crosley, before the Committee.

Here follows the Part of the Appendix, N' XVI. of my Answer to Mr. Mudge, which relates to the Watch Green, when corrected for the Errors discovered by- Mr. Graham.

Mr. Mundy reported from the Committee, to whom the Bill to enlarge the Term and Powers of an Act, passed in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for repairing and widening the Road leading from Penistone Bridge, in the County of York, to

Griudleford Bridge, in the County of Derby, and the Roads severally leading from Bamford over

Yorkshire Bridge, to the Guide Post on Thornhill Moor, to or near the Eighth Mile Stone on Hathersage Moor, and to the Village of Darwent, in the said County of Derby, was committed; That the Committee had examined the Allegations of the Bill, and found the same to be true; and that the Committee had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Amendments were Once read throughout; and then a Second Time, One by One; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were agreed to by the House.

A Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, for exempting the Inhabitants of Darwent from paying Tolls.

And the said Clause was Twice read; 'and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrossed.

A Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, for including several small Ships in One Adjudication.

And the said Clause was Twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, directing that Prize Agents shall advertize in the Gazette the Time of registering their Account of Sales.

And the said Clause was Twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the BUI.

Sir William Dolben reported from the Committee, Report on appointed to enquire into a Method of making the improving Approach to both Houses of Parliament more con- the AP* venient, by removing the Building at the End of the {^Homo Court of Exchequer which extends into the Street be- of Parlia-tween New Palace Yard and Saint Margaret Street, or ment. such Part of the said Building as shall be found necessary for the Purpose before-mentioned, and the Sheds and Buildings thereunto annexed; and also, to prepare a Plan of such Work, and an Estimate of the Expence thereof, and report the same, with their Observations and Opinion thereupon, from Time to Time, to the House; That the Committee had made a further Progress in the Matters to them referred, and had directed him to make a Report thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Your Committee, having taken into their Consideration that the Public House situate in New Palace Yard, and known by the Sign of The Coach and Horses, would be cut through by the Line described in their former Report, thought proper to call before them

William Withers, the Person who now occupies the said Public House; who being examined, informed your Committee, That he holds it under a Lease

from

"from John WalkerHeneage, fisqutre, granted to Thomas

Coles and William Williams (dated the 20th of Mdy 1786) ten- Ten Years from Michaelmas 1786, and assigned from the said Coles and Williams to one Benjamin Brown, by an Indorsement on the said Lease, bearing Date the 2d Day of March 1787; and froth the said Benjamin Brown assigned to the Witness, by Indenture, dated the 24th Day of December' 1787; and that the Annual Rent thereof is 12/. — And being further examined, he said, That the House consists of a Tap Hoorn and Cellar, and other small Partitions on the Ground Floor, and of Two Rooms in an Upper Story; and that if it should be found expedient to take away Part of the present Building to the Westward, and an Addition could be made thereto on the jEast Side, as large and commodious as the Part taken away, it would be equally as convenient for him; but if he Should be immediately turned out, the Value of the Damage to be sustained by him would amount to between 100 /. and 600 /.

Your Committee thereupon directed Mr. Groves to inspect the said Building, and the Premisses adjacent thereto, and inform your Committee, whether such Alterations could be carried into Effect, and at what Rxpence. — And,

Air. Groves having inspected the same accordingly, informed your Committee, That, supposing the said Public House, or Part thereof, was taken down, there is ample Room for erecting or completing a. Building of the same Description a little to the Eastward of the Spot where the present Building stands; and that if Part of the old Materials of the Buildings to be taken down were used, he thinks it might be built or repaired in a substantial Manner, and so as not to endanger the adjoining Buildings in case of Fire, for the Sum of no/.

Upon the Whole, yortr Committee are inclined to be of Opinion, that it would be most advisable to rebuild or repair the said Public House, in such a Manner as that it may not be liable to the same Objections as at present; and this Mode seems to your Committee to be the more proper, as by that Means the Compensation to Mr. Heneage may be lessened, by the Amount of the Value of the Rent paid to him for the said Public House.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

at A Message by Mr. Quarme, Yeoman Usher of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty's Commission for declaring His Royal Assent to several Acts agreed upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate Attendance of this Honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported, Thit the House, at the Desire of thfe Lords authorized by virtue. of His Majesty's Commission afore mentioned, had been at the House of Peers, where a Commission under the Great Seal was read, giving, declaring, and notifying the Royal Assent to the several Public and Private Bills therein mentioned; and also impowering His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, His Royal Highness the Duke of York, His Royal Highness the Duke of Clarence, His Royal Highness the Duke of Gloucester, the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, and several other Lords, to declare and notify the Royal Absent to the said BilU; and that the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, and the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, and the.Eatl Graliam, named alsp in the said Commission, did accordingly declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills: Which. Treaty with TRANSLATION of a Treaty between HeaseCasseL His Majesty and the Landgrave of Hesse Cosset,

signed at Cosset the loth of 1793.

Re it known to those whom it may concern, That His Majesty the King of Geat , and his Serene

Highness the Landgrave of Hesse Cosset, in Consideration of the strict Ties which unite the Interest of their respective Houses, and having judged that, in the present Situation of Affairs, it would contribute to the reciprocal Welfare of Great Britain and of Hesse, to cement and strengthen, by a new Treaty of Alliance, the Connection which subsists between them; His Britan-nick Majesty, in order to regulate the Objects relative to this Alliance, has thought proper to send to Cosset the Right honourable Thomas Earl of Elgin and of Kinkar-dine, Baron Bruce of Kinross, His Minister Plenipotentiary; and his Serene Highess has nominated, on His Pari; for the same Purpose, the Baron Maurice Frederick of Munchausen, his actual Minister of State, Privy Councillor, and Knight of the Order of the Golden Lion, and his Director of the College and Treasury of War, and John Francis Kunckel, Privy Councillor of War; who, being furnished with the -oecessary full Powers, have agreed to take for Basis of the present Treaty the Treaties which were formerly concluded between Great Britain and , to adopt such Parts of them as may be applicable to the present Circumstances, or to settle by new Articles those Points which it may be necessary to regulate otherwise. Every Thing which shall not otherwise be settled, shall be deemed subsisting in full Force, in the Manner expressed in the above-mentioned Treaties: And, as it is not possible to specify each particular Case, every Thing which shall not appear to be determined in a precise Manner, either in the present Treaty, or in the former Treaties, shall be settled with Equity and good Faith, in Conformity to the same Principles, which it is agreed on both Sides to adopt for the Regulation of such Cases, whether during the Course of the War, or after its Conclusion.

*1.

There shall be, therefore, in virtue of this Treaty, between His Majesty the King of Great Britain, and his Serene Highness the Landgrave of Hesse Cassel, their Successors and Heirs, a strict Friendship, and a sincere, firm, and constant Union, so that the one shall consider the Interests of the other as his own, and shall strive to promote them with good Faith, as much as possible, and mutually to prevent and remove all Disturbance and Injury.

Two Divisions; The First, consisting of 4,000 Men, shall be composed of a Corps of Infantry with the Artillery-men, and of a Regiment of Cavalty. — Formerly the Signature of Treaties preceded for some Time the Period of the Requisition for the March of the Troops; but as in the present Circumstances there is no Time to be lost, the Day of the Signature of the present Treaty is deemed to be also the Period of the Requisition, and the First Division of 4,000 Men shall be in Readiness to pass in Review before the Commissary of His Britannick Majesty on the 8th of next Month,

and to begin its March the following Day for the Place of its Destination. — The Second Division, consisting also of 4,000 Men, and composed of a Corps of Infantry, of a Battalion of Chasseurs, and of Two Regiments of Cavalry, shall be in Readiness to pass in Review the 5th of June, and shall be ready to march in Eight Weeks, from the Day of the Conclusion of the present Treaty, or even sooner, if it is possible. These Troops shall not be separated, unless the Cause of War should require it, but shall continue under the Orders of their Hessian Chief, under the Command, however, of the General to whom His Britannick Majesty shall intrust that of His whole Army; and the Second Division shall only be conducted to those Places where the First shall be, unless it should be contrary to the Plan of Operations.

IV.

Each Battalion of Infantry of this Corps of Troops shall be provided with Two Field Pieces, and the Officers, Cannoneers, and other Men and Equipage attached to them.

V.

In order to defray the Expences to which the Serene Landgrave shall be put, by equipping the above-mentioned Corps of 8,000 Men, His Majesty the King of Great Britain promises to pay to his Serene Highness for each Horseman or Dragoon, properly armed and mounted, 80 Crowns Banco, and for each Foot Soldier 30 Crowns Banco: This Levy Money for the First Division shall be paid Fifteen Days after the Signature of the present Treaty. With regard to the Levy Money for the Second Division, One Half thereof shall he paid on the 8th of next Month, and the other Half on the Day on which the Second Division shall begin its March. The Levy Money shall be paid for the same Description of Persons for whom it was given in the former Alliances.

II.

With this View, it is agreed, that all the former Treaties, especially those of Guaranty, shall be deemed to be renewed and confirmed by the present Treaty, in all their Points, Articles, and Clauses, and shall have the same Force, as if they were herein inserted Word for Word, in as much as the same is not derogated from by the present Treaty.

III.

His Majesty the King of Great Britain desiring to secure for His Service in Europe a Body of the Troops of the Serene Landgrave, and his Serene Highness, wishing for nothing more than to give His Majesty real Proofs of his strong Attachment for Him, engages, by virtue of this Article, to keep in Readiness for this Purpose, during the Space of Three successive Years, reckoning from the Day of the Signature of the present Treaty, a Body of 8,000 Men, as well Infantry as Cavalry or Chasseurs, including Officers. This Subsidy shall commence from the Day of the Signature of this Treaty; and it shall be paid at the Rate of Two hundred and Twenty-five thousand Crowns Banco per Annum; the Crown being reckoned at Fifty-three Sols of Holland, or at Four Shillings and Nine Pence Three Farthings English Money.

TRANSLATION of a Convention between His Majesty and the Empress of Russia, signed at London the 25th of March 1793.

Their Majesties the King of Great Britain, and the Empress of all the Russias, equally convinced of the Importance and Advantage to the Two Monarchies of the Extension of the Commerce which has hitherto subsisted between their respective Subjects, have acknowledged the Necessity of immediately providing for this Object by preliminary Stipulations, till a definitive Arrangement for a Treaty of Commerce can be agreed upon between the Two Crowns. For this Purpose they have chosen and authorized; viz. His Britannick Majesty, the most illustrious and most excellent Lord fViUicnnWynd Baron Grenville of

hVotton, One of His Majesty's Privy Council, and His Principal Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs; and her Majesty the Empress of all the Russias, the most illustrious and most excellent Lord Count Simon Woronzcrw, Lieutenant General of the Armies of her said Imperial Majesty, her Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary to His Britannick Majesty, and Knight of the Orders of St. Alexander Newsky, of the Military Order of St. George of the Third Class, and of St. Vladimir Great Cross of the First Class; who, after communicating to each other their full Powers, and finding them to be in good arid due Form, have agreed upon the following Articles:

Article I.

The Treaty of Friendship, Commerce and Navigation, concluded at St. Petersburgh in the Year 1706, between the Two Monarchies, shall resume its Force and Activity, which shall continue in all the Clauses and Stipulations during the Space of Time hereafter fixed; and the Two high contracting Parties engage to employ themselves, in the Interval, in the Arrangement of a new Treaty of Commerce, for the Purpose of securing, in a permanent Manner, whatever may tend to consolidate and to extend the Commerce and the Navigation of the British and Russian Subjects. In consequence whereof His Britannick Majesty, and her Majesty the Empress of all the Russias, engage and promise reciprocally to execute, observe, and accomplish, in all Points, the above-mentioned Clauses and Stipulations of the Treaty of Commerce of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Sixty-six, as if they were inserted here Word for Word, and in the same Manner in which they were executed, observed, and accomplished, before the Year 1787, being the Date of the Expiration of the said Treaty; with Exception only of those Alterations which are agreed upon by the present Act, and which will be mentioned in the following Articles.

A. 1793.

Article II.

The College of Commerce being no longer a Court of Justice, Law Suits, and other Affairs of English Merchants established in Russia, shall be judged and regulated by the Tribunals established for this Purpose, in the same Manner as is practised with regard to other Nations who have Treaties of Commerce, In Return for which, the Russian Subjects established in England shall be under the Jurisdiction of the same Tribunals before which the Affairs of other Nations are brought, who have Treaties of Commerce with England.

Article III.

Her Imperial Majesty of all the Russias, in Continuation of the Encouragements which she has uniformly granted in her States to the Commerce and Navigation of British Subjects, engages that they shall enjoy in her Ports in the Black Sea, and the Sea of Asoph, all the Advantages and Diminutions of Custom-house Duties which are specified in the Sixth Article of the Edict preceding the General Tariff of the Year 1782, and which is of the following Tenor:

" Although this General Tariff is to serve also for " all our Ports situated on the Black Sea, and the Sea " of Azoph, we, however, diminish in the said Ports, by " One Fourth Part, the Duties fixed in this Tariff, in " order to encourage Commerce for the Utility of our " Subjects, and of "the Nations with which we shall " stipulate reciprocal Advantages in this Respect, in " Compensation for the Privileges which those Nations " shall grant to our Commerce; excepting, however, " from this Diminution, the Merchandize specified by " Name in the present Tariff, as liable to pay the same " Duties in the Ports of the Black Sea as in the other " Custom-houses of our Empire, as also those for " which the present Tariff fixes particular Duties in the " Ports of the Black Sea."

Article IV.

The present Arrangement of Commerce, on which their Majesties the King of Great Britain and the Empress of all the Russias are agreed, and by which they confirm the Whole of the Treaty of 1766, the Alterations above agreed upon excepted, shall subsist and be obligatory during the Space of Six Years, this Terra being fully sufficient for coming to a definitive Agreement on all the Stipulations of a new Treaty of Commerce, calculated to perpetuate and to extend the Advantages of their respective Subjects. The high contracting Parties engage, in consequence of this Act, to provide, in the most effectual Manner, and according to the Forms established in each of the Two Countries, for the entire Execution of all that is stipulated, without the smallest Restriction.

Article V.

His Britannick Majesty, and her Imperial Majesty of all the Russias, engage to ratify the present Act; and the Ratifications shall be exchanged within the Space of Three Months, or sooner if it can be done, reckoning from the Day of Signature.

In Witness whereof, we, the under-signed Plenipotentiaries of their Majesties the King of Great Britain and the Empress of all the Russias, have signed the present Convention, and have caused it to be sealed with our Arms.

Done at London, the Twenty-fifth Day of March, One thousand Seven hundred and Ninety-three.

Signed,

Grenville. (L.S.) S. Comte Woronxmi, (L.S.)

TRANSLATION of Coovwtion between His Majesty and the Empress of signed

at London the 35th of 1793.

The Persons who have exercised the Powers of Government in France, after having plunged their Country into the most dreadful Miseries, having adopted towards the other Powers of Europe, Measures equally unjust and offensive, conducting themselves in that Respect by Principles incompatible with the Security and Tranquillity of all independent States, and even with the Existence of all social Order, and having actually rendered themselves guilty of the most unjust and injurious Aggression, by laying an Embargo on all the British and Russian Ships which were in the Ports of France; an Aggression followed by a Declaration of War against His Majesty, and

His Ally the Republic of the United Provinces; their Majesties the King of Great Britain, and the Empress of all the Russias, have thought proper to concert together upon the Means of opposing a sufficient Barrier to the Dangers which threaten all Europe, in consequence of such Principles, Views, and Conduct.

Their Majesties have therefore authorized their respective Ministers; to wit, the King of Great Britain, the most illustrious and most excellent Lord William. Wyndham, Baron Grenville of Wotton, One of His Majesty's Privy Council, and His Principal Secretary of State for the Department of Foreign Affairs; and her Majesty the Empress of all the Russias, the most illustrious and most excellent Lord Count Simon de JVoronzow, Lieutenant General of her Imperial Majesty's Armies, her Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary to the King of Great Britain, and Knight of the Orders of St. Alexander Newsky, of the Military Order of St. George of the Third Class, and of St. Vladimir, Grand Cross of the First Class; who, after having communicated to each other their respective full Powers, have agreed to the following Articles:

Article I.

Their Majesties, in Conformity to the ancient Ties of Friendship, by which they and their august Predecessors have been united, and which they are desirous of cultivating and extending as much as possible, will exert all their Endeavours, and will concert together ultimately for assisting and succouring each other mutually, in the Course of the present War, in order to procure for themselves at the Peace, that Satisfaction and Security which they have a Right to expect, and to guaranty for the future the public Tranquillity and Security of Europe.

Article II.

For this End, their Majesties engage to employ their respective Forces, as far as the Circumstances in which they may find themselves shall permit, in carrying on the just and necessary War in which they are engaged against France; and they reciprocally promise not to lay down their Arms but by common Consent, without having obtained Restitution of all the Conquests which France may have made, upon either of their said Majesties, or upon such other of the Powers, Friends or Allies of their said Majesties, to whom they shall judge proper to extend this Guaranty, by common Consent.

Article III.

Their said Majesties reciprocally engage to shut all their Ports against French Ships, not to permit the Exportation, in any Case, from their said Ports for France, of any Military or Naval Stores, or Corn, Grain, Salt Meat, or other Provisions; and to take all other Measures in their Power for injuring the Commerce of France, and for bringing her by such Means, to just Conditions of Peace.

Vo L.48.

rumu 943

Article IV,

Their Majesties engage to unite all their Efforts to prevent other Powers, not implicated in this War, from giving, on this Occasion of common Concern to every civilized State, any Protection whatever, directly or indirectly, in consequence of their Neutrality, to the Commerce or Property of the French, on the Sea, or in the Ports of France.

Article V.

Their Majesties desiring mutually and ardently to confirm and consolidate, as much as possible, the Friendship and Union now subsisting between them, and to protect and extend the Commerce between their respective Subjects, will authorize their Ministers to proceed without Delay, to the Formation of a definitive Arrangement for a Treaty of Alliance and Commerce. In the mean Time, and until that happy Work can be effected, they have agreed to renew provisionally the Treaty of 1766, by a preliminary Agreement of the same Date with this Convention, and exchanged in like Manner between the above-mentioned Ministers.

Article VI.

His Britannick Majesty and her Imperial Majesty 1 of all the Russias, engage to ratify the present Convention, and the Ratifications thereof shall be exchanged in the Space of Three Months, or sooner if it can be done, to be computed from the Day of the Signature.

In Witness whereof, we, the under-signed Plenipotentiaries of their Majesties the King of Great Britain, and the Empress of all the Russias, have signed the present Convention, and have caused the Seals of our Arms to be affixed thereto. Done at London, this Twenty-fifth of March, in the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Ninety-three.

(L. S.) Grenville. (L. S.) S. Comte JVoronzmo.

TRANSLATION of a Treaty between His Majesty and the King of Sardinia, signed at London, the 25th of April 1793.

Their Majesties the King of Great Britain and the King of Sardinia, finding themselves engaged in a War against France, in consequence of the most injurious Acts of Violence and Aggression, which they have respectively experienced from that Country, their above-mentioned Majesties have agreed to make a common Cause in this War, and to concert together on the Means of providing for their mutual Defence and Safety, as well as for the general Interests of Europe.

Their above-mentioned Majesties in consequence have named and constituted for this Purpose; to wit, His Britannick Majesty the most illustrious and most excellent Lord William Grenville of Wotton, Privy Counsellor of His before-named Majesty, and His Principal Secretary of State for the Foreign Department; and his Sardinian Majesty the most illustrious and most excellent Lord Philip de St. Martin de Front, Gentleman of the Chamber to his before-named Majesty, Colonel of Cavalry and Dragoons, and his Envoy Extraordinary to His Britannick Majesty; who, after having duly communicated their respective full Powers, have agreed upon the following Articles:

Article I.

His Sardinian Majesty engages to keep on foot, during the whole Course of the present War, an Army of Fifty Thousand Men, to be employed for the Defence of his Dominions, as well as to act against the common Enemy: His Britannick Majesty engaging, on His Side, to send into the Mediterranean a

respectable

Treaty with Sardinia.

17° Ju

A. 1793.

respectable Fleet of Vessels of War, to be employed accordingly as Circumstances shall permit, against the Naval Forces which the Enemy may have in that Part of the World. Their before-named Majesties will-ultimately concert as to the Destination and Employment of the respective Forces above-mentioned.

Article II.

His Britannick Majesty engages to furnish to his

Sardinian Majesty, during the whole Course of the War, a Subsidy of Two hundred Thousand Pounds Sterling per Annum, to be reckoned from the Day of the Signature of the present Treaty; which Subsidy shall be paid to him punctually every Three Months, in Advance, to be reckoned from the above Day.

Article III.

His Britannick Majesty engages not to conclude a Peace with the Enemy, without comprehending in it the entire Restitution to his Sardinian Majesty of all the Parts of his Dominions, which belonged to him at the Commencement of the War, and of which the aforesaid Enemy has obtained Possession, or of which it may hereafter obtain Possession, during the Course of Hostilities. In Return, his Sardinian Majesty will continue firmly and inseparably united and attached to the common Cause, and to the Interests of His Britannick Majesty in this War, not only for so long Time as the War may last in Italy, or in the Southern Parts of Europe, but until the Conclusion of Peace between Great Britain and France.

Article IV.

If one or the other of the Two high contracting Parties shall happen to be attacked, molested, or disturbed in any of his Estates, Rights, Possessions, or Interests, at any Time, or in whatever Manner it may be, by Sea or by Land, in consequence, or in Resentment of the Articles or Stipulations contained in the present Treaty, or of the Measures to be taken by the said contracting Parties, by virtue of this Treaty, the other contracting Party engages to succour him, and to make common Cause with him, in the Manner which is stipulated by the above Articles.

Article V.

The present Treaty shall be ratified by both Parties, and the Exchange of the Ratifications shall take place in the Space of Two Months, or sooner if possible.

In Faith of which, we, the undersigned Ministers Plenipotentiary of their Majesties the King of Great Britain and the King of Sardinia, have signed this present Treaty, and have caused to be affixed the Seal of our Arms.

Done at London this Twenty-fifth Day of April, One Thousand Seven hundred and Ninety-three.

Grenville (L. S.) St. Martin de Front (L. S.)
