A Motion was made, and the Question being put, Motion for That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, Address for to lay before His Majesty, the humble Representations of His faithful Commons in the present awful and momentous Crisis, a Duty which they feel themselves Neg. more especially called upon to perform at this Juncture, as a long and eventful period may probably elapse before His Majesty can again have an Opportunity of collecting, through their Representatives, the real Sentiments and Wishes of His People:

In the Name of the People of Great Britain, His Majesty's faithful Commons are bound to declare, that they concurred in the Measures necessary to carry on the present War for the Objects of Defence and Security, and for those Objects only:

That any Plan of Aggrandizement, founded on the present distressed Situation of France, much less any Purpose of establishing among the French People any particular Form of Government, never would have had their Concurrence or Support:

In expressing these their Sentiments and Opinions, on entering into the present War, His Majesty's faithful Commons are sensible that they are only repeating those benevolent Declarations which true Policy, and a careful Attention to the real Interests of the British

Nation,

Ration, induced His Majesty to use in His most gracious Speech from the Throne, at the beginning of the present Session of Parliament, and in repeated Messages to this House:

To represent to His Majesty, that though his faithful Commons have the most perfect Reliance on His Majesty's sacred Word and Promise, solemnly pledged to this Country and to Europe, not to interfere in the Internal Affairs of France, or to enter into the Views and Projects of other Powers, who, in the present War, ipay be actuated by Motives far different frofn those which govern the Conduct of His Majesty, yet they feel it to be their indispensable Duty to call His Majesty's most serious Attention to some of the Circumstances which have occurred since the Commencement of the present unfortunate Contest:

The French Arms, which, after a successful Invasion of Brabant, had threatened the Security of His Majesty's Allies The States General, have since been confined within their own Territory, and are now occupied in Defence of their Frontier Towns against the united Forces of His Majesty and His Allies; the Danger apprehended from the former Conquests and Aggrandizement of the French Nation, appears therefore to be no longer a Subject of just U neasiness or Alarm:

Some of the Powers engaged in the Confederacy against France have, on the other Hand, openly avowed, and successfully executed, Plans of Domination and Conquest, not less formidable to the General Liberties of Europe — The rapacious and faithless Dismemberment of the unhappy Kingdom of Poland, without having produced, as far as it appears to this House, any Remonstrance from His Majesty's Ministers, has excited in His Majesty's faithful Commons the highest Indignation at so daring an Outrage on the Rights of independent Nations, and the keenest Solicitude to rescue the Honour of the British Government, from the Suspition of having concurred or acquiesced in Measures so odious in their Principle, and so dangerous in their Example, to the Peace and Happiness of Mankind:

The severe Calamities which, since the Commencement of the present War, this Nation has already experienced, the Shock given to Commercial Credit, and the alarming Consequences which the Failure of the Mercantile and Manufacturing Interests threatens to the Public Revenue, and to the general Prosperity of the Country, cannot have failed to attract His Majesty's Attention, and to excite in His benevolent Mind a sincere Desire to relieve His People from Distresses, a Termination of which they cannot hope for but in the speeedy Re-establishment of Peace:

His Majesty's faithful Commons therefore make it their most earnest and solemn Request, that His Majesty, taking into His Consideration all the above Circumstances, will not fail to employ the earliest Measures for procuring Peace on such Terms, as are consistent with the professed Objects of the War, and with that good Faith, strict Justice, and liberal and enlightened Policy, which have hitherto peculiarly distinguished the British Nation;

ment; That the Committee had examined the same accordingly; and had agreed upon a Report, which they had directed him to make to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the same, together with an Appendix thereunto, in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Report was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Your Committee have arranged their Proceedings under the following Heads:

1st. The ancient Constitution of the Royal Burghs, and the Modes in which the Magistrates and Common Councils were elected:

I Idly. The present Mode of Election of the Magistrates and Common Councils:

Illdly. 'Whether Taxes have been imposed without the Authority of Parliament, or a greater Sum levied in Name of, or together with the Cess, Stent, or Land Tax, than is paid to Government, and is expended in the Collection, taken together:

IVthly. The Amount of the Annual Revenues of the Royal Burghs:

Vthly. Whether the Lands and other heritable Property of the Royal Burghs have been alienated by the Magistrates and Common Councils, and in what Manner; and whether Debts have been contracted, or the Common Property dilapidated.

1st. With respect to the ancient Constitution, of the Royal Burghs, and the Modes in which the Magistrates and Common Councils were elected.

It is stated in the Petitions, that by the ancient Con- Lfges Bur-stitutions of the Royal Burghs, and by the express goruui et Words of their Charters, the Magistrates and Common Councils were elected Annually, by the free Suffrage of U the Burgesses; but that, by Acts of the Scottish Parliament 1469 and 1474, it was ordained, that the Old Council should chuse the New, that the New and the Old Councils should chuse the Officers, and that Four Persons out of the Old should be chosen Yearly into the New Councils.

In Obedience to an Order for Copies of the Charters, and Setts of the Royal Burghs, Sixty-three of the Royal Burghs produced Copies of Charters. The Town Clerk of Kirkwall certified, that the Charters of that Burgh could not be read by him; and the Burghs of Loch-maben and Crail did not make any Return at all to the Order respecting the Charters.

All the Charters, with the Exception of Glasgow, are granted to the Burgesses alone; or to the Burgesses and Inhabitants; or to the Provost, Burgesses, and Community; or to the Aldermen and Community; or to the Merchants, Burgesses, and Community; or to the Provost, Baillies, Council, Burgesses, Community, and Incorporations; or to the Burgesses, together with the Provost, Baillies, and Incorporations; or to the Burgesses, together with the Provost, Baillies, and Council; or to the Provost, Baillies, Council, and Community. The Charter to Glasgow in 1690 confirms all former Charters granted Communitati vel Gildae Mecha-nicis, ac singulis Societatibus, et Diaconis ejusdem; and then the Charter is granted, de novo, Civitati et Concilio Burgali.

The Charters of Eighteen of the Burghs, so far as produced, do not contain any Clauses respecting the Elections. But,

Ist. Although many of the Burghs appear to have been possessed of great Number of Charters, yet, in general, only One or Two Charters have been produced to the House of Commons. Thus Edinburgh has produced only One Charter, but that Charter confirms Twenty-four other Charters; which are not produced;

Stirling has produced only Two Charters, confirming Twelve or Fifteen other Charters; Inverkeithing has produced only One Charter, confirming Eight others; and a very great Number of the other Burghs have

produced

Report respecting the Royal Burghs of Scotland*

It appears that the last Charter to Selkirk contains the Grant of a Provost, but makes no Alteration on the Clause of Klee t ion in the former Charter.

produced Charters, which confirm many other Charters that are not produced.

2dly, Many of the Charters are very ancient; but there is no Instance of a Clause of Election being introduced into any Charter before 1469; and even after that Period it appears that some Charters do, and others do not contain Clauses of Election, though granted in Favour of the same Burgh. — Thus Selkirk has produced Three Charters, only Two of which contain Clauses of Election; Banff has produced Three Charters, only One of which contains a Clause of Election; Stirling has produced Two Charters, and only One of them contains a Clause of Election.

3dly, It appears, that Burghs, some of whose Charters contain Clauses of Election, have not produced those Charters. Thus Elgin, in 1789, returned Two Charters, granted in the 13th and 14th Centuries, without Clauses of Election; but, on the 28th March 1793, a Third Charter was produced, containing a Clause of Election in Favour of the Burgesses. The Burgh of Pittenweem produced One Charter dated in 1593, which did not contain a Clause of Election; but a Copy of a Charter, certified by the proper Officer, from the public Records of Scotland, has been produced, containing a Clause of Election, dated 24th February, in the 28th Year of King Janies. Lochma-ben is in a similar Situation: That Burgh did not produce any Charter at all; but a certified Copy was procured from the Records of a Charter in 1612, containing a Clause of Election in Favour of the Burgesses.

The Charters in Favour of Forty-six of the present Royal Burghs contain Clauses respecting the Elections. Copies of those Clauses are annexed in the Appendix (A.) According to which, the Right of electing, or voting in the Elections, appears to your Committee to be as follows.

In Thirty-two Burghs, the Right of Election is granted either to Burgesses or Inhabitants alone, or to both, or either of them, joined with the Magistrates or other Persons in Office, or with the Community 32

In Eleven Burghs, the Right of Election is granted to the Provost, Baillies, Council, and Community - - - - -11

43

But Two Burghs, Bruntisland and Selkirk, have produced Two Charters, each containing Clauses of Election; by the One of which the Right is granted to the Bur-

fesses, and by the other to the Provost, laillies. Council, and Community; and in Rothsay, the Recital mentions, that the Burgesses had been in all past Times in the Use and Possession of Election; but the new Clause of Election is granted to the Provost, Baillies, Council, and Community; deducting, therefore, those Burghs whose Charters are Twice stated 3

Total Number of Royal Burghs - 66

In Pittenweem and Whithorti the Right of Election was limited, with the Consent of the Prior and Convent of Pittenweem and Candide Cross respectively. In Culross, Inverary, Wick, and Cambelton, the Right of electing the Magistrates, but not of the Council, was limited to be made with the Consent of, or out of, Lists of a certain Number, to be given by particular Persons.

In Twenty-five of the Forty-six Burghs whose Charters contain Clauses of Election, the Election is appointed to be made Yearly. In Eighteen there is no Regulation how often the Election is to be made. In One Burgh the Election is to be made in the ordinary Way and Time; and in Three Burghs the Electors are empowered to depose or remove the Persons elected for reasonable Causes, when it shall appear expedient to them.

The Burgh of Aberdeen is One of the Eighteen whose Charters do not contain any Clause of Election. But Extracts from the Records of Election in that Burgh, from the End of the 14th to the End of the 16th Century (the Appendix (B.) contains a Note of the particular Years extracted, and Copies of the Records of Election for the Years 1399, 1408, 1435, J439> H74, 1475, M77, 1494, 1502, 1509, 1523, 1526, 1536, 1537, 1543, 1580) and several Acts of the Town Council of that Burgh, Decrees of the Court of Session, and a Writ under the Privy Seal respecting the Elections in that Burgh about the End of the 16th Century, have been produced. From these Papers it appears, that till the Year 1590, the Provost, Four Baillies, and Four Common Serjeants, were elected Annually in the Liber Communitatis, Curia Capitalis Burgi de Aberdeen, or Curia Capitalis Ballivorum de Aberdeen, holden on the First Monday or Tuesday after Michaelmas Yearly, by the express Votes of all the Citizens and Burgesses, or, as it is sometimes said of the whole Community, taken upon Rolls regularly called, and in which the Names of all the Persons absent were marked, frequently to a very considerable Number. Sometimes, however, the Records do not mention the Description of the Electors; and for 100 Years before 1590, One Person or another of the Name of Menzies was Annually elected Provost by the Electors, the Burgesses, Citizens, or Comburgesses, with One Exception in the Year 1535, when Andrew Cullane was elected Provost. In some Instances, particularly in 1399, t435, 1475, 1477, ar*d 1481, the Common Council also appears to have been elected in the Head Court, and at the same Time with the Magistrates. In 1408 and 1469 the Names of the Common Council are entered after the Election of Magistrates, at the Head Court, without mentioning that they were elected. And in the Years 1469, 1477, and 1481, the Names of the Common Council are entered, or they are mentioned, to be elected after some private Business had been done after the Election of the Magistrates.

The Common Council, however, appear to have been in general chosen in the Curia Gildae, or Curia Ballivorum Gildse, holden the Friday after the Head Court, where all the Brethren of the Guild were obliged to attend, and where their Names were entered in Rolls regularly called, and the Names of those absent marked in the same Manner as at the Head Court. In general, the Names of the Common Council are entered every Year, either before or after the other Business of the Meeting, and sometimes it appears to be the only Business of the Meeting. At other Times, the Election is particularly entered thus; Subscripti electi fuerunt in Communes Consiliarios, viz*. 1439 an<* 1474; and in 1474 the Record bears, that they were elected pro Anno sequente. In the Head Court, in the Year 1475 and 1477, the Council are also said to be elected pro Anno sequente vel instanti.

About the Middle of the 16th Century, it appears,

that

that the Council themselves, at Three different Times, elected, -named, or admitted certain Persons into the Council at the Curia Gild®; in the First Instance, after the Names of the Council had been entered in the ordinary Manner; in the Two others, before the Entry of the Names of the Council. The First Instance of this is in 1549, when Two Persons were added to the Council; and there are two other Instances, in 1580, when Five Persons were added, because some of the Old Council were dead, and in 1587, when Eight were added, without any. Reason except that the Recora says it was according to the Use. No other Instances appear; but in a Note upon the Margin of the First Instance of the Admission, Naming, or Election of Councillors by the Council in 1549, it is said, " that there are many similar Elections of Members of the Common Council by the " Council themselves alone, sometimes on the Occasion of the Annual Election at Michaelmas, and at " other Times when any Vacancy happened." The Annual Election is also mentioned in the Year 1580, when the Record states, " that the Council, understanding that ane certain Number of the auld Council, elected and chosen the last Year, are departed " and deceased, at the Pleasure of God, to the Num-."* her of 5, and therefore they thought it expedient to " adjoin Five others."

It appears to your Committee, that in the Records of Aberdeen produced, the Council is not mentioned particularly to have been elected, except in the Head Court in the Years 1399, 1435, 1475> *477. and 1481, and in the Guild Court in 1439 aQd *474; the Names of the Council being in general entered Yearly, in the Manner already mentioned at the Guild Court, where all the Brethren of the Guild were-obliged to attend; and in no Instance is the Description. of the Electors of the Common Council in general particularly mentioned. For in the Three Instances, 154-9, 1580, and 1587, certain Persons are named or chosen by the Council to be added to the Council, without saying how the other Members of the Council were elected. Those Three Instances appear at a very late Period of the Records, - and the First of them, is only about' Forty Years before the Action which, was brought in 1590. It appears also, that the Auditors of Accounts were elected at the Guild Court. In no Instance is the Description of the Electors ,of. the Auditors entered in the Record; but in general their Names appear to be entered at the Guild Court, in the same Manner as those of the Common Council, sometimes particularly mentioning that they were elected, and' sometimes not.

The Dean of Guild, and Master of Kirk and Bridge-Work, -are not mentioned in the Records till 1502. In general they are mentioned to be elected, sometimes before and sometimes, after the Entry of the Names of the Common Council, at the Guild Court; but there is no Description of the Electors,_ except in the Ten. Years from 1726 to 1736 inclusive, when they are-said at first to have been elected by the Advice of the Provost and Council, and in the Five last Years to have been chosen directly, by the Provost- and Council.. Thus in the Year 1526 it is said, that the Deans of Guild, and Masters of Kirk Work were elected by the Awyss (Advice) of the Provost, Baillies, and Council. . In 1528, the Deans of Guild are said to be chosen in the same Manner, but the Master of Kirk Work is said to be chosen directly by. the Provost and Council. In 1529, 1530, 1531, the Election is ip. the same Manner. In 1532, 1533, 1534, 1535, and 1536,. it is said that both the Deans of Guild, and Master of Kirk Work, were chosen by- the Provost and Council.' Copies of the-Records of Election 1523,. 1526, 1536, 1537, and 1538, are annexed in the Appendix, (B).

On the 20th of July 1591, and before Judgment was pronounced, in this Action, a Writ was issued under the Privy Seal of King James VI, in which it is stated, " That the Council of Aberdeen had continued since their First Election unaltered or changed " for the Space of 40 or 50 Years, according to the " Consuetude of the Burgh observit the Space of 100 " Years before; that the Act of Parliament about " changing the Yearly Council had never taken " Effect in that Burgh; and that the Persons once " lawfully chosen on Council had continued till the " Time of their Death, subject to the Tryal of the " Neighbours of the said Burgh; and in case of any

Fault or Crime, the same has been ordourlie tried " on the Guild Court Day, after the Election of the " Magistrates, and those found guilty removed, and " others placed in their Rooms, from which great " Tranquility and Concord has followed in the said " Burgh; and in respect of many other Inconveniences which the Yearly changing of the Council might <c carry with it, the Annual Disorder and Dissention,

" and the infinite Confusion and Peril which commonly " accompanies all new Changes in Commonwealths,

" it is declared, that the same Council shall remain in

<lall Time coming; and in case of their Decease, or " tried Unworthiness, that the other Members of the " Council shall elect others in their Places, it being <l understood that the same Council shall be Yearly

" thereafter elected by Vote of Council, and such other " Ceremonies as are accustomed in Election of Magistrates within Burgh, notwithstanding the Act of " Parliament concerning the Yearly Change and " Election, which is dispensed with in that Part concerning the changing the Council only."

Notwithstanding this Dispensation, and the Perils of Changes, the Magistrates and Council, little more than Two Months afterwards, on the 1st of October 1591, made an Act of Council, in which they assert strongly, " That it/ was the aniient Custom of the " Burgh to continue the Council to the Day of their " Death, unless tried and found guilty of some Crime, (.‘ which was the Cause of the great flourishing of tho " Burgh, and the avoiding the Inconveniences of " Yearly Change; but that the present Age had produced restless and unquiet Spirits, seeking Change " and Alterations, quarrelling the Council that had " been for 50 Years by past, accusing the Provost; " Baillies, Dean of Guild, Treasurer, and other Office " Men, of unlawful Usurpations of thair Offices, and " pursuing them, and the Persons of the Council, before the Lords for the same; therefore; to remove " the Occasion of great Discord that had fallen out " within the Burgh, and greater likely to ensue if not " prevented, die Council ordered the Acts of Parliament to be followed ;" that isj the Old Council to " choose the New, Four Persons, of the Old to be chosen Yearly into the New Council, and the New and Old Council to chuse the Magistrates. The Election for the Year 1591 appears accordingly to have been made in that Manner; but it also appears, that Four of the Deacons of Trades refused to give any Vote in the Election although required.

That this Mode of Election did not. satisfy the Citizens appears from an Act of the Council on tho 25thi. December 1591, about Two. Months after this. This Fact of the Self-election of the Councils, or the perpetuating the Power of leading Men in the Council, appears from the First Sett of Dunfermline, N° 26, and also from the very strong Evidence of the Sett of Stirling. By the old Sett of that Burgh, N# 5, Eleven out of Twenty-one of the Council were ordered by the Sett to be changed Yearly, and the Magistrates could not be continued in the same Office above Two Years. The Election 1773 was declared void, as being brought about by undue Influence and Corrupt Practices, and the Burgh was deprived of Magistrates and Council. A Petition was presented to the king in' Council for a Warrant to restore the Magistrates and Council, and to make some Alterations in the Sett; and upon the Opinions of the then Attorney and Solicitor General, tind the Lord Advocate for Scotland, tipon a Reference to them arid a Comriiittee' of thd Privy Council, a new Sett was given, by Which His Majesty in Council directs, that iri order to prevent " Abuses to which the old Practice was liable," a Majority of the Council shall be chosen by the Merchants arid Trades every Year, and Two Thirds Of the Council shall be elected Yearly. The following Account of the Effect of the former Sett appears, as . stated in the Petition on which the Warrant fot* the hew Sett proceeds: " Eleven Members were Chahged or turned out of the Couricii, Yearly; but the Guildry or Meixharits had rib Choice in the Merrihers brought into Council out of their Own Nhm-|* her, neither had they any Choice of thfeir ovvtt Dean . " of Guild, he being elected arid preserited to titerif by the Common Council. That although no Person could by Election be continued in the Magis- t.racy of said Burgh longer than TwO Years at One " Time, yet One Magistrate might, and by Practifcb " often did, continue in Couricii as One of the SfeVdri " Ordinary Merchant Councillors, Or be fnade Dean !" of Guild* and so. remain iri any of these Offices frit " another Year, and could be again re-elected ak Pri>-yost or Baillie for anothef Year, whereby the leading " Members in the Council had it in their Power to " perpetuate themselves in Office, and to maridge arid u do in all Matters in the Burgh as they thought xt proper."

Your Committee have thought. It unnecessary to fenter into any Detail of the Various Modes of electing the Magistrates, except in so far as they come within the Description of Members of the Common Councils. Iri some Instances, the Magistrates are elected but of the Members of the Couricii, as in Aberdeen, and in others, out of Persons not in the Council. Iri general, the Council for the preceding Year form the Majority of the Electors Of the Magistrates for the next Year; but ih Four Instances, Anstruther Easter, Kilrenny, Kirkwall, Wick, and perhaps One or TVo more, the Magistrates are chosen by a popular Election. Wherever that is the Case, however, they are choseh out of Lists or Ledts given Ky ‘the Council, either of themselves, or other Persons. Thus in Anstruther Easter, the Majority of the Couricii continue withofat Election; the Four Magistrates are chosen by the Burgesses out of Lists of Nine Persons for Bailltes giveri by the Baillies, of which there are always Three, and of Three for the Treasurer given by himself, of which he is always Ope. The Case is similar in Kilrenny and Kirkwall. In Wick, if the Successor of the Earl of Caithness has riot resumed the Right of consenting to the Choice of the Magistrates, which it is said in the Sett he had relinquished, the Magistrates are elected by the Burgesses, and those Magistrates elect the Council, Jf the Earl's Successors have resumed the Eight of Assenting to the Election of Magistrates, of which no Evidence appears in the Papers produced, the Eight

of Election is virtually exercised by him'; for the Burgesses must elect Magistrates to whose Appointment he, will consent, and those Magistrates, iri so far as appears from the Sett, have the Right of noriiinating the Council.

With Respect to the particular Modes of Election in each Burgh, and the various and minute Regulations, respecting the Number and Description of the Magistrates and Members of Council, the Leets or Lists iri choosing Magistrates, Councillors, arid Deacons, arid1 ethdr Usages of a! like Nature, the Setts differ very widely, and do riot appear to depend on any certain or Uniform Authority. A great Part of them appear to have ariseif frorri local Usages. Thus Wigtown certifies to the' Convention in 1709, that the Sett had been Observed for Fifteen Years and upwards; Cupar, iri 1710, that the Sett had been observed Forty Years arid upwards, and riiany others. Indeed a Nufnbef of the Setts produced appear to have been copied from the Record the Convention established in 1708. Others of the Setts, Sach as Crailf, Banff, Kirkwall, Kinghorri, and Rutherglen, appear to have beeh framed by the Town Couricils. Some Setts originally framed or altered by the Town Councils, have received the Approbation of the General Convention of Royal Burghs. Other Setts, such as Perth, Duirifertriline, Inverness, Kirkaldy, InvbrkeitHing, Rigid, Taih, Glasgow, Aberdeen, Edinburgh Queensferry,. arid Saricjuhar, seem to owe their Forte to tteciSidifs of private Persons, or of Com-ffiittefes of the general Cotivention, ‘ on Arbitrations, fnade tb therri by rersoris who at the Time appear to have bfebri in the Offices of the Magistracy, Council, CrdiitlH, br Trades, tholteh yorir Committee cannot disedver iri dhy of the Papei's produced, what Authority such Persons had tb'stibmit the public Righto Of thl Coiriparii6s/of Corporations, or other Privileges, bfelbnging either to rite m of tb the Trades or Burgesses at large.

It does not appear to your Committee, that any of the Setts, fexcept Aberdeen, and perhaps Cupar, and One Or Tri o mOfe, are according to the Acts of Parliament hientione^ in the Papers produced, neither do they appear to be in Conforriiity with the Charters Which contain ClaUSes of Election'; and it is evident^ that neither In the Acts of Parliament nor in the -Chatters is there arty Foundation or Authority for riiany Of the local Usages that have been introduced respecting th'e Modes of Election in particular Burghs. It ftppeairs, that m'ariy of the Setts have befen altered, either rriote or less materially, in the Course of the present Century, either by the Authority of the Town Councils themselves, ‘aided hi general by the Appro-, bation Of the Coriventibh, or by the Convention, or by Decrees Arbitral of private Fersoris, or by Usage. Tea Burghs, Kircudbright, Durafermline, Culross, North Berwick, Queensferry, Rutherglen, Kirkaldy, St. Andrew's, Dysart, and Irvine, where the Exaction, besides what is paid Government, and the Expence of collecting, amounts to £912. 19 5-, have neither

carried it to the Account of the Revenue, nor made any Excuse whatever for the extra Exaction.

The Magistrates of Edinburgh, Aberdeen, Banff, and Inverness, where the extra Exaction (the Reason or Excuse for which is entered at the Bottom of the First Table) amounts to above £9,000, do not carry it to the Account of the Annual Revenue.

Although the Magistrates of Aberdeen and Banff say that the extra Exaction is imposed by Authority, and Acts of Head Courts in General Meetings of the Inhabitants, for the Expence of Wells, paving and lighting the Streets, &c. it appears to your Committee, that in none of the Returns, except Aberdeen and Banff, is any Tax said to be imposed by the Authority of Head Courts in General Meetings of the Inhabitants; and that neither in these Two Burghs, in Edinburgh, in Inverness, nor in any of the Burghs where an extra Exaction appears, is there any Act of Parliament, or other similar Authority, for imposing the Taxes or extra Exactions, the £ 1,250 per Annum levied in Edinburgh, by Act of Parliament, for the Town Guard, beipg perfectly distinct from the Sums said to be imposed with the Land Tax.

The other Fifteen Burghs in the Two First Tables carry the extra Exaction to the Account of the Annual Revenue, either wholly, or more generally in Part, after deducting certain Payments which have no Relation whatever to the Land Tax, or to the Expence of collecting it Thus the Magistrates of Brechin admit, that in the Year 1788 they levied £ 80, or more than double £ 39. 10 s. paid to the Receiver General, After deducting £7. gs. 10 d. as the Expence of levying the Assessment, they likewise deduct £16. 2 7 for

Eque and Missive Dues, and Commissioners Expences to Convention, Articles which appear to have no Relation to the Laind Tax, and to be merely a Part of the ordinary Expence of every Royal Burgh. Nothing more than the Balance of £17. 10$. 5d. or Excrescence, as it is called, of the Cess, after those Deductions, is carried to the Account of the Revenue: The same is the Case in Sanquhar 8nd Forfar.

The Magistrates of Forfar say, that the extra Exaction, more than Two Thirds of the Sum paid Government, is owing to an Increase of Inhabitants, nothing more being levied from Individuals than formerly.

As the Magistrates of Nairn say that the Burgesses cheerfully acquiesce in the Exaction, because they have Access to the Towns Commons, Mosses, and Quarries, without any Payment, your Committee have examined the Charter of Naim produced, and it appears to be granted to the Provost, Baillies, Burgesses, and Inhabitants. No other Reasons or Excuses for the extra Exaction appear in the Papers produced.

From the Return of the Burgh of Campbelton it appears, that for the First Nine of the Ten Years, the Sum actually levied is specified, without mentioning whether any Deduction has been made for Deficiencies in the Collection. In the Tenth Year, the Sum imposed on the Inhabitants is mentioned, being nearly Five Times the Amount of the whole Sum paid to Government; but of that Sum it is said only Four Fifths can be made effectual, leaving One Fifth, or a Sum nearly equal to what is paid Government for Deficiencies in that Year. Now it appears your Committee, that more than Forty of the Burghs have given no Account of any Sums allowed for Deficiencies in the Collection, the Accounts appearing to be the Sums actually levied, and not the Sums imposed on the Inhabitants.

It likewise appears to your Committee, that the Salaries to the Collectors, and Expence of collecting the Cess, is fixed at the Discretion of the Magistrates and Town Councils; that it is very different in different Burghs, and in many Instances amounts to a most extravagant Rate on the Sum paid Government. In Ten Burghs no Salary is returned, viz*. Annan, where no Cess is levied from the Inhabitants, M it ia paid out of the Baits of a Fishing belonging to them; and Forfar, North Berwick, Sanquhar, Rutherglen, Canapbeftop^ Fortrose, Kintore, and Dumbarton, where the Cess seems to be collected by the Treasurer or others, without any Salary, along with the other Branches of the Burgh Revenue; and Forres, where the Magistrates return, that no Salary is fixed for the Collector, but the Persona liable in Payment make him what Satisfaction they please for his Trouble.

A Table of the Rate of the Expence on the Sum paid Government in Forty-five other Burghs, is annexed in the Appendix (D.) amounting from to 39 per Cent,

on the Sum paid to Government.

Vthly, Whether the Lands and other Heritable Property of the Royal Burghs have been alien* ated by the Magistrates and Common Councils, and in what Manner; and whether Debts have been contracted, and the common Property dilapidated.

The Charters of the Royal Burghs, produced, contain Grants and Confirmations of many Lands, Fishings, and other real Property; but as in general the Description is by the Name or Boundaries, the precise Value or Extent of the Property does not appear from the Charters: There is only One Instance, where it is in some Measure ascertained. By a Charter in 1536, King James grants to the Baillies, Burgesses, and Community of Selkirk, Licence to break and till Yearly

1,000 Acres of their Common Lands of their said Burgh, in what Part thereof they pleased, with Power to them either to occupy the Lands, or to lease them to Tenants as they shall think most expedient

Although the precise Value and Extent of the common Properly of the Burghs granted by the Charters cannot be ascertained, it appears to your Committee, that within Eighteen Years after the Act 1469, it was enacted, by an Act of the Scottish Parliament, 1487, Cap. 108, that the Election of Officers in Boroughs should be made " of the best and worthiest Indwellers " of the Town, and not by Partiality or Mastership.'' It appears to your Committee, that before the new System of Burgh Government was introduced by the Act 1469, there is no Instance of any Complaint that Elections had been made by Partiality or Mastership.

By the Act of the Scottish Parliament, about Sixteen Years after, in 1503, Cap. 80, it was enacted, " That u all Officers having Office of jurisdiction within Burgh " should be Annually changed, and that none have " Jurisdiction within Boroughs, unless they use Merchandize within the same.'7

The Act 26 of the Scottish Parliament, held in the Year 1535, Thirty-tvto Years after, proceeds on the following Narrative: " Because all our Sovereign Lord " Burrowes are put to Poverty, wasted, and destroyed " in their Goods and Policy, and almost ruinous, thro' " Fault of using of Merchandize, and thro' being of " Oudaadsmen, Provost, Baillies, and Aldermen within " Burgh, for their own particular Weil, in consuming " of the common Good of Burrows, granted to them " by our Sovereign Lord and his Predecessors Kings " of Scotland, for the Uphold of Honesty and Policy " within Burgh."

The Act of the Parliament of Scotland, in the Year 1609, Cap. 8, Seventy-four Years after, discharging Noblemen and Gentlemen to be elected Officers of Boroughs, proceeds on this Narrative: " Neither yet " the Course intended by his Majesty for discharging " Noblemen and Gentlemen to be elected Provosts u and Magistrates of Burrowes (whereof none should " be capable but Burgesses, actual Traffickers, and

Inhabitants of the said Boroughs) has taken such u Effect as is maist necessary for Preservation of the

Liberties and good Estate of the said Boroughs, and M hindering the Dissipation of their common Good, u and perverting of their Privileges."

In the Year 1684, Seventy-five Years after, King Charles the Second granted a Commission for enquiring into the Affairs of Boroughs. In that Commission his Majesty expressly says, " We understanding that in many of our Royal Burghs the common Property " and Revenues have, by the Magistrates for the " Time, been either profusely dilapidated, or pri-vateiy peculated, and for the most Part have been " applied to Ends and Purposes totally different from uthose directed by Law, or by the beneficent Donations made by us and our illustrious Ancestors, but " more particularly that our Royal Burghs, without Vo i/. 48.

Ymii.

" any Necessity, have contracted Debts, and that after Report " Grants and Donations altogether sufficient for the respecting " Discharge of these Debts were made by ns and our g*r tf Predecessors, and after Burthens were imposed by ScotLad " the Consent of the Citizens for Payment of these " Debts, yet they for the greater Part, in most of our " Royal Burghs, remain unpaid, and the Revenues " arising from the common Good, from our most liberal and beneficent Gifts, and the voluntary Contributions of the Citizens, have been wasted and " misapplied; from whence there have proceeded not " only numberless Murmurs and Complaints in Burghs,

" but also those that prefer their private Advantage " to the common Interest of the Burghs, and to the

Dignity and Office of Magistracy, have excited " Factions and Divisions in order to procure themselves to be elected to the Offices of Magistracy,

" and in order that they, their Friends, Relations, and " Dependants might be continued in that Office,

" from whence they might take Occasion to squander " the Properties and Revenues of the Burgh in rewarding their Friends, and supporting their Factions in the Burgh: Whereas, if they were strictly " compelled to render an Account of the public Property and Revenue of the Burgh, to prove that the " same were necessarily and profitably applied to the " common Uses and Affairs of the Burgh, to render " an Account of their Dilapidations and Misapplications, and to pay and indemnify the same to the " Burgh, and if they were otherwise fined and punished, as the Laws of the Kingdom require, for their " corrupt Administration, then these Evils would in a " great Measure be remedied and prevented, from " whence Murmurs and Complaints would cerise,

" Contentions for the Office of Magistrates would be " restrained and mitigated, and Merchants and Manufacturers, and other Citizens of Burghs, would diligently and peaceably follow their Callings and Profeesions, and our Burghs be well and peaceably " governed, Ac." The Commission, which is in Latin, is annexed in Appendix (F.)

In the Claim of Righte presented to King William and Queen Mary, on the 11th April 1689, Five Years after, One of the Grievances specially mentioned is the subverting, by the abdicated Family, the Rights of the Royal Boroughs, the Third Estate of Parliament " imposing on them not only Magistrates, but also the " Town Councils and Clerks, contrary to their Liberties " and express Charters."

One of the Special Articles of Grievances presented to King William, in pursuance of the Claim of Rights of the 13th of April 1689, was " That the Grievances " of the Boroughs be considered and redressed in " Parliament."

By the Act of Union, " The Rights and Priviledges of the Royal Burghs in Scotland shall remain entire after the Union, and notwithstanding " thereof."

The Act of the Scottish Parliament, in the Year 1693, Cap. 28, anent the common Good of Royal Borrowes, proceeds in this Narrative, " That the " Royal Burrows of the Kingdom, erected and provided with their respective public Goods and Revenues, are of late, through the Mal-administration " of the Magistrates and others, to whom the Management of the public Goods and Revenues have u been committed, fallen into great Debts and Burthens,

" to the Diminution of the Dignity of the Estate of " Burrows, &c."

In the next Year, 1694, a Commission, proceeding on the same Narrative, was granted by the Crown " to certain Persons, for enquiring into the Administration of Boroughs."

In the Year 1691, John Anderson, then Provost of Glasgow, in the Name and- Behalf of that Borough, presented a Supplication to the General Convention

of

of Royal Boroughs, which is of the following Tenor: " That whir the Town of Glasgow, having of a considerable Time by gone flourished in its Trade and " Inhabitants, and paid a large Share of the Public " Burthens due and payable by the State of Burrowes; " true it is, that of late the said Burgh is become " altogether incapable of Subsistence, in regard of these " heavy Burthens that ly thereupon, occasioned by " the vast Soumes that have been borrowed by the " late Magistrates, and the Misapplying and Dilapi-"dation of the Tounes Patirmony, in suffering their " Debts to swell, and employing the common Stock " for their own sinistrous Ends and Uses, whirin, if " the Petitioner should be express in the Particular, "it would accordingly tend to the Dishonor and " Disparagement of those whose Duty it was to have " been the Patriots and Supporters of the Place. And that the General Convention of the Royal Burghs of Scotland did themselves entertain, with Regard to the general Administration of the Burghs, the Sentiments contained in the above-mentioned Supplication from the Burrowe of Glasgow, appears from an Act of the General Convention in the Year 1691, which states that there were " Many Complaints " given in to the respective General Conventions of " Burrowes these several Years by past by many particular Burghs, yea universally by the Whole Royal " Burroughs, complaining of their Poverty, Want, " and Decay of Trade, and that they are not rightly " adjusted in the Taxt Roll as to the Quota and Proportion of Burden; and considering that there has *' been Remedies proposed, yet none has been received with that universal Satisfaction as a general " Search and Inquirie to be made into the State and " Condition of every Burgh as to thir Trade and common Good, by a Visitation to be made over the " whole Burroughs, which, although not practised " formerly, yet its thought to be the most just and " equal Way how to adjust the Taxt Roll, if impartiallie gone about; therefore the Convention ordains every particular Royal Burgh within the " Kingdom to be visited as to their Trade and common Good, conform to the Instructions hereunto " subjoined, and for that Effect appoints and nominates " Four Visitors, &c\"

In the Year 1789, an Order was made for an Account of all Lands and other Heritable Property, sold, feued, or alienated by the Magistrates since the Union, specifying the Price for which the same were sold, and the Rent received for the last Year the same were let prior to the Alienation.

The Burghs of Fortrose, Pittenweem, and Loch* maben, did not make any Returns to this Order. Very voluminous Accounts were produced by many of the other Burghs.

On examining those Accounts your Committee have found it impossible to make any general and accurate State of the Transactions respecting the Alienation of the Lands. In some Instances the Lands are sold for an Annual Feuduty or Ground Rent, without any Price; in others for a Price without any Feuduty; and in others both for a Feuduty and a Premium. In a great many Instances, the Rents of the Property, previous to the Alienation, is not specified. In some Cases the Property is said to have been Waste; in others, that the Rent, the Price on the Feuduty, could not be ascertained. In some cases the Prices received is not mentioned. The Dates of the Sales are omitted in Dumbarton. In Annan, the Magistrates say, that they alienated Lands to a considerable Amount with the Consent of the Inhabitants; but neither the Dates of the Sales, the Names of the Lands, the former Rent, the Price received, or any other Particulars, are mentioned. In some Cases, as Dumfries, the Lands are said to have been in the Occupation of the Burgesses as common Pasturage, so that the former Rent or Value does not appear. The Return for the Burgh of Edinburgh bears to be an Account of those Lands only which belonged to the Burgh at the Union, and have been alienated since that Time; but the Return does not specify the Sale of any Lands, or other Real Property which they had acquired since the Union, and in Consequence the whole of the Alienations in that Burgh is made to amount only to £. 6,000 since the Year 1707, though the Return of the Revenue states that the Feuduty or Quit Rent of Lands payable to the Burgh amounts to above £. 1,800, of which more than £. 900 is paid for Lands over which the Royalty of the Burgh was extended by 22 Geo. II, Chap. 26. There is no Account of the Sales of the Lands of Hospitals, except in the Return of the Burgh of Dundee.

There is One Instance of the Deficiency and Uncertainty of the Returns respecting the Alienations, which your Committee think it necessary to mention. The Return of Haddington states, that in 1730, and afterwards, the Barony of Gladsmuir wras feued at the Rent for which the I^nds were held in Lease, converted into a Feuduty or Quit Rent, and the Whole of that Feuduty appears by the Return of the Revenue to be about £.48. By an Act of the Council of Haddington, in January 1727, it appears that a Mr. Men* zies, of Letham, offered to take a common improving Lease of the Barony at the Rent of £. 100 per Annum, and to consent that certain Parts of the Lands, and sufficient Pasturage for the Cattle of the Burgesses, and the Liberty of raising Coal, should be excepted from the Lease. It appears that this Offer was not accepted; that the Lands were leased at £48, and soon after that the Leases were changed into Feus or perpetual Rights, without any Price or Premium, and the Rent converted into a Feuduty. The Whole of this Transaction was made by private Sale, except one Parcel of 28 Acres feued by public Auction, 1745, at £. 6. 19». 6d.; but in 1756 this Feuduty is reduced to more than One Third less, without any Reason being given for the Reduction.

By an Act of Council of Haddington, 20th January 1733, appears, that " those Feus were granted " clandestinely, and when there was not a Quorum of " disinterested Persons present; and therefore the " Council unanimously condescended, that the said " Charters be reduced^ and Process be intented for " that Purpose."

961

Two Facte appear from the Returns; that the Magistrates and Council possess the Power of selling and alienating the Common Lands of the Burghs granted to the Burgesses by their Charters, or purchased with their common Monies, Property, or Revenues, and that this Power may be exercised in any Manner the Magistrates and Council think proper.

In the whole of the Alienations since the Union, there does not appear above One hundred Instances where the Property was sold by Public Sale or Auction; about that Number of Instances are mentioned in the Returns, although the Order for an Account of the Alienations does not direct that it should be specified, whether they were made by public and private Sale. The Amount of the Debts contracted by the Magistrates and Town Councils, nor the Causes for which they were contracted, nor the Uses to which the Money was applied, do not appear from the Accounts, no Order having been made for an Account of the Debts of the Royal Burghs, or the Causes of their Contraction, or the Application of the Money; but that the Council may and do contract Debts is established, not only by the Acts of Parliament and Commissions already mentioned, but likewise by the Accounts from Perth, Stirling, and Two or Three of the smaller Burghs, where the Debts are mentioned. The Debts of Perth exceed 16,000l. and i,oooo/. of that Sum Iras contracted in the Year 1788. The Debts of Stirling exceed 5,000l. The Three other small Burghs are in Debt from 1,200l. to 700l. each In many Instances it appears that Lands have been sold for the Payment of Debts, It likewise appears, that in the Year 1722, the Burgh of Edinburgh was in Debt above 47,500 /., as Provision is made for Payment of that Sum, at least, of their Debt, during the Continuance of an Act of 9 Geo. I. Cap. 14. afterwards extended and continued to 1799 by 1 Geo. II. Cap. 22. Glasgow and Arbroath also appear to have contracted very considerable Debts, by several Acts of Geo. I. and II. and 27 Geo. III. Chap. 46. imposing and continuing a Duty of Two Pennies 00 the PiBt of Ale for Payment of those Debts, and other Purposes.

In some of the Burghs possessed of landed Property it appears, that no Sales to any considerable Amount have been made since the Union; and in those Burghs, such as Kircudbright, Dumfermline, and Selkirk, the greatest Part of their Revenue consists of the Rents of their Lands.

In those Burghs which have sold Lands since the Union, it appears to your Committee, that the gross Amount of the Prices of the Lands alienated, so far as stated in the Returns, may amount to about One hundred thousand Pounds Sterling. Taking the Rents as at the Period of the Sale, and without Reference to the present Value of the Property sold, and supposing that all the Property, the Rent of which is not ascertained, specified, or mentioned in the Returns was Waste, it would appear that the whole Feuduty received in all the Burghs is more than equal to the

Rent said to have been received for the Lands at the Report n Time of the Alienation, besides the Prices received ?|>ectl.nK on the Alienation. Of those Prices, so far as specified of°j^,tlai in the Returns, it appears to your Committee, that scarcely any Part now remain with the Burghs. The only Instance where Money is returned as Part of the common Property is in the Burgh of Ayr. The Magistrates sold some Lands in 1757 for above 7,000l., and by the Return of the Revenue of that Burgh in 1788, it appears that the Burgh was then possessed of

2,000 /. in Money, the Interest of which is entered as One of the Articles of the Revenue.

From a Consideration of the different Authorities and Papers produced, it appears, that from a very early Period after the Year 1469, when a new Mode -of electing the Magistrates and Common Council was introduced, by which the Old Council were authorized to choose the New, the Administration of the Affairs of the Royal Burghs appears to have been Matter of great and frequent Complaint in several of the Royal Burghs, as repeatedly declared by the Parliament, and by the executive. Government of Scotland, by the Claim of Rights, by Supplications of individual Burghs to the General Convention, and by the Acts of the General Convention itself; that the Principle of Election introduced by that Statute still continues to act universally, or almost universally, in the Royal Burghs, although with respect to the particular Modifications of that Principle^ and the various Ways in which it has been carried into Effect, the Modes of Election in the Burghs appear to be widely different, to depend on no certain or uniform Authority, and to be maintained in direct Contradiction to the Clauses of Election in a great Majority of the Charters; that Taxes have been imposed without the Authority of Parliament, and greater Sums levied in the Name of, or together with the Land Tax, than what is paid to Government, and the Expence of collecting taken together; and that the Powers exercised by the Town Councils, before the Union, of contracting Debts, disposing of the common Revenues, and alienating the common Property and common Lands of the Burghs at their Pleasure, remain unaltered and undiminished.

In Conclusion, your Committee think it their Duty to state, that the Petitioners, in their Petitions, proffered additional Evidence by the oral Testimony of Witnesses, and otherwise, to substantiate the different Allegations in the Petitions, in case it should appear to be necessary, particularly as to Grievances stated in the Petitions, to which tnc Papers ordered and returned do not apply, such as the actual Mismanagement and Misapplication of the Revenues, the Contractions of Debts, the Want of a Jurisdiction of Accounts, the Neglect of Police, Partiality in quartering Soldiers and apportioning the Cess, and the refusing the Burgesses Access to the Accounts and Records of the Burghs.

Appendix, (C.)

ABSTRACT of the Setts of the Royal Burghs.

I. EDINBURGH.

Two Decrees Arbitral 2 Acts of Counsel

'1658 & 1673} concerning the Sett3-

Council consists of 17 Merchants, 6 Deacons, and 2 Trades Counsellors, in all 25. These shorten the Leets for 14 Deacons, and elect 6 of them Council Deacons; they may continue 2 Years. The 14 Deacons are elected as follows: Each Corporation or Trade vote a List, or Leet, of 6, which they give in to the Council, who return 3 of the 6 for the Election of a Deacon, who is chosen by a Majority of the Votes of the Members of the respective Corporations. The 25 Members of Council elect 3 Merchants and 2 Trades Counsellors. The Old and New Council, consisting of 30 Leet for the Office Bearers, who are elected by them and the 8 Deacons not of the Council, making in all 38, Thereafter the Council consists, as formerly, of 25; but the 8 Extra Deacons have a Vote in every Case exceeding the Value of 1/. 13#. 4 d. The Magistrates consist of a Lord Provost, Dean of Guild, and Treasurer, each of whom may be re-elected for 1 Year more, and Baillies, who cannot be re-elected into the same Office the succeeding Year, and they must be

II. PERTH.

Act of Convention, 1658, on a Submission, reduced the Council from 38 to 26, by striking off or debarring Two Trades Counsellors, but does not mention the Mode of Election.

The Sett mentioning the Mode of Election returned to the Convention in Consequence of the Order 1708.

Council consists of 26, to wit, 14 Merchants and 12 Tradesmen. Merchant Counsel are elected by such Members of the Old Town Council as are Merchants, but the old Magistrates continue 1 Year as Counsellors. The Trades Counsellors are elected by the Council out of Leets given in by the Trades.

Provost, 3 Baillies, and Dean of Guild, are Merchants; the Treasurer a Merchant and Tradesman per Vices, elected by the Town Council out of Leets given by the old Magistrates and Council; 4th Baillie is a Tradesman elected by the Council out of Leets given by the Corporation of Trades per Vices. Magistrates cannot be reelected above 2 Years; but no Restriction as to the Re-election ol Counsellors, nor to the Election of the same Magistrates after they have been One Year out of Office.

After the Election, Deacons are elected by each Corporation of Trades without Controul from the Council, and they with the Trades Baillie and Trades Counsellors elect a Convener, who is not a Member of the Council; nor are the Deacons Members of Council, ex Officio.

III. DUNDEE.

Provost, 4 Baillies, Dean of Guild, and Treasurer and Counsellors, in all 20.

The Council, out of Leets made by themselves, choose 5 Merchants and 3 Trades Counsellors. The Old and New Council make Leets for Magistrates, Copies of which are given to the Trades, and the Election of those Magistrates is made by the Old and New Council, and 9 Deacons.

The Sett does not contain any Restriction against the Re-election of any Person in Office or in Council; Deacons not Counsellors ex officio; no Leets for them.

IV. ABERDEEN.

Established by Act of the Town Council 1591, and Decrees of Lords of Session approving the Alteration as according to the Acts of Parliament, tho' contrarie to former Practice.

Approved by Decrees Arbitral, King James .'jth, 1592.

Altered by Decrees Arbitral of Commissioners of Convention, 1596, giving the 6 Deacons of Trades not in Council a Vote in the Election of the Magistrates.

Council consists of 19, who choose 13 new Brethren of the Guild, and continue of the old, making 17, and choose Two of the Deacons, making in all 19.

Afterwards the New and Old Guild Council, consisting of 30, with 6 Deacons of Trades not in Council, and Deacons of Old and New Council, in all 40, elect Provost, Baillies, and other Officers, out of the Council.

No Leets for Deacons who are not Counsellors ex Officio.

V. STIRLING.

The Town Council by the Old Sett consisted of 7 Deacons chosen out of Leets made by the Trades, shortened by the Council to 2 Persons, and One of these Two chosen by each Trade, who was a Counsellor ex Officio, and 14 Merchant Counsellors elected by the Old Council, in all 21.

The Provost, 4 Baillies, Dean of Guild, and Treasurer, were chosen out of Leets of Persons in Council by the New and Old Council.

Seven Merchant Counsellors, and Deacons, being a Majority of the Council, changed Yearly.

Magistrates not to continue in the same Office longer than 2 Years.

No Restriction against Re-election of Magistrates or Counsellors changed after they had been One Year out of Office or Council.

By New Sett given 23d May 1781.

A Poll Election was given in the First Instance, and thereafter the Number of the Council the same as before, to be elected thus: 7 Deacons chosen by the Members of each Trade, without Leets or Controul from Council, as formerly, Counsellors ex officio; 4 New Merchant Counsellors, One of whom to be Dean of Guild to be elected by the Merchants or Members of the Guildry; 3 new Merchant Counsellors, to be elected by the Old Council, who vote off or remove 7 of the Old Merchant Council; 7 Merchant Counsellors, who remain without Election; in all 21. These 21 elect from themselves the Magistrates, except the Dean of Guild. The Old Council name Deacons, who cannot be re-elected for the next Year.

VI. LINLITHGOW.

The Number of Council, 19 Merchants and 18 Trades, in all 27, elected thus:

Each of the 8 Corporations of Trades gives a Leet of 3 Persons, of which the Council and Deacon of the Trade expunge One, and in his Stead add the then Deacon, and the Person so expunged presides at the Election respectively of each of the Deacons.

VII. SAINT ANDREWS.

Decreet Arbitral on Submission to Convention, 8th July 1740, after the Sett, and concerns an Election prior to the Submission.

The Council consists of 29; Provost, Dean of Gild, 4 Baillies, and Treasurer, Merchants or Guildry, and 14 Gild Brethren, Merchant Counsellors, and the Convener and 7 Deacons, Trades Counsellors, elected thus-

The Old Council choose 3 new Merchant Counsellors; the Trades choose a Convener, and 7 Deacons; and the other 18 Members of Council remain without Election; in all 29.

The 7 Magistrates are elected out of the 21 Counsellors, by the Old and New Council of 32.

There appears to be no Leets of Deacons; but the old Magistrates are always put in the Leets for electing the new.

Ry the Decreet Arbitral, Regulation is made concerning the Residence of Magistrates, and that the Dean of Guild, Baillies, and Treasurer, shall not be continued in the same Office above 3 Years; and that no Tradesman shall be elected as Guild Counsellor, unless he renounce his Trade, and the Privilege of being a Deacon in future.

VIII. GLASGOW.

Sett, 1711. Altered by Council in 1748, and approved by Convention.

Council 29 or 33 in certain Cases.

By the Sett, they are elected thus:

The Council of 29 or 33 elect the Provost and 3 Baillies out of very complex Leets of the Council, made by the Magistrates; then the Provost and 3 Baillies so elected for that Year, and the Provosts and Baillies for the 2 preceding Years, in all 12, of whom there is in Council at the Time a Majority, or 8 out of 12, elect the Counsellors, viz. 13 Merchants and 12 Trades; in all 29.

The Magistrates and Council of the Year, with the Deacons of Trades, to whom are added as many Merchants as make the Number of Merchants equal to the Trades, elect the Dean of Guild out of a Leet from the Merchants House, and the Deacon Convener out of a Leet from the Trades House, who either may or may not be Members of Council; but if not, are extra Counsellors ex Officio. The Master of Works, and Treasurer, are elected by the New Council, and if not Members of Council, they are extraordinary Members ex Officio. In all extra Counsellors.

The Provost Baillies last elected, Dean of Guild, and Deacon Convener, are continued in the Council a Year after the Expiry of their Offices.

The 2 Senior Merchants, and 2 SeniorTrades Counsellors, not in the Magistracy, nor in preceding Article, shall be disqualified from sitting in Council for 3 Years.

IX. AIR.

Council consists of a Provost, 2 Baillies, Dean of Guild, Treasurer, and 10 Merchant and 2 Trades Counsellors, in all 17, elected thus:

The Old Council of 17 elect Merchants and 2 Tradesmen of different Crafts new Counsellors for the ensuing Year, which, with the Old Council of 17, make 23.

Those 23 make Leets of themselves for Provost, Treasurer, Dean of Guild, and Baillies, and then the said 23, along with Three Deacons of the other Crafts, in all 26, elect the 5 Magistrates out of the said Leets, Four of the Merchant, and 2 of the Trades Counsellors, go out of Council each Year.

The Sett contains no Regulation for the Change of any other Members of the Council than the Merchants and 2 Trades Counsellors; and there is no Restriction against the Re-election of the Counsellors so changed, after they have been 1 Year out of the Council.

X. HADDINGTON. — Act of Town Council, on Act of Convention, 1655.

Council consists of 16 Merchants and 9 Trades, elected thus:

The Magistrates and Merchant Council, in N* 16, elect new Merchant Counsellors, in Place of who are put off Yearly, at the Conclusion of the whole Elections, by the Magistrates, Treasurer, and new Merchant Counsellors; 12 Merchant Counsellors remain without any Election; and 7 Deacons and 2 Trades Counsellors are chosen by the Trades; in all 25.

The Trades Baillie is always One of the Trades Counsellors, and as such is chosen by the Trades; and the other Magistrates are chosen out of the new and old Merchant Council, by the new and old Merchant and Trades Council of 31.

Leets for Magistrates.

The Council consists of 2 Baillies and 21 Counsellors, Tradesmen.

The Old Council chooses the New out of Leets given by each Member of Two Persons.

Each of the Baillies makes a Leet of 6, 12 in all, out of which the Old and New Council choose 6, that Six the Two Baillies are elected.

The Baillies and New Council choose the Treasurer out of the Leet of Two, given by the surer.

No Restriction as to Re-election either of Magistrates or Counsellors.

XII. KIRKA

Decreet Arbitral concerning the Sett by the Earl of Rothes, dated 1662, and Sett altered or explained 29th August 1721, on a Submission to Convention. Council consists of 10 Seafaring Men, 8 Merchants, and 3 Tradesmen; in all 21.

The Old Council choose the New; and the New and Old Council, with the whole Deacons, choose the 5 Magistrates.

No Counsellor can continue above Two Years together, unless an Officebearer; and the Deacons are joined with Counsel in setting Tacks, contracting Debt, and common Works.

No Restriction as to Re-election of Magistrates, and no Restriction against re-electing a Counsellor after he has been One Year out of Council.

XIII. MONTROSE.

Council consists of 17 Merchants and 2 Tradesmen, including the Magistrates, making 19.

The Old Council choose the New. Only 7 old Magistrates continue Counsellors One Year longer ex Officio. The Old and New Council, out of Leets, elect of the Magistrates, and the New Council elect the other 3. No Limitation as to Re-election of Counsellors; but the Provost, Treasurer, and Hospital Master cannot continue in those Offices above 2, nor the Baillies above 3 Years; but no Restriction against re-electing them after being One Year out of Office, though in Council as old Magistrates.

XIV. CUPAR. — Said to have been observed 40 Years before 1710, and upwards.

The Council consists of a Provost, 3 Baillies, Dean of Guild, and Treasurer, 13 Guild or Merchant Counsellors, and 8 Deacons Trades Counsellors; in all 27. Elected thus:

The 13 Merchant Council choose the like Number to succeed them the ensuing Year, called the New Council; and the Old and New Council and 8 Deacons elect 5 of the Magistrates; and the Dean of Guild is elected by the whole Guild Brethren of the Burgh.

After the Election, 4 of the Old Council are chosen, One by each of the Provost and 3 Baillies, called the Adjoined Council, who are Members of the Council for that Year, but have no Vote at next Election. There is no Restriction against the Re-election either of Provost or Counsellors, at least after they have been One Year out of Office. The other Magistrates cannot continue in their Offices above 2 Years together; but there is no Limitation of re-electing them after being One Year out of Office.

XV. ANSTRUTHEREASTER.

Council consists of 19, apparently without Distinction of Merchants and Trades, viz*. 3 Baillies, 1 Treasurer, and 15 Counsellors.

The Old Council nominate new Counsellors, and Annually put off of the old, and the other 11 Counsellors remain without Change.

The Magistrates are elected by the whole Burgesses out of a Leet of 9 Persons for the Baillies, given by the 3 Baillies, of which Number they are always 3; and out of a Leet of 3 Persons for the Treasurer, given by himself, and of which Number he is always One.

XVI. DUMFRIES.

Council consists of a Provost, 3 Baillies, Dean, Treasurer, 12 Merchant Counsellors, and 7 Deacons Trades Counsellors; in all 25. Elected thus:

Four new Merchant Counsellors are chosen by the Magistrates and Old Council; 8 Merchant Counsellors continue without Election; 7 Deacons Trades Counsellors are elected by the Trades without Leets. The 6 Magistrates are elected as under, out of Leets of the Old and New Merchant Council of 22; and at the Conclusion of the whole Election, 4 of the old Merchant Counsellors are voted off by a Council of the 6 new Magistrates, 4 new Merchant Counsellors, and 7 Deacons; in all 17.

The whole Old Council of 25, the new Merchant Counsellors, and Tradesmen added to the Deacons, in all 33, make Leets of the Members of the Old and New Merchant Council for Magistrates; and out of those Leets the 33 elect the 6 Magistrates.

Only of the 18 Merchants, including Magistrates in Council, are Annually changed, and 14 Merchants must remain; but the Magistrates cannot continue in the same Office without Intermission above Two Years.

The 7 Deacons either may or may not be re-elected.

Certain Relations, such as Father and Son, Brethren, &c. cannot be on the Magistracy at the same Time under a Penalty of £. 1,000 Scots, and several similar Regulations, enacted by Acts of the Town Council, are read at every Election.

XVII. INVERNESS.

First Sett by Committee of Convention 1676 Orders, that the Council shall consist of 21, conform to the Sett made by the Town Council in 1648; and on Account of the Complaint of the Continuance of the Council many Years before, enacts, that 5 new Counsellors shall be chosen every Year, and that the Council shall choose Magistrates out of their own Number. The Provost not to continue above 3 Years, nor the other Magistrates above 2 Years without Intermission, without Prejudice to their being re-chosen after being One Year out of those Offices.

Explained by a Committee of Convention, upon a Submission, in 1709.

Altered by Act of Council, Approved by Convention, in 1722; against which Alteration and Approbation the Commissioner from Dundee protested; to which the Commissioner for Inverness answered, that their Sett was neither according to their Charter nor Act of Parliament, but was given them by, and is alterable by Convention.

The Mode of Election appears to be this:

The Provost, Baillies, Dean of Guild, and Treasurer, continue Counsellors for the Year after they go out of Office, and cannot be any of the Five Merchant Counsellors turned off.

The Town Council choose 5 new Merchant Counsellors, and remove 5 of the old; so that 13 Merchant Counsellors continue without Election.

The 6 incorporated Trades shall choose each one Deacon, and those Deacons shall elect a Convener, who is ex Officio a Counsellor; out of the remaining Deacons the Town Council shall elect 2 Trades Counsellors; in all 21.

The 5 old Merchant Counsellors being removed, the Council, out of their own Number, shall choose the

Magistrates.

Report respecting the Royal Burghs of Scotland.

XVIII. BRUNTISLAND.

Produced Submission, dated 22d and 29th February 1728, between Guildry and Convener of the Trades, whose Subscription by Act of Council is declared as good as if both Parties had subscribed, and they particularly submit with Power to annul a Decreet of Declarator ito Favour of the Trades and Decreet Arbitral thereon.

Decreed 1st. That the Council shall consist of 14 Merchants, actual Traffickers, Burgesses, (residing and bearing Scotland Lot) and of 7 Tradesmen, Burgesses, Freemen, bearing Scotland Lot; in all 21, elected thus:

The Old Council shall choose the New Council, and the New Council shall choose 3 Baillies out of the Merchant Council, who cannot continue above 2 Years in that Office. Counsellors shall ndt' continue longer than 3 Years, till 1 Year out of Council; and that after the Election Anno 1729, 3 Guild Councellors at least shall be changed every Year, and that the Sett, except so fer as altered by the Decreet, shall remain in full Force.

XIX. INVERKEITHING.

Produced 1st. Sett, as in Books of Convention 1709.

2. Decreet of the Convention, admitting Deacons to Council, 7th July 1742.

By 1st. Sett. — Council consists of at least 15, without Distinction of Merchants and Trades, viz*, a Provost, 2 Baillies, Dean of Guild, and Treasurer, and 10 or more Burgesses, Inhabitants. Elected thus:

The Magistrates and Council when any of the Old Council are desirous of an Ease, and have demitted their Offices, shall choose others in their Room. The Magistrates are elected by the Council out of Leets of themselves.

By Act Convention 1742, a Petition of the Deacons and Dean of Guild to the Convention, praying, that the 5 Deacons might be Counsellors ex officio, was approved by the Convention, provided the Deacons should have no Convener, and that the Gild Counsellors should exceed the Number of Deacons, and that the Deacons hereafter to be elected shall be elected conformable to the Sett of the Burgh of Culross; which Sett says nothing about their Election. By this it appears that 5 Deacons are added to the former Number, so that the Council is 20. There is no Provision for any Change of 15 of the Council, except by Death or Resignation.

Council consists of 17 Merchants, Sailors, and Brewers, and 5 Deacons, in all 22; the Provost and 2 Baillies being chosen out of the 17. Elected thus:

Six New Counsellors are elected each Year by the Counsel and Deacons, in Place of 6 that go off, and the other 11 of the Merchant Counsel remain without Election. The 5 Deacons are supposed to be chosen by the Trades; but the Sett says nothing respecting their Election.

XXI. BRECHIN.

The Council consists of U Merchants and Two Tradesmen residing in the Burgh, in all 13, of whom 7 are a Quorum. Elected thus:

The Old Council always choose the Whole of the New Council, and there is no Restriction against their re-electing themselves.

The Provost, One Baillie, Dean of Guild, and Treasurer, are elected by the New Council and Six Deacons, out of a Leet from the 11 Merchant CounsdktrB (made by the Old and New Council) of Two for Provost and Four for Baillies. Lord Panmure, in virtue of a Contract, not produced, in 1630, names the other Baillie out of the Leet of made by the Council.

Deacons not Counsellors ex Officio, and no Leets appear for them.

XXII. IRVINE.

Council consists of 15 Merchants, in which are included Provost, 2 Baillies, Dean of Guild, and Treasurer, and 2 Trades Counsellors; in all 17. Elected thus:

The Old Council elect the 2 new Merchant Counsellors and Two Trades Counsellors, whom they must change every Year; the Remainder of the Council, viz*. 13, may or may not be re-elected, at the Discretion of the Council.

The Council elects the Magistrates out of Leets of their own Number made by themselves, but the Provost and Baillies cannot continue in that Office above 2 Years.

Deacons not Members ex Officio^ and no Leets as to them.

XXIII. KIRCUH B RIG HT — Recorded, 1707, in Books Convention, appears to depend on

Usage, as set forth in Petition, with some Alterations on Overtures approved by Act of Council.

Council consists of the Provost, 2 Baillies, Treasurer, and Thirteen Counsellors; in all 17. Elected thus:

Two or 3 new Counsellors are elected Yearly by the Magistrates and Council, in Place of the same Number they put off; the other 1 o or 11 Counsellors remain without Change.

The Magistrates are elected by the New Council along with One Person named by the Community to represent them, who has a Vote in the Election of Magistrates only, but not of the New Council, and that besides the Ordinary Town Council of 17 > but the said Representative for the Community is no further a Member of the Town Council, and has no Vote but simply in the said Election.

Nothing said about Deacons. By the first Overture it is declared, that the Constitution shall continue unalterable, except in so far as it may be innovate by any of the Overtures following.

XXIV. IVIGTO N. — Certificate by the Council in 1709, that the Sett for 15 Years by past and

upwards has been.

Council consists of a Provost and 2 Baillies, who do not continue in that Office more than 2 Years, 15 Counsellors, one of whom Treasurer, and the Town Clerk, in all 19. Elected thus:

The Council Annually put off 3 Counsellors, and elect the same Number; the other Thirteen Counsellors may remain in Office without Change. The Sett does not say any Thing respecting the Election of the 3 Magistrates.

XXV. PITTENWEEM. — Sett said to have been punctually observed since the' Erection of the Burgh.

The Council consists of Baillies, a Treasurer, and 19 Counsellors; in all 24. Elected thus:

The Old Council elect the Baillies out of a Leet of 12, of which the Old Baillies and Old Treasurer must be in the Number leeted; the Treasurer out of a Leet of Three, and the 19 other Members of the New Council without any Leet or Provision against re-electing themselves.

XXVI. DUMFERMLINE. — Act of the Convention making the Sett, dated Dumfermline, 13th July 1718, not produced but recited in Deereet 1724, produced.

By the Sett 1718, the Council consisted of a Provost, 2 Baillies, Dean of Guild, and Treasurer, and Four Counsellors, all Merchants, and 7 Trades Counsellors. Elected thus:

The Old Council to choose the New, and these Two the Officers.

Act of the Convention, 13th July 1724, alters the above Sett made by the Convention in 1718, upon and as recited in a Petition of John Wilson, Weaver, for himself and in Name of a Number of Burgesses. The Committee find no Rule of Election, except the Decreet Arbitral 1718, which was a very indistinct Rule, and that it was in the Power of Merchants and Trades to re-elect themselves to the Day of their Death without any Change.

XXVII. DUMBARTON.

The Council consists of 10 Merchants, including Provost, 2 Baillies, Dean of Guild, and Treasurer, and 5 Tradesmen; in all 15. Elected thus:

The Old Council choose the 5 Merchant and 5 Trades Counsellors; and the Old Provost, 2 Old Baillies, Dean of Guild, and Treasurer, in all 5, continue in virtue of their Offices Counsellors for the Year ensuing.

This New Counsel so chosen, with the Deacons of Crafts in Number 5, proceed to the leering and electing the Provost, Eldest Baillie, Youngest Baillie, Dean of Guild, Treasurer, and other Officers, out of the Council; and the new Treasurer, if he be not a Member of the New Council, is Supernumerary to the 15.

There is no Restriction against the Re-election of either Magistrates or Counsellors.

XXVIII. RENFREW.

Council consists of 19, including a Provost and 2 Baillies. Elected thus: >

The Old Council elect the New Council thus:

The Provost makes each Counsellor in his Turn retire, and in his Absence it is put to the Vote whether the Person absent shall be continued a Counsellor for the Year ensuing or not; then in case of the Removal or Death of any Counsellor, each Counsellor present names a Burgess, and the Council is made up to 19 out of those Burgesses having the greatest Number of votes.

The New Council elect the Provost and Baillies out of Leets made by the Council; but the Provost must have been 2 Years a Counsellor before his Election; and the Provost and Baillies are continued Counsellors for 2 Years after the Expiry of their Offices, but no longer, unless re-elected.

There is no Restriction against the Re-election of the whole Council by themselves, without Limitation of Time, or Change of Persons, the Vote put being " Continue the former Counsellor or not."

XXIX. DUNBAR.

Council consists of a Provost, 3 Baillies, and Treasurer, and 15 Counsellors; in all 20. Elected thus:

The Magistrates and Old Council, out of a Leet made by themselves of 8, chuse New Counsellors, and the Old and New Council choose the 5 Magistrates out of Leets made by themselves, and then the old and new Magistrates and Treasurer put off such of the old Counsellors as they think proper.

There is no Provision for any Change in the Council, except the Annually put off; so the Majority of the Council must continue without Election; and no Restriction against Re-election of Magistrates.

XXX. LANER K. — 29 June 1710, the Act of Council states;

" We, according to our ancient Custom, as gathered from our ancient Records, and according to our present " Use, make up our Sett as follows: "

Council consists of 17 Persons, without Distinction of Merchants and Trades, including the Magistrates, of whom the Deacon Convener is always One. Elected thus:

The Old Council choose the New without any Provision against re-electing themselves. The Council, with the Deacons of Trades, choose the Baillies and Treasurer out of Leets of die 17 Counsellors made by the Council; the Provost is One of the 17 chosen by the New Council.

There is no Provision against the Re-election of the same Magistrates and Counsellors.
